definition.simple: Someone who calls themselves your "account manager" and pushes you to deposit more, trade more, or hand over your login.
definition.balanced: They may be friendly, then urgent. They may ask for remote access to your phone or computer, or offer to trade for you. Never share your MetaTrader login or passwords, and never let anyone trade your account for you.

definition.simple: The price at which you can buy right now.
definition.balanced: The lowest price sellers are currently accepting. When you buy at market, you buy at the ask.

glossary.example: If EUR/USD shows 1.1000 / 1.1002, the ask is 1.1002.

definition.simple: When an option holder exercises, a seller of that option is chosen to carry out the deal. That seller has been assigned.
definition.balanced: An assigned call seller must sell the underlying at the strike; an assigned put seller must buy it at the strike. With an American-style option, assignment can come before expiry. The seller does not choose when.

definition.simple: An option whose strike price is equal, or very close, to the current price of the underlying.
definition.balanced: It has no [[intrinsic-value]], so its premium is all [[time-value]]. At expiry an option exactly at the money is worth nothing.

definition.simple: An indicator that shows how far price has typically moved per candle recently. It says nothing about direction.
definition.balanced: True range is the largest of: high minus low, the gap from the previous close to the high, and the gap from the previous close to the low. ATR averages true range over a set period, often 14. It is measured in price units, so on EUR/USD 0.00120 means 12 pips. It describes the past, so it is slow to show a sudden change in volatility.

glossary.example: Previous close 1.10000, high 1.10300, low 1.10050: the ranges are 25, 30 and 5 pips, so the true range is 30 pips.

definition.simple: Testing your trading rules on past price data to see how they would have behaved.
definition.balanced: A backtest applies fixed rules to historical bars. It can show how often the rules found trades, how they handled different conditions, and where they broke down. It cannot show what will happen next. Results depend on [[sample-size]] and can be distorted by [[look-ahead-bias]], [[overfitting]] and [[survivorship-bias]].

glossary.example: You step through 50 past setups in Replay, following your plan exactly, and record each result.

definition.simple: When later futures months are priced lower than nearer ones.
definition.balanced: The [[futures-curve]] slopes down. The shape can change at any time and is not a forecast. Compare [[contango]].

glossary.example: Fictional: near month 48.00, next month 47.20.

definition.simple: A snapshot of what a company owns, what it owes, and what is left for the owners, on one day.
definition.balanced: Assets = liabilities + equity. Key lines for beginners: cash, debt, and equity (what would be left for shareholders if everything were sold at book value and all debts paid). Debt − cash = [[net-debt]].

definition.simple: The money in your account, not counting trades that are still open.
definition.balanced: Your deposits plus or minus the results of closed trades and charges such as [[swap|swaps]]. Profits and losses on open trades are not in the balance until the trades close. See also [[equity]].

definition.simple: The first currency in a pair. Buying the pair means buying this currency.

glossary.example: In GBP/USD the base currency is GBP.

definition.simple: The difference between the spot price of something and the price of a futures contract on it.
definition.balanced: Often defined as spot − futures, though some sources use futures − spot, so check which is meant. Basis tends to shrink toward zero as [[expiry]] nears, but it can widen or narrow along the way.

glossary.example: Fictional: spot 50.00, near-month future 50.60. Basis (spot − futures) = −0.60.

definition.simple: The price at which you can sell right now.
definition.balanced: The highest price buyers are currently offering. When you sell at market, you sell at the bid.

glossary.example: If EUR/USD shows 1.1000 / 1.1002, the bid is 1.1000.

definition.simple: Three lines around price: a moving average in the middle, and bands above and below that widen when price has been jumpy and narrow when it has been calm.
definition.balanced: With the common (20, 2) settings, the middle line is a 20-period simple moving average. The bands sit 2 standard deviations of the last 20 closes above and below it. A touch of a band is not a signal by itself. In a strong trend price can ride along one band for many candles. Narrow bands show that recent movement was small, not which way the next move will go.

glossary.example: Middle 1.10000 and standard deviation 0.00150: upper band 1.10300, lower band 1.09700.

definition.simple: The price where a position neither gains nor loses.
definition.balanced: For an option held to expiry: call breakeven = strike + premium; put breakeven = strike − premium. Fees move it further away.

definition.simple: When price moves out of a range or through a support or resistance area.
definition.balanced: There is no single definition. Many traders only count a breakout when a candle closes beyond the level, sometimes by a set distance. A move only by the wick, which then closes back inside, usually does not count. Many breakouts fail and turn into [[false-breakout|false breakouts]].

definition.simple: How a company makes money: what it sells, to whom, and how it covers its costs.
definition.balanced: Understanding the business model tells you what drives revenue and costs, and so what could go wrong. Ask: who pays, how often, what does it cost to serve them, and how easily could they switch?

glossary.example: A fictional food maker sells packaged meals to shops; most of its cost is ingredients and factories.

definition.simple: The price difference between two contract months of the same futures market, or a position that buys one and sells the other.
definition.balanced: Calendar spread = later month − nearer month. [[rollover|Rolling]] a position trades this gap. Spread positions still carry risk, because the gap itself can move.

glossary.example: Fictional: next month 51.30 − near month 50.60 = 0.70 per unit.

definition.simple: A right to buy the underlying at the strike price. The buyer pays a premium for it.
definition.balanced: At expiry a call is worth price − strike per unit if the price is above the strike, and nothing otherwise. A call buyer can lose at most the premium paid. A call seller receives the premium and must sell at the strike if [[assignment|assigned]]; an [[uncovered-option|uncovered]] sold call has no fixed limit on loss.

definition.simple: A chart shape that shows how price moved in one time period: where it opened, its highest and lowest points, and where it closed.
definition.balanced: The thick part is the body, between the open and the close. The thin lines are wicks (or shadows), reaching to the high and low. A candle is usually coloured one way when the close is above the open and another way when it is below. Colours depend on your app settings.

glossary.example: Open 1.10000, high 1.10250, low 1.09900, close 1.10180: the close is above the open, so it is an up candle with an 18-pip body.

definition.simple: Holding a currency with a higher interest rate against one with a lower rate, to earn the difference over time.
definition.balanced: The interest arrives as a [[swap]] for each night the position is held, after the broker's markup. If the higher-yielding currency falls, the price loss can be much larger than the interest earned.

definition.simple: The report that shows the actual cash coming in and going out over a period.
definition.balanced: It splits cash into operating (the day-to-day business), investing (such as capital expenditure) and financing (borrowing, repaying, dividends). Comparing operating [[cash-flow]] with [[earnings]] shows whether profit is turning into cash.

definition.simple: The actual cash moving into and out of a company over a period.
definition.balanced: Operating cash flow is the cash the day-to-day business brings in. It can differ from [[earnings]] because profit counts sales when they are made, even if customers have not paid yet. Profit that rarely turns into cash is a warning sign worth investigating.

glossary.example: Profit 52.5 million USD but operating cash flow only 2 million USD: the profit is not arriving as cash (fictional).

definition.simple: Selling a put option while setting aside enough cash to buy the underlying at the strike if assigned.
definition.balanced: The cash set aside is strike × units per contract × contracts. It means the purchase can be paid for; it does not reduce the loss. If the price falls far below the strike, the seller still buys at the strike.

definition.simple: Ending a futures contract with a cash payment of the price difference, with nothing delivered.
definition.balanced: At [[expiry]], each position is settled against a final settlement price set by the contract's rules. Compare [[physical-settlement]].

definition.simple: The public body that sets a country's main interest rate and looks after its currency.
definition.balanced: Most central banks aim for stable prices, and some also for jobs or growth. They change the policy [[interest-rate]] and give guidance about future moves. Their decisions and statements can move currencies sharply.

glossary.example: Hypothetical: a fictional central bank holds rates but says it may cut later. Its currency may weaken, or not move if this was already expected.

definition.simple: Two roughly parallel sloping lines that a trend's swings have stayed between.
definition.balanced: In a rising channel, one line joins the higher lows and a parallel line runs over the highs. The lines depend on which swing points you choose, so write the rule down. A close beyond a line, by an amount you set in advance, says the old pattern stopped. It does not say what comes next.

glossary.example: Lows at 100.0 and 104.0, 20 candles apart, give a slope of 0.2 per candle.

definition.simple: A basic raw material that is much the same whoever produces it, such as gold, oil, natural gas, wheat or coffee.
definition.balanced: Commodities are often grouped as metals (gold, silver), energy (crude oil, natural gas) and agricultural goods (grains, soft crops, livestock). Their prices move with supply and demand, [[inventory-report|inventories]], [[seasonality]], weather, politics and currencies. Traders can gain exposure through futures contracts, funds or CFDs, each with its own costs and risks.

definition.simple: Something that lets a company keep earning good profits even when rivals try to compete.
definition.balanced: Examples of possible advantages: lower costs, a trusted brand, customers who find it hard to switch. Advantages can fade, so they are judgements, not facts. High margins and [[return-on-capital]] held for many years are one clue, not proof.

definition.simple: The figure most forecasters expect a release to show, before it comes out.
definition.balanced: The consensus is often a median of analyst forecasts. Prices may already reflect it before the release. That is why the gap between actual and expected, the [[surprise]], often matters more than the number itself.

glossary.example: Hypothetical: the consensus for a fictional inflation release is 2.5%.

definition.simple: A period when price moves sideways in a fairly narrow box, often after a bigger move.
definition.balanced: Highs stop rising and lows stop falling. You can measure the box against [[atr|ATR]] to see how narrow it is. A consolidation can end with a [[breakout]] in either direction, or last much longer than expected.

glossary.example: Highs near 82.40 and lows near 80.10 for 30 candles, with ATR 1.10: a box about 2.1 ATR tall.

definition.simple: When later futures months are priced higher than nearer ones.
definition.balanced: The [[futures-curve]] slopes up. A long position that keeps [[rollover|rolling]] in contango buys each new month at a higher price, which can cost money even if spot does not move. It is a shape, not a signal.

glossary.example: Fictional: near month 50.60, next month 51.30.

definition.simple: The month in which a particular futures contract expires. Each month is a separate contract with its own price.
definition.balanced: A market can list several contract months at once. Prices differ between them, which forms the [[futures-curve]]. Which months exist, and which one is most traded at a given time, depends on the contract.

definition.simple: How much one lot or one futures contract represents.
definition.balanced: For forex, the units of the [[base-currency]] in 1.00 [[lot]]: often 100,000, but brokers can set it differently. For a futures contract, the quantity of the underlying in one contract, set in its specification (for example 100 units). Check the exact specification for each symbol or contract you trade.

definition.simple: How much two markets tend to move together.
definition.balanced: Correlation runs from −1 (opposite moves) to +1 (moving together). It changes over time. Two trades on pairs that move together can act like one bigger trade, so your total risk is higher than each trade alone suggests.

glossary.example: A learner buys two pairs that both have USD as the quote currency. If USD strengthens, both trades may lose at once.

definition.simple: Selling a call option on units of the underlying you already own.
definition.balanced: If the call is exercised, the owned units are delivered at the strike, so the loss on the call is offset by the units. In return for the premium, the seller gives up gains above the strike and still carries nearly all the risk of the underlying falling; the premium cushions a fall only slightly.

definition.simple: Two currencies quoted against each other, like EUR/USD. The price says how much of the second you need for one of the first.
definition.balanced: A forex quote of the form BASE/QUOTE: the price of one unit of the [[base-currency]] in units of the [[quote-currency]].

glossary.example: EUR/USD 1.1000: one euro costs 1.10 US dollars.

definition.simple: A practice trading account that uses pretend money. Nothing you do on it can win or lose real money.
definition.balanced: A broker account funded with virtual money. Prices are usually real or close to real, but fills, costs, and emotions can differ from a live account.

definition.simple: When a company creates and sells new shares, each existing share becomes a smaller slice of the company.
definition.balanced: Companies issue new shares to raise cash, pay debts, or pay staff and lenders. Your number of shares stays the same, but your percentage of the company falls. Repeated dilution is common in small companies that keep running short of cash, and it can push the share price down over time.

glossary.example: Fictional: you own 10,000 of 20 million shares (0.05%). The company issues 10 million more. You now own 10,000 of 30 million (about 0.033%).

definition.simple: Spreading money across different investments so that one going wrong does less damage.
definition.balanced: It only helps if the holdings do not all move together. Positions that depend on the same currency, sector or commodity behave like one larger bet, and [[correlation|correlations]] tend to rise when markets are stressed.

definition.simple: The yearly dividend per share as a percentage of the share price.
definition.balanced: Dividend yield = dividend per share ÷ share price. It rises when the price falls, so a very high yield can be a sign that buyers expect the dividend to be cut. It is based on past payments, which are not promised.

glossary.example: Dividend 0.435 USD per share ÷ price 6.80 USD = about 6.4%.

definition.simple: Part of a company's profit paid out in cash to its shareholders.
definition.balanced: The company decides whether to pay a dividend and how much. It can raise, cut or stop it. A dividend paid from borrowing rather than from [[free-cash-flow]] may not last.

glossary.example: A company pays 87 million USD in dividends across 200 million shares: about 0.435 USD per share.

definition.simple: How far your account has fallen from its highest point.
definition.balanced: Drawdown = (peak − current) ÷ peak. After a drawdown d, you need a gain of d ÷ (1 − d) to get back to the peak. A 20% drawdown needs a 25% gain. A 50% drawdown needs 100%.

glossary.example: Peak 10,000 USD, now 8,000 USD: drawdown is 2,000 ÷ 10,000 = 20%.

definition.simple: A company's regular report of its revenue, profit and other figures for the latest period.
definition.balanced: Listed companies publish results on a regular schedule set by their market's rules. Prices often move sharply around a report, and they react to the figures compared with what was expected, not to whether the figures are good or bad. See [[surprise]].

definition.simple: The profit left for the owners after every cost, interest and tax has been paid.
definition.balanced: Earnings (net income) = revenue − cost of sales − operating expenses − interest − tax. It is the last line of the [[income-statement]]. Earnings are an accounting figure: they can differ a lot from the cash the business actually collected, so compare them with [[cash-flow]].

glossary.example: Revenue 1,040, all costs, interest and tax 926: earnings = 114 (fictional, millions USD).

definition.simple: A list of upcoming economic releases and central-bank events, with their times.
definition.balanced: Calendars usually show the time, country, event, an importance rating, the [[consensus-forecast]], the previous figure, and the actual once released. Check the time zone. Spreads often widen around high-importance events.

glossary.example: A learner checks the calendar each Monday and marks events for the currencies they trade.

definition.simple: A regular release showing how many jobs were added or lost and how many people are unemployed.
definition.balanced: Jobs reports usually include jobs added, the unemployment rate and wage growth. Markets compare each figure with the [[consensus-forecast]]. Earlier months may be revised, which can change the reaction.

glossary.example: Hypothetical: a fictional country was expected to add 150,000 jobs and added 90,000.

definition.simple: The company's profit divided by its number of shares: how much profit belongs to each share.
definition.balanced: EPS = net income ÷ shares outstanding. It lets you compare profit with the price of one share. If a company issues many new shares, EPS can fall even when total profit rises.

glossary.example: Net income 114 million USD ÷ 200 million shares = 0.57 USD per share.

definition.simple: Your balance plus or minus the profit or loss on your open trades right now.
definition.balanced: Equity = [[balance]] + floating profit − floating loss on open positions. It changes every time prices move. [[free-margin|Free margin]] and [[margin-level]] are both worked out from equity.

glossary.example: Balance 1,000 USD and an open trade showing −150 USD: equity is 850 USD.

definition.simple: The rule for when an option can be exercised, set in the contract's specification.
definition.balanced: American style allows exercise on any trading day up to expiry. European style allows it only at expiry. The names do not tell you where a contract trades, so read the specification of the exact contract.

definition.simple: Using the right an option gives: buying the underlying at the strike (call) or selling it at the strike (put).
definition.balanced: Only the holder decides whether to exercise. When it happens, a seller is given the obligation through [[assignment]]. When exercise is allowed is set by the [[exercise-style]], and some contracts settle in cash instead of delivering the underlying. Check the exact contract.

definition.simple: The average result per trade you would get over many trades, if your numbers held.
definition.balanced: Expectancy = [[win-rate]] × average win − loss rate × average loss. It is often given in R. It is arithmetic on your inputs. Real win rates and averages change, and a positive past figure does not guarantee a future one.

glossary.example: Example inputs: win rate 40%, average win 2R, average loss 1R. Expectancy = 0.40 × 2 − 0.60 × 1 = +0.2R per trade.

definition.simple: The date a futures contract or an option stops trading and is settled.
definition.balanced: After expiry the contract no longer exists. Before it, a holder can close the position, [[rollover|roll]] it to a later month, or let it go to [[physical-settlement|physical]] or [[cash-settlement|cash]] settlement. The dates are set in each contract's specification and differ between contracts. Depending on the contract and the broker, an option that is in the money at expiry may be exercised automatically, so check the rules. An option that is out of the money then expires worthless.

definition.simple: A breakout that does not continue: price moves through a level, then soon comes back inside.
definition.balanced: You only know a breakout was false afterwards. Rules that wait for more confirmation can avoid some false breakouts, but they enter later, at a worse price, and still get caught by some.

glossary.example: Price closes 8 pips above resistance at 1.25600, then the next two candles close back at 1.25550 and 1.25400.

definition.simple: A drawing tool that marks set percentages of a price move, such as 38.2%, 50% and 61.8%, as lines on the chart.
definition.balanced: It is a convention some traders watch, not a prediction. The levels depend on which swing you anchor to, and with several levels close together, many pullbacks end near one by chance. Use it as a ruler for describing depth.

glossary.example: Move from 40.00 to 50.00: the 50% level is 45.00 and the 61.8% level is 50.00 − 6.18 = 43.82.

definition.simple: A government's decisions on spending and taxes.
definition.balanced: Spending more or taxing less can support growth but may add to [[government-debt]]. Fiscal policy is set by government, while [[monetary-policy]] is usually set by a [[central-bank]]. The two can pull in the same or opposite directions.

definition.simple: The shares that are actually available for the public to trade. Shares held by insiders or locked up are usually left out.
definition.balanced: A company can have many shares outstanding but a small float if most are held by insiders or cannot be sold yet. A low float means a modest amount of buying or selling can move the price a lot, which makes sharp spikes and sharp falls more likely.

glossary.example: Fictional: 50 million shares outstanding, 45 million held by insiders. The float is about 5 million shares.

definition.simple: Following your trading plan in real time on a demo or paper account, where you cannot see the future.
definition.balanced: A forward test comes after a [[backtest]]. It adds things a backtest misses: waiting in real time, changing spreads, slippage, and your own emotions. On a [[demo-account]] the money is pretend, so fills and feelings can still differ from real trading.

definition.simple: The cash left after the business pays to keep itself running and growing.
definition.balanced: Free cash flow = operating cash flow − capital expenditure (money spent on equipment, buildings, software). It is the cash available to pay debt, pay [[dividend|dividends]], or save. Negative free cash flow is normal for some growing firms, but it has to be funded by cash, borrowing or new shares.

glossary.example: Operating cash flow 150, capital expenditure 32: free cash flow = 118 (fictional, millions USD).

definition.simple: The part of your equity that is not tied up as margin. It shrinks as open trades lose money.
definition.balanced: Free margin = [[equity]] − used [[margin]]. It is roughly what is left to absorb further losses or to open new trades. When it nears zero, a [[margin-call]] or [[stop-out]] gets close.

glossary.example: Equity 850 USD and used margin 200 USD: free margin is 650 USD.

definition.simple: An agreement, traded on an exchange, to buy or sell something at a set price on a set future date.
definition.balanced: A standardised contract whose rules are set in its specification: [[contract-size]] or [[multiplier]], [[tick-size]], [[contract-month|contract months]], [[expiry]] and settlement method. Buyers and sellers put down [[margin]], and gains and losses are settled daily through [[mark-to-market]]. Every contract has its own specification.

glossary.example: Example index future (fictional specs): multiplier 10 USD per point, tick size 0.25, cash-settled.

definition.simple: The line you get by plotting the prices of one futures market across its contract months.
definition.balanced: A curve sloping up into later months is in [[contango]]; sloping down is [[backwardation]]. The shape can change, and it is not a forecast of the future spot price.

definition.simple: A jump in price with no trading in between, for example from Friday's close to Monday's open.
definition.balanced: When the market reopens, or after sudden news, price can start at a level far from the last one. Orders resting inside the gap, including a [[stop-loss]], fill at the first available price, which can be much worse than their level.

glossary.example: A buy trade's stop sits at 1.09500. The market closes at 1.09800 and reopens at 1.09200. The stop fills near 1.09200, not 1.09500.

definition.simple: The total value of goods and services an economy produces over a period. Its change is the usual measure of growth.
definition.balanced: Usually reported as a percentage change, for example on the previous quarter. Early figures are estimates and are often revised. Growth is read together with [[employment-report|employment]] and [[inflation]], not alone.

glossary.example: Hypothetical: output rises from 500.0 to 503.0 billion WMK. Growth = 3.0 ÷ 500.0 = 0.6%.

definition.simple: The chance that conflicts, sanctions, trade rules or political changes disrupt how goods are produced, shipped or sold.
definition.balanced: Commodities are often produced in a few places and shipped along a few routes, so politics can affect supply or how it reaches buyers. Prices may rise on worry alone, before anything is actually lost, and fall back if the worry fades. Treat geopolitical stories as scenarios with several possible outcomes, never as certain price calls.

definition.simple: The total amount a government has borrowed and not yet repaid.
definition.balanced: Often compared with [[gdp]] as debt ÷ GDP. A yearly deficit (spending above revenue) adds to the debt. Higher [[interest-rate|interest rates]] raise the cost of carrying it as old debt is refinanced. How much debt is 'too much' is debated, not a fixed line.

glossary.example: Hypothetical: debt 480 billion WMK, GDP 800 billion WMK. Debt ÷ GDP = 60%.

definition.simple: An approach that looks for companies whose revenue and profit may grow fast, often accepting a high price for them.
definition.balanced: Growth investors often accept a high [[pe-ratio|P/E]] and low or negative free cash flow today in exchange for expected future growth. The risk: if growth slows, the high price can fall a long way even while the business keeps growing.

definition.simple: How big future price swings are expected to be, worked backwards from option prices.
definition.balanced: Higher implied volatility usually goes with higher premiums, because bigger swings make a large move more likely. It is an estimate drawn from prices, not a forecast that will come true, and it can fall quickly, lowering premiums even when the underlying price does not move.

definition.simple: The part of the data used to build or tune a rule.
definition.balanced: In-sample results flatter a rule because the rule was shaped to fit them. Judge a rule on [[out-of-sample]] data instead.

glossary.example: +18R over 60 in-sample trades fell to +2R over 25 out-of-sample trades.

definition.simple: An option that would be worth something if it expired now: a call with the price above the strike, or a put with the price below it.
definition.balanced: The amount it is in the money per unit is its [[intrinsic-value]]. Being in the money does not mean the buyer is in profit: the premium paid has to be covered first.

definition.simple: The report that shows revenue, costs and profit over a period.
definition.balanced: It runs from the top line to the bottom line: [[revenue]] − cost of sales = gross profit; − operating expenses = operating profit; − interest − tax = net income ([[earnings]]). Divide net income by the number of shares to get [[eps]].

definition.simple: A fund that holds the companies in a market index, so one purchase spreads money across many of them.
definition.balanced: It aims to follow the index, not to beat it. It still falls when the whole market falls, and its yearly fee is taken whatever the result.

definition.simple: When two indicators tend to say the same thing because they are calculated from the same prices.
definition.balanced: RSI, MACD and moving averages all use recent closing prices, so they often turn together. Their agreement is closer to one reading than to two confirmations. Information from a different source, such as structure or volume, is less likely to repeat it.

glossary.example: RSI 14 crosses above 50 and MACD crosses above zero on the same candle: largely the same message twice.

definition.simple: A line or chart calculated from past prices, such as an average, to summarise what price has done.
definition.balanced: Indicators only rearrange information already on the chart: past prices, and sometimes volume. They do not see the future. Each has settings, such as a period, and the result changes when the settings change. Each has market conditions where it gives many misleading readings.

definition.simple: How fast prices of everyday goods and services are rising.
definition.balanced: Inflation is usually reported as the percentage change in a price index over a year or a month. Central banks watch it closely. Higher-than-expected inflation can raise expectations of higher [[interest-rate|interest rates]], but the market reaction is never certain.

glossary.example: Hypothetical: a fictional country's prices rise from an index of 100 to 103 in a year, which is 3% inflation.

definition.simple: The deposit needed for each contract to open a futures position.
definition.balanced: A good-faith deposit, not the price of the contract and not the most you can lose. Exchanges set minimums and brokers may ask for more; both can raise it, sometimes at short notice. See also [[maintenance-margin]].

definition.simple: The price of borrowing money, shown as a percentage per year.
definition.balanced: A [[central-bank]] sets a short-term policy rate. Other rates follow it. In forex, the rate gap between two currencies affects [[swap]] costs and can shape demand for a currency. Expectations about future rates often matter as much as today's rate.

glossary.example: Hypothetical: a fictional central bank raises its policy rate from 3.00% to 3.25%.

definition.simple: What an option would be worth if it expired right now. It is never below zero.
definition.balanced: Call: price − strike, or 0 if that is negative. Put: strike − price, or 0 if that is negative. At expiry an option is worth only its intrinsic value.

definition.simple: A regular report of how much of a commodity is held in storage, and how much that changed since the last report.
definition.balanced: A fall in stored amounts is called a draw; a rise is called a build. Traders compare the change with what was expected. A bigger draw than expected can suggest supply is tighter than thought, and a surprise build the opposite. As with any release, what moves price is the [[surprise]], and even that reaction is not certain.

glossary.example: Fictional: consensus −1.5 million barrels, actual −4.2 million. The draw was 2.7 million barrels bigger than expected.

definition.simple: A scheme that pretends to be an investment or trading opportunity in order to take your money or account details.
definition.balanced: Common signs: promised or "guaranteed" returns, pressure to act fast, requests for your login or passwords, payment to unusual accounts or in crypto, and firms you cannot find on a [[regulator]]'s official register.

definition.simple: An indicator that reacts only after price has already moved, because it is built from past prices.
definition.balanced: All averages lag. A longer period gives a smoother line but more lag. A shorter period reacts faster but changes direction more often for no lasting reason, which gives more false signals.

glossary.example: A 5-period average of closes at 1.1010, 1.1020, 1.1030, 1.1040 and 1.1100 is 1.1040, which is 60 pips below the last close.

definition.simple: Borrowed buying power that lets a small deposit control a bigger position. It makes both gains and losses bigger.
definition.balanced: The ratio between the size of a position and the [[margin]] needed to open it. At 1:100 leverage, 1 unit of margin controls 100 units of position, so a 1% price move changes the position's value by an amount equal to the whole margin.

definition.simple: An order to buy at a lower price than now, or sell at a higher price than now.
definition.balanced: A buy limit sits below the current [[ask]]; a sell limit sits above the current [[bid]]. It aims to fill at your price or better. If price does not reach it, it does not fill.

definition.simple: How easily you can buy or sell without moving the price much. More buyers and sellers usually means more liquidity.
definition.balanced: The depth of buying and selling interest. Lower liquidity usually means wider [[spread|spreads]], bigger jumps, and more difficulty getting out at the price you want. It varies by instrument, time of day, and market conditions.

definition.simple: Using information in a test that you could not have known at the time of the trade.
definition.balanced: Examples: drawing a level using a candle that formed after your entry, or reading a bar's close before that bar has finished. It makes a [[backtest]] look better than real trading could be. Replay helps by hiding future bars.

glossary.example: You mark a "clear" support line on a chart, but the bounce that made it clear happened after your planned entry.

definition.simple: Several losing trades in a row.
definition.balanced: Losing streaks are normal, even for a plan that works over time. If each trade loses with chance L, independently, the chance the next N trades all lose is L to the power N. Over many trades, the chance of seeing some streak is much higher. Never raise size to win losses back.

glossary.example: With an example 50% loss chance, the next 5 trades all lose with chance 0.5^5 = 3.125%.

definition.simple: A unit for the size of a forex trade.
definition.balanced: By common convention a standard lot is 100,000 units of the base currency, a mini lot 10,000, and a micro lot 1,000. Check your broker's contract size, because it can differ.

definition.simple: An indicator that shows the gap between a faster and a slower average of price, plus an average of that gap.
definition.balanced: With the common settings, the MACD line is the 12-period EMA minus the 26-period EMA. The signal line is a 9-period EMA of the MACD line. The histogram is the MACD line minus the signal line. It is built from averages, so it lags. Some apps draw the MACD line as bars, so check what each part shows in yours.

glossary.example: EMA 12 = 1.10350 and EMA 26 = 1.10200, so the MACD line is 0.00150.

definition.simple: The lower level your account must stay above while you hold a futures position.
definition.balanced: If daily [[mark-to-market]] losses take the account below the maintenance margin, a [[margin-call]] follows. You must add money, often back up to the [[initial-margin]], or the broker can close the position. The rules differ between brokers and contracts.

definition.simple: A warning from your broker that your account is low compared with the margin your trades need.
definition.balanced: When your [[margin-level]] falls to a level set by the broker, the broker warns you and may stop you opening new trades. If losses continue, a [[stop-out]] can follow. The level differs between brokers and account types.

definition.simple: Your equity compared with the margin in use, shown as a percentage. Lower means closer to trouble.
definition.balanced: Margin level = [[equity]] ÷ used [[margin]] × 100%. Brokers use it to decide when to warn you ([[margin-call]]) and when to close trades ([[stop-out]]). The exact levels are set by each broker.

glossary.example: Equity 850 USD, used margin 200 USD: margin level = 850 ÷ 200 × 100% = 425%.

definition.simple: The gap between your estimate of what something is worth and the price you pay, kept as room for the estimate to be wrong.
definition.balanced: Measured as (estimated value − price) ÷ estimated value. It protects only against errors in the estimate no larger than the gap, and the estimate itself rests on assumptions.

glossary.example: Estimated value 50, price 40: margin of safety = 10 ÷ 50 = 20%.

definition.simple: Money your broker sets aside from your account while a leveraged trade is open. It is a deposit, not the most you can lose.
definition.balanced: The collateral required to open and hold a leveraged position. If losses reduce your equity too far, the broker may ask for more money (a margin call) or close positions. Losses can be larger than the margin.

definition.simple: Valuing an open futures position at each day's settlement price, and moving that day's gain or loss into or out of the account.
definition.balanced: Gains and losses are settled in cash every day, not only when you close. A run of losing days can bring a [[margin-call]] even if you planned to hold longer.

glossary.example: Fictional: 1 contract at 10 USD per point. Today's settlement is 15 points lower than yesterday's, so 150 USD leaves the account today.

definition.simple: What the market says the whole company is worth: share price × number of shares.
definition.balanced: Market cap = share price × shares outstanding. It measures size in the market's eyes, not quality. A high market cap with small profits means buyers expect a lot of future growth. It moves every time the share price moves.

glossary.example: Price 14.40 USD × 100 million shares = 1,440 million USD market cap.

definition.simple: An order to buy or sell straight away at the best price available now.
definition.balanced: A buy at market fills at or near the [[ask]]; a sell at market fills at or near the [[bid]]. You get speed, but the exact price is not fixed, so [[slippage]] can happen.

definition.simple: The type of market in a period: trending or ranging, and calm or jumpy compared with its own past.
definition.balanced: Classify with a written rule, for example by comparing the net move with ATR, and current ATR with its longer average. The label lags because it uses past candles, and regimes change without warning. Rules often behave very differently from one regime to another, so review test results by regime.

glossary.example: Net move 150 pips over 20 candles with ATR 40 pips is 3.75 ATR: trending under a 3 ATR rule.

definition.simple: The pattern of swing highs and swing lows on a chart, used to describe whether price is trending or moving sideways.
definition.balanced: Higher highs and higher lows describe an uptrend. Lower highs and lower lows describe a downtrend. Overlapping swings describe a range. When an uptrend makes a new low below its last higher low, people say the structure is broken. That is a change in description, not a promise that price will now fall.

definition.simple: The idea that a price that has moved far from its recent average tends to drift back towards it.
definition.balanced: It describes some quiet, sideways markets better than trending ones. In a trend, a price that looks stretched can keep moving the same way for a long time, so mean-reversion rules need a [[market-regime]] filter and a stop.

definition.simple: A company whose total market value is very small compared with most listed companies.
definition.balanced: Size here means market value: share price × shares outstanding. A low share price does not by itself make a company small, and a higher share price does not make it big. Where the 'microcap' line sits depends on who is drawing it. Microcaps often have little trading, few analysts following them, and less information available.

glossary.example: Fictional: 0.25 USD × 40 million shares = 10 million USD market value.

definition.simple: What a central bank does to influence interest rates and the money supply, usually to keep inflation steady.
definition.balanced: The main tool is the policy [[interest-rate]]; banks may also use guidance about future moves and other tools. Markets react to expected future policy as much as to today's decision. Compare [[fiscal-policy]].

definition.simple: The average closing price over the last few candles, drawn as a line that updates with each new candle.
definition.balanced: A simple moving average (SMA) weights each close equally. An exponential moving average (EMA) gives more weight to recent closes, so it reacts faster. Both lag price. In sideways markets price crosses back and forth over the line many times.

glossary.example: A 20-period MA on an H1 chart averages the last 20 hourly closes.

definition.simple: Looking at the same market on two or three timeframes: a higher one for context and a lower one for detail.
definition.balanced: The views often disagree: a daily uptrend can contain a 1-hour fall. Choose your timeframes before you look. The timeframe used for the stop sets its distance, and so the size. Agreement between timeframes is two views of the same prices, not a forecast.

glossary.example: Daily chart: uptrend. 1-hour chart: falling for 15 hours. Both can be true: a pullback inside the daily uptrend.

definition.simple: The money value of a one-point move in a futures price, for one contract.
definition.balanced: [[notional-value|Notional value]] = price × multiplier. Some contracts give a [[contract-size]] in units instead; the idea is the same. Multipliers differ between contracts, so take the number from the exact contract's specification.

glossary.example: Fictional: multiplier 10 USD per point. A 15-point move = 15 × 10 = 150 USD per contract.

definition.simple: Debt minus cash: how much a company would still owe if it used all its cash to repay debt.
definition.balanced: Net debt = debt − cash. If it is negative, the company has net cash. Compare net debt with operating profit or cash flow: the same debt is much riskier for a company whose profit is shrinking.

glossary.example: Debt 160, cash 71: net debt = 89 (fictional, millions USD).

definition.simple: The full value of the position a contract controls.
definition.balanced: For a future, notional value = price × [[multiplier]] × contracts. Profit and loss come from the notional value, not from the [[margin]]. Notional ÷ margin shows the [[leverage]].

glossary.example: Fictional: price 4,000 × multiplier 10 USD = 40,000 USD for 1 contract.

definition.simple: Short for open, high, low and close: the four prices that describe one period on a chart.
definition.balanced: Open is the first price in the period, close is the last, high is the highest and low is the lowest. Candlesticks and OHLC bars show the same four numbers in different shapes. MetaTrader charts usually show bid prices, so a buy fills at the ask, a little above what the chart shows.

glossary.example: A 1-hour period that opens at 1.25400, reaches 1.25450, falls to 1.25000 and ends at 1.25100 has O 1.25400, H 1.25450, L 1.25000, C 1.25100.

definition.simple: The price of an option. The buyer pays it and the seller receives it.
definition.balanced: It is usually quoted per unit of the [[underlying]], so the money for one contract is premium × units per contract. Before expiry the premium is [[intrinsic-value]] plus [[time-value]]. For a buyer it is the most that can be lost; for a seller it is the most that can be made.

definition.simple: The person who sells an option. They receive the premium and take on the duty to buy or sell if assigned.
definition.balanced: The premium is the most a writer can make. A writer of an [[uncovered-option|uncovered]] call has no fixed limit on loss; a writer of a put can lose up to (strike − premium) × units if the price falls to zero. Brokers usually require approval and [[margin]] before you can write options.

definition.simple: A contract that gives its buyer a right, but not a duty, to buy or sell something at a set price by or on a set date. The seller takes on the duty.
definition.balanced: The buyer pays a [[option-premium|premium]] for the right. A [[call-option]] is a right to buy; a [[put-option]] is a right to sell, at the [[strike-price]], until or at [[expiry]]. The seller, or [[option-writer|writer]], must deliver, or pay the cash difference, if the buyer [[exercise|exercises]]. Each contract's specification sets the [[underlying]], how many units it covers, the [[exercise-style]] and how it settles.

definition.simple: The list of buy orders and sell orders waiting at each price, with how many shares are wanted at each.
definition.balanced: A deep order book has lots of shares waiting near the current price. A thin one has only a few. In a thin book, a large [[market-order|market order]] uses up the best price and then fills at worse and worse prices. The visible book can also change or vanish in an instant.

glossary.example: Fictional bids: 3,000 shares at 0.40, 2,000 at 0.38, 5,000 at 0.35. Selling 10,000 at market fills at all three levels, an average of 0.371.

definition.simple: Trading that happens through dealer networks rather than on a main stock exchange. Many very small companies trade this way.
definition.balanced: Rules on listing and reporting for OTC-traded shares are often lighter than on a main exchange, and they vary by market and by tier. That can mean less information, fewer buyers and sellers, and wider [[spread|spreads]]. Trading OTC is not a scam in itself, but it means you need to check more for yourself.

definition.simple: Data kept aside and not used to build or tune a rule, then used once to test it.
definition.balanced: Out-of-sample results are usually weaker than [[in-sample]] ones, because tuning picks up some noise. Once you change a rule because of out-of-sample results, that data has become in-sample and you need fresh data.

glossary.example: Tune on candles 1–400, then test the finished rules once on candles 401–600.

definition.simple: An option that would be worth nothing if it expired now: a call with the price below the strike, or a put with the price above it.
definition.balanced: Its premium is all [[time-value]]. If it is still out of the money at expiry it expires worthless and the buyer loses the whole premium.

definition.simple: Labels for an indicator reading that is high (overbought) or low (oversold) compared with its usual range.
definition.balanced: For RSI, 70 and 30 are common default lines. The labels say price has moved a lot in one direction recently. They do not say it must turn. In a strong trend, overbought or oversold readings can last a long time.

definition.simple: Adding or tuning rules until they fit past data very well, so they explain the past but may fail on new data.
definition.balanced: Each extra filter that removes a few past losers makes old results look better. But those filters were chosen after seeing the answers. The fix is to keep rules simple and test any changed rule on new data you have not seen.

glossary.example: After 30 trades you add four new filters that would have avoided 8 past losers. The new rules have been tested on zero new trades.

definition.simple: How much a test result changes when you nudge a setting, such as an average length from 20 to 18 or 22.
definition.balanced: If neighbouring settings give similar results, the result is less fragile. A single sharp peak surrounded by losses is a warning sign of [[overfitting]]. Low sensitivity does not prove a rule has an edge; it only shows the result does not hinge on one exact number.

glossary.example: Lengths 16 to 24 give −4R, −1R, +12R, −2R, −5R: the +12R at length 20 stands alone and is fragile.

definition.simple: The share of profit a company pays out as dividends.
definition.balanced: Payout ratio = dividends ÷ net income. A ratio near or above 100% leaves little profit to reinvest, pay debt or absorb a bad year, so the dividend may be at risk.

glossary.example: Dividends 87 ÷ net income 114 = about 76% (fictional, millions USD).

definition.simple: How many years of today's profit you pay for in the share price. Price ÷ earnings per share.
definition.balanced: P/E = share price ÷ [[eps]]. A high P/E means buyers expect profits to grow; a low P/E can mean low expectations, or a business in trouble. P/E says nothing on its own about whether a company is good, and it is meaningless when earnings are zero or negative.

glossary.example: Price 6.80 USD ÷ EPS 0.57 USD = a P/E of about 11.9.

definition.simple: The P/E ratio divided by the expected yearly growth rate of earnings, in percent.
definition.balanced: A rough way to compare price with growth. It inherits all the uncertainty of the growth forecast, and it means little for companies with tiny or negative earnings.

glossary.example: P/E 30 and expected growth 15% a year: PEG = 30 ÷ 15 = 2.0.

definition.simple: An order that waits until price reaches a level you chose, then opens a trade.
definition.balanced: An instruction to open a trade later, at a set price. The main types are [[limit-order|limit orders]] (buy below or sell above the current price) and [[stop-order|stop orders]] (buy above or sell below it). If price never reaches the level, nothing happens.

definition.simple: A share in a very small company that trades at a low price per share. Penny stocks are often hard to sell quickly and easy to push around.
definition.balanced: There is no single worldwide definition. Different markets, regulators and brokers draw the line in different ways, some by price per share and some by company size. What they share is the risk: low [[liquidity]], wide [[spread|spreads]], thin information, and a higher chance of [[stock-promotion|promotions]] and [[pump-and-dump]] schemes.

glossary.example: Fictional: a share priced at 0.25 USD in a company worth 10 million USD in total, with only a few thousand shares traded on a typical day.

definition.simple: Ending a futures contract by actually delivering the goods for payment.
definition.balanced: A buyer who holds a physically settled contract into its delivery period can be required to pay for and receive the goods. Practice traders who want only price exposure close or [[rollover|roll]] before the dates in the specification. Compare [[cash-settlement]].

definition.simple: How much money you make or lose when price moves one pip in your favour or against you.
definition.balanced: Pip value = position size in units × pip size. The answer is in the [[quote-currency]]. If your account is in a different currency, convert it at the current rate.

glossary.example: 10,000 units of EUR/USD: 10,000 × 0.0001 = 1 USD per pip.

definition.simple: A standard small step in a currency price. For most pairs it is 0.0001.
definition.balanced: For most currency pairs a pip is a move in the fourth decimal place (0.0001). For pairs quoted in Japanese yen it is usually the second decimal place (0.01). Many brokers show one extra digit, called a pipette (a tenth of a pip).

glossary.example: EUR/USD moving from 1.1000 to 1.1050 is a 50-pip move.

definition.simple: One tenth of a pip. It is the extra last digit many platforms show.
definition.balanced: Many brokers quote most pairs to 5 decimal places and yen pairs to 3. The last digit is a pipette, worth one tenth of a [[pip]]. A move of 10 pipettes is a move of 1 pip.

glossary.example: EUR/USD moving from 1.10000 to 1.10007 is a move of 7 pipettes, or 0.7 pips.

definition.simple: Choosing how big a trade is so that hitting the stop loses only the amount you planned.
definition.balanced: Size in lots = money at risk ÷ (stop distance in pips × [[pip-value]] for 1 lot). Round down to your broker's size step, so the real risk stays at or under the plan. Costs such as the [[spread]] add to the loss.

glossary.example: Example: risk 100 USD, stop 40 pips, pip value 10 USD per lot. Size = 100 ÷ (40 × 10) = 0.25 lot.

definition.simple: A few quick questions you answer before every trade: Is it in my plan? Is a stop loss set? Is the risk within my limit? Is important news due soon for this market? Am I calm, and not trying to win back a loss?
definition.balanced: The checklist sits between your [[trading-plan]] and the order button. If an answer raises a caution (for example no stop, risk over your limit, news due soon, not calm, or not sure), you wait or skip that trade. It catches rushed or emotional trades before they happen.

definition.simple: When the market's price already reflects news that people expected, so the news itself may move the price very little.
definition.balanced: Prices move ahead of events as traders act on what they expect. When the event matches expectations, the reaction may be small, or opposite to the 'obvious' direction as traders take profits. It is hard to know exactly how much is priced in, so treat it as a working guess.

glossary.example: Hypothetical: a rate rise is widely expected and the currency rose for weeks before. The rise happens, and the currency slips as early buyers sell.

definition.simple: A score for how well you followed your plan on a trade. It never uses profit or loss.
definition.balanced: It rewards a stop set before entry, risk within your limit, an entry that matched your rules, and a completed review. A winning trade that broke rules does not score well. A losing trade that followed the plan can score well.

glossary.example: A trade where you moved your stop and still won scores lower than a planned trade that hit its stop.

definition.simple: How much of each dollar of revenue is left as profit.
definition.balanced: Gross margin = gross profit ÷ revenue. Operating margin = operating profit ÷ revenue. Net margin = net income ÷ revenue. A thin margin leaves little room: a small rise in costs can wipe out the profit.

glossary.example: Operating profit 40 on revenue 450: operating margin = 8.9% (fictional, millions USD).

definition.simple: A move against the trend that leaves the trend's structure intact.
definition.balanced: In an uptrend, a pullback falls but stays above the last higher low. At the time, a pullback and the start of a [[reversal]] look the same; only later candles show which it was.

glossary.example: Uptrend low 4,580, high 4,700. Price dips to 4,620, still above 4,580: a pullback so far.

definition.simple: A scheme where people hype a small, thinly traded asset to push its price up, then sell to the buyers they attracted.
definition.balanced: The promoters buy first, spread excited messages, and sell into the rising price. When they stop buying, the price can fall quickly and late buyers may not be able to sell at a good price. It is often seen with very small stocks and coins.

definition.simple: A right to sell the underlying at the strike price. The buyer pays a premium for it.
definition.balanced: At expiry a put is worth strike − price per unit if the price is below the strike, and nothing otherwise. A put buyer can lose at most the premium paid. A put seller receives the premium and must buy at the strike if [[assignment|assigned]], so the seller's largest loss comes if the price falls to zero.

definition.simple: The second currency in a pair. The price is measured in this currency, and profit or loss first appears in it.

glossary.example: In GBP/USD the quote currency is USD.

definition.simple: A result measured in units of the amount you risked. 1R is the planned loss.
definition.balanced: R-multiple = profit or loss ÷ planned risk. A win of twice the risk is +2R. A full stop-out is −1R. Slippage can make a loss worse than −1R. Using R lets you compare trades of different sizes.

glossary.example: You risked 50 USD and made 75 USD. That trade was +1.5R.

definition.simple: A second scam aimed at people who already lost money: someone offers to "recover" the money for an upfront fee.
definition.balanced: They may claim to be lawyers, investigators or officials, and may know details of your first loss. Never pay anyone upfront to get money back. Report the loss through official channels in your country instead.

definition.simple: A government or official body that licenses and supervises financial firms in a country or region.
definition.balanced: Many regulators keep a public register of firms they authorise. To check a broker, find the regulator's own official website yourself, search its register, and make sure the firm's exact name, address and website match. Rules differ between countries, so also check what applies where you live.

glossary.example: Examples of regulators include the FCA, ASIC and CySEC.

definition.simple: A comparison of one market with another, or with an index, usually as a ratio of their prices.
definition.balanced: A rising ratio means the first market did better over that window, even if both fell. The result depends on the window chosen and can change at any time. It is not [[rsi|RSI]], which looks at one market on its own.

glossary.example: A goes from 50 to 47 (−6%); the index goes from 4,000 to 3,600 (−10%). A shows relative strength, but still fell.

definition.simple: A price area where rising price has stopped and turned down before.
definition.balanced: Like support, resistance is a zone drawn from past turning points. It shows where sellers outweighed buyers before. It is not a wall, and price can push through it.

definition.simple: When price breaks a level, then comes back to touch it from the other side.
definition.balanced: After a breakout above resistance, price may return to that area. Sometimes the old resistance acts as support and price moves away again. Sometimes price falls straight back through it. A retest is something to watch, not a signal that works by itself.

definition.simple: The full spread of trade results: not just the average, but the middle result, the range and the worst runs.
definition.balanced: An average can hide that most trades lost while a few big winners pulled it up. Look at the median, the share of the total from the best one or two trades, the longest losing run and the deepest [[drawdown]]. With few trades, all of these are very uncertain.

glossary.example: Results +3, −1, −1, −1, +2, −1, −1, +4, −1, −1 R: average +0.2R, but median −1R.

definition.simple: How much operating profit a company earns on all the money tied up in it, from lenders and owners.
definition.balanced: In this app: return on capital = operating profit ÷ (debt + equity). Other sources define it slightly differently. A business that earns a high return on capital for years may have a [[competitive-advantage]], but past returns are not promised.

glossary.example: Operating profit 156 ÷ (debt 100 + equity 654) = about 20.7% (fictional, millions USD).

definition.simple: Profit as a percentage of the owners' money in the business.
definition.balanced: ROE = net income ÷ equity. It can look high simply because the company borrowed a lot and has little equity, so read it alongside debt and [[return-on-capital]].

glossary.example: Net income 114 ÷ equity 654 = about 17.4% (fictional, millions USD).

definition.simple: All the money a company brings in from selling its products or services, before any costs.
definition.balanced: Revenue is the first line of the [[income-statement]]. Growing revenue is not the same as growing profit: if costs grow faster, profit can fall while revenue rises.

glossary.example: A shop sells 10,000 items at 5 USD each: revenue is 50,000 USD.

definition.simple: A change in the direction of a trend: the old structure breaks and a new one forms.
definition.balanced: An uptrend reverses when price breaks below its last higher low and then makes lower highs and lower lows. You only know afterwards, and a new trend can turn again. Every reversal starts out looking like a [[pullback]].

glossary.example: Uptrend low 4,580 breaks with a close at 4,560; then a lower high at 4,650 and a lower low at 4,540.

definition.simple: A company swaps several old shares for one new share. You have fewer shares at a higher price, and your total value is unchanged on the day.
definition.balanced: In a 1-for-10 reverse split, every 10 shares become 1 and the price is multiplied by about 10. Nothing about the business changes. Companies sometimes do it to lift a falling share price above a level they need. Repeated reverse splits alongside repeated [[dilution]] are a warning sign worth investigating.

glossary.example: Fictional: 10,000 shares at 0.12 USD (1,200 USD) become 1,000 shares at 1.20 USD (still 1,200 USD).

definition.simple: The chance that losses push your account down to a level where you must stop.
definition.balanced: Risk of ruin depends on win rate, reward to risk, risk per trade and where you set the ruin level. It can only be estimated, for example by simulation. Risking a smaller share of the account each trade usually lowers it a lot.

glossary.example: Example: a learner sets ruin as a 50% [[drawdown]] and runs simulations at 1% and at 5% risk per trade to compare.

definition.simple: The money you would lose on one trade if the stop loss is hit, often set as a share of your account.
definition.balanced: Risk per trade = account balance × the risk percentage you chose. Rules such as 1% are learning examples, not a right number for everyone. The real loss can be larger than planned if the [[stop-loss]] slips.

glossary.example: Example only: a 10,000 USD account with a 1% example rule risks 100 USD per trade.

definition.simple: How much you plan to gain compared with how much you plan to lose on a trade.
definition.balanced: Reward to risk = distance to [[take-profit]] ÷ distance to [[stop-loss]]. A 2:1 trade aims to make twice what it risks. A bigger ratio needs a lower [[win-rate]] to break even, but price may reach the target less often.

glossary.example: Stop 30 pips away, target 60 pips away: reward to risk is 60 ÷ 30 = 2, written 2:1.

definition.simple: Closing a futures contract that is near expiry and opening the same position in a later month.
definition.balanced: Rolling is two trades, so it has costs, and the new month is bought or sold at its own price. The price gap between the months is a [[calendar-spread]]. Some brokers roll positions automatically, others do not, so check.

definition.simple: An indicator from 0 to 100 that compares the size of recent up moves with recent down moves.
definition.balanced: RSI = 100 − 100 ÷ (1 + RS), where RS is the average gain divided by the average loss over a set period, often 14. Readings above 70 or below 30 are often labelled [[overbought-oversold|overbought or oversold]]. In a strong trend RSI can stay at those levels for a long time while price keeps going.

glossary.example: Average gain 6 pips, average loss 2 pips: RS = 3, so RSI = 100 − 100 ÷ 4 = 75.

definition.simple: How many trades (or results) you are judging from. A small sample says little.
definition.balanced: With few trades, luck can make bad rules look good or good rules look bad. With 10 trades, changing one result moves the win rate by 10 percentage points, and adding one more trade moves it by up to about 9. With 50 trades, changing one result moves it by 2. More trades make the picture steadier, but even a large sample from the past does not promise the future.

glossary.example: Winning 4 of your first 5 replay trades tells you very little about your rules.

definition.simple: Patterns that tend to repeat at certain times of year, such as crops arriving at harvest or more fuel used for heating in winter.
definition.balanced: Seasons change supply (planting, harvest) and demand (heating, cooling, travel). Markets usually know the calendar, so normal seasonal changes are often already priced in. What moves prices is a season that turns out different from what was expected. A seasonal tendency is never a guarantee.

definition.simple: A small piece of ownership in a company. Own one share and you own a tiny part of the business.
definition.balanced: Each share gives a claim on part of the company's profits and assets, and usually a vote. Your fraction of the company = your shares ÷ all the shares outstanding. The price of a share is set by buyers and sellers on a [[stock-exchange]], not by the company.

glossary.example: A fictional company has 100 million shares. Owning 1,000 of them means owning 1,000 ÷ 100,000,000 = 0.001% of it.

definition.simple: Selling something you have borrowed, hoping to buy it back cheaper later. If the price rises instead, you lose.
definition.balanced: With shares, a short seller borrows them, sells them, and must later buy them back to return them. The loss has no fixed limit because the price can keep rising. For small, thinly traded shares, borrowing may be impossible or expensive, brokers may not allow it, and sudden spikes can force short sellers to buy back at very bad prices.

definition.simple: A chat group or service that sends "buy" and "sell" calls, often for a fee.
definition.balanced: Some are run by people who earn from fees or referrals, not from trading. Claimed results are usually screenshots you cannot check. Following signals also skips your own [[trading-plan]] and risk rules.

definition.simple: The difference between the price you expected and the price you actually got.
definition.balanced: It happens when price moves between sending an order and filling it, or when there is not enough volume at the requested price. It can be against you or in your favour. It is more likely in fast markets, around news, and in thin [[liquidity]].

definition.simple: The gap between the [[ask]] price and the [[bid]] price. It is a cost you pay every time you trade.
definition.balanced: Ask minus bid. A trade opened and closed immediately at market loses the spread. Spreads change with liquidity and can widen around news and outside busy hours.

glossary.example: Bid 1.1000, ask 1.1002: the spread is 0.0002, which is 2 pips.

definition.simple: A market where buyers and sellers trade shares under set rules.
definition.balanced: An exchange lists companies that meet its rules, matches buy and sell orders, and publishes prices. Each listed company has a short [[ticker]] code. Many exchanges trade only during set hours, so prices can [[gap]] between one session and the next.

definition.simple: Marketing that pushes people to buy a particular share, often through newsletters, social media, emails or chat groups.
definition.balanced: Some promotions are paid for by the company or by shareholders who may want to sell. The excited tone, the price targets and the urgency are designed to make you act before checking. A heavy promotion of a tiny, thinly traded share is one of the classic setups for a [[pump-and-dump]].

glossary.example: Fictional: 'This tiny miner could go up 10 times by Friday!' with a small-print note that the writer was paid by a shareholder.

definition.simple: An order that closes your trade if price moves against you to a level you chose in advance. It limits how much you planned to lose.
definition.balanced: A pending order placed at the price where your trade idea is proven wrong. It becomes a market order when reached, so in fast markets or gaps it can fill at a worse price than the stop level.

definition.simple: An order to buy once price rises to a level above now, or sell once it falls to a level below now.
definition.balanced: A buy stop sits above the current [[ask]]; a sell stop sits below the current [[bid]]. When price reaches the level, it becomes a [[market-order]], so the fill can be worse than the level. A [[stop-loss]] works the same way.

definition.simple: When the broker closes your trades for you because your account cannot support them any more.
definition.balanced: If your [[margin-level]] falls to the broker's stop-out level, the broker starts closing open positions, often the biggest loser first. You do not choose the price. The level is set by each broker. In fast markets the account can lose more than expected before the close happens.

definition.simple: What it costs to keep a physical commodity until later: warehouse or tank space, insurance and the money tied up.
definition.balanced: Because holding a physical commodity costs money, a price for delivery later is often higher than the price for delivery now. When storage space is scarce or costly, that gap can widen. When supply is tight right now, buyers may pay more for the near delivery instead, and the gap can turn the other way.

glossary.example: Fictional: storage, insurance and financing cost 0.40 USD per unit per month. A price for delivery in one month might sit about 0.40 above today's price.

definition.simple: The fixed price at which an option lets its holder buy (call) or sell (put) the underlying.
definition.balanced: Options on the same underlying and expiry are listed at several strikes, and each is a separate contract with its own premium. Where the strike sits against the current price decides whether an option is [[in-the-money|in]], [[at-the-money|at]] or [[out-of-the-money|out of]] the money.

definition.simple: A sudden, unexpected change in how much of something can be produced or delivered, such as a mine flooding or a pipeline closing.
definition.balanced: A negative supply shock removes supply and can push prices up, especially if [[inventory-report|inventories]] are low. How much it matters depends on its size, how long it lasts, whether other producers can make up the gap, and what the market had already expected. Prices can jump on the news and fall back once the picture is clearer.

definition.simple: A price area where falling price has stopped and turned up before.
definition.balanced: Support is an area, not an exact line, because wicks and the [[spread]] blur the edges. It describes where buyers outweighed sellers in the past. It can break at any time, and a broken support area sometimes acts as resistance later.

glossary.example: Price turned up from 1.08020, 1.07980 and 1.08050. You might mark a support zone from 1.07980 to 1.08050.

definition.simple: The difference between the actual figure and what was expected.
definition.balanced: Surprise = actual − [[consensus-forecast]]. A big surprise often brings a bigger move, but the direction is not certain. Other parts of the report, revisions, and what traders had already priced in can change the reaction.

glossary.example: Hypothetical: expected 2.5%, actual 2.9%. The surprise is +0.4 percentage points.

definition.simple: Judging only from the things that "survived" or got noticed, while ignoring the ones that failed or vanished.
definition.balanced: In trading, it happens when you copy a method because you heard it worked, without seeing the similar methods that failed and were forgotten. The failures are missing from what you look at, so the method looks better than it is. Testing only the periods you remember as good is a related error called selection bias, or cherry-picking.

glossary.example: You copy a method because a fictional forum post says it worked. Nobody posts about the similar methods that stopped working, so you only ever see the survivor.

definition.simple: A charge or credit for keeping a trade open overnight.
definition.balanced: A daily adjustment for holding a leveraged position past the broker's daily cut-off time. It can be negative or positive, and it differs for buys and sells, between symbols and between brokers. Some brokers apply several days' worth on one night of the week. Check your broker's contract specification.

definition.simple: A turning point at the top: a high with lower highs on both sides of it.
definition.balanced: People define it in different ways. One common rule is a candle whose high is above the highs of the two candles before and the two candles after it. Because you need the later candles, a swing high is only confirmed after some time has passed.

definition.simple: A turning point at the bottom: a low with higher lows on both sides of it.
definition.balanced: Like a swing high, it depends on the rule you use, and it is only confirmed after the candles that follow it have formed.

definition.simple: An order that closes your trade when price reaches the profit level you chose.
definition.balanced: A level attached to an open trade. A buy is closed at the [[bid]], so its take profit triggers when the bid reaches the level. A sell is closed at the [[ask]], so its take profit triggers when the ask reaches it. It is the partner of the [[stop-loss]].

definition.simple: The smallest step a futures price can move.
definition.balanced: Prices move in whole ticks. The tick size is set in the contract specification, and differs between contracts. Together with the [[multiplier]] it sets the [[tick-value]].

glossary.example: Fictional contract with a tick size of 0.25: price can move from 4,000.00 to 4,000.25, but not to 4,000.10.

definition.simple: How much money one tick of price movement is worth for one contract.
definition.balanced: Tick value = [[tick-size]] × [[multiplier]] (or × [[contract-size]]). Profit or loss = ticks moved × tick value × contracts. Never assume two contracts share a tick value.

glossary.example: Fictional: tick size 0.25 × multiplier 10 USD = 2.50 USD per tick, per contract.

definition.simple: A short code of letters that stands for a company's shares on an exchange.
definition.balanced: Tickers save space on quote screens. Similar-looking tickers can belong to very different companies, and the same company can have different tickers on different exchanges, so check the full name before you act.

definition.simple: The way an option's time value tends to shrink as expiry gets closer, if nothing else changes.
definition.balanced: It works against option buyers and for option sellers. It is why an option can lose value even when the underlying moves the right way, if the move is too small or too slow. At expiry, time value is gone.

definition.simple: The part of an option's premium above its intrinsic value. It is what buyers pay for the chance the price moves further before expiry.
definition.balanced: Time value = premium − intrinsic value. It tends to be larger with more time left and with higher [[implied-volatility]]. It shrinks as expiry nears ([[time-decay]]) and is zero at expiry.

definition.simple: How much time each candle on a chart covers, for example 15 minutes, 1 hour or 1 day.
definition.balanced: Common labels: M1, M5, M15, M30 (minutes), H1, H4 (hours), D1 (day), W1 (week). Four H1 candles together cover the same time as one H4 candle. The same market can look like it is rising on one timeframe and falling on another, because each looks at a different stretch of time.

glossary.example: On a forex weekday there are 24 H1 candles, so 100 H1 candles cover about 4 days.

definition.simple: A pause in trading a share. While it lasts, you cannot buy or sell it at all.
definition.balanced: An exchange or regulator may halt a share pending news, after a very sharp price move, or when there are questions about the company's information. A halt can last minutes or much longer. When trading restarts, the price can open far from where it stopped, so a [[stop-loss]] gives no protection during the pause.

definition.simple: A record of each trade: what you planned, what you did, what happened, and what you learned.
definition.balanced: A good journal records entry, stop, target, size, exit, result in pips, money and R, your reasons, emotions, rule breaks and a chart screenshot. Reviewing it shows patterns that single trades hide. The result of a trade is recorded separately from the quality of the decision.

definition.simple: A short written set of rules for how you trade: what, when, how you enter and exit, and how much you risk. You write it before you trade, while you are calm.
definition.balanced: It covers instruments, sessions, timeframe, entry, exit, [[stop-loss]] and [[take-profit]] rules, risk per trade, a daily loss limit, a maximum number of trades, and when to stop. Change it between sessions, not during a trade, and keep each version so you can compare them.

glossary.example: A plan might say: "EUR/USD only, London session, 1-hour chart, stop on every trade, example risk 1% per trade, stop for the day after 2 losses."

definition.simple: The part of the day when a major financial centre, such as London or New York, is open and active. Session times are conventions and shift with daylight saving.
The general direction price has moved in: up, down or sideways.
definition.balanced: An uptrend is often described as a series of higher [[swing-high|swing highs]] and higher [[swing-low|swing lows]]. A downtrend has lower highs and lower lows. When neither is clear, the market is called sideways or ranging. A trend describes the past. It can stop or turn at any time.

glossary.example: Swing lows at 1.09500, 1.09850 and 1.10100, with swing highs at 1.10200 and 1.10600, form higher lows and higher highs: an uptrend so far.

definition.simple: A sold option without the holding or cash that would cover the obligation if assigned.
definition.balanced: An uncovered sold call has no fixed limit on loss, because the price of the underlying can keep rising. Losses can be many times the premium received. Brokers usually require special approval and margin for it.

definition.simple: The thing an option or other derivative is based on, such as a share, an index or a futures contract.
definition.balanced: An option's value at expiry depends only on the underlying's price against the [[strike-price]]. The contract specification names the underlying and how many units of it one contract covers.

definition.simple: Judging what a company might be worth compared with the price you would pay for it.
definition.balanced: Simple valuation tools compare the price with profit, cash or dividends: [[pe-ratio|P/E]], earnings yield (EPS ÷ price) and [[dividend-yield]]. A good business can be a poor investment if the price already assumes more than it later delivers. Every valuation rests on guesses about the future.

definition.simple: An approach that looks for companies whose price seems low compared with their profits, cash or assets.
definition.balanced: Value investors look for a low price relative to earnings, cash flow or book value. The risk: some companies are cheap for a reason, such as a shrinking business, and stay cheap or get cheaper.

definition.simple: A share that looks cheap on its figures but is cheap because the business is declining.
definition.balanced: A low [[pe-ratio]] can mean earnings are about to fall. Checking why the price is low, and whether cash flow supports the profits, is the defence.

definition.simple: Setting the stop from how much the market moves, such as 2 × ATR, then sizing so the loss at the stop is a fixed amount.
