definition.balanced: Size = money at risk ÷ (stop distance × value per unit of price), rounded down. A jumpier market gets a wider stop and a smaller size. If the smallest possible size is still too big, skip the trade. ATR is backward-looking, and gaps can still push a loss past the stop.

glossary.example: Risk 100 USD, ATR 0.80, stop 2 × ATR = 1.60: 100 ÷ 1.60 = 62.5, so 62 shares.

definition.simple: How much and how fast a price moves up and down.
definition.balanced: High volatility means bigger swings, in both directions. It often rises around news. Wider swings need wider stops for the same idea, which means a smaller size for the same money at risk. [[slippage|Slippage]] and wider spreads are more common when volatility is high.

glossary.example: A pair that usually moves 50 pips a day moves 150 pips on a news day.

definition.simple: How much was traded during a candle, such as the number of shares or contracts.
definition.balanced: Stocks and futures report volume from their exchange. Forex has no single exchange, so platforms usually show tick volume: how many times the broker's price changed. Compare a bar with its recent average. Heavy volume shows more participation; it does not show direction or what happens next.

glossary.example: Average volume 400,000 shares; today 1,000,000 shares, so relative volume is 2.5.

definition.simple: Testing in steps: tune rules on one block of history, test them unchanged on the next block, then slide forward and repeat.
definition.balanced: Only the joined test blocks are judged, since each was tested with rules tuned on earlier data. It shows how rules cope as conditions change. It is still a test of the past with a limited sample, and any leak of future data spoils it.

glossary.example: Tune on candles 1–200, test 201–300; tune on 101–300, test 301–400; and so on.

definition.simple: A quick move one way that triggers a trade, followed by a quick move back that stops it out.
definition.balanced: Common for trend and breakout rules in sideways markets: price crosses an average or a level, the rule enters, and price returns. A run of whipsaws produces many small losses.

glossary.example: Price closes above a rising average at 1.1020, the rule buys, and two candles later it closes back below at 1.1005: a whipsaw.

definition.simple: The share of your trades that make money.
definition.balanced: Win rate = winning trades ÷ all trades. On its own it says little: a high win rate with small wins and big losses can still lose money. Break-even win rate = 1 ÷ (1 + reward to risk), before costs.

glossary.example: 6 winners out of 20 trades is a 30% win rate.

disclosures.title: Futures losses can exceed margin
body: The [[margin]] a futures broker requires is a deposit, not the most you can lose. Losses on a futures position can be larger than the margin you put up.
Prices can gap past your [[stop-loss|stop loss]], and contract specifications differ between contracts. Always check the specification of the exact contract.

disclosures.title: Before you start: simulation and education only
body: TradeLab is a learning app. It is not a broker, a signal service, or financial advice for your situation.
Everything you trade here is simulated or on a demo account. TradeLab never places real trades, never asks for broker logins, and never handles money.
Trading strategies can lose money. Past performance does not guarantee future results.
Scores and certificates in TradeLab measure learning and discipline. They are not licences and they do not show that you are likely to make money.

disclosures.title: Leverage makes losses bigger too
body: [[leverage|Leverage]] lets a small deposit control a much larger position. It increases losses in exactly the same way it increases gains.
A small price move against a leveraged position can use up your [[margin]] quickly. Practise sizing so that one losing trade costs only a small, planned amount.

disclosures.title: Options can lose the whole premium, or far more
body: A bought [[option]] can expire worthless, and the whole [[option-premium|premium]] paid is lost. A sold option can lose far more than the premium received, and an [[uncovered-option|uncovered]] sold call has no fixed limit on loss.
Options are complex, and contract specifications differ. Always check the specification of the exact contract. In this app, options are for study in simulation only.

disclosures.title: Penny stocks: thin trading and manipulation risk
body: Penny stocks and microcaps can be illiquid: few buyers and sellers, wide [[spread|spreads]], and prices that jump sharply. It can be hard to sell when you want to.
They are a common target for promotions and pump-and-dump schemes. Often the best decision is to stay out.

disclosures.title: Practice is not a green light
body: Completing lessons, simulations, and demo practice shows what you have learned. It does not show that you are ready to trade real money.
Simulated and demo results can differ from real trading, where costs, fills, and emotions are different.

questions.prompt: Fictional weekly report: consensus a draw of 2.0 million barrels, actual a draw of 0.5 million. What is the surprise?

options.text: −1.5 million barrels, a bigger draw than expected
options.explanation: No: the actual draw was smaller than expected, so the surprise is positive.

options.text: +1.5 million barrels
options.explanation: Right: −0.5 − (−2.0) = +1.5. Less was drawn than expected.

options.text: −2.5 million barrels
options.explanation: No: that adds the two draws together.

questions.prompt: A fictional mine that supplies a small share of a metal closes for a week while stored stocks are high. What is the most accurate view?

options.text: The price must rise sharply, since any supply loss lifts prices
options.explanation: No: size, duration and stored stock all matter, and no reaction is certain.

options.text: Any effect is likely to be small or brief, since stored stocks are high
options.explanation: Right: the mine is small, the closure is short and stocks are high. The reaction is still a scenario, not a fact.

options.text: It could cause a lasting shortage once stored stocks run down
options.explanation: No: the closure lasts a week and stored stocks are high, so a lasting shortage is unlikely.

questions.prompt: Fictional crop: stock 40, harvest 90, use 110 (million tonnes). What is the stock-to-use ratio at year end?

options.text: About 36%
options.explanation: No: that is 40 ÷ 110, the starting stock only.

options.text: About 18%
About 22%
options.explanation: No: that divides 20 by the harvest (90) instead of by use (110).

questions.prompt: Fictional commodity at 800 USD. The rate moves from 1 USD = 1.25 WMK to 1 USD = 1.50 WMK. What happens for a Westmark buyer?

options.text: Nothing changes, since the USD price is unchanged
options.explanation: No: the buyer pays in WMK, and the exchange rate moved.

options.text: It gets 200 WMK cheaper
options.explanation: No: more WMK per USD makes it dearer for the Westmark buyer, not cheaper.

options.text: It costs 200 WMK more: 1,200 instead of 1,000

questions.prompt: Fictional curve: immediate 30.00, 1-month 29.40, 2-month 28.90. Which statement is right?

options.text: It is in contango, so the market predicts a rise
options.explanation: No: later months are cheaper, and a curve is not a forecast anyway.

options.text: Backwardation, which often points to tight supply now
options.explanation: Right: later dates are priced lower; near delivery is valued more today.

options.text: It is in backwardation, so the price will soon fall to 28.90
options.explanation: No: the shape is right, but a curve is not a forecast of the future price.

questions.prompt: A fictional harvest report shows a bigger crop than expected, yet the price rises. Which explanation fits best?

options.text: It was already priced in, or other news dominated
options.explanation: Right: if a big crop was already priced in, or weather news elsewhere mattered more, the price can rise anyway.

options.text: The report must have been wrong, so traders ignored it
options.explanation: No: the number does not need to be wrong for the price to rise.

options.text: Bigger crops can raise prices, as more supply means more trading
options.explanation: No: more supply tends to weigh on price. More trading does not lift it.

questions.prompt: Fictional GDP release: consensus +0.4% on the quarter, actual +0.1%. What is the surprise?

options.text: +0.3 points
options.explanation: No: surprise is actual minus consensus, and the actual is lower.

options.text: +0.1 points
options.explanation: No: that is the actual figure, not the gap.

options.text: −0.3 points
options.explanation: Right: 0.1 − 0.4 = −0.3 points, weaker than expected.

questions.prompt: In most countries, who sets the policy interest rate?

options.text: The finance ministry
options.explanation: No: the government sets taxes and spending, which is fiscal policy.

options.text: The country's central bank
options.explanation: Right: the policy rate is the central bank's main monetary-policy tool.

options.text: The statistics office
options.explanation: No: statistics offices publish data such as GDP and inflation; they do not set rates.

questions.prompt: Hypothetical: government debt 300 billion WMK, yearly GDP 600 billion WMK. What is debt as a share of GDP?

options.explanation: No: that divides GDP by debt. Divide debt by GDP.
No: check the division. 300 ÷ 600 = 0.5.
No: that is the debt in billions, read as a percentage.

questions.prompt: Suppose traders' bets imply a 90% chance of a 0.25-point rate rise. The fictional central bank holds rates instead. Measured against what was priced in, what is the surprise?

options.text: −0.225 points
options.explanation: Right: priced in = 0.90 × 0.25 = 0.225 points, and 0 − 0.225 = −0.225.

options.text: 0 points, as rates did not move
options.explanation: No: the market expected a rise, so no change is itself a surprise.

options.text: −0.25 points
options.explanation: No: that assumes the rise was certain. It was priced at 90%.

questions.prompt: The price of fictional Westmark's main export falls 15%. What is most accurate about WMK?

options.text: WMK must fall 15% too, matching its export
options.explanation: No: there is no one-to-one link, and other forces can outweigh it.

options.text: It tends to weigh on WMK; other forces also matter
options.explanation: Right: lower export earnings can reduce demand for WMK, as a tendency, not a rule.

options.text: Buyers abroad now need less WMK, which may push it up
options.explanation: No: needing less WMK means less demand for it, which tends to weigh on it, not lift it.

questions.prompt: Two fictional inflation releases show the same consensus and actual. After one, the currency rises and holds; after the other, it spikes and falls back. What best explains the difference?

options.text: One release must have been reported wrongly
options.explanation: No: both numbers can be correct. The setup before them differed.

options.text: One release may have had a bigger surprise than the other
options.explanation: No: the same consensus and actual means the same surprise. The setup before them differed.

options.text: More was priced in before the second, so traders took profit
options.explanation: Right: when many traders bought early, good news can be when they take profit.

questions.prompt: Your first 6 replay trades were all losses. What is the most sensible view?

options.text: The rules are broken, so drop them now and start again with a different method
options.explanation: No: 6 trades is a tiny sample. Losing streaks happen even with sound rules.

options.text: Too early to judge; check you followed the plan and keep collecting trades
options.explanation: Right: a small sample says little.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of look-ahead bias?

options.text: Drawing support on a past chart using a low that formed after your entry
options.explanation: Right: you used information that did not exist at the time.

options.text: Testing on a quiet, ranging period you chose in advance
options.explanation: No: no future information is used. Picking periods before you look, including quiet ones, is a good way to reduce selection bias.

questions.prompt: You only test periods you remember as big trends. What bias is this?

options.text: Look-ahead bias
options.explanation: No: look-ahead bias is using future information.

options.text: Selection bias
options.explanation: Right: this is selection bias, also called cherry-picking. You only test what stood out, and leave out the rest.

options.text: Survivorship bias
options.explanation: No: survivorship bias is copying a method because it is one of the ones that happened to work. Picking only the periods you remember is selection bias.

questions.prompt: You add a filter that removes 5 past losers. How do you know if it helps?

options.text: The past results improved, so it helps
options.explanation: No: it was chosen from those trades. That is overfitting.

options.text: Test it as a new plan version on fresh periods
options.explanation: Right: only new data can show that.

questions.prompt: Fictional test: 40 trades, 12 wins of +3R, 28 losses of −1R. Net result?

options.explanation: No: that ignores the losses.
No: 36R − 28R is positive.

questions.prompt: What can a 50-trade replay test show you?

options.text: Whether the plan has a real edge that will keep working on a live account in future
options.explanation: No: past tests promise nothing about the future.

options.text: How your rules behave in different conditions and how well you follow them
options.explanation: Right: it is a learning tool, not a forecast.

questions.prompt: You buy USD/JPY. What are you doing?

options.text: Buying dollars and paying with yen
options.explanation: Right: buying the pair means buying the base (USD) with the quote (JPY).

options.text: Buying yen with dollars
options.explanation: No: that would be selling USD/JPY.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a major pair?

options.text: AUD/USD
options.explanation: Right: the US dollar paired with a major currency.

options.text: EUR/JPY
options.explanation: No: there is no US dollar, so it is a cross.

options.text: USD/TRY
options.explanation: No: the Turkish lira makes it an exotic.

questions.prompt: You sell EUR/USD at market. Which price do you get?

options.text: The bid (the lower price)
options.explanation: Right: sells fill at the bid.

options.text: The ask (the higher price)
options.explanation: No: the ask is the price you can buy at.

questions.prompt: Bid 1.30000, ask 1.30020 on a 10,000-unit trade where 1 pip is worth 1 USD. What does the spread cost?

options.text: 0.20 USD
options.explanation: No: 0.00020 is 2 pips, not 0.2 pips.

options.text: 2 USD
options.explanation: Right: 2 pips × 1 USD per pip = 2 USD.

options.text: 20 USD
options.explanation: No: that would be 20 pips, or a 100,000-unit trade.

questions.prompt: Which statements about trading sessions are true? Choose all that apply.

options.text: Spreads can widen in quiet hours
options.explanation: True: lower activity often means wider spreads.

options.text: Session times shift with daylight saving
options.explanation: True: London and New York change their clocks.

options.text: The market is busiest on Sunday afternoon
options.explanation: False: the main market is closed at the weekend.

questions.prompt: A EUR/USD candle: open 1.09200, high 1.09350, low 1.09150, close 1.09300. How big is its body?

options.text: 10 pips
20 pips
options.explanation: No: that is the range, high minus low.

options.text: 100 pips
options.explanation: No: 0.00100 is 10 pips. On EUR/USD one pip is 0.00010.

questions.prompt: Four H1 candles have highs 1.2510, 1.2525, 1.2518 and 1.2505. What is the high of the H4 candle they make?

options.explanation: Right: the H4 high is the highest of the four highs.
No: that is the last candle's high.
No: that is the average of the four highs. The H4 high is the highest one.

questions.prompt: Swing highs 1.3200, 1.3150, 1.3080. Swing lows 1.3100, 1.3020. What do the swings describe?

options.text: A downtrend so far
options.explanation: Right: lower highs and lower lows.

options.text: An uptrend so far
options.explanation: No: the highs and lows are both falling.

options.text: A range between 1.3020 and 1.3200
options.explanation: No: the swings step down rather than overlap.

questions.prompt: Swing highs keep turning near 1.1100 and swing lows near 1.1020. What is this, and how high is it?

options.text: A range about 80 pips high
An uptrend about 80 pips high
options.explanation: No: the swings are not rising.

options.text: A range about 8 pips high
options.explanation: No: 0.0080 is 80 pips.

questions.prompt: An uptrend's last higher low is 1.27400. A candle closes at 1.27350. What is the best description now?

options.text: Uptrend structure broken; direction unclear
options.explanation: Right: a lower low breaks the pattern, but a downtrend also needs a lower high.

options.text: A confirmed downtrend has started, so this is a signal to sell
options.explanation: No: a break of structure changes the description. It is not a signal.

options.text: The uptrend is still intact, since it was only a small dip
options.explanation: No: price closed 5 pips below the last higher low, so the pattern of higher lows is broken.

questions.prompt: The D1 chart shows an uptrend. The M15 chart shows the last 3 hours falling. What is true?

options.text: Both can be true at once
options.explanation: Right: a short fall can sit inside a longer rise.

options.text: One of the charts must be wrong
options.explanation: No: they show the same prices over different windows of time.

quizzes.title: Checkpoint: forward testing, journaling and psychology

questions.prompt: What is the main goal of forward testing on demo?

options.text: To prove the plan makes money, so you know it is safe to move to a real account
options.explanation: No: 20 demo trades is a small sample and proves nothing about future profit. No demo result shows that you are ready to trade real money.

options.text: To see if you can follow your plan live, and learn real costs and reactions
options.explanation: Right: it is about execution and learning.

questions.prompt: Which trade earns the higher process score?

options.text: Won 50 USD after moving the stop further away to give the trade room
options.explanation: No: moving the stop away is a rule break, and profit never counts.

options.text: Lost the planned 20 USD with every rule followed
options.explanation: Right: process is scored, not profit.

questions.prompt: Put the review steps in order. Which comes right after "rules followed?"

options.text: The one lesson you will carry into your next session
options.explanation: No: the result comes first, kept separate from decision quality.

options.text: Result, kept separate from decision quality
options.explanation: Right: thesis → plan vs. actual → rules followed? → result → one lesson → next goal.

options.text: Thesis
options.explanation: No: the thesis is the first step.

questions.prompt: Planned stop 25 pips, fill 3 pips worse, pip value 2 USD. Actual risk?

options.text: 50 USD
options.explanation: No: that is the planned risk.

options.text: 56 USD
options.explanation: Right: 28 pips × 2 USD = 56 USD.

options.text: 44 USD
options.explanation: No: a worse fill adds pips, it does not remove them.

questions.prompt: After three losses, you feel the urge to win it back. Which response fits a good plan?

options.text: Take a bigger trade now
options.explanation: No: that is revenge trading and sizing up after losses.

options.text: Stop or pause as your plan says, and note the feeling
options.explanation: Right: the plan is there for this moment.

questions.prompt: Why are imported MT demo trades kept separate from replay and paper trades?

options.text: So different sources never mix in your results
options.explanation: Right: each source has different conditions.

options.text: Because imported trades do not count toward your progress at all
options.explanation: No: they count, they are just labelled by source.

questions.prompt: Fictional jobs report: consensus +200,000 jobs, actual +260,000. What is the surprise?

options.explanation: No: surprise is actual minus expected, and actual is higher.
No: that is the actual figure, not the gap.

questions.prompt: A fictional country's inflation comes in above the consensus. What is the most accurate statement?

options.text: Its currency will rise, because inflation above the consensus always makes the central bank raise rates at once
options.explanation: No: a rise is one possible reaction, not a certainty, and a central bank does not always respond at once.

options.text: The currency may rise as markets expect higher rates, but it may fall or not move if this was priced in
options.explanation: Right: the mechanism is a tendency, and the reaction is uncertain.

questions.prompt: A fictional central bank cuts rates by more than expected. What might happen to its currency?

options.text: It may weaken, as rates are lower than expected, but the reaction is not certain
options.explanation: Right: a lower-than-expected rate is a negative surprise for the currency, as a tendency only.

options.text: Nothing, because a rate decision only matters once the next inflation figure is published
options.explanation: No: rate decisions and guidance can move currencies sharply, straight away.

questions.prompt: Buy 0.20 lot EUR/USD (pip value 2 USD), stop 25 pips. A release makes the stop fill 8 pips past its level. What is the loss?

options.text: 50 USD
options.explanation: No: that is the planned loss, 25 × 2.

options.text: 66 USD
16 USD
options.explanation: No: that is only the slippage part, 8 × 2.

questions.prompt: What often happens to spreads around a major economic release?

options.text: They often widen
options.explanation: Right: liquidity can thin out and prices move fast, so trading costs often rise.

options.text: They narrow
options.explanation: No: spreads usually get wider, not narrower, around big news.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that a release was 'priced in'?

options.text: Traders had already acted on what they expected, so the price already reflected it
options.explanation: Right: that is why an expected number may cause little move.

options.text: The broker added a fee to the price during the release
options.explanation: No: it is about expectations already being in the price.

questions.prompt: A 3-period SMA uses closes 1.3000, 1.3030 and 1.3060. What is it?

options.explanation: No: that is the last close.
No: that is the sum. Divide by 3.

questions.prompt: Using the simplified formula, average gain 9 pips and average loss 3 pips give what RSI?

options.explanation: No: that would be the result if gains and losses were swapped.
No: RSI reaches 100 only when there are no losses at all. Here the average loss is 3 pips. RS = 9 ÷ 3 = 3, and RSI = 100 − 100 ÷ (1 + 3) = 75.

questions.prompt: RSI 14 has been above 70 for 15 candles in a strong uptrend. What should you conclude?

options.text: Recent up moves have been much bigger than down moves
options.explanation: Right: that is what RSI measures. It does not say when the move ends.

options.text: Price is overbought, so it must fall soon
options.explanation: No: overbought readings can last while price keeps rising.

questions.prompt: EMA 12 = 1.08420 and EMA 26 = 1.08300. The signal line is 0.00150. What is the MACD histogram?

options.explanation: No: that is the MACD line. The histogram is MACD line minus signal line.
No: check the sign. The MACD line is below the signal line.

questions.prompt: Previous close 1.15000. Candle high 1.15400, low 1.15200. What is the true range?

options.text: 40 pips
options.explanation: Right: high − previous close = 40 pips, larger than high − low (20) and low − previous close (20).

options.text: 20 pips
options.explanation: No: high − low misses the gap up from the previous close.

options.text: 0.4 pips

questions.prompt: Each option pairs a tool with a condition where it often misleads. Which pairs are right? Select all that apply.

options.text: Moving-average crosses: a sideways range
options.explanation: Right: price crosses a flat average again and again.

options.text: Bollinger Band touch as a reversal signal: a strong trend
options.explanation: Right: price can ride one band for many candles.

options.text: ATR: it is never misleading
options.explanation: No: ATR describes the past, so it can be far too low just before a sudden news move.

questions.prompt: Price has turned down three times near 1.0900. What is that area called?

options.text: Resistance
options.explanation: Right: rising price has turned down there before.

options.text: Support
options.explanation: No: support is where falling price has turned up.

options.text: A breakout zone
options.explanation: No: a breakout is a close beyond a level. Here price keeps turning down before it gets through.

questions.prompt: Swing lows at 1.25030, 1.24980 and 1.25070. What support zone do they make, and how wide is it?

options.explanation: Right: from the lowest to the highest low, 1.25070 − 1.24980 = 0.00090 = 9 pips.
No: 0.00090 is 9 pips, not 90.

options.text: Exactly 1.25030
options.explanation: No: support is better drawn as a zone than a single price.

questions.prompt: Resistance zone tops at 1.10500. Your rule: a breakout is a close at least 5 pips above it. Which candle counts?

options.text: Close 1.10560
options.explanation: Right: 1.10560 − 1.10500 = 6 pips, which is at least 5.
No: only the wick went above. It closed inside the zone.

options.text: Close 1.10530
options.explanation: No: that is only 3 pips above the zone.

questions.prompt: Buy 0.10 lot (pip value 1 USD) on a breakout at 1.26680 with a stop at 1.26450. It turns into a false breakout and the stop fills at its level. What is the loss?

options.text: 23 USD
2.30 USD
options.explanation: No: 0.00230 is 23 pips, not 2.3.

options.text: 230 USD
options.explanation: No: that would need a pip value of 10 USD.

questions.prompt: Price breaks above resistance, then comes back down to that level from above. What is this called?

options.text: A retest
options.explanation: Right: price returns to test the level it broke.

options.text: A guaranteed buy signal
options.explanation: No: the old resistance may act as support, or price may fall straight through.

questions.prompt: Which statement about false breakouts is true?

options.text: You usually only know a breakout was false afterwards
options.explanation: Right: at the moment of the break, both kinds can look the same.

options.text: Waiting for a second close beyond the level removes them all
options.explanation: No: stricter rules skip some, enter later, and still get caught by others.

options.text: They only happen to beginners who enter too early
options.explanation: No: they are a normal part of how price moves.

questions.prompt: What is the main job of a trading plan?

options.text: To guarantee profits
options.explanation: No: nothing can guarantee profits.

options.text: To make decisions in advance, so your trading is consistent and reviewable
options.explanation: Right: rules made while calm, then followed and checked.

options.text: To list every market situation you might meet, and exactly what to do in each
options.explanation: No: no plan can list everything. A plan should be short enough to follow.

questions.prompt: A demo balance is 8,000 USD. The example daily loss limit is 2%. Risk per trade is 80 USD. After how many full losses do you stop?

options.explanation: No: one loss is 80 USD, and the limit is 160 USD.
Right: 2% × 8,000 = 160 USD, and 160 ÷ 80 = 2 losses.
No: 4 losses would be 320 USD, double the limit.

questions.prompt: Which rule is clear enough to test?

options.text: "Sell when it feels toppy"
options.explanation: No: this cannot be checked on a chart.

options.text: "Sell when a 1-hour candle closes below the last swing low"
options.explanation: Right: anyone can check this at the time.

questions.prompt: Stop distance 25 pips, pip value 2 USD, risk limit 40 USD. Does the trade fit?

options.text: Yes: the stop is only 25 pips, which is well inside a 40-pip limit
options.explanation: No: the limit is 40 USD of risk, not 40 pips. 25 × 2 = 50 USD, which is over the limit.

options.text: No: 25 × 2 = 50 USD is over the 40 USD limit, so reduce size or skip
options.explanation: Right: the money at risk breaks the limit.

questions.prompt: You are angry after a loss. Your checklist asks "Am I calm?" What do you do?

options.text: Answer yes, since the setup matches your plan anyway
options.explanation: No: the checklist only works if you answer honestly, even when the setup looks good.

options.text: Answer no, and wait or skip for now
options.explanation: Right: not being calm raises a caution, so you wait or skip that trade.

questions.prompt: Why is the plan versioned?

options.text: So you can go back to an older version whenever a new one has a losing week or two
options.explanation: No: judging a version by a week or two of results is chasing outcomes. Changes belong between sessions, recorded so you can compare how each version was followed.

options.text: So each change is recorded and you can compare how each version was followed
options.explanation: Right: versions let you learn from changes instead of drifting.

questions.prompt: You sell GBP/USD at market. Bid 1.27000, ask 1.27015. Which price do you get, assuming no slippage?

options.explanation: Right: market sells fill at the bid.
No: that is the ask, where buys fill.

questions.prompt: EUR/USD bid is 1.08000. You want to sell if price rises to 1.08400. Which order?

options.text: Sell stop at 1.08400, above the price
options.explanation: No: a sell stop goes below the current price. A sell order placed above the price is a sell limit.

options.text: Sell limit at 1.08400
options.explanation: Right: a sell limit sits above the current price.

options.text: Buy limit at 1.08400
options.explanation: No: that would open a buy, and a buy limit sits below the price.

questions.prompt: You hold a buy trade with a take profit at 1.10500. Which price must reach 1.10500 to close it?

options.text: The bid
options.explanation: Right: a buy is closed by selling, at the bid.

options.text: The ask
options.explanation: No: the ask closes sell trades.

options.text: The mid price
options.explanation: No: trades close at the bid or the ask, not halfway between. A buy closes by selling, at the bid.

questions.prompt: Sell 0.10 lot EUR/USD (pip value 1 USD) at 1.10000, stop loss 1.10300. The market gaps and the stop fills at 1.10450. What is the loss?

options.text: 30 USD
options.explanation: No: that is the planned loss. The gap made the fill worse.

options.text: 45 USD
4.50 USD
options.explanation: No: 0.00450 is 45 pips, not 4.5.

questions.prompt: Which kind of stop promises to close at exactly its level?

options.text: Any stop loss, as long as it was set before entry
options.explanation: No: when to set it does not matter here. A normal stop becomes a market order and can slip, especially in gaps.

options.text: A guaranteed stop, if your broker offers one
options.explanation: Right: only a guaranteed stop promises the level, and it usually costs extra.

options.text: A stop placed far from the price
options.explanation: No: distance does not stop a gap from jumping past it.

quizzes.title: Checkpoint: pips, lots, leverage and margin

questions.prompt: USD/JPY moves from 151.30 to 150.80. How many pips is that?

options.text: 50 pips
options.explanation: Right: the move is 0.50, and on a yen pair 0.50 ÷ 0.01 = 50 pips.

options.text: 5 pips
options.explanation: No: 5 pips on a yen pair would be 0.05.

options.text: 5,000 pips
options.explanation: No: that uses 0.0001 as the pip, which is wrong for yen pairs.

questions.prompt: EUR/USD, 0.30 lot with a 100,000-unit contract, account in USD. What is one pip worth?

options.text: 0.30 USD
options.explanation: No: that would be 3,000 units, which is 0.03 lot.

options.text: 3 USD
30 USD
options.explanation: No: that would be 3.00 lots.

questions.prompt: EUR/USD at 1.2000, 0.10 lot (10,000 EUR), leverage 1:30, account in USD. What margin is required?

options.explanation: No: that forgets to convert 10,000 EUR into USD first.

options.text: 400 USD

options.explanation: No: that is the full trade value, before leverage.

questions.prompt: Balance 1,500 USD, open loss 300 USD, used margin 600 USD. What is the margin level?

options.explanation: No: that uses the balance. Margin level uses equity, which includes the open loss.
No: that divides margin by equity, which is the wrong way round.

questions.prompt: Which statements are true? Choose all that apply.

options.text: Leverage magnifies losses as well as gains
options.explanation: True: profit and loss come from the full trade size.

options.text: Swaps can be positive or negative and vary by broker
options.explanation: True: check your broker's contract specification.

options.text: Stop-out levels are the same at every broker
options.explanation: False: each broker sets its own margin call and stop-out levels.

questions.prompt: Example rule: risk 1% of the current balance. Your balance is 12,000 USD. How much do you risk?

options.text: 120 USD
12 USD
options.explanation: No: that is 0.1%.
No: that is 10%.

questions.prompt: Example risk 120 USD. Stop 60 pips. Pip value 10 USD per 1.00 lot. What size keeps the risk at 120 USD?

options.text: 0.20 lot
options.explanation: Right: risk per lot = 60 × 10 = 600 USD, and 120 ÷ 600 = 0.20 lot.

options.text: 2.00 lots
options.explanation: No: that would risk 1,200 USD.

options.text: 0.12 lot
options.explanation: No: that would risk 0.12 × 600 = 72 USD.

questions.prompt: A plan uses 1.5:1 reward to risk. What win rate does it need to break even, before costs?

options.explanation: No: that is the loss rate at break-even.
No: that is the break-even win rate for 2:1.

questions.prompt: Example inputs: win rate 35%, average win 2.5R, average loss 1R. What is the expectancy per trade?

options.explanation: Right: 0.35 × 2.5 − 0.65 × 1 = 0.875 − 0.65 = 0.225R. It is arithmetic on example inputs, not a promise.
No: you must subtract the losses, 0.65 × 1.
No: the wins outweigh the losses with these inputs.

questions.prompt: Your example account is 25% below its peak. What gain gets it back to the peak?

options.text: 25%, the same as the fall
options.explanation: No: the gain is measured on a smaller balance.

options.text: About 33.3%

options.explanation: No: 50% would be needed after a 33.3% drawdown.

questions.prompt: You followed your plan and lost 5 trades in a row. Which response fits sound risk management?

options.text: Raise the risk on the next few trades so one good win recovers the losses faster
options.explanation: No: bigger size after losses deepens drawdowns and raises the risk of ruin.

options.text: Keep or lower the risk, pause, and review the trades against the plan
options.explanation: Right: losing streaks are normal even for a sound plan.

options.text: Stop using stop losses until you win again
options.explanation: No: that removes the limit on each loss.

questions.prompt: What makes a strategy rules-based?

options.text: Entry, exit, stop and size are defined exactly
options.explanation: Right: then anyone applying it to the same chart makes the same trades.

options.text: It uses at least one indicator
options.explanation: No: an indicator can still be read by feel.

options.text: It has made money in a backtest before
options.explanation: No: results say nothing about whether the rules are exact.

questions.prompt: Average 1.3500 now, 1.3420 ten candles ago; latest close 1.3460. What do the simplified trend rules allow?

options.text: A long, because the average is rising
options.explanation: No: a long also needs a close above the average, and 1.3460 is below 1.3500.

options.text: No entry: below a rising average
options.explanation: Right: a long needs a close above a rising average; a short needs a close below a falling one. Neither holds.

options.text: A short, because the close is below the average
options.explanation: No: a short also needs a falling average, and this one rose from 1.3420.

questions.prompt: A long fills at 1.0850 with ATR 0.0025. Where is a 2 × ATR stop?

options.text: 1.0825, one ATR below
options.explanation: No: that is 1 × ATR. The rule uses 2 × 0.0025 = 0.0050.

options.text: 1.0900, above the entry
options.explanation: No: a long's stop is below the entry.

questions.prompt: Previous 20 candles' high 1.2740, low 1.2610. Today's high is 1.2755 but it closes at 1.2735. Is there a long signal?

options.text: No: the close is inside the channel
options.explanation: Right: the rules use closes, and 1.2735 is below 1.2740.

options.text: Yes: the high went above 1.2740
options.explanation: No: an intraday spike that closes inside the channel is not a signal.

options.text: Yes, if volume was high
options.explanation: No: these simplified rules have no volume condition; the close decides.

questions.prompt: You compared 8 lookbacks on the same years and kept the best. What should you do next?

options.text: Use it at once, as it was the best
options.explanation: No: the best of several settings on one data set usually flatters the result.

options.text: Test it on data you did not use to choose it
options.explanation: Right: an out-of-sample check shows how much of the result was fitted to noise.

options.text: Keep adjusting it until every year is positive
options.explanation: No: tuning until everything looks good is overfitting.

questions.prompt: Why does this module teach generic versions rather than named traders' systems?

options.text: Named systems are known to have stopped working
options.explanation: No: the module makes no claim about how any named system performs.

options.text: Generic versions are proven to work better
options.explanation: No: nothing here is proven to work; the versions are for learning and testing.

options.text: Named versions need a person to check their sources first
options.explanation: Right: attributions, rules and results for named traders are added only after human review against reliable sources.

quizzes.title: Checkpoint: scams, brokers and your progress review

questions.prompt: A fictional "account manager" asks for your MetaTrader login to "help". What do you do?

options.text: Share it if it is only a demo account
options.explanation: No: never share MetaTrader logins with anyone.

options.text: Refuse and stop contact
options.explanation: Right: no genuine helper needs your login.

questions.prompt: Which is a red flag?

options.text: "Returns guaranteed, 8% every week"
options.explanation: Right: no one can guarantee trading returns.

options.text: "Trading carries a risk of loss"
options.explanation: No: that is an honest warning.

questions.prompt: You lost money to a fake platform. Someone offers to recover it for an upfront fee. What do you do?

options.text: Pay the fee, since getting most of the money back is worth a small cost
options.explanation: No: never pay to recover money. This is a recovery scam.

options.text: Refuse and report the loss through official channels
options.explanation: Right: an upfront recovery fee is a second scam.

questions.prompt: How should you check a broker's regulation?

options.text: Trust the licence number and regulator logo shown on the broker's own website
options.explanation: No: numbers and logos can be copied.

options.text: Search the regulator's official register yourself and match every detail
options.explanation: Right: the official register, reached by you and not through a link you were sent, is the check that counts.

options.text: Ask a signal group if it is safe
options.explanation: No: chat groups are not a reliable source.

questions.prompt: A chat suddenly fills with hype about a tiny coin "about to explode". What might this be?

options.text: A pump-and-dump
options.explanation: Right: hype to push the price up so the promoters can sell.

options.text: A safe bet
options.explanation: No: sudden hype about a small asset is a warning sign.

questions.prompt: What does the Practice Progress Review give you?

options.text: A "ready to trade" badge once you pass every checkpoint and your demo trades make a profit
options.explanation: No: it shows no "ready" badge, never uses profit, and is never a readiness verdict.

options.text: What you have studied and practised, and which gaps remain, with links to practise them
options.explanation: Right: it is a learning assessment, with no pass or fail.

quizzes.title: Checkpoint: futures contracts, margin and expiry

questions.prompt: Fictional contract: tick size 0.1, tick value 1 USD. You sell 2 contracts at 250.0 and buy them back at 248.5. What is the result?

options.text: A 15 USD gain
options.explanation: No: that is 15 ticks × 1 USD for one contract. You hold 2.

options.text: A 30 USD gain
options.explanation: Right: 1.5 ÷ 0.1 = 15 ticks in your favour, and 15 × 1 USD × 2 = 30 USD.

options.text: A 30 USD loss
options.explanation: No: you sold first and price fell, so the move was in your favour.

options.text: A 3 USD gain
options.explanation: No: that multiplies the 1.5-point move by 2 contracts without converting to ticks and money.

questions.prompt: Fictional contract: 25 USD per point, maintenance margin 2,500 USD. Balance 4,000 USD. You sell 1 contract at 1,200.0. At what price does a margin call start?

options.explanation: No: a short loses when price rises, so the margin-call price is above the entry.
No: that uses the maintenance margin alone, 2,500 ÷ 25 = 100 points. Use the balance above maintenance.
No: that is where the whole 4,000 USD balance is gone, 4,000 ÷ 25 = 160 points.

questions.prompt: Fictional contract: multiplier 50 USD per point, price 2,000, initial margin 5,000 USD. What leverage does 1 contract carry?

options.text: 20 times
50 times
options.explanation: No: 50 is the multiplier, not the leverage.

options.text: 2.5 times
options.explanation: No: that divides the margin by the price. Leverage = notional ÷ initial margin.

questions.prompt: A fictional futures curve is in backwardation. What does that mean?

options.text: Later months are priced higher than nearer ones
options.explanation: No: that is contango.

options.text: Spot prices may fall to meet the later months
options.explanation: No: the curve's shape is not a forecast of spot prices.

options.text: Later months are priced lower than nearer ones
options.explanation: Right: in backwardation the curve slopes down into later months.

questions.prompt: You hold a bought contract that is physically settled (fictional), and you only want price exposure. What should your plan include?

options.text: Hold to expiry, since every future settles in cash
options.explanation: No: settlement differs by contract. This one is physically settled.

options.text: You must close or roll before the last day in the spec
options.explanation: Right: the specification sets the dates, and acting before them avoids the delivery process.

options.text: Nothing, since delivery rules only affect sellers
options.explanation: No: with physical settlement, a buyer who holds on can be required to take delivery.

questions.prompt: A fictional contract needs 3,000 USD initial margin. What is the most you could lose on 1 bought contract?

options.text: There is no fixed limit, and it can exceed 3,000 USD
options.explanation: Right: the loss depends on how far price moves against the full notional value, and can exceed the margin and the account.

options.text: Exactly 3,000 USD, since margin caps the loss
options.explanation: No: margin is a deposit, not a limit on losses.

options.text: Only the gap between initial and maintenance margin
options.explanation: No: falling below maintenance brings a margin call, but losses can keep growing.

questions.prompt: Bought with your own cash, which of these makes you a part-owner of a company?

options.text: An ordinary share
options.explanation: Right: a share is a small piece of ownership in a company.

options.text: A forex position
options.explanation: No: a retail forex position is a contract on an exchange rate, not part of a company.

options.text: An index future
options.explanation: No: a future is a contract on a price, not ownership of any company.

questions.prompt: Illustrative: 0.10 lot EUR/USD (10,000 EUR) at 1.2000, account in USD, leverage 1:30. What does a 1% move against you cost?

options.text: 12 USD
options.explanation: No: that is 1% of 1,200, not of the 12,000 USD trade value.

options.text: 400 USD
options.explanation: No: that is the margin, 12,000 ÷ 30, not the loss.

options.text: 120 USD
options.explanation: Right: 10,000 × 1.2000 = 12,000 USD, and 1% of that is 120 USD, which is 30% of the 400 USD margin.
No: that would be a 10% move.

questions.prompt: Which statement about trading hours is most accurate?

options.text: They depend on the venue, and activity varies within them
options.explanation: Right: hours are set by the exchange or broker, and liquidity rises and falls within them.

options.text: Every one of the five markets trades all day, every day
options.explanation: No: most have closures, and some have long breaks.

options.text: All five markets open and close at exactly the same times
options.explanation: No: hours differ between markets, exchanges and products.

questions.prompt: A fictional stock shows bid 1.00 USD and ask 1.04 USD. You buy 1,000 shares and sell straight away. Ignoring commission, what does the round trip cost?

options.text: 4 USD
options.explanation: No: the spread is 0.04 USD on each of 1,000 shares.
No: that is what you paid, not what you lost.

options.text: 0.04 USD
options.explanation: No: that is the spread on one share only.

options.text: 40 USD
options.explanation: Right: (1.04 − 1.00) × 1,000 = 40 USD, before price moves at all.

questions.prompt: A friend says: 'Penny stocks are a cheap way to start.' What is the best reply?

options.text: True: a low share price means low risk
options.explanation: No: price per share says nothing about risk.

options.text: Low price is never the same as low risk or cost
options.explanation: Right: thin trading and wide spreads can make them costly and hard to exit.

options.text: True, as long as you buy a lot of shares to spread it out
options.explanation: No: buying more of one thinly traded stock adds to the risk instead of spreading it.

questions.prompt: Which is the best reason to choose a market to study first?

options.text: It is the market most talked about online this month
options.explanation: No: popularity says nothing about whether it fits your time, account or risk.

options.text: A stranger posted a big profit from it online
options.explanation: No: one claimed result is not evidence, and may not be true.

options.text: Its hours and smallest trade size fit your time and risk
options.explanation: Right: fit with your schedule and your risk per trade is a sound starting point.

questions.prompt: What does the buyer of a call option hold?

options.text: The duty to buy the underlying at the strike
options.explanation: No: the buyer has a right, not a duty. The seller carries the obligation.

options.text: The right to buy the underlying at the strike, until or at expiry
options.explanation: Right: a call is a right to buy at the strike; the buyer can choose not to use it.

options.text: The right to sell the underlying at the strike
options.explanation: No: that is a put.

questions.prompt: Fictional: you buy 2 puts, strike 25.00, premium 1.00 USD per unit, 100 units per contract. At expiry the price is 22.00. What is your profit or loss?

options.text: A 600 USD gain
options.explanation: No: that is the value at expiry, 3.00 × 100 × 2. Take away the 200 USD premium paid.

options.text: A 200 USD gain
options.explanation: No: that is the result for one contract. You bought 2.

options.text: A 400 USD gain
A 400 USD loss
options.explanation: No: the price fell below the strike, which helps a put buyer.

questions.prompt: Fictional: you buy a call, strike 80.00, premium 3.50 USD per unit. What is the breakeven price at expiry?

options.explanation: Right: call breakeven = strike + premium = 80.00 + 3.50.
No: that is the put formula, strike − premium.
No: at the strike the call is worth nothing and the premium is lost.

questions.prompt: Fictional: you buy 3 calls at a premium of 0.70 USD per unit, 100 units per contract. What is the most you can lose, fees aside?

options.text: 70 USD
options.explanation: No: that is the premium for one contract. You bought 3.

options.text: 210 USD
options.explanation: Right: 0.70 × 100 × 3 = 210 USD, the whole premium paid.

options.text: There is no fixed limit
options.explanation: No: a bought option can lose at most its premium.

questions.prompt: You sell a call without owning the units it covers. Which statement is true?

options.text: The most you can lose is the premium received
options.explanation: No: the premium is the most you can make.

options.text: The loss is capped at the strike × units
options.explanation: No: that is close to a sold put's worst case, not a sold call's.

options.text: The loss has no fixed limit, because the price can keep rising
options.explanation: Right: an uncovered sold call loses more for every rise above strike + premium.

questions.prompt: Fictional: you sell 1 put, strike 45.00, premium 2.00 USD per unit, 100 units per contract. At expiry the price is 41.00. What is your profit or loss?

options.text: A 200 USD gain
options.explanation: No: you keep the premium only if the put expires worthless. It ended 4.00 in the money.

options.text: A 400 USD loss
options.explanation: No: that forgets the 200 USD premium you received.

options.text: A 4,300 USD loss
options.explanation: No: that is the worst case if the price fell to 0, (45.00 − 2.00) × 100.

options.text: A 200 USD loss
options.explanation: Right: the put is worth 4.00, so −(4.00 − 2.00) × 100 = −200 USD.

questions.prompt: Fictional: share at 62.00. A call with strike 60.00 is quoted at 3.10 USD per unit. What are its intrinsic value and time value?

options.text: Intrinsic 2.00, time value 1.10
Intrinsic 3.10, time value 0
options.explanation: No: the whole premium is intrinsic only at expiry.

options.text: Intrinsic 0, time value 3.10
options.explanation: No: the price is above the strike, so the call is in the money.

questions.prompt: If nothing else changes, what tends to happen to an option's time value as expiry gets closer?

options.text: It grows
options.explanation: No: less time left means less chance of a further move.

options.text: It shrinks, and is zero at expiry
options.explanation: Right: that is time decay. At expiry only intrinsic value remains.

options.text: It stays the same until the last day
options.explanation: No: time value tends to shrink over the option's life, not all at once.

questions.prompt: Implied volatility for an option rises while the underlying price stays the same. What usually happens to the premium?

options.text: It usually rises
options.explanation: Right: bigger expected swings make a large move more likely, so premiums are usually higher.

options.text: It falls to its intrinsic value
options.explanation: No: only expiry removes all time value.

options.text: Nothing: only the underlying price matters
options.explanation: No: before expiry, expected volatility and time left also affect the premium.

questions.prompt: Before studying a real option, which set of items should you read in its specification?

options.text: Last month's return and the most popular strike
options.explanation: No: neither is part of the contract's specification.

options.text: The premium only
options.explanation: No: the premium alone does not tell you what the contract covers or how it ends.

options.text: Underlying, units per contract, call or put, strike, expiry date, exercise style and settlement
options.explanation: Right: these define what one contract is and how it ends. Check the exact contract each time.

questions.prompt: Fictional Company X: 0.05 USD a share, 1,000 million shares. Fictional Company Y: 20 USD a share, 2 million shares. Which is bigger by market value?

options.text: Company Y, because its share price is 400 times higher
options.explanation: No: Y is 20 × 2 million = 40 million USD. Share price alone does not show size.

options.text: Company X, at 50 million USD
options.explanation: Right: 0.05 × 1,000 million = 50 million USD, against 40 million USD for Y.

options.text: They are the same size by market value
options.explanation: No: 50 million USD and 40 million USD are different.

questions.prompt: Simulated penny stock: bid 0.18, ask 0.20. You buy 10,000 shares and sell at once. What do you lose to the spread?

options.text: 20 USD

options.explanation: No: that is what you get back when you sell, 10,000 × 0.18.
No: that is what you paid, 10,000 × 0.20.

options.text: 200 USD

questions.prompt: A fictional company went from 80 million to 200 million shares in two years, then did a 1-for-10 reverse split. What is the most reasonable reading?

options.text: Repeated dilution plus a reverse split: check cash and financing first
options.explanation: Right: this pattern is a common warning sign that a company keeps funding itself by issuing shares.

options.text: The reverse split made holders 10 times richer
options.explanation: No: the share count fell by the same factor, so holders gained nothing from the split itself.

options.text: Holders lost 90% of their value, as they now hold a tenth of the shares
options.explanation: No: each share is now priced about 10 times higher, so the split itself leaves the value of the holding unchanged.

questions.prompt: Which group of signs most strongly suggests a possible pump and dump?

options.text: Paid promotion, no revenue, and insiders selling during the hype
options.explanation: Right: together these suggest the people behind the hype may be selling to new buyers.

options.text: Steady small revenue, on-time reports and very little daily trading
options.explanation: No: this describes a quiet, illiquid share. Liquidity is a risk, but this is not a pump pattern.

options.text: A share that trades over the counter and has a website
options.explanation: No: neither of these is a red flag on its own.

questions.prompt: You bought 3,000 shares at 0.50 with a stop at 0.45. The share is halted, then reopens at 0.30. Roughly what is the loss?

options.text: 150 USD, the planned loss
options.explanation: No: (0.50 − 0.45) × 3,000 = 150 is the plan. The stop could not fill during the halt.

options.text: About 600 USD, four times the plan
options.explanation: Right: (0.50 − 0.30) × 3,000 = 0.20 × 3,000 = 600 USD, four times the plan, and possibly worse in a thin market.

options.text: Nothing; a halt cancels trades
options.explanation: No: a halt pauses trading. Your position stays open.

questions.prompt: A small, honest-looking company files on time and has steady revenue, but trades only 5,000 shares a day. You want to buy 20,000. What is the best approach?

options.text: Buy all 20,000 at market, since the business looks sound
options.explanation: No: a sound business does not fix liquidity. Your order is 4 days of normal volume.

options.text: Treat it as a likely scam and report it to the regulator
options.explanation: No: nothing here suggests fraud. Not every small share is a scam.

options.text: Go much smaller, use limit orders, or stay out
options.explanation: Right: 20,000 ÷ 5,000 = 4 days of volume. Size down to what you could exit, or stay out.

questions.prompt: A fictional company has 80 million shares at 2.50 USD. What is its market cap?

options.text: 32 million USD
options.explanation: No: that divides 80 by 2.50.

options.text: 200 million USD
options.explanation: Right: 2.50 × 80 million = 200 million USD.

options.text: 82.5 million USD
options.explanation: No: the price and shares are multiplied, not added.

questions.prompt: You own 5,000 of a company's 10 million shares. Then it issues 10 million new shares. What is your stake now?

options.text: 0.05%, unchanged
options.explanation: No: there are now 20 million shares, so your slice is smaller.

options.text: 0.1%, it doubled
options.explanation: No: you have the same shares out of a larger total.

options.text: 0.025%, it halved

questions.prompt: Share A trades 3 million shares a day; Share B trades 15,000. Which statement fits?

options.text: A 10,000-share order is harder to fill in B
options.explanation: Right: it is two thirds of B's daily volume but a tiny part of A's.

options.text: B has more liquidity, because fewer people own it
options.explanation: No: less trading usually means less liquidity.

options.text: Volume makes no difference to filling orders
options.explanation: No: thin volume can mean wider spreads and worse fills.

questions.prompt: Dividend 0.60 USD per share, EPS 0.80 USD, price 12.00 USD. What are the yield and the payout ratio?

options.text: Yield 6.7%, payout 133%
options.explanation: No: that uses EPS instead of the dividend for the yield (0.80 ÷ 12.00), and turns the payout ratio upside down (0.80 ÷ 0.60).

options.text: Yield 5%, payout 75%
Yield 7.5%, payout 5%
options.explanation: No: these mix up the two formulas.

questions.prompt: A company reports profit up 8%. Buyers expected up 15%. Which is true?

options.text: The price must rise because profit grew
options.explanation: No: the price reacts to results compared with expectations.

options.text: The report has no effect on the price
options.explanation: No: prices often move sharply around reports.

options.text: The price may fall on the miss
options.explanation: Right: a miss against expectations can push the price down.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of style and main risk is right?

options.text: Value: the firm may be cheap for a reason
options.explanation: Right: a low price can reflect a shrinking business.

options.text: Growth: the dividend may turn out too high
options.explanation: No: the main growth risk is that growth slows while the price assumes it will not.

options.text: Long-term: no exit plan is needed at all
options.explanation: No: long-term investors still need to know what would make them sell.

questions.prompt: Revenue 500, cost of sales 300, operating expenses 120, interest 10, tax 20 (fictional, millions USD). What is net income?

options.explanation: No: that is operating profit, before interest and tax.
No: that is gross profit.

questions.prompt: Net income 50 million USD, 25 million shares, price 30 USD. What is the P/E?

options.explanation: No: that divides the price by total profit, not by EPS.
No: that multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.prompt: Debt 300, cash 80, operating profit 50, equity 200 (fictional). What are net debt and return on capital?

options.text: Net debt 380; return on capital 25%
options.explanation: No: net debt subtracts cash, and return on capital uses debt plus equity.

options.text: Net debt 220; return on capital 10%
Net debt 220; return on capital 17%
options.explanation: No: return on capital uses debt plus equity, 500, not debt alone.

questions.prompt: Net income has grown for three years, while operating cash flow fell close to zero. Which is the best reading?

options.text: Profit is not becoming cash; find out why
options.explanation: Right: this is a warning sign to investigate, with several possible causes.

options.text: Cash flow does not matter if profit grows
options.explanation: No: profit is an accounting figure; cash is what was collected.

options.text: The company is certain to fail soon
options.explanation: No: the figures raise questions; they do not prove an outcome.

questions.prompt: A fictional firm has steady margins and a high return on capital, but trades on a P/E of 70. Which is true?

options.text: A strong business is a good buy at any price
options.explanation: No: the price can assume more than the business delivers.

options.text: A high P/E proves the business is weak
options.explanation: No: a high P/E reflects expectations, not weakness.

options.text: The price assumes a lot of future growth
options.explanation: Right: if growth falls short, the price can drop while the business stays strong.

questions.prompt: A fictional firm has a P/E of 4 and a dividend yield of 15%. Revenue has fallen for three years and the dividend was just cut. What fits?

options.text: It is clearly a bargain at this price
options.explanation: No: low ratios can reflect a shrinking business; it may be cheap for a reason.

options.text: It may be cheap for a reason
options.explanation: Right: falling revenue and a dividend cut explain why buyers pay so little.

options.text: The 15% yield will be paid
options.explanation: No: the yield uses past payments, and this dividend was just cut.

quizzes.title: Checkpoint: regimes, sizing and honest testing

questions.prompt: Stock at 30.00, ATR 14 = 0.75, stop = 2 × ATR. You risk 150 USD. How many shares?

options.text: 200 shares
options.explanation: No: that uses a 1 × ATR stop of 0.75. The stop is 1.50.

options.text: 100 shares
50 shares
options.explanation: No: that would need a 3.00 stop, which is 4 × ATR.

questions.prompt: Rule: trending if net move over 20 candles ≥ 3 × ATR; low volatility if ATR ≤ 0.75 × its 100-candle average. Net move 40 pips, ATR 20 pips, average ATR 30 pips. Label?

options.text: Trending, low volatility
options.explanation: No: 40 ÷ 20 = 2 ATR, below the 3 ATR needed for a trend.

options.text: Ranging, normal volatility
options.explanation: No: 20 ÷ 30 ≈ 0.67, which is 0.75 or less, so low volatility.

options.text: Ranging, low volatility
options.explanation: Right: 2 ATR is below 3, and 20 ÷ 30 ≈ 0.67 is at most 0.75.

questions.prompt: 10 trades: one of +6R and nine of −1R. What is the average result per trade?

options.explanation: Right: 6 − 9 = −3R in total, and −3R ÷ 10 = −0.3R.
No: that leaves out the nine losses.
No: −1R is the median, the middle trade. The average is −3R ÷ 10.

questions.prompt: A plan needs RSI above 50, MACD above zero and price above SMA 20. What is a fair description?

options.text: Three separate confirmations that add up
options.explanation: No: all three come from recent closes, so they often agree for the same reason.

options.text: Closely linked readings of recent direction
options.explanation: Right: correlated indicators largely repeat one message.

options.text: A filter set that removes false signals
options.explanation: No: no combination of indicators removes false signals.

questions.prompt: In a walk-forward test, why judge only the joined test blocks?

options.text: They contain more trades than tuning blocks
options.explanation: No: they often contain fewer. The point is what the rules had seen.

options.text: They remove the need for a demo forward test
options.explanation: No: a forward test on a demo account is still the next step.

options.text: The rules never saw those candles in tuning
options.explanation: Right: the rules had not seen those candles when they were set.

questions.prompt: Which set of results is least likely to be fragile?

options.text: +4R, +5R, +4R at average lengths 18, 20, 22
options.explanation: Right: neighbouring settings agree, so the result does not hinge on one number.

options.text: −3R, +14R, −2R at average lengths 18, 20, 22
options.explanation: No: a lone peak with losing neighbours is a sign of overfitting.

options.text: +14R at length 20, nothing else tested
options.explanation: No: without neighbours you cannot see how sensitive it is.

questions.prompt: Average volume is 120,000 contracts. Today 300,000 trade. What is the relative volume?

options.text: 180,000 more, so 1.8 times
0.4 times the average
options.explanation: No: that is average ÷ today. Divide today by the average.

options.text: 2.5 times the average

questions.prompt: Swing low 80.00, swing high 100.00. Where is the 61.8% retracement?

options.explanation: No: that is the 38.2% level: 100.00 − 7.64.
No: 61.8% is a share of the move, not a price.

questions.prompt: Downtrend; the last lower high is 1.3400. Price rallies to 1.3350 and turns down. Is the downtrend structure intact?

options.text: No: any rally ends a downtrend
options.explanation: No: rallies within a downtrend are normal. The question is whether one breaks the last lower high.

options.text: Yes: price stayed below 1.3400
options.explanation: Right: 1.3350 is below 1.3400, so this is a pullback so far.

options.text: No: 1.3350 marks the reversal
options.explanation: No: nothing broke. A reversal needs the structure to break first.

questions.prompt: Stock A falls from 80 to 76. Its index falls from 2,000 to 1,800. What is true?

options.text: A outperformed, so A went up
options.explanation: No: A fell 5%. It just fell less than the index.

options.text: The ratio fell because both prices fell
options.explanation: No: 76 ÷ 1,800 is higher than 80 ÷ 2,000, so the ratio rose.

options.text: A fell less, so the ratio rose
options.explanation: Right: A fell 5%, the index 10%.

questions.prompt: You bought 100 shares at 25.50 with a stop at 24.00. The stock closes at 25.00 and opens at 23.50. Roughly what is the loss?

options.text: 150 USD, as planned
options.explanation: No: the open is below the stop, so the stop fills near 23.50, not 24.00.

options.text: About 200 USD
options.explanation: Right: (25.50 − 23.50) × 100 = 200 USD, not the planned 150.

options.text: About 50 USD
options.explanation: No: 50 USD is only the extra loss from the gap: (24.00 − 23.50) × 100.

questions.prompt: Which pairs show a way these tools can mislead? Select all that apply.

options.text: Channel lines: redrawn after every candle
options.explanation: Right: lines that keep moving to fit price say nothing.

options.text: Volume: never, since it counts real trades
options.explanation: No: heavy-volume moves can fail, and forex tick volume is only a stand-in.

options.text: Fibonacci: near-misses look like hits
options.explanation: Right: with five levels close together, many turns land near one by chance.

lessons.title: Futures curves, storage and spreads: a first look

inOneLine.simple: A commodity has different prices for delivery at different dates. Lining them up gives a [[futures-curve|curve]]. Later dates priced higher is called [[contango]]; later dates priced lower is called [[backwardation]].
inOneLine.balanced: The shape of the curve reflects [[storage-cost|storage costs]], financing and how tight supply is right now. When near-term supply is plentiful, contango is common; when it is tight, buyers may pay more for near delivery, giving backwardation. The gap between two dates is a calendar spread. The futures module covers contracts in depth.

explain.simple: Many commodities trade through [[futures-contract|futures contracts]]: agreements to buy or sell a set amount at a set price on a future date. There is usually a separate price for each delivery month. Plot those prices from nearest to furthest and you get a futures curve. If the later months cost more, the curve slopes up. This is called contango, and one common reason is the cost of storing, insuring and financing the commodity until then. If the later months cost less, the curve slopes down. This is called backwardation, and it often shows that people want the commodity now, for example when supply is short. All prices here are fictional.
explain.balanced: The curve shape matters to anyone who holds a position over time. A contract converges towards the price for immediate delivery as it nears expiry. In contango, someone who keeps buying later, more expensive contracts and letting them run down towards a lower near price loses that gap each time if nothing else changes. In backwardation the effect works the other way. The difference between two delivery months is a calendar spread, and spreads can move even when the overall price level does not. This is an introduction: contract details, rolling and margin are covered in the futures module.

assumptions: Fictional commodity. Price for immediate delivery: 50.00 USD per unit
1-month contract: 50.40. 2-month: 50.80. 3-month: 51.20
Fictional storage, insurance and financing cost: 0.40 USD per unit per month
steps: The curve slopes up, so it is in contango. Here the step matches the 0.40 monthly carrying cost.
Calendar spread between 3-month and 1-month = 51.20 − 50.40 = 0.80 USD.

If you buy the 1-month contract at 50.40 and the immediate price is still 50.00 at expiry, the contract ends near 50.00: a loss of about 0.40 per unit, or 400 USD on 1,000 units, even though 'the price did not move'.

assumptions: Same fictional commodity, but after a supply disruption
Immediate: 50.00. 1-month: 49.20. 2-month: 48.50
steps: Each later month is cheaper: 49.20 < 50.00 and 48.50 < 49.20. The curve slopes down: backwardation.
Buyers are paying 50.00 − 49.20 = 0.80 more to get the commodity now rather than in a month.
This often signals that supply is tight today. It is a reading of the present, not a forecast that prices will fall.

lessons.explainSimpler: There is a price for now and a price for later. If later costs more, that's contango, often because storing things costs money. If now costs more, that's backwardation, often because people need it now.
lessons.commonMistake: Reading the curve as a forecast. A 3-month price above today's price does not mean the market predicts a rise. It mostly reflects storage, financing and current supply.

quickCheck.prompt: Fictional curve: immediate 80.00, 1-month 80.60, 2-month 81.20. What shape is this?

options.text: Backwardation, because later dates are cheaper
options.explanation: No: the later dates here are more expensive, not cheaper.

options.text: Flat, because the gaps are equal
options.explanation: No: equal steps up still make an upward slope.

options.text: Contango, because later dates cost more
options.explanation: Right: later months are priced higher, 80.00 → 80.60 → 81.20.

quickCheck.prompt: Same fictional curve: what is the 2-month minus 1-month calendar spread?

options.explanation: No: that is 2-month minus immediate, 81.20 − 80.00.
No: a spread subtracts the two prices; it does not add them.

quickCheck.prompt: A fictional curve is in steep backwardation. What does it most likely tell you?

options.text: Near delivery is valued more, often because supply is tight now
options.explanation: Right: buyers pay extra to get it now. It is a reading of today, not a forecast.

options.text: The market predicts the price will fall to the later levels
options.explanation: No: the curve shape is not a forecast of the future price.

options.text: Buyers may want later delivery more than delivery now
options.explanation: No: in backwardation the later months are cheaper, so buyers value near delivery more, not later.

doItNow.instructions: Draw two fictional futures curves with four points each: one in contango and one in backwardation. Label each point with a price. For each, work out the spread between the last and first contract, and write one sentence on what might cause that shape.

lessons.title: Inflation, interest rates and currency effects

inOneLine.simple: A commodity's price can change because of the money it is priced in, not just because of the commodity itself.
inOneLine.balanced: When a commodity is quoted in one currency, a change in that currency changes the cost for buyers who use other currencies. Higher [[interest-rate|interest rates]] raise the cost of holding something that pays no interest, like a metal in a vault. [[inflation|Inflation]] links are often talked about but are not reliable rules.

explain.simple: Many international commodity prices are quoted in a single currency. If that currency gets weaker, buyers who pay with another currency need less of their own money to buy the same amount, so demand from them may rise. If it gets stronger, the commodity costs them more. Interest rates matter too. Gold and silver pay no interest. If savings accounts pay more, holding metal means giving up more interest, which some traders see as a reason to hold less. All countries, currencies and numbers here are fictional.
explain.balanced: Traders often describe gold as a hedge against inflation or as a place people go in uncertain times. Treat these as possible tendencies, not rules: there can be long stretches when the link does not hold, and other forces such as rates, currency moves and positioning can dominate. Inflation can also push up commodity prices directly, because commodities are part of what goes into the inflation number. The direction of cause and effect is often unclear. Read every link here as a hypothesis to test, not a certainty.

assumptions: A fictional commodity quoted at 2,000 USD per unit, unchanged in USD
A buyer in fictional Westmark pays in WMK
Exchange rate moves from 1 USD = 1.50 WMK to 1 USD = 1.35 WMK
steps: Before: 2,000 × 1.50 = 3,000 WMK per unit.
After: 2,000 × 1.35 = 2,700 WMK per unit.
The USD price did not move, but the Westmark buyer now pays 300 WMK less, 10% cheaper.
Cheaper for buyers in other currencies can mean more demand, which is one reason a weaker quoting currency is sometimes linked to higher commodity prices. A tendency only.

assumptions: You hold 10,000 USD of a fictional metal that pays no interest
A fictional savings rate rises from 1% to 5% a year
steps: At 1%: interest given up by holding metal = 10,000 × 0.01 = 100 USD a year.
At 5%: interest given up = 10,000 × 0.05 = 500 USD a year.
The cost of holding the metal instead of cash rose by 400 USD a year.
Some holders may switch to cash, which can weigh on the price. Others may hold for different reasons, so the effect is not certain.

lessons.explainSimpler: Sometimes the commodity has not changed; the money has. And when cash pays more interest, holding a metal that pays nothing costs more.
lessons.commonMistake: Treating 'gold rises with inflation' or 'commodities rise when the dollar falls' as rules. They are tendencies that often fail, especially over shorter periods.

quickCheck.prompt: Fictional commodity: 50 USD per unit. The rate moves from 1 USD = 2.00 WMK to 1 USD = 2.20 WMK. What is the new WMK price?

options.text: 100 WMK
options.explanation: No: that is the old price, 50 × 2.00.

options.text: 110 WMK
options.explanation: Right: 50 × 2.20 = 110 WMK, so it costs Westmark buyers 10% more.
No: you multiply by the exchange rate, not add it.

quickCheck.prompt: Why might higher interest rates weigh on a metal that pays no interest?

options.text: Holding it means giving up more interest than before
options.explanation: Right: the opportunity cost of holding it rises. A tendency, not a rule.

options.text: Higher rates raise the metal's storage cost
options.explanation: No: rates do not change what a vault or insurance costs. The main effect is the interest you give up by holding the metal.

options.text: Holders pay interest on the metal they own
options.explanation: No: nobody charges interest for owning it. The cost is the interest you give up by not holding cash or bonds instead.

quickCheck.prompt: Which statement about inflation and commodities is most accurate?

options.text: Gold always rises whenever inflation goes up, without exception
options.explanation: No: the link is a tendency that can fail for long periods.

options.text: Inflation has no link to commodities
options.explanation: No: commodities feed into inflation and can be affected by it.

options.text: Links exist, but they are not reliable rules
options.explanation: Right: treat each link as a hypothesis, not a certainty.

doItNow.instructions: Work out by hand: take a fictional commodity at 1,500 USD per unit and work out its price in WMK at three exchange rates: 1.20, 1.40 and 1.60 WMK per USD. Then work out the yearly interest given up by holding 5,000 USD of a non-interest-paying metal at rates of 2% and 4%.

lessons.title: Seasons, weather, geopolitics and supply shocks

inOneLine.simple: Harvests, winters and political events change how much of a commodity is available. Prices react most when what happens differs from what was expected.
inOneLine.balanced: [[seasonality|Seasonal]] patterns are usually known in advance and often priced in. [[supply-shock|Supply shocks]] and [[geopolitical-risk|geopolitical]] events are not. Their effect depends on size, duration, spare supply and stored stock, and early price jumps can reverse once the picture clears.

explain.simple: Many crops are harvested once a year, so new supply arrives in a rush and then has to last until the next harvest. In places that heat homes with natural gas, demand usually rises in cold months. These patterns repeat, so traders expect them. What surprises the market is a harvest much smaller or bigger than expected, or a winter much colder or milder than normal. Supply can also be cut suddenly: a mine floods, a pipeline breaks, a port closes, or a conflict blocks a shipping route. All places, firms and figures in this lesson are fictional.
explain.balanced: A useful way to judge a disruption is to ask four questions. How big is it, as a share of total supply? How long will it last? Can other producers or stored stock fill the gap? What had the market already expected? A small, short outage when storage is full may barely matter. A large, open-ended one when storage is low can move prices a lot. Political events are especially uncertain: prices may rise on worry before any supply is lost, then fall back if the worry fades. Treat every story as a set of scenarios, not a price call.

assumptions: Fictional grain market in a fictional region, in million tonnes
Stock left from last year: 30. Expected harvest: 120. Expected use: 125
Then a drought cuts the harvest by 10%
steps: Expected supply = 30 + 120 = 150. Expected stock left at year end = 150 − 125 = 25.
Stock-to-use = 25 ÷ 125 = 20%.
With the drought, harvest = 120 × 0.90 = 108. Supply = 30 + 108 = 138.
Stock left at year end = 138 − 125 = 13, so stock-to-use = 13 ÷ 125 = 10.4%, about half the earlier cushion.
A thinner cushion can make prices more sensitive. Whether they rise depends on how much of the drought was already expected.

assumptions: Fictional region where natural gas heats homes
Typical use: 60 units a day in summer, 90 units a day in winter
steps: Winter use is 90 − 60 = 30 units a day higher.
30 ÷ 60 = 0.5, so winter use is 50% above summer use.
This pattern is known, so prices often reflect it before winter arrives.
What can move prices is a winter much colder or milder than forecasters expected.

lessons.explainSimpler: Everyone knows winter comes and harvests happen. Prices move when the winter or the harvest turns out different from what people guessed, or when something suddenly cuts supply.
lessons.commonMistake: Assuming a scary headline means prices must keep rising. Markets may have priced in the worry already, the disruption may be short, or other supply may fill the gap.

quickCheck.prompt: Fictional crop: stock 20, harvest 100, use 105 (million tonnes). What stock is left at year end?

options.text: 5 million tonnes
options.explanation: No: that leaves out the 20 already in stock.

options.text: 15 million tonnes
