options.explanation: Right: 20 + 100 − 105 = 15 million tonnes.

options.text: 25 million tonnes
options.explanation: No: that adds the 5 shortfall to the stock instead of taking it away: 20 − 5 = 15.

quickCheck.prompt: A fictional pipeline closes for a few days while storage is unusually full. What is a reasonable expectation?

options.text: Prices must rise strongly for weeks after any outage
options.explanation: No: a short outage with full storage may have only a small or brief effect.

options.text: Any effect is likely small or brief, since full storage covers the gap
options.explanation: Right: size, duration and stored stock all shape the reaction, which stays uncertain.

options.text: Prices may spike for months, since outages are rare
options.explanation: No: a few days of outage with full storage gives little reason for a long spike, rare or not.

quickCheck.prompt: Why does a normal seasonal rise in heating demand often move prices less than expected?

options.text: Seasonal demand does not affect commodity prices at all
options.explanation: No: it does affect them, but the effect is usually expected in advance.

options.text: Governments fix prices during winter
options.explanation: No: this is not a general rule, and it is not the reason here.

options.text: The market already knows the calendar and prices it in
options.explanation: Right: the surprise is a season that differs from what was expected.

doItNow.instructions: In Chart Lab, load the News shock scenario with the Volume pane on, then the High volatility scenario. For the News shock, mark the first jump and note whether price held, partly reversed or fully reversed. Write one sentence on how a supply disruption story could produce each of those three paths.

lessons.title: Supply, demand and inventory reports

inOneLine.simple: When more is produced than used, stored amounts rise. When less is produced than used, they fall. An [[inventory-report|inventory report]] shows which is happening.
inOneLine.balanced: Inventory change ≈ supply − demand over the period. A draw (fall) bigger than expected can suggest tighter supply; a surprise build the opposite. As with any release, the [[surprise]] against the [[consensus-forecast|consensus]] matters more than the headline, and the reaction is never certain.

explain.simple: Think of a giant tank. Production and imports pour in; factories, refineries and buyers take out. If more goes in than comes out, the level rises: that is a build. If more comes out, the level falls: that is a draw. Many commodities have regular reports on stored amounts. Before each report, forecasters publish what they expect. Prices often react to the gap between the actual change and the expected change, not to the change itself. All countries, reports and figures here are fictional.
explain.balanced: Supply comes from production, imports and stored stock; demand from use and exports. Production can take months or years to change, so short-term moves are often about stocks in storage. Reports have several parts, such as crude, fuel products and regional figures, and they can disagree. Traders may also have expected something different from the published consensus. So a big draw might lift prices, do nothing, or even be followed by a fall if it was already priced in. Treat each report as a scenario with several possible outcomes.

assumptions: Fictional country: Northland. Fictional weekly report on crude oil in storage
Supply into storage this week: 10.0 million barrels; taken out: 11.5 million
Consensus forecast: a draw of 0.5 million barrels
steps: Inventory change = 10.0 − 11.5 = −1.5 million barrels, a draw.
Surprise = actual − consensus = −1.5 − (−0.5) = −1.0 million barrels.
The draw was 1.0 million barrels bigger than expected, which hints at tighter supply.
Scenario thinking: price might rise, rise then fade, or barely move. Do not pick one as certain.

assumptions: Same fictional Northland report, a different week
Consensus: a draw of 0.5 million barrels
Actual: a build of 0.8 million barrels
steps: Surprise = +0.8 − (−0.5) = +1.3 million barrels.
More is in storage than expected, which hints at looser supply or weaker use.
Story 1: prices fall as traders see more supply than they thought.
Story 2: fuel stocks drew sharply in the same report, and that detail dominates. Prices hardly move.
Same headline surprise, different outcomes, depending on the details and on what was priced in.

lessons.explainSimpler: Watch the tank level and compare it with what people guessed. A bigger fall than guessed can mean tight supply, but the market may already have guessed right.
lessons.commonMistake: Reading a draw as 'bad' because a number fell. A draw means more was used than added, which points to tighter supply, not weaker demand. And the sign of the surprise matters more than the sign of the change.

quickCheck.prompt: Fictional report: consensus a build of 1.0 million barrels, actual a draw of 2.0 million. What is the surprise?

options.text: +3.0 million barrels
options.explanation: No: actual minus consensus is −2.0 − (+1.0), which is negative.

options.text: −1.0 million barrels
options.explanation: No: that adds the two numbers instead of subtracting.

options.text: −3.0 million barrels
options.explanation: Right: −2.0 − (+1.0) = −3.0 million barrels, a much tighter week than expected.

quickCheck.prompt: Stored amounts of a commodity fall more than expected. What is the most accurate reading?

options.text: Supply is likely tighter than thought, but the price reaction is not certain
options.explanation: Right: a tendency only. It may have been priced in, or other details may dominate.

options.text: Demand is weak, so the price will certainly fall this week
options.explanation: No: a draw means use exceeded supply, and no reaction is certain.

options.text: Supply may be looser than thought, so prices may slip
options.explanation: No: a bigger draw than expected points to tighter supply, not looser.

quickCheck.prompt: In one week, 8.0 units go into storage and 6.5 units come out. What happened?

options.text: A build of 1.5 units
options.explanation: Right: 8.0 − 6.5 = +1.5, so stored amounts rose.

options.text: A draw of 1.5 units
options.explanation: No: more went in than came out, so the level rose.

options.text: A build of 14.5 units
options.explanation: No: that adds the flows instead of subtracting them.

doItNow.instructions: Open the Fundamental Analysis Lab and work through the fictional weekly crude inventory scenario. Before you look at the reactions, write down the surprise and two different ways price could react. Then compare your list with the reactions in the scenario.

lessons.title: What commodities are: metals, energy and crops

inOneLine.simple: A [[commodity]] is a basic raw material, such as gold, silver, crude oil, natural gas or wheat. Each one has its own drivers, units and risks.
inOneLine.balanced: Commodities fall into broad groups: metals, energy and agriculture. They are priced per unit (an ounce, a barrel, a bushel and so on), and traders usually get exposure through [[futures-contract|futures contracts]], funds or CFDs rather than owning the physical goods.

explain.simple: Precious metals like gold and silver are used in jewellery and industry, and some people hold them as a store of value. Energy commodities like crude oil and natural gas power transport, industry and heating. Agricultural commodities like wheat, corn, coffee and sugar depend on growing seasons and weather. Because one barrel of oil is much like another, prices are driven mainly by how much is produced and how much is wanted. Each commodity is quoted in its own unit, and the size of a contract varies, so always check the unit before working out money. All prices in this lesson are simulated or fictional.
explain.balanced: Different commodities respond to different things. Energy prices are sensitive to production decisions, [[inventory-report|inventories]], [[seasonality|seasonal]] demand and [[geopolitical-risk|geopolitics]]. Crops respond to planting, weather and harvests. Precious metals are often linked by traders to [[interest-rate|interest rates]], [[inflation]] and currency moves. These links are tendencies, not rules. Commodities can be very [[volatility|volatile]], and the way you trade them matters: a futures contract has an expiry date, and a fund or CFD may have costs that ordinary shares do not. The futures module goes deeper into contracts.

assumptions: Simulated Practice commodity priced at 50.00 USD per unit
You buy 100 units in paper trading
Price later moves to 52.50 USD
steps: Price change = 52.50 − 50.00 = +2.50 USD per unit.
Profit = 2.50 × 100 = 250 USD (before costs).
If price had fallen 2.50 instead, the loss would be 2.50 × 100 = 250 USD.
The money result depends on the unit and the position size, so check both before every trade.

assumptions: Same simulated Practice commodity: bid 49.95, ask 50.05
You buy 200 units and sell straight away
steps: Spread = 50.05 − 49.95 = 0.10 USD per unit.
Cost of the round trip = 0.10 × 200 = 20 USD.
The price must rise 0.10 before this trade breaks even.
Spreads in some commodities can widen around reports and when trading is quiet, so this cost is not fixed.

lessons.explainSimpler: Commodities are the raw stuff the world runs on. Their prices mostly move on how much there is and how much people need.
lessons.commonMistake: Treating all commodities as one market. Gold, natural gas and coffee have very different drivers, units, seasons and volatility.

quickCheck.prompt: Simulated commodity: you buy 40 units at 120.00. It falls to 117.50. What is the result before costs?

options.text: −100 USD

options.explanation: No: that is the change per unit. Multiply by the 40 units.

options.text: +100 USD
options.explanation: No: the price fell, so a buyer loses.

quickCheck.prompt: Which pair belongs to the energy group?

options.text: Gold and silver
options.explanation: No: these are precious metals.

options.text: Wheat, corn and coffee beans
options.explanation: No: these are agricultural commodities.

options.text: Crude oil and natural gas
options.explanation: Right: both are energy commodities.

doItNow.instructions: In Paper trading, open the Practice commodity (prices are simulated). Write down its unit, bid, ask and spread. Work out what a 1.00 move would mean in money for a 50-unit position. Then place a small practice trade with a stop-loss and record why you chose that size.

lessons.title: Currencies and commodities: how they link

inOneLine.simple: A currency's value is pulled by interest rates, trade and mood. Commodity prices are pulled by supply and demand, and by the currency they are priced in. Each can affect the other.
inOneLine.balanced: Rate gaps between countries, trade flows and risk mood all feed currency valuation. For a [[commodity]], supply, demand and inventories matter, and a price set in one currency changes in local terms when exchange rates move. A country that exports a commodity can see its currency react to that commodity's price, as a tendency, not a rule.

explain.simple: Why would anyone want a country's currency? To buy its goods, to earn its interest rates, or to invest there. If a country sells a lot of one commodity abroad, buyers need its currency to pay, or the sellers bring the money home and swap it into local currency. So when that commodity's price falls, fewer foreign earnings may flow in, and the currency may weaken. It works the other way too: a commodity priced in one currency gets more expensive for buyers whose own currency weakens, even if the price on the screen has not changed.
explain.balanced: None of these links is fixed. A currency can rise on a rate surprise while its main export falls in price. Commodity prices respond to production, inventories, demand and storage, and to the currency they are quoted in. When you study a link, write it as a chain and test each step: commodity price → export earnings → demand for the currency. Any step can break. For how rates feed into currencies, see the lesson on interest rates and central banks. Westmark, WMK and its export are fictional.

assumptions: Fictional Westmark exports a fictional commodity, priced in USD
Hypothetical exports: 2 million units a year
Hypothetical price falls from 80 USD to 68 USD per unit
Volumes assumed unchanged to keep the steps clear
steps: Export earnings before = 2,000,000 × 80 = 160 million USD.
Export earnings after = 2,000,000 × 68 = 136 million USD.
Drop = 160 − 136 = 24 million USD, which is 24 ÷ 160 = 15%.
Fewer USD earnings to swap into WMK may mean less demand for WMK, so WMK may weaken.
It could also hold up, for example if Westmark's interest rates rise at the same time. Scenario, not forecast.

assumptions: A fictional commodity priced at 50 USD per unit, unchanged
Hypothetical exchange rate moves from 2.00 to 2.20 WMK per USD (WMK weakens)
steps: Cost in WMK before = 50 × 2.00 = 100 WMK.
Cost in WMK after = 50 × 2.20 = 110 WMK.
Change = (110 − 100) ÷ 100 = 10% more expensive for Westmark buyers, with no change in the USD price.
Higher local costs can feed into Westmark's inflation, which links back to central-bank policy.

lessons.explainSimpler: If a country sells lots of one thing abroad, its money can follow that thing's price. And when a currency weakens, things priced in other currencies get dearer for its people.
lessons.commonMistake: Treating a link as a law, for example 'commodity up, exporter's currency up' every time. Rates, risk mood and other news can easily outweigh it.

quickCheck.prompt: A fictional commodity costs 40 USD. The rate moves from 1.50 to 1.80 WMK per USD. How much more does it cost Westmark buyers?

options.text: 20% more
30% more
options.explanation: No: 0.30 is the change in the rate, not the percentage change in cost.

options.text: No change
options.explanation: No: the USD price is unchanged, but WMK buyers need more WMK to pay it.

quickCheck.prompt: Fictional: Westmark's main export falls in price, but Westmark raises rates by more than expected the same week. What could happen to WMK?

options.text: It must fall, because the export price fell
options.explanation: No: the rate surprise pulls the other way, so a fall is not certain.

options.text: The forces cancel out, so WMK may stay flat
options.explanation: No: the two forces need not be the same size, so nothing makes them cancel. Several reactions are plausible.

options.text: No clear call: the two forces pull opposite ways
options.explanation: Right: two forces pull in opposite directions, so several reactions are plausible.

doItNow.instructions: In the Fundamental Analysis Lab, open any Westmark macro scenario and write the chain of links from the release to WMK, one arrow at a time. Under each arrow, write one thing that could break that link.

lessons.homework: Make up a fictional country that exports one fictional commodity. Write two short scenarios: one where its currency follows the commodity price, and one where something else outweighs it.

lessons.title: Growth, jobs and inflation as a set

inOneLine.simple: Growth, jobs and inflation are three views of the same economy. Read them together, not one at a time.
inOneLine.balanced: [[gdp|GDP]] growth, the [[employment-report]] and [[inflation]] each tell part of the story. A central bank weighs them as a set, so markets do too. When they point the same way the picture is clearer; when they disagree, reactions are harder to read.

explain.simple: GDP measures how much an economy produces; its change is called growth. The employment report shows how many people have jobs and how many are looking. Inflation shows how fast prices are rising. You met jobs and inflation in the forex lessons on [[interest-rate|interest rates]] and on expected vs. actual. Here the point is to read them as a group. Strong growth, falling unemployment and rising inflation can all push the same way: towards higher rates. Weak growth with high inflation pulls in two directions at once.
explain.balanced: Each release has quirks. GDP comes out less often than jobs data and is often revised. Job numbers can be noisy month to month. Inflation can be driven by a few volatile prices. So one figure rarely changes the picture alone; a run of figures that agree carries more weight. A useful habit is a three-line summary after each release: growth up, flat or down; jobs stronger or weaker; inflation above, near or below target. Then ask what a [[central-bank]] facing that mix might do, and treat the answer as a scenario, not a forecast. Westmark and WMK are fictional.

assumptions: Fictional country: Westmark, currency WMK
Hypothetical output: 500.0 billion WMK last quarter, 503.0 billion WMK this quarter
Hypothetical unemployment: 4.8% last month, 4.5% this month
Hypothetical inflation 3.4%; central-bank target 2%
steps: Unemployment change = 4.5% − 4.8% = −0.3 points: fewer people looking for work.
Inflation gap = 3.4% − 2% = 1.4 points above target.
All three point the same way: a growing economy, a tight jobs market, prices rising fast.
Scenario: markets may expect rates to stay high or rise. If that was already expected, WMK may barely move. It is not a forecast.

assumptions: Fictional Westmark, the next quarter
Hypothetical output falls from 503.0 to 501.5 billion WMK
Hypothetical unemployment rises from 4.5% to 4.9%
Hypothetical inflation 3.8%; target 2%
steps: Unemployment change = 4.9% − 4.5% = +0.4 points: the jobs market weakened.
Inflation is 3.8% − 2% = 1.8 points above target, higher than before.
The set now disagrees: weak growth and jobs argue for lower rates, high inflation for higher ones.
Possible reactions run both ways. Scenario thinking: list what would make each one more likely, such as what the central bank says next.

lessons.explainSimpler: Ask three questions: is the economy growing, are jobs getting easier or harder to find, and are prices rising fast? If all three answers agree, the picture is clearer. If not, expect a messier reaction.
lessons.commonMistake: Reacting to one release alone, such as a single strong GDP figure, without checking jobs and inflation, or without noticing that the figure may be revised later.

quickCheck.prompt: Hypothetical output rises from 800 to 806 billion WMK in a quarter. What is the growth rate?

options.explanation: No: 6 is the change in billions. Divide it by the starting level, 800.
No: that is 6 ÷ 1,000. Divide by the starting level, 800.

quickCheck.prompt: Fictional data: output shrinking, unemployment rising, inflation well above target. What is most accurate?

options.text: The data clash: weak growth and jobs against high inflation
options.explanation: Right: weak growth and jobs pull one way, high inflation the other.

options.text: Rates must be cut, because growth is negative
options.explanation: No: high inflation argues against cuts, and nothing is certain.

options.text: Inflation may fall soon, so the bank can safely cut
options.explanation: No: nothing in the data says inflation will fall soon, so a cut is far from safe.

doItNow.instructions: Open the Fundamental Analysis Lab and choose the Westmark growth scenario. Before reading the reactions, write the three-line summary: growth, jobs, inflation. Then pick the reactions you think are plausible and compare your reasons with the explanations.

lessons.title: Central banks vs governments: policy and debt

inOneLine.simple: The central bank steers interest rates; the government decides spending, taxes and borrowing. Both affect the economy, and they do not always pull the same way.
inOneLine.balanced: [[monetary-policy|Monetary policy]] is set by the [[central-bank]], mainly through the policy [[interest-rate]]. [[fiscal-policy|Fiscal policy]] is the government's spending and taxes. Deficits add to [[government-debt]], and higher rates make that debt more costly to carry.

explain.simple: A central bank usually tries to keep inflation steady by raising or cutting interest rates, as you saw in the lesson on rates and central banks. A government decides how much to spend and how much to tax. When it spends more than it collects, it borrows the difference, and the total borrowed is government debt. People often compare debt with the size of the economy, GDP. Higher interest rates mean the government pays more on new borrowing, which can squeeze its budget over time.
explain.balanced: The two policies can work together or against each other. A central bank raising rates to cool inflation while the government cuts taxes to boost spending is a tug of war; markets then have to guess which force wins. Large or fast-rising debt can make lenders ask for higher interest, which can affect the currency and other markets, but there is no fixed level at which debt becomes 'too much', and reactions differ between countries and times. Read debt and deficit news as one input among many. All figures here are hypothetical and Westmark is fictional.

assumptions: Fictional Westmark, currency WMK
Hypothetical yearly GDP: 800 billion WMK
Hypothetical government debt: 480 billion WMK
Hypothetical yearly spending 340 billion WMK; tax and other revenue 310 billion WMK
steps: Deficit = 340 − 310 = 30 billion WMK, which is 30 ÷ 800 = 3.75% of GDP.
The deficit is borrowed, so debt next year ≈ 480 + 30 = 510 billion WMK.
Growth in the economy can slow the rise in the debt ratio even while the debt itself grows.

assumptions: Same hypothetical debt of 480 billion WMK, GDP 800 billion WMK
Hypothetical average interest rate on the debt: 2%
Simplification: all debt is refinanced at a new rate of 3%. In reality debt is refinanced bit by bit over years
steps: Interest cost at 2% = 480 × 0.02 = 9.6 billion WMK a year.
Interest cost at 3% = 480 × 0.03 = 14.4 billion WMK a year.
Extra cost = 14.4 − 9.6 = 4.8 billion WMK, which is 4.8 ÷ 800 = 0.6% of GDP.
So a central-bank decision on rates feeds into the government's budget. That link is why traders watch both.

lessons.explainSimpler: The central bank sets the price of borrowing. The government decides how much it spends and borrows. When rates go up, the government's borrowing costs more.
lessons.commonMistake: Mixing up the two: thinking the government sets interest rates, or that a central bank decides taxes. Another mistake is treating one debt or deficit number as a sure sign of a crisis or of a currency move.

quickCheck.prompt: Hypothetical: spending 220 billion, revenue 200 billion, GDP 500 billion. What is the deficit as a share of GDP?

options.explanation: No: 20 is the deficit in billions. Divide it by GDP, 500.
No: that divides the deficit by revenue, 200. Divide by GDP.

quickCheck.prompt: Which of these is fiscal policy?

options.text: The central bank raises its policy rate
options.explanation: No: that is monetary policy.

options.text: The government cuts income tax rates
options.explanation: Right: taxes and spending are fiscal policy.

options.text: A bank publishes its inflation target
options.explanation: No: an inflation target is part of monetary policy.

doItNow.instructions: Open the Fundamental Analysis Lab and choose the Westmark budget scenario. Work out the surprise in the deficit, read what was priced in, and mark which reactions are plausible. Write one sentence on how a central-bank rate rise and a bigger deficit could pull the currency in different directions.

lessons.title: Expectations: what was already priced in

inOneLine.simple: Prices move on what people expect before news arrives. When the news comes, what matters is how different it is from what was already in the price.
inOneLine.balanced: The [[surprise]] against the [[consensus-forecast]] is a start, but what was [[priced-in|priced in]] also depends on how traders were positioned. That is why the same number can bring different reactions on different days.

explain.simple: You learned in the forex lesson on expected vs. actual that surprise = actual − consensus. This lesson adds a second layer. Before a release, traders act on what they expect, so the price already reflects some outcome. If many have already bought on a hoped-for number, a good number may bring little more buying, and some may sell to take profit. If nobody was prepared, the same number can bring a bigger, longer move. So ask two questions: how big was the surprise, and what was the market already set up for?
explain.balanced: Clues to what is priced in include how far the price moved in the run-up, how one-sided commentary has been, and, for rate decisions, how likely traders' bets make each outcome. None of these is exact, so treat 'priced in' as a working guess. A simple way to measure a rate decision against expectations: expected change = probability × size. The real surprise is the actual change minus that expected change, not minus zero. All scenarios here use fictional Westmark data and are not forecasts.

assumptions: Fictional Westmark central bank, policy rate 3.00%
Suppose traders' bets imply about an 80% chance of a 0.25-point rise and a 20% chance of no change
Two possible outcomes, both made up
steps: Expected change = 0.80 × 0.25 = 0.20 points. Most of the rise is already priced in.
Outcome A, a 0.25 rise: surprise against what was priced = 0.25 − 0.20 = +0.05 points. Small.
Outcome B, no change: surprise = 0 − 0.20 = −0.20 points. Four times larger, in the opposite direction.
So 'no change' can move WMK more than a rise, because it was the outcome fewer people prepared for. Possible, not certain.

assumptions: Fictional Westmark inflation release: consensus 3.0%, actual 3.4%
Context 1: WMK was flat beforehand, and few traders had bet on a high number
Context 2: WMK had risen for weeks, and many traders had bet on a high number
steps: Surprise in both = 3.4 − 3.0 = +0.4 points. The number is identical.
Context 1: little was priced in, so WMK may rise and hold as traders adjust.
Context 2: much was priced in, so WMK may spike, then fall back as early buyers take profit.
Same number, different setup, different plausible reactions. The two Westmark inflation scenarios in the Fundamental Analysis Lab let you try this.

lessons.explainSimpler: News that everybody expected is old news. It moves price less, and sometimes the 'wrong' way, because people acted on it early.
lessons.commonMistake: Measuring a surprise only against the published consensus and ignoring how the market was positioned. Another mistake is being sure you know what is priced in. It is always an estimate.

quickCheck.prompt: Suppose traders' bets imply a 60% chance of a 0.50-point rate cut and 40% of no change. How much of a cut is priced in?

options.text: 0.50 points
options.explanation: No: that assumes the cut is certain. Multiply by the 60% chance.

options.text: 0.60 points
options.explanation: No: that is the probability, not the size of the cut.

options.text: 0.30 points
options.explanation: Right: 0.60 × 0.50 = 0.30 points expected.

quickCheck.prompt: Two fictional releases have the same consensus and actual. Why might the reactions differ?

options.text: One of the two releases must contain an error
options.explanation: No: the numbers can be correct; the setup before them differed.

options.text: Traders were positioned differently beforehand
options.explanation: Right: what was priced in and how traders were positioned change the reaction.

options.text: The surprise may have been bigger in one of them
options.explanation: No: the same consensus and the same actual means the same surprise. The setup before them differed.

doItNow.instructions: In the Fundamental Analysis Lab, open the two Westmark inflation scenarios, the calm one and the crowded one. Work out the surprise in each, then read what was priced in. For each, write the reaction you think is most plausible and one that would prove you wrong.

lessons.homework: Before the next release you see on an economic calendar, write down the consensus and one sentence on what you think is already priced in. After the release, note what happened, without judging yourself on whether you guessed right.

lessons.title: What a futures contract is: specs, expiry and settlement

inOneLine.simple: A futures contract is an agreement to buy or sell something at a set price on a set future date. Its rules are written in the contract specification.
inOneLine.balanced: A [[futures-contract]] is a standardised agreement traded on an exchange. Its specification sets the [[multiplier]] or [[contract-size]], the [[tick-size]], the [[contract-month|contract months]], the [[expiry]] date, and whether it ends in [[physical-settlement]] or [[cash-settlement]].

explain.simple: When you buy a share, you own a small piece of a company. When you buy a futures contract, you own nothing yet. You have agreed a price for a deal that completes later. Each contract has a rule book called the specification. It says how big one contract is, the smallest price step, which months you can trade, and the last day of trading, called expiry. At expiry, the contract either ends with the real goods being delivered, or with a cash payment of the difference. Every contract has its own rules, so you must read the specification of the exact contract you study.
explain.balanced: Each contract month is a separate contract with its own price. Close to expiry, trading activity often moves to the next month, so the contract you see on a chart may change. The [[notional-value]] of one contract is price × multiplier (or price × contract size). That is the size of the exposure you control, which is usually far bigger than the [[margin]] you put down. Settlement method matters: with physical settlement, a buyer who holds to the end can be required to take delivery, which most practice traders close or roll well before. Exchanges set and can change specifications, so never copy them from a chart, a forum or memory. All examples here use fictional specifications.

assumptions: Example index future (fictional specs): multiplier 10 USD per point, tick size 0.25
Fictional contract months: March, June, September and December
Cash-settled at expiry (fictional rule)
Price today 4,000.00 points
steps: Notional value of 1 contract = 4,000 × 10 USD = 40,000 USD.
Notional value of 2 contracts = 2 × 40,000 = 80,000 USD.
You buy 1 contract at 4,000.00 and hold it to expiry. The final settlement price is 4,020.00.
Gain = (4,020 − 4,000) × 10 USD = 20 × 10 = 200 USD, paid in cash. Nothing is delivered.
If the final price were 3,980.00 instead, the loss would be 20 × 10 = 200 USD, taken in cash.

assumptions: Example commodity future (fictional specs): contract size 100 units of a fictional commodity, priced in USD per unit
Physically settled at expiry (fictional rule)
Price today 50.00 USD per unit
steps: Notional value of 1 contract = 100 × 50.00 = 5,000 USD.
If you hold a bought contract into the delivery period, the rules could require you to pay for and receive 100 units.
A practice trader who only wants price exposure must close or roll the position before the last day set in the specification.
Same idea of 'a deal for later', but a very different ending. That is why the settlement method is part of the specification you check.

lessons.explainSimpler: A futures contract is a promise to trade later at today's agreed price. The rule book tells you its size, its price steps, when it ends, and how it ends: with goods or with cash.
lessons.commonMistake: Thinking all futures work the same way. Contracts differ in size, tick size, months, expiry dates and settlement. Another mistake is forgetting that a contract expires: unlike a share, you cannot hold the same contract forever.

quickCheck.prompt: Fictional contract: multiplier 20 USD per point, price 2,500.00. What is the notional value of 1 contract?

options.explanation: No: that is the price in points. Multiply it by the 20 USD multiplier.

options.text: 125 USD
options.explanation: No: that divides instead of multiplying. Notional = price × multiplier.

quickCheck.prompt: A fictional contract is cash-settled. You hold 1 bought contract to expiry. What happens?

options.text: The price gap is settled in cash; nothing is delivered
options.explanation: Right: cash settlement pays the difference against the final settlement price. Nothing is delivered.

options.text: You take delivery of the goods
options.explanation: No: that describes physical settlement, not cash settlement.

options.text: You may be moved to the next month automatically
options.explanation: No: a contract ends at expiry. Moving to a later month is a separate choice called rolling.

doItNow.instructions: Open the futures contract calculator. Enter the example index future's fictional specs from this lesson (tick size 0.25 and tick value 2.50 USD, which is 0.25 × the 10 USD multiplier) and check that 1 contract at 4,000.00 shows a notional value of 40,000 USD. Then make up a second fictional contract with a different multiplier (tick value = tick size × multiplier) and compare the notional values. Write down, in one line each, the six things you would check in a real contract's specification before studying it.

lessons.homework: Write a one-page 'spec card' template with blank fields for contract size or multiplier, tick size, tick value, contract months, expiry, settlement method, initial margin and maintenance margin. Fill it in for the two fictional contracts in this lesson.

lessons.title: Rollover, basis, contango and backwardation

inOneLine.simple: Each contract month has its own price. Lining them up shows the futures curve, and moving from one month to the next is called rolling.
inOneLine.balanced: The [[futures-curve]] is in [[contango]] when later months are priced higher and in [[backwardation]] when they are lower. [[basis|Basis]] compares the spot price with a futures price. A [[rollover]] closes one month and opens the next, at the price gap between them: a [[calendar-spread]].

explain.simple: The spot price is the price for buying the thing now. Futures prices for later months can be higher or lower than spot. If later months cost more, the curve slopes up: that is contango. If later months cost less, it slopes down: that is backwardation. Before your contract expires, you can close it, let it settle, or roll it: sell the month you hold and buy a later one. Rolling is two trades, so it has costs, and you buy the new month at its own price, not at the old one.
explain.balanced: Curve shape can reflect things like storage and financing costs, current supply and demand, and expectations, but the reasons differ by market and can change. Neither shape is a signal by itself. A futures price tends to move toward the spot price as expiry nears, so a long position that keeps rolling in contango can lose even if spot does not move; in backwardation the effect can run the other way. Basis is often defined as spot − futures, but some sources use futures − spot, so check which one is meant. All prices here are fictional.

assumptions: Example commodity future (fictional specs): 100 units per contract, prices in USD per unit
Fictional prices: spot 50.00, near month 50.60, next month 51.30
Basis defined here as spot − futures
Fees left out
steps: Later months are higher (50.60, then 51.30), so the curve is in contango.
Basis for the near month = 50.00 − 50.60 = −0.60 USD per unit.
Calendar spread, next − near = 51.30 − 50.60 = 0.70 USD per unit, which is 0.70 × 100 = 70 USD per contract.
To roll a long position, sell the near month at 50.60 and buy the next month at 51.30. You now hold exposure at the higher price.
Scenario: if spot stays at 50.00 and the next month's price moves to spot by its expiry, the long loses (51.30 − 50.00) × 100 = 130 USD, plus fees on every trade.

assumptions: Same fictional contract
Fictional prices: spot 49.00, near month 48.00, next month 47.20
steps: Later months are lower (48.00, then 47.20), so the curve is in backwardation.
Basis for the near month = 49.00 − 48.00 = +1.00 USD per unit.
Calendar spread, next − near = 47.20 − 48.00 = −0.80 USD per unit, or −80 USD per contract.
Rolling a long here buys the next month at a lower price than the month you sell. That is not free money: the curve can change shape at any time, and the spot price can fall.

lessons.explainSimpler: Each month has its own price. If later months cost more, that is contango; if they cost less, backwardation. Rolling means swapping your month for a later one at its own price.
lessons.commonMistake: Comparing a futures chart with the spot price and calling the gap a mistake, or joining two contract months on one chart without noticing the jump between them. Another mistake is thinking rolling is free: it is two trades, each with costs, at whatever price gap the curve shows that day.

quickCheck.prompt: Fictional prices: near month 70.00, next month 71.50, the month after 72.80. What shape is the curve?

options.text: Backwardation
options.explanation: No: backwardation means later months are priced lower.

options.text: Contango
options.explanation: Right: later months are priced higher, so the curve slopes up.

options.text: Flat
options.explanation: No: the prices rise from month to month, so the curve is not flat.

quickCheck.prompt: Fictional: spot 30.00, near-month future 30.45. Using basis = spot − futures, what is the basis?

options.explanation: No: that is futures − spot. Here basis is spot − futures.
No: that adds the prices instead of taking one from the other.

doItNow.instructions: Using the fictional contract in this lesson, work out by hand the calendar spread and the near-month basis for both curves. Then open the futures contract calculator, enter a tick size of 0.01 and a tick value of 1 USD (100 units × 0.01), and use it to check the 130 USD loss in the roll scenario (buy at 51.30, exit at 50.00).

lessons.homework: Make up a fictional curve of four contract months twice: once in contango and once in backwardation. For each, write the calendar spread between each pair of neighbouring months.

lessons.title: Leverage, gaps and forced liquidation

inOneLine.simple: Futures let a small deposit control a large position, so a small price move can wipe out the deposit, and a gap can push the loss past your stop.
inOneLine.balanced: Risk comes from [[notional-value]], not from [[margin]]. A [[gap]] can fill a [[stop-loss]] far past its level, and a broker can close positions at the market price when margin runs short. Losses can exceed the margin and the account.

explain.simple: With futures, the money you put down is a small part of the position's full value. That is leverage. A move of a few percent in price can equal the whole margin. Markets can also jump between one price and the next, for example after a close or sudden news. A stop loss is an order, not a guarantee: in a gap it fills at the first available price. And if your account falls below the maintenance margin and you do not add money, the broker can close your position for you, at whatever price it can get.
explain.balanced: Plan risk from the stop distance and the money per point, then add room for gaps and [[slippage]]. Margin requirements can be raised during fast markets, which can cause a margin call without any new loss. Forced liquidation does not wait for a good price, and in thin trading it can fill badly. Holding several contracts multiplies everything. A simple check before any futures trade: what would a 2.5% move against me cost, as money and as a share of my account?

assumptions: Example index future (fictional specs): multiplier 10 USD per point, tick size 0.25
Fictional margins: initial 2,000 USD, maintenance 1,600 USD per contract
Account balance 3,000 USD; buy 1 contract at 4,000.00
Stop loss at 3,980.00
Price closes at 3,990.00 and reopens at 3,820.00 after news
steps: The gap jumps over the stop. It fills near the first price, 3,820.00.
Actual loss = (4,000 − 3,820) × 10 = 180 × 10 = 1,800 USD. That is 1,800 ÷ 200 = 9 times the planned loss.
Account = 3,000 − 1,800 = 1,200 USD. Without a stop, the position would still be open with the account below the 1,600 USD maintenance margin, so a margin call would follow.
This is a made-up case to show the mechanism. It is not a prediction of how often gaps happen.

assumptions: Same fictional contract and margins
Account balance 10,000 USD
Price 4,000.00; compare holding 1 contract with holding 4
steps: 4 contracts need initial margin of 4 × 2,000 = 8,000 USD, so the account allows it.
Notional for 4 contracts = 4 × 40,000 = 160,000 USD, which is 160,000 ÷ 10,000 = 16 times the account.
A 100-point move against you, only 100 ÷ 4,000 = 2.5%, loses 100 × 10 × 4 = 4,000 USD: 40% of the account.
With 1 contract the same move loses 100 × 10 = 1,000 USD: 10% of the account.
The margin let you open 4. It did not tell you whether 4 was a sensible risk.

lessons.explainSimpler: A small deposit holds a big position. A small move can take the deposit, a jump can skip your stop, and the broker can close you out at a bad price.
lessons.commonMistake: Sizing a futures trade by how many contracts the margin allows. Size it from the money you can afford to lose if price moves past your stop, and remember that a gap can make the real loss much bigger than the planned one.

quickCheck.prompt: Example index future (fictional: 10 USD per point). Buy 1 at 4,000.00 with a stop at 3,990.00. Price gaps and the stop fills at 3,950.00. What is the loss?

options.text: 100 USD
options.explanation: No: that is the planned loss, 10 points × 10 USD. The fill was worse.

options.text: 500 USD
400 USD
options.explanation: No: that is only the part beyond the stop, 40 × 10. Count from the entry.

quickCheck.prompt: Which statement about futures margin is true?

options.text: Losses stop once the margin is used up
options.explanation: No: losses can keep growing past the margin and even past the account balance.

options.text: Losses are never capped at the margin
options.explanation: Right: profit and loss come from the full notional value.

options.text: Margin can never change after you open
options.explanation: No: exchanges and brokers can raise margins, sometimes at short notice.

doItNow.instructions: In the paper trading simulator, open the Practice index future and read its notes on margin per contract and the stop-out. Before each trade, write the stop distance in points, the money at risk for 1 contract, and the money lost if price moved 2.5% against you. Place 5 paper trades of 1 contract, each with a stop loss, and record any fill worse than your stop.

lessons.homework: Write one futures rule for your plan: the most money you will risk per trade, and how you will size contracts from it rather than from the margin allowed.

lessons.title: Initial margin, maintenance margin and margin calls

inOneLine.simple: You put down a deposit to open a futures trade. Every day, gains and losses are added to or taken from your account, and if it falls too low you must add money or be closed out.
inOneLine.balanced: [[initial-margin|Initial margin]] is needed to open; [[maintenance-margin]] is the lower level the account must stay above. Through [[mark-to-market]], each day's gain or loss is settled in cash. Falling below maintenance brings a [[margin-call]]. Required margin is not the maximum loss.

explain.simple: Initial margin is a good-faith deposit for each contract, not the price of the contract. Each trading day the position is valued at that day's settlement price, and the gain or loss moves into or out of your account. This is called mark-to-market. If the account falls below the maintenance margin, you get a margin call: you must add money, or the broker can close your position. Margin is only a deposit. A large move can take more than the margin, and even more than your whole account.
explain.balanced: Exchanges set minimum margins and brokers may ask for more; both can raise margins at short notice, often when markets are moving fast. Rules on how much to add after a margin call differ: in this lesson's example the broker asks you to top the account back up to the initial margin. The price that triggers a margin call depends on your balance, not only the margin: margin-call price for a buyer = entry − (balance − maintenance margin × contracts) ÷ (money per point × contracts). Notional ÷ initial margin shows the [[leverage]] built into the trade.

assumptions: Example index future (fictional specs): multiplier 10 USD per point, tick size 0.25
Fictional margins: initial 2,000 USD, maintenance 1,600 USD per contract
Account balance before the trade: 2,000 USD
Buy 1 contract at 4,000.00
Fictional rule: after a margin call you must top up to the initial margin
steps: Notional value = 4,000 × 10 = 40,000 USD. Leverage = 40,000 ÷ 2,000 = 20 times.
Day 1 settles at 3,985.00: change = −15 points × 10 = −150 USD. Account = 2,000 − 150 = 1,850 USD, still above 1,600.
Day 2 settles at 3,955.00: change = −30 points × 10 = −300 USD. Account = 1,850 − 300 = 1,550 USD, below 1,600.
Margin call: top up to 2,000 USD, so add 2,000 − 1,550 = 450 USD, or the broker may close the position.
A 200-point fall, only 200 ÷ 4,000 = 5% of the price, would lose 200 × 10 = 2,000 USD: the whole initial margin.

assumptions: Same fictional specs and margins
Account balance before the trade: 5,000 USD
Sell (go short) 1 contract at 4,000.00
steps: For a short, losses come from price rising.
The whole balance is gone at 4,000 + 5,000 ÷ 10 = 4,500.00.
Price can keep rising past 4,500.00. At 4,600.00 the loss would be 600 × 10 = 6,000 USD, which is 1,000 USD more than the account held.
Extra cash moves the margin-call price further away. It does not cap the loss.

lessons.explainSimpler: Margin is a deposit that gets topped up or drained every day. If it drains below a line, you must refill it or lose the position. And the loss can be bigger than the deposit.
lessons.commonMistake: Treating the initial margin as the price of the trade or as the most you can lose. Your profit and loss is based on the full notional value, and it is settled every day, so a run of bad days can force a margin call well before you planned to exit.

quickCheck.prompt: Fictional margins: initial 2,000 USD, maintenance 1,600 USD. You opened with 2,000 USD. Your account holds 1,700 USD after today's mark-to-market. What happens?

options.text: Nothing yet: still above maintenance
options.explanation: Right: 1,700 is above 1,600, so there is no margin call yet, even though the account is below the initial margin.

options.text: A margin call: you are below initial margin
options.explanation: No: in this example the call comes when the account falls below the maintenance margin, 1,600 USD.

options.text: The trade is closed with a 300 USD gain
options.explanation: No: the account has fallen by 300 USD, which is a loss, and nothing forces a close yet.

quickCheck.prompt: Example index future (fictional: 10 USD per point). Balance 3,000 USD, maintenance 1,600 USD, buy 1 contract at 4,000.00. At what price does the margin call start?

options.explanation: No: that uses the maintenance margin alone, 1,600 ÷ 10. Start from the balance above maintenance.
No: that is where the whole 3,000 USD balance is gone.

doItNow.instructions: Open the futures contract calculator and enter this lesson's fictional specs (tick size 0.25 and tick value 2.50 USD, which is 0.25 × 10) and margins, with a 2,000 USD balance and a buy at 4,000.00. Check that it shows a notional value of 40,000 USD, leverage of 20 and a margin-call price of 3,960.00. Then raise the balance to 3,000 USD and to 5,000 USD and write down how the margin-call price moves. Note the price where the balance would be gone, and remember price can go further than that.

lessons.homework: Make a mark-to-market table for 5 made-up settlement prices on the example index future. For each day, write the daily gain or loss, the account balance, and whether a margin call would happen.

lessons.title: Tick size, tick value and multipliers

inOneLine.simple: Futures prices move in fixed small steps called ticks, and each tick is worth a set amount of money per contract.
inOneLine.balanced: [[tick-value|Tick value]] = [[tick-size]] × [[multiplier]] (or × [[contract-size]]). Profit or loss = number of ticks moved × tick value × number of contracts.

explain.simple: A tick is the smallest step a futures price can move. The tick size is how big that step is, for example 0.25 of a point. The tick value is how much money one tick is worth for one contract. To find it, multiply the tick size by the multiplier, which is the money value of one whole point. Once you know the tick value, profit and loss is simple counting: how many ticks did price move, times the tick value, times how many contracts you hold.
explain.balanced: Two contracts can show prices that look alike yet be worth very different amounts per point. A 10-point move might be 100 USD on one contract and 500 USD on another. That is why the calculator asks you to enter the specification instead of assuming one. Some contracts quote a multiplier, others a contract size in units; both lead to the same idea of money per point. Exchanges can set different tick sizes for different contracts, and specifications can change, so check the exact contract each time. All specs in this lesson are fictional.

assumptions: Example index future (fictional specs): multiplier 10 USD per point, tick size 0.25
Buy 2 contracts at 4,000.00
Sell to close at 4,012.50
Fees left out to keep the steps clear
steps: Tick value = 0.25 × 10 USD = 2.50 USD per tick, per contract.
Ticks moved = 12.50 ÷ 0.25 = 50 ticks.
Profit = 50 ticks × 2.50 USD × 2 contracts = 250 USD.
Check another way: 12.50 points × 10 USD × 2 contracts = 250 USD. Both methods agree.

assumptions: Example commodity future (fictional specs): contract size 100 units, tick size 0.01 USD per unit
Sell (go short) 3 contracts at 62.40
Price rises and you buy back to close at 62.85
Fees left out
steps: Tick value = 0.01 × 100 units = 1.00 USD per tick, per contract.
Price move = 62.85 − 62.40 = 0.45, against a short position.
Ticks moved = 0.45 ÷ 0.01 = 45 ticks against you.
Loss = 45 × 1.00 USD × 3 contracts = 135 USD.
Compare: a fictional contract with a multiplier of 50 USD per point would turn a 10-point move into 10 × 50 = 500 USD per contract, five times the 100 USD on the 10 USD contract.

lessons.explainSimpler: Count the steps price moved, then multiply by what one step is worth, then by how many contracts you hold.
lessons.commonMistake: Assuming every contract has the same tick value or multiplier, or using a number remembered from somewhere else. Always take tick size, tick value and multiplier from the specification of the exact contract you are looking at.

quickCheck.prompt: Fictional contract: tick size 0.5, multiplier 5 USD per point. What is the tick value?

options.text: 5.00 USD
options.explanation: No: that is the value of a whole point. One tick is only half a point here.

options.text: 2.50 USD
options.explanation: Right: 0.5 × 5 USD = 2.50 USD per tick, per contract.
No: that divides 5 by 0.5. Tick value = tick size × multiplier.

quickCheck.prompt: Example index future (fictional specs: tick 0.25, tick value 2.50 USD). You buy 1 contract at 4,000.00 and sell at 3,995.00. What is the result?

options.text: A 5 USD loss
options.explanation: No: that is the move in points, not in money.

options.text: A 50 USD gain
options.explanation: No: price fell after you bought, so this is a loss.

options.text: A 50 USD loss
options.explanation: Right: 5 points ÷ 0.25 = 20 ticks, and 20 × 2.50 USD = 50 USD lost.

quickCheck.prompt: Two fictional contracts both move 10 points. Why might the money result differ?

options.text: Each contract has its own multiplier
options.explanation: Right: money per point comes from each contract's own specification.

options.text: Points are always worth 1 USD
options.explanation: No: a point is worth whatever the specification says.

options.text: One may have a smaller tick size
options.explanation: No: tick size sets the smallest step, not the money per point. The multiplier decides what 10 points is worth.

doItNow.instructions: Work out both examples in this lesson by hand first. Then open the futures contract calculator, enter the same fictional specs, entries and exits, and check your P/L and tick count. Finally, enter a made-up contract with a tick size of 0.1 and a tick value of 5 USD, and find how much a 3-point move is worth for 2 contracts.

lessons.title: ATR and Bollinger Bands: measuring volatility

inOneLine.simple: ATR and Bollinger Bands measure how much price has been moving. Neither tells you which way it will move next.
inOneLine.balanced: [[atr|ATR]] averages the true range of recent candles. [[bollinger-bands|Bollinger Bands]] put bands 2 standard deviations around a 20-period average. Both describe past volatility and are slow to react to sudden changes.

explain.simple: ATR answers: how far has price typically moved per candle lately? On EUR/USD H1, an ATR of 0.00120 means about 12 pips per candle. That helps you see if a stop is tiny compared with normal movement. Bollinger Bands draw a line above and below an average. When price has been jumpy, the bands spread out. When it has been calm, they squeeze together. Neither tool says up or down.
explain.balanced: True range = the largest of high − low, |high − previous close| and |low − previous close|, so it includes gaps. ATR 14 averages it, with smoothing in most apps. ATR is backward-looking: before news it may be low, and then one candle is several times larger. Bollinger (20, 2): middle = SMA 20, bands = middle ± 2 × the standard deviation of the last 20 closes. A touch of the upper band is not "too high". In strong trends price can ride a band for many candles. A squeeze shows recent calm, and the move that follows can go either way, or not come at all.

assumptions: Illustrative EUR/USD H1 candle
Previous close 1.10000; this candle: high 1.10300, low 1.10050
steps: |High − previous close| = 1.10300 − 1.10000 = 30 pips.
|Low − previous close| = 1.10050 − 1.10000 = 5 pips.
True range = the largest = 30 pips. It is bigger than the candle itself because price gapped up from the previous close.
If ATR 14 is 12 pips, a 5-pip stop is less than half a typical candle's movement and could be hit by ordinary noise. A wider stop needs a smaller position to keep the same money at risk.

assumptions: Illustrative Bollinger (20, 2) on EUR/USD H4
Middle line (SMA 20) = 1.10000; standard deviation of the last 20 closes = 0.00150
steps: Price closes at 1.10320, above the upper band. In a strong uptrend this can happen candle after candle. Selling only because price is outside the band would mean selling into that trend.

lessons.explainSimpler: ATR is how big the waves have been. Bollinger Bands draw a lane that widens with bigger waves. Neither tells you which way the next wave goes.
lessons.commonMistake: Treating a Bollinger Band touch as a reversal signal, or a squeeze as a sign of which way price will break. Another mistake is trusting ATR right before major news, when the next candle may be far bigger than recent ones.

quickCheck.prompt: Previous close 1.20000. Candle high 1.20100, low 1.19750. What is the true range?

options.text: 35 pips
options.explanation: Right: high − low = 35 pips, which is larger than 10 pips (high − previous close) and 25 pips (previous close − low).

options.text: 3.5 pips
options.explanation: No: 1 pip is 0.00010, so a gap of 0.00350 is 35 pips, not 3.5. True range is the largest of high − low (35), high − previous close (10) and previous close − low (25).

options.text: 25 pips
options.explanation: No: that is only previous close − low.

quickCheck.prompt: Bollinger Bands are squeezed very tight. What does that tell you?

options.text: Recent price movement has been small
options.explanation: Right: narrow bands only describe recent calm.

options.text: A breakout upward is due next
options.explanation: No: a squeeze says nothing about direction, and a big move may not come at all.

quickCheck.prompt: ATR 14 on EUR/USD H1 reads 0.00090. What does it mean?

options.text: Price has moved about 9 pips per candle recently, in either direction
options.explanation: Right: ATR measures size of movement, not direction.

options.text: Price will rise 9 pips next hour
options.explanation: No: ATR has no direction and does not forecast.

options.text: Price has moved about 90 pips per candle recently, in either direction
options.explanation: No: 0.00090 is 9 pips, not 90, because 1 pip is 0.00010.

doItNow.instructions: On your demo account, add a moving average, Bollinger Bands, RSI, MACD and ATR to a EUR/USD chart, check their settings, then remove them. Follow the task card.

lessons.homework: In Chart Lab, choose the News shock scenario, turn on Bollinger (20, 2) and show ATR 14 below the chart. Long-press to compare the ATR just before the shock with the range of the shock candle. Then choose the Strong uptrend scenario and find a stretch where price rode along the upper band. Finally, pick one indicator from this module and write two sentences: what it measures, and one market condition where it misleads.

lessons.title: Backtesting with Replay, and why sample size matters

inOneLine.simple: A [[backtest]] tests your plan on past charts. A small [[sample-size|sample]] says little, so you need many trades before you judge.
inOneLine.balanced: Replay shows past charts one bar at a time and hides the future, so you can follow your plan as if it were live. Each trade is one data point. With few trades, luck dominates the result.

explain.simple: Before you practise a plan on a demo account, test it on the past. Go to Practice → Replay. Replay shows an old chart one candle at a time. You cannot see what comes next. Follow your plan exactly: same entry rule, same stop, same target, same size. Record every trade in the Journal. Then look at what happened. But be careful. A handful of trades tells you almost nothing. Five wins in a row can be luck. Five losses in a row can be bad luck. That is why this module asks for 50 replay trades, not 5.
explain.balanced: Each trade is one result, a bit like one coin toss. With 10 trades, changing one result (a win that becomes a loss) moves the win rate by 10 percentage points, and adding one more trade moves it by up to about 9. With 50 trades, changing one result moves it by 2 points, and adding one moves it by up to about 2. A larger sample gives a steadier picture, but 50 trades is still a small sample. It is enough to learn how your rules behave and how well you follow them. It is not enough to know that the rules have an edge, and nothing from the past promises the future.

assumptions: Fictional replay results, illustrative only
After 10 trades: 6 wins, 4 losses
After 11 trades: one more loss
steps: Win rate after 10 trades = 6 ÷ 10 = 60%.
Win rate after 11 trades = 6 ÷ 11 ≈ 54.5%.
One trade moved the win rate by about 5.5 percentage points.
The "60%" was never a stable number. It was 10 coin tosses.

assumptions: Fictional replay results, illustrative only
After 50 trades: 25 wins, 25 losses
After 51 trades: one more loss
steps: Win rate after 50 trades = 25 ÷ 50 = 50%.
Win rate after 51 trades = 25 ÷ 51 ≈ 49.0%.
One trade moved the win rate by about 1 percentage point.
Steadier, but still a small sample. Use it to learn about your rules and your discipline, not to predict future results.

lessons.explainSimpler: Ten trades is a rumour. Fifty trades is a first draft. Neither is a promise.
lessons.commonMistake: Judging a plan after a few trades: giving up after 3 losses, or getting excited after 4 wins. Both are reacting to noise.

quickCheck.prompt: You won 4 of your first 5 replay trades. What does this tell you?

options.text: The plan works: 80% is a strong win rate
options.explanation: No: 5 trades is far too few. Luck can easily explain 4 wins out of 5.

options.text: Very little yet; keep following the plan and collecting trades
options.explanation: Right: a small sample says little.

quickCheck.prompt: How does Replay help you test fairly?

options.text: It hides future bars, so you decide without knowing what comes next
options.explanation: Right: you trade the chart as it was at the time.

options.text: It shows the whole finished chart at once, so you can spot the best entries
options.explanation: No: that is the opposite. Seeing the whole finished chart leads to look-ahead bias. Replay hides future bars.

quickCheck.prompt: With 20 trades, roughly how much does one extra trade move the win rate?

options.text: About 1 percentage point
options.explanation: No: that is closer to 100 trades.

options.text: About 5 percentage points
options.explanation: Right: one result out of 20 is worth 1 ÷ 20 = 5 points. Adding a 21st trade moves it by a little less.

options.text: About 20 percentage points
options.explanation: No: that would be about 5 trades.

doItNow.instructions: Open Practice → Replay. Take 10 replay trades following your saved plan exactly: same entry, stop, target and size rules. Log each one in the Journal. Do not change any rule yet.

lessons.title: Look-ahead, selection and survivorship bias

inOneLine.simple: Three common test errors: using information you could not have known ([[look-ahead-bias]]), only testing the periods you remember as good (selection bias, or cherry-picking), and copying a method only because it is one that happened to work ([[survivorship-bias]]).
inOneLine.balanced: All three make a backtest or a method look better than real trading could be. Replay reduces look-ahead bias by hiding future bars. You reduce selection bias by choosing test periods before you look, across different market conditions. You reduce survivorship bias by testing a method yourself instead of trusting that it worked for someone.

explain.simple: Look-ahead bias means using the future by accident. For example, you draw a support line on an old chart. But the bounce that made the line obvious happened after your entry. At the time, you could not have known it was support. Replay helps, because it hides bars that have not happened yet. Selection bias, or cherry-picking, means only testing the periods that suit your rules. Maybe you only replay charts with big, clean trends because those are the ones you remember. The quiet, choppy periods are missing from your test. Survivorship bias means only seeing the winners. Maybe you copy a method only because you heard it worked for someone. You never hear about the similar methods that failed and were dropped.
explain.balanced: To limit look-ahead bias: mark levels only with bars visible at that point, decide on a bar only after it closes, and never skip forward to "check" before deciding. To limit selection bias: pick your replay periods before you look at them, and include trending, ranging, quiet, busy and news-driven periods. Write down every trade, including the ones you would rather forget. A test that only includes good-looking periods tells you how your rules do in good-looking periods. To limit survivorship bias: treat a method you heard about as an idea to test, not as proof. The stories you hear come from the methods that happened to work; the ones that failed are rarely mentioned.

assumptions: Fictional example on EUR/USD, illustrative prices
Learner tests a "buy at support" rule on a full, finished chart
Support is drawn at 1.08000 using a low that formed 2 days after the planned entry
steps: On the finished chart, 1.08000 looks like strong support, so the buy looks great.
But at the planned entry time, that low had not happened yet.
The trade could not have been taken that way in real time. This is look-ahead bias.
In Replay, the future low is hidden, so the line cannot be drawn there yet. The test becomes honest.

assumptions: Fictional learner, 30 replay trades
24 trades chosen from periods the learner remembered as "strong trends"
6 trades from random periods
steps: The 24 remembered-trend trades look good.
The 6 random-period trades look worse.
Most of the test came from the conditions the learner already knew suited the rules. That is selection bias, also called cherry-picking.
The fix: choose periods first, then replay them, and include ranges and quiet markets.

lessons.explainSimpler: Look-ahead bias: peeking at the answers. Selection bias: only sitting the tests you know you will pass. Survivorship bias: only hearing from the people who passed.
lessons.commonMistake: Testing on a fully visible chart and "spotting" setups after the fact. Nearly everything looks obvious in hindsight.

quickCheck.prompt: You mark a resistance level using a high that formed after your planned entry. What is this?

options.text: Look-ahead bias
options.explanation: Right: you used information that did not exist at the time.

options.text: Survivorship bias
options.explanation: No: survivorship bias is copying a method because it is one of the ones that happened to work, while the failures are forgotten.

quickCheck.prompt: You only replay periods with strong trends because those are the charts you remember. What is the risk?

options.text: None: trends are where you would actually trade
options.explanation: No: your rules will also meet ranges and quiet markets, and you cannot always tell in advance which period you are in.

options.text: Your test leaves out conditions where the rules may fail, so it looks better than it is
options.explanation: Right: this is selection bias, also called cherry-picking.

quickCheck.prompt: You copy a method only because you heard it made money for someone. Which bias is this a risk of?

options.text: Survivorship bias
options.explanation: Right: you hear about the methods that happened to work, not the similar ones that failed. Test it yourself before trusting it.

options.text: Look-ahead bias
options.explanation: No: look-ahead bias is using information that did not exist at the time of the trade.

options.text: Selection bias in your test periods
options.explanation: No: selection bias is choosing only the test periods that suit your rules. Here the problem is which methods you hear about.

doItNow.instructions: Before opening Replay, write a list of 4 periods to test: one trending, one ranging, one quiet, and one around a news event. Then open Practice → Replay and take your next 10 trades across those periods, following your plan. Decide only on closed bars.

lessons.title: Overfitting, and reviewing 50 replay trades

inOneLine.simple: [[overfitting|Overfitting]] means adding rules until the past looks perfect. Review your 50 replay trades for process first, and test any rule change on new data.
inOneLine.balanced: Each new filter that removes a few past losers improves the old results, but it was chosen after seeing them. Keep rules simple, change one thing at a time, save a new plan version, and test the change on periods you have not used.

explain.simple: After some replay trades, you will see losers and think, "If I had added one more rule, I would have avoided that one." Then another rule. Then another. Soon the rules fit the past perfectly. This is overfitting. The rules were shaped by the answers, so they may not work on new charts. When you review your 50 replay trades in the Journal, start with the process. Did you follow the plan on each trade? Were stops and size right? Only then look at results, and remember 50 trades is still a small sample.
explain.balanced: A useful review asks: how many trades followed every rule? Which rules were broken, and how often? Did results differ across trending, ranging and news periods? What was the result in R (multiples of the planned risk), and how spread out was it? If you want to change a rule, change one thing, save it as a new plan version, and replay fresh periods with it. A change that only helps the trades you already saw is not evidence of anything.

assumptions: Fictional set of 50 replay trades, illustrative only
20 wins of +2R each; 30 losses of −1R each
R = the planned risk on each trade
All 50 trades followed the plan
steps: Total from wins = 20 × 2R = +40R.
Total from losses = 30 × −1R = −30R.
Net = +10R. Average per trade = 10R ÷ 50 = +0.2R.
This is one small sample from the past. A few different trades could flip the sign. It says how this test went, not what will happen next.

assumptions: Fictional learner, 30 replay trades so far
Learner adds 4 new filters after reviewing the losers
The filters would have removed 8 past losing trades and 1 past winner
steps: On the old 30 trades, results now look much better.
But the filters were chosen by looking at those exact trades.
Number of new trades the changed plan has been tested on: zero.
The learner saves it as a new plan version and replays 20 fresh periods before judging it.

lessons.explainSimpler: Overfitting is tailoring a suit to fit one photo of a person. It may not fit the person when they move.
lessons.commonMistake: Judging a replay test by profit alone. A profitable test full of rule breaks tells you less than a flat test where every rule was followed.

quickCheck.prompt: After reviewing losers, you add 3 rules that would have avoided them. What should you do next?

options.text: Trust the new rules; they removed the past losses
options.explanation: No: they were chosen from the answers. That is overfitting.

options.text: Save a new plan version and test it on periods you have not used yet
options.explanation: Right: only new data can show whether a change helps.

quickCheck.prompt: 50 trades: 15 wins of +2R, 35 losses of −1R. What is the net result in R?

options.explanation: No: check the losses. 35 × −1R = −35R.
No: 30R − 35R is −5R.

quickCheck.prompt: When reviewing your replay trades, what should you look at first?

options.text: The total profit or loss
options.explanation: No: results from a small sample say little.

options.text: Whether each trade followed the plan
options.explanation: Right: process first. You cannot judge rules you did not follow.

doItNow.instructions: Finish 50 replay trades in Practice → Replay, all following the same plan version. Then review them in the Journal: count rule breaks, compare trending, ranging and news periods, and write down one rule you might test next and why.

lessons.homework: Write three sentences: what the 50 trades taught you about your rules, about your discipline, and what they cannot tell you.

lessons.title: Bid, ask, and the spread

inOneLine.simple: You buy at the higher price and sell at the lower one. The gap between them is a cost on every trade.

explain.simple: Every quote shows two prices. The [[bid]] is the price you can sell at. The [[ask]] is the price you can buy at, and it is slightly higher. The gap is the [[spread]]. If you buy and then sell straight away, you lose the spread. So every trade starts a little behind.
explain.balanced: A buy order fills at the ask and is closed by selling at the bid. A sell order fills at the bid and is closed by buying at the ask. The spread is therefore paid on every round trip. It changes with [[liquidity]] and often widens around major news and when the market is quiet.

assumptions: EUR/USD bid 1.10000, ask 1.10015 (5-digit quote)
Trade size 0.10 lot = 10,000 EUR
Account in USD; 1 pip on EUR/USD = 0.0001
steps: Cost of the spread on this trade = 1.5 × 1 USD = 1.50 USD, paid even if price never moves.

assumptions: GBP/USD bid 1.25000, ask 1.25030
Trade size 1 standard lot = 100,000 GBP
steps: Spread = 0.00030 = 3 pips.
One pip on 100,000 GBP = 10 USD.
Spread cost = 3 × 10 = 30 USD for one round trip.

lessons.explainSimpler: Buying costs a little more than selling. That little difference is a fee you pay on every trade.
lessons.commonMistake: Placing a stop loss or target without allowing for the spread. A sell trade's stop is hit by the ask price, which can trigger it even when the chart's bid line never touched your level.

quickCheck.prompt: You want to buy EUR/USD at market. Which price do you get?

options.text: The ask
options.explanation: Right: buys fill at the ask, the higher price.

options.text: The bid
options.explanation: No: the bid is the price you can sell at.

options.text: The mid price, halfway between bid and ask
options.explanation: No: market orders do not fill at the mid. Buys fill at the ask.

quickCheck.prompt: Bid 1.2000, ask 1.2003. What is the spread in pips?

options.text: 0.3 pips
options.explanation: No: 0.0003 is three steps of 0.0001.

options.text: 3 pips
30 pips
options.explanation: No: 30 pips would be 0.0030.

doItNow.instructions: In MetaTrader on your demo account, tap EUR/USD in the quotes list. Read the bid and the ask, work out the spread in pips, and write it down.

lessons.homework: Check the EUR/USD spread in MetaTrader around the London open and again late in the evening, and note both.

lessons.title: Breakouts

inOneLine.simple: A breakout is when price moves out through a support or resistance zone. Decide in advance what counts as one.
inOneLine.balanced: Define a [[breakout]] with a written rule, for example "a candle closes at least 5 pips beyond the zone". Without a rule, every wick through a line looks like a breakout afterwards.

explain.simple: Price can poke through a level and come straight back. So people use rules. A common one is to wait for a candle to close beyond the zone, not just touch it with a wick. Some add a small extra distance, called a filter. The rule is your choice. What matters is that you write it down before you look, and use it the same way every time.
explain.balanced: A wick-only move outside the zone that closes back inside does not meet a close-based rule. A bigger filter means fewer breakouts are counted, but you enter later and further from the level, so a [[stop-loss]] on the other side of the zone is wider. A breakout can continue, stall, or fail. Many fail, which is why the next lesson is about [[false-breakout|false breakouts]]. Breakouts around news can come with [[slippage]] and wider [[spread|spreads]].

assumptions: Illustrative EUR/USD H1 prices
Resistance zone 1.10450–1.10500
Your written rule: a breakout is a close at least 5 pips above the top of the zone, so at or above 1.10550
steps: Candle A: high 1.10560, close 1.10470. The wick went above 1.10550, but the close is inside the zone. Not a breakout under this rule.
Candle B: close 1.10580. That is 1.10580 − 1.10500 = 8 pips above the zone, which is at least 5. This counts as a breakout.
If you bought at 1.10580 with a stop just below the zone at 1.10430, the stop distance would be 1.10580 − 1.10430 = 15 pips.
Counting it as a breakout says nothing about whether price will keep rising.

assumptions: Illustrative USD/JPY H4 prices; 1 pip = 0.01
Support zone 149.80–149.90
Rule: a breakdown is a close at least 10 pips below the bottom of the zone, so at or below 149.70
steps: A candle closes at 149.75. That is 149.80 − 149.75 = 0.05 = 5 pips below the zone. Not enough under this rule.
The next candle closes at 149.62. That is 149.80 − 149.62 = 0.18 = 18 pips below. This counts.
With a 5-pip filter, the first candle would have counted. The rule you choose changes which moves you call breakouts.

lessons.explainSimpler: A breakout is price leaving the box. Decide before you look what "leaving" means, for example a close outside it.
lessons.commonMistake: Calling every wick through a line a breakout, or changing the rule after the fact so the chart fits. Another mistake is assuming a breakout will run far.

quickCheck.prompt: Resistance zone tops out at 1.25000. Your rule: a breakout is a close at least 5 pips above it. A candle has high 1.25080 and close 1.24980. Is it a breakout?

options.text: No: it closed back inside the zone
options.explanation: Right: only the wick went above. The close at 1.24980 is below 1.25000.

options.text: Yes: the high went 8 pips above the zone, past the 5-pip filter
options.explanation: No: your rule is about the close, not the wick. The close was below 1.25000.

quickCheck.prompt: You make your breakout filter bigger, from 5 to 15 pips. What usually changes?

options.text: Fewer moves count as breakouts, and entries are later
options.explanation: Right: a stricter rule waits for more distance, so it confirms less often and later.

options.text: False breakouts stop happening, because the filter screens them all out
options.explanation: No: a filter only changes which moves count. Some breakouts that pass it still fail.

options.text: Nothing changes
options.explanation: No: the filter changes which candles meet the rule.

doItNow.instructions: Write a breakout rule in one sentence, for example "a close at least 5 pips beyond the zone". Then open the Breakout or fake? drill in Practice and apply that same rule to every chart.

lessons.title: How to check a broker

inOneLine.simple: Check a broker on the [[regulator]]'s own official register, found by you, not through a link the broker gives you. Then check the rules where you live.
inOneLine.balanced: Examples of regulators include the FCA, ASIC and CySEC. Search the register for the firm's exact name, and make sure the website, address and contact details match. Firms can copy a real firm's name, so details matter. Being regulated does not mean trading is safe or profitable.

explain.simple: Before you ever think about a broker, check who they are. A broker should be authorised by a financial regulator. Examples of regulators include the FCA, ASIC and CySEC. Each country has its own. Find the regulator's official website yourself, for example by typing the regulator's name into a search engine and checking you are on the official site. Do not use a link from the broker or from a chat. On the register, search for the broker's exact name. Check that the website address and contact details match what the broker uses. Then check the rules for traders where you live, because they differ between countries.
explain.balanced: Things to note from the register: the exact legal name, the status (for example authorised, or not), the website addresses listed, and any warnings. If the name matches but the website or phone number does not, treat it as a possible clone of a real firm. Some regulators also publish warning lists of unauthorised firms. A clean register entry is only a first check. It does not mean the broker suits you, and it says nothing about whether trading will make money. This app does not recommend any broker.

assumptions: Fictional broker "Example Broker A (fictional)", all details made up
Its website is example-broker-a.invalid (a made-up address) and its phone number starts +00 111
The learner finds the regulator's official site on their own
steps: The register shows a firm called "Example Broker A Ltd (fictional)" with status "authorised".
The website listed on the register is different from the one the learner was sent.
The phone number on the register is also different.
Same name, different details: this could be a clone. The learner uses only the contact details on the register, or walks away.

assumptions: Fictional broker "Example Broker B (fictional)", all details made up
The learner searches two regulators' official registers
steps: No firm with that name appears on either register.
The broker's website says it is "fully regulated" but gives no regulator or number.
The learner cannot confirm the claim on any official register.
Result of the check: unverified. The learner does not use it, and notes the name in their journal.

lessons.explainSimpler: Check the ID yourself, at the official office, not with a card the stranger hands you.
