lessons.commonMistake: Trusting a regulator logo or licence number on the broker's own website. Anyone can copy a logo. Check on the regulator's own site.

quickCheck.prompt: Where should you check whether a broker is regulated?

options.text: On the broker's own website
options.explanation: No: logos and numbers can be copied.

options.text: On the regulator's own official register, found by you
options.explanation: Right: the official source is the check that counts.

quickCheck.prompt: The register shows a firm with the right name but a different website and phone number. What does this suggest?

options.text: It is fine; the name matches, and websites often change
options.explanation: No: scammers can copy a real firm's name. The website and phone number must match the register too.

options.text: It could be a clone; use only the details on the register or walk away
options.explanation: Right: every detail should match.

quickCheck.prompt: A broker passes your register check. What does that show?

options.text: That it is safe and recommended, so you can deposit without more checks
options.explanation: No: being on a register is a first check, not a recommendation. You still check local rules and costs, and it says nothing about whether trading makes money.

options.text: That it appears on an official register; you still check local rules and costs
options.explanation: Right: it is a first check, not a recommendation.

doItNow.instructions: Do a broker check on the broker behind your MetaTrader demo account. Find the relevant regulator's official website yourself, search its register for the broker's exact name, and note whether the name, website and contact details match. Then look up the rules for traders where you live. Write down what you found and anything you could not confirm.

lessons.title: Candlesticks and OHLC

inOneLine.simple: Each candle shows four prices for one period: where it opened, how high and low it went, and where it closed.
inOneLine.balanced: A [[candlestick]] draws the [[ohlc]] prices: the body runs from open to close, and the wicks reach to the high and low.

explain.simple: Pick one candle on a chart. It covers one stretch of time, such as one hour. The thick body runs from the opening price to the closing price. If the close is above the open, price rose during that hour and the candle is an up candle. If the close is below the open, it is a down candle. The thin lines above and below the body are wicks. They show the highest and lowest prices reached. Colours depend on your app, so check which colour means up.
explain.balanced: Body size = |close − open|. Range = high − low. Upper wick = high − the higher of open and close. Lower wick = the lower of open and close − low. Body plus both wicks equals the range. A long wick shows price went somewhere and came back within the period, but not why or what happens next. MetaTrader charts usually show bid prices, so a buy fills at the ask, which sits one [[spread]] above the chart.

assumptions: Illustrative prices
One 1-hour EUR/USD candle: open 1.10000, high 1.10250, low 1.09900, close 1.10180
steps: The close (1.10180) is above the open (1.10000), so this is an up candle.

assumptions: Illustrative prices
One 1-hour GBP/USD candle: open 1.25400, high 1.25450, low 1.25000, close 1.25100
steps: The close (1.25100) is below the open (1.25400), so this is a down candle.
Upper wick = 1.25450 − 1.25400 = 5 pips. Lower wick = 1.25100 − 1.25000 = 10 pips.
The 10-pip lower wick shows price dipped to 1.25000 and came back up a little before the hour ended. It does not tell you what the next candle will do.

lessons.explainSimpler: A candle is a tiny summary of one time period: start price, end price, top and bottom.
lessons.commonMistake: Reading a single candle as a prediction, for example "a long lower wick means price will rise". One candle only describes what already happened in one period.

quickCheck.prompt: A candle opens at 1.08500 and closes at 1.08350. What kind of candle is it?

options.text: A down candle
options.explanation: Right: the close is below the open, so price fell over the period.

options.text: An up candle
options.explanation: No: it opened at 1.08500 and closed lower, at 1.08350. An up candle closes above its open.

quickCheck.prompt: A EUR/USD candle has high 1.10400 and low 1.10120. What is its range?

options.text: 28 pips
2.8 pips
options.explanation: No: 0.00280 is 28 pips, because 1 pip is 0.00010.

options.text: 280 pips
options.explanation: No: that would be a range of 0.02800.

quickCheck.prompt: What do the wicks of a candle show?

options.text: The highest and lowest prices in the period
options.explanation: Right: the wicks run from the body out to the high and the low.

options.text: The opening and closing prices of the period
options.explanation: No: the open and close are the two ends of the body.

options.text: Where price will go next
options.explanation: No: a candle only describes the past period.

doItNow.instructions: Open Chart Lab on a candlestick chart. Long-press on 5 different candles to read their open, high, low and close. For each one, say whether it is an up or down candle and work out its range in pips.

lessons.title: Channel breakouts and choosing a lookback

inOneLine.simple: A channel marks the highest high and lowest low of the last few candles; a close beyond it is a breakout signal, and a shorter channel on the other side is the exit.
inOneLine.balanced: Most breaks fail and fall back inside, so the rule relies on the occasional break that becomes a long move. The lookback length changes the trades completely, and choosing it on past data is a common way to overfit.

explain.simple: The simplified version here uses the previous 20 daily candles for the entry [[channel]] and the previous 15 for the exit. A close above the 20-candle high enters long; a close below the 15-candle low exits. The channel leaves out the current candle, so a break means a close beyond every candle in the lookback. In Chart Lab, the Channel 20 overlay draws the 20-candle entry channel; count the 15-candle exit level from the candles. This is a simplified educational version, not any trader's system.
explain.balanced: A short lookback gives more signals and more [[false-breakout|false breakouts]]; a long one gives fewer, later signals. Comparing lookbacks is useful, but only if the final choice is tested on data that was not used to make it ([[out-of-sample]]). Gaps through the channel mean fills can be worse than the level, and the exit channel always gives back part of a gain before it triggers.

assumptions: Illustrative GBP/USD daily chart (simulated)
Previous 20 candles: high 1.3150, low 1.2980; previous 15 candles' low 1.3060
Account 10,000 USD (simulated); 1 pip = 1 USD per 10,000 units
steps: Today closes at 1.3165, above 1.3150: a long signal.
The order fills at the next open, 1.3170. The stop at the 15-candle low, 1.3060, is 110 pips away.
1% risk = 100 USD. 100 ÷ 110 ≈ 0.91 USD per pip, about 9,090 units. Round down to 9,000 units.
Check: 9,000 units = 0.90 USD per pip; 0.90 × 110 = 99 USD at the stop.

assumptions: Illustrative practice test, not real results
Lookbacks of 10, 20, 40 and 60 candles compared on simulated years 1–3, then checked on year 4
steps: On years 1–3, the 40-candle lookback did best: +0.30R per trade.
Year 4 was not used to choose it. There, the 40-candle lookback gave +0.05R per trade.
The drop suggests part of the year 1–3 result came from fitting that data's noise.
Out-of-sample results are the fairer guide, and they are usually weaker than the best in-sample result.

lessons.explainSimpler: Draw a box around recent prices. Buy when price closes above the top, and get out if it falls below a smaller box.
lessons.commonMistake: Counting an intraday spike above the channel as a breakout. The simplified rules use closes only, so a candle whose high pierced the channel but closed inside it is not a signal.

quickCheck.prompt: The previous 20 candles' highest high is 0.6850. Which daily close triggers a long?

options.text: 0.6840, after a high of 0.6862
options.explanation: No: the high pierced the channel, but the close is inside it.

options.text: 0.6850, exactly equal to the high
options.explanation: No: the close must be above the channel high, not equal to it.
Right: 0.6855 is a close above 0.6850.

quickCheck.prompt: A lookback chosen because it did best on years 1–3 does worse on year 4. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: It was partly fitted to the noise in years 1–3
options.explanation: Right: the best of many settings on one data set usually looks better than it is.

options.text: The year 4 data might be faulty
options.explanation: No: weaker out-of-sample results are normal, not a sign of bad data.

options.text: A shorter lookback is always better than a longer one
options.explanation: No: no lookback is always better; each trades differently.

doItNow.instructions: In Chart Lab, choose Breakout and turn on Channel 20. Mark each close beyond the channel. Then choose False breakout and count how many breaks fell back inside within 5 candles.

lessons.homework: Write down two lookbacks you would compare, and how you would keep some data aside to check the one you choose.

lessons.title: Currency pairs: base and quote

inOneLine.simple: A forex price tells you how much of one currency you need to buy one unit of another.
inOneLine.balanced: Every forex quote is a [[currency-pair]]: the price of one unit of the [[base-currency]] expressed in the [[quote-currency]].

explain.simple: In forex you always swap one currency for another, so prices come in pairs, like EUR/USD. The first currency (EUR) is the base. The second (USD) is the quote. The number shows how many US dollars one euro costs. If you buy EUR/USD, you buy euros and pay with dollars. If you sell EUR/USD, you sell euros and receive dollars.
explain.balanced: A [[currency-pair]] such as EUR/USD is read as 'one unit of the [[base-currency]] costs this many units of the [[quote-currency]]'. Buying the pair means going long the base and short the quote; selling means the opposite. When the price rises, the base has strengthened against the quote.
explain.advanced: A forex quote is an exchange rate between two currencies. Long EUR/USD is economically long EUR and short USD. Profit and loss are first measured in the quote currency and must be converted into your account currency when the two differ.

assumptions: EUR/USD is quoted at 1.1000
Ignore spread and costs for now
steps: 1 EUR costs 1.1000 USD.
To buy 1,000 EUR you need 1,000 × 1.1000 = 1,100 USD.
If EUR/USD rises to 1.1100, those 1,000 EUR are worth 1,110 USD: the euro strengthened against the dollar.

assumptions: USD/JPY is quoted at 150.00
Ignore spread and costs
steps: Here USD is the base and JPY is the quote: 1 US dollar costs 150 Japanese yen.
If USD/JPY falls to 148.00, one dollar buys fewer yen: the dollar weakened against the yen.

lessons.explainSimpler: EUR/USD = 1.1000 means: one euro costs 1.10 dollars. Buying the pair means buying euros.
lessons.commonMistake: Reading the pair backwards. In EUR/USD the price is in dollars per euro, not euros per dollar. If you buy expecting the dollar to get stronger, you have the trade the wrong way round.

quickCheck.prompt: In GBP/USD, which currency is the base?

options.text: GBP
options.explanation: Right: the first currency in the pair is the base.

options.text: USD
options.explanation: No: USD is second, so it is the quote currency the price is measured in.

quickCheck.prompt: EUR/USD moves from 1.1000 to 1.0900. What happened?

options.text: The euro weakened against the dollar
options.explanation: Right: one euro now buys fewer dollars.

options.text: The euro strengthened against the dollar
options.explanation: No: a lower price means one euro is worth fewer dollars.

options.text: Nothing changed for the euro
options.explanation: No: the price of a euro in dollars fell.

doItNow.instructions: Write down three currency pairs you have seen. For each one, name the base and the quote currency, and say what 'buying' that pair means.

lessons.title: Drawdowns, losing streaks and risk of ruin

inOneLine.simple: Losing runs happen to every trader. Deep falls are much harder to climb back from, so keep each loss small.
inOneLine.balanced: After a [[drawdown]] d, you need a gain of d ÷ (1 − d) to get back. [[losing-streak|Losing streaks]] are normal, and [[risk-of-ruin|risk of ruin]] rises fast as risk per trade grows.

explain.simple: A drawdown is how far your account has fallen from its highest point. Losses and gains are not equal: lose 50% and you need 100% just to get back. Losing streaks are normal, even for a plan that works over time. If you trade long enough, you will see one. Small risk per trade keeps a streak from becoming a disaster. Never raise size to win it back.
explain.balanced: Recovery needed = d ÷ (1 − d): 10% needs 11.1%, 20% needs 25%, 50% needs 100%. If each trade loses with chance L, independently, the chance that the next N trades all lose is L^N. The chance of seeing such a run somewhere in many trades is much higher. Risk of ruin is the chance of falling to a level where you must stop. It depends on win rate, reward to risk, risk per trade and your ruin level, and is best explored by simulation. Watch [[correlation]] too: two trades on pairs that move together can lose together, like one bigger trade.

assumptions: Example account with a peak of 10,000 USD
Drawdowns of 10%, 20% and 50% from that peak
No deposits or withdrawals
steps: 10% drawdown: account at 9,000 USD. Gain needed = 0.10 ÷ 0.90 = 11.1%.
20% drawdown: account at 8,000 USD. Gain needed = 2,000 ÷ 8,000 = 0.20 ÷ 0.80 = 25%.
50% drawdown: account at 5,000 USD. Gain needed = 0.50 ÷ 0.50 = 100%.
The deeper the fall, the faster the climb back grows. Small losses keep you in the shallow part.

assumptions: Example loss chance per trade: 50%, and each trade is independent of the last
Example rule: 1% of current balance risked per trade, on a 10,000 USD account
Stops fill at their level, no costs
steps: Chance the next 5 trades all lose = 0.5^5 = 0.03125, about 3.1%.
Chance of at least one run of 5 losses somewhere in 100 trades is about 81%. Over many trades, a streak is likely.
5 losses at 1% each: 10,000 × 0.99^5 = 9,509.90 USD, a drawdown of about 4.9%.
That streak is unpleasant but survivable. The same streak at a much bigger risk per trade would be far deeper.

lessons.explainSimpler: Falling down a hole is quick. Climbing out takes longer the deeper it is. Expect losing runs, and keep each loss small so you never fall too far.
lessons.commonMistake: Thinking a losing streak means the plan is broken, or that a win is now 'due'. Each trade is a new event. The other big mistake is raising size to recover losses, which makes ruin more likely.

quickCheck.prompt: Your example account falls 30% from its peak. What gain do you need to get back?

options.text: 30%, the same as the loss
options.explanation: No: the gain is measured on a smaller balance, so it must be bigger.

options.text: About 42.9%

options.explanation: No: 0.30 ÷ (1 − 0.30) is about 42.9%, not double the drawdown.

quickCheck.prompt: You have had 6 losses in a row while following your plan. What is a sound response?

options.text: Double the size, because a win is due
options.explanation: No: a win is not due, and bigger size after losses deepens the drawdown.

options.text: Keep or cut the risk, pause, and review the trades against the plan
options.explanation: Right: streaks are normal. Review whether the rules were followed before changing anything.

options.text: Delete the losing journal entries so they do not drag down your statistics
options.explanation: No: losing trades are part of the honest record.

quickCheck.prompt: You buy EUR/USD and GBP/USD, each risking your example 1%. Why might your real risk be higher than 1%?

options.text: The pairs may move together, so both can lose at once
options.explanation: Right: correlated trades can act like one bigger trade, here up to about 2%.

options.text: It cannot: each trade is only 1%
options.explanation: No: two trades that each risk 1% can lose about 2% together.

doItNow.instructions: Open Learn → Calculators. In Losing streak chance, keep 100 trades and a 50% example loss chance, and try streaks of 5, 8 and 10. Then in Risk of ruin (simulated), compare risk per trade of 1%, 2% and 5% with the other inputs unchanged. Write down what you notice.

lessons.homework: Write one rule for what you will do after a losing streak, for example pause and review after a set number of losses. Add it in More → Risk rules.

lessons.title: Jobs data: expected vs. actual

inOneLine.simple: Markets react to the gap between what was expected and what came out, not to the number alone.
inOneLine.balanced: [[surprise|Surprise]] = actual − [[consensus-forecast]]. A bigger surprise often means a bigger move, but the direction can still go either way, or the news may already be priced in.

explain.simple: Before a release such as an [[employment-report]], forecasters publish what they expect. Prices start to reflect that guess. When the real number comes out, traders compare it with the guess. Better than expected and worse than expected are what move prices. A number that matches the guess may cause little change. But the reaction is never certain. The first jump can reverse within minutes.
explain.balanced: A jobs report has several parts: jobs added, the unemployment rate, wages, and revisions to earlier months. They can point in different directions. Traders may also have expected something different from the published consensus. So the same surprise can bring different reactions: a lasting move, a spike that reverses, or almost nothing. Read each case as a set of possible scenarios. All examples here are fictional.

assumptions: Fictional country: Westmark, currency WMK
Hypothetical consensus: +150,000 jobs; unemployment 4.5%
Hypothetical actual: +90,000 jobs; unemployment 4.3%
steps: Jobs surprise = 90,000 − 150,000 = −60,000. Weaker than expected.
Unemployment surprise = 4.3% − 4.5% = −0.2 points. Lower unemployment is stronger than expected.
The two parts disagree. WMK could fall on the weak jobs number, rise on the low unemployment, or swing both ways.
Scenario thinking: list each possible reaction and what would make it more likely. Do not pick one as certain.

assumptions: Fictional Westmark inflation release
Hypothetical consensus 2.5%, hypothetical actual 2.9%
Three made-up market stories for the same number
steps: Surprise = 2.9% − 2.5% = +0.4 points, higher than expected.
Story 1: traders now expect higher rates, and WMK rises and holds.
Story 2: many traders had already bet on a high number. WMK spikes, then falls back as they take profits.
Story 3: a bigger story elsewhere dominates the day, and WMK hardly moves. Same number, three different outcomes.

lessons.explainSimpler: It is not 'good news, price up'. It is 'better or worse than people guessed'. Even then, the market can surprise you.
lessons.commonMistake: Reading only the headline number and ignoring the forecast. Another mistake is assuming the first move after a release will continue. It often reverses.

quickCheck.prompt: Hypothetical release: consensus 3.0%, actual 3.4%. What is the surprise?

options.text: +0.4 points
options.explanation: Right: 3.4 − 3.0 = +0.4 points.

options.text: −0.4 points, a negative surprise
options.explanation: No: surprise is actual minus expected, and actual is higher.

options.text: 3.4 points
options.explanation: No: that is the actual figure, not the gap.

quickCheck.prompt: A fictional jobs report comes out exactly in line with the consensus. What is the most accurate expectation?

options.text: No move at all, because there is no surprise to react to
options.explanation: No: other parts of the report and revisions can still move price.

options.text: Often a smaller reaction, but other details can still move price either way
options.explanation: Right: no headline surprise, but wages, revisions or the unemployment rate may matter.

options.text: A large move in the direction of the recent trend, since the news was as expected
options.explanation: No: an in-line release gives no headline surprise, and it does not decide the direction of any move.

quickCheck.prompt: Why can a better-than-expected number still be followed by the currency falling?

options.text: Traders may have expected even better, or already bought before the release
options.explanation: Right: if it was priced in, some traders sell into the news.

options.text: The number must have been wrong, so the market ignores it
options.explanation: No: the number does not need to be wrong. What traders expected, and how they were already positioned, can matter more than the headline.

doItNow.instructions: News scenarios: make up three fictional releases, each with a consensus and an actual. For each, work out the surprise and write two different ways the currency could react, with a reason for each.

lessons.title: False breakouts and retests

inOneLine.simple: A false breakout goes through a level, then comes back inside. You only know it was false afterwards.
inOneLine.balanced: A [[false-breakout]] meets your breakout rule, then fails. Waiting for more confirmation, such as a [[retest]], avoids some false breakouts but costs a later, worse entry and still catches some.

explain.simple: Imagine price closes above resistance, so it looks like a breakout. Then the next candles fall back into the old range. That was a false breakout. Anyone who bought on the first close may hit their stop loss. There is no way to tell for certain at the moment of the breakout which kind it will be. What you can control is your plan: where your stop goes, how much you risk, and what would show you were wrong.
explain.balanced: Ways people try to filter false breakouts include waiting for a second close beyond the level, waiting for a retest that holds, or only taking breakouts in the direction of the longer-timeframe [[trend]]. Each one trades fewer false signals for later entries and missed moves. None removes false breakouts. In ranges, false breakouts at the edges are common. Practise judging them in replay, where future candles stay hidden.

assumptions: Illustrative GBP/USD H1 range: support 1.25000, resistance 1.25600 (60 pips high)
Breakout rule: close at least 5 pips above 1.25600
Buy 0.10 lot at the breakout close 1.25680; pip value 1 USD; stop loss 1.25480
No slippage, and the spread is ignored to keep the numbers simple
steps: The breakout close at 1.25680 is 8 pips above 1.25600, so it meets the rule.
Stop distance = 1.25680 − 1.25480 = 20 pips. Planned loss = 20 × 1 USD = 20 USD.
The next two candles close at 1.25550 and 1.25400, back inside the range. The stop at 1.25480 is hit on the way down.
Loss = 20 USD. Looking back, this was a false breakout. At the time of entry, it looked the same as a breakout that works.

assumptions: Same illustrative resistance at 1.25600 on a different day
Rule B: wait for a second H1 close above 1.25650 before buying
steps: First close above: 1.25680. Under rule A you would have bought here.
Second close: 1.25740. Under rule B you buy here, 1.25740 − 1.25680 = 6 pips higher.
If the second candle had closed back inside, rule B would have skipped a false breakout that rule A took.
But when the move continues, rule B always pays a later price, and if price fails after the second close, rule B loses too. Neither rule is safe.

lessons.explainSimpler: A false breakout is a door that opens and slams shut. You cannot tell which doors will stay open, so plan for both.
lessons.commonMistake: Thinking false breakouts mean someone is "hunting stops" every time, or that a special trick can always spot them. Most of the time you cannot tell in advance. Size your trade so the loss is acceptable if it fails.

quickCheck.prompt: Resistance is 1.30000. A candle closes at 1.30080, then the next two close at 1.29950 and 1.29800. What was it?

options.text: A false breakout
options.explanation: Right: it closed above, then fell back below the level.

options.text: A successful breakout
options.explanation: No: price did not stay above the level.

quickCheck.prompt: Buy 0.10 lot (pip value 1 USD) at 1.10580 with a stop at 1.10430. It turns into a false breakout and the stop fills at its level. What is the loss?

options.text: 15 USD
1.50 USD
options.explanation: No: 0.00150 is 15 pips, not 1.5.

options.text: 150 USD
options.explanation: No: that would need a pip value of 10 USD.

quickCheck.prompt: What is the trade-off of waiting for a retest before entering?

options.text: It can skip some false breakouts, but you may miss moves or enter later
options.explanation: Right: every filter costs something.

options.text: It removes false breakouts completely
options.explanation: No: a retest can hold and then fail as well.

doItNow.instructions: Start a replay on the false breakout scenario. Before each new candle, decide: breakout, false breakout, or not sure yet. Write down your call, then reveal the next candle. Repeat on the breakout scenario and compare.

lessons.title: Fills, slippage and gaps

inOneLine.simple: The price you ask for is not always the price you get. A stop loss is not a guaranteed price.
inOneLine.balanced: [[slippage|Slippage]] and [[gap|gaps]] mean orders, including stops, can fill at worse prices than planned, unless your broker offers a guaranteed stop.

explain.simple: A fill is the price your order actually gets. In a calm market it is usually close to what you saw. When prices move fast, for example around big news, your order can fill at a different price. This is slippage. It can be worse or better. A gap is a jump in price, for example from Friday's close to Monday's open. If your stop loss sits inside the gap, it fills at the first price after the gap, which can be far worse. Your loss can then be bigger than you planned.
explain.balanced: A [[stop-loss]] and a [[stop-order]] become market orders when triggered, so they take the next available price. [[liquidity|Thin liquidity]], news releases and market opens raise the risk of slippage and gaps. Some brokers offer a guaranteed stop, usually for an extra cost; only that kind of stop promises the exact price. Plan your size so that a worse-than-planned fill would still be survivable.

assumptions: Illustrative prices
Account currency USD
Buy 0.10 lot EUR/USD at 1.10000; pip value 1 USD
Stop loss at 1.09500 (50 pips below)
Market closes with the bid at 1.09800 and reopens with the bid at 1.09200
steps: Planned loss = 50 × 1 USD = 50 USD.
The reopen price 1.09200 is already below the stop, so the stop triggers.
Actual loss = 80 × 1 USD = 80 USD, 30 USD more than planned.

assumptions: Illustrative prices
Buy 0.10 lot EUR/USD at market; pip value 1 USD
The ask on screen is 1.10012
steps: Case A: the fill is 1.10020. Slippage = 0.8 pips against you = 0.80 USD.
Case B: the fill is 1.10008. Slippage = 0.4 pips in your favour = 0.40 USD.
Check the fill price in your trade history, not just the price you saw before tapping.

lessons.explainSimpler: Your stop loss is an instruction to get out, not a promise of the exact price. If price jumps past it, you get out at the next price available.
lessons.commonMistake: Believing a stop loss caps the loss exactly at its level. It caps it only in normal conditions. In a gap or a fast market, the loss can be larger. Only a guaranteed stop, if your broker offers one, promises the level.

quickCheck.prompt: Your buy trade's stop is at 1.09500. The market reopens at 1.09300. Roughly where does the stop fill?

options.explanation: Right: the stop becomes a market order and takes the first available price after the gap.

options.text: Exactly 1.09500
options.explanation: No: a normal stop is not a guaranteed price. Price never traded at 1.09500.

quickCheck.prompt: Which statements about slippage are true? Choose all that apply.

options.text: It can be in your favour or against you
options.explanation: True: the fill can be better or worse than the price you saw.

options.text: It is more likely around big news
options.explanation: True: prices move fast and liquidity can thin out.

options.text: A normal stop loss prevents it
options.explanation: False: a normal stop becomes a market order and can slip too.

doItNow.instructions: In MetaTrader, open the History tab on your demo account. For your last few closed trades, compare the price you expected with the open and close prices shown. Note any slippage in pips.

lessons.homework: Before the next weekend, write down what would happen to a demo trade's stop loss if the market reopened past it, and how much you would lose at 0.10 lot.

lessons.title: Forward testing your plan on a demo account

inOneLine.simple: A [[forward-test]] means following your plan in real time on a [[demo-account]], where you cannot skip ahead.
inOneLine.balanced: Replay tests the past. A forward test adds what replay leaves out: waiting in real time, changing spreads, [[slippage]], and your own reactions. Demo money is pretend, so it still differs from real trading.

explain.simple: After replay, the next step is to follow the same plan on your MetaTrader demo account, in real time. This is a forward test. It feels different. You have to wait for setups. Spreads widen and narrow. Orders can fill at a slightly different price. You may feel bored, impatient or tempted to break a rule. All of that is useful to learn. Before each demo trade, run the pre-trade checklist. Then place the trade exactly as your plan says, with a stop loss. The goal for this module is 20 or more demo trades, each logged in the Journal with a screenshot.
explain.balanced: Keep the plan version fixed during the forward test, so results are comparable. Compare demo fills with your planned prices: the gap between them shows real costs like the [[spread]] and slippage that replay may not show. Remember the limits. Demo trades use pretend money, so the fear of real loss is missing, and some brokers' demo fills may differ from live fills. And 20 trades is a small sample. The forward test is about whether you can follow your plan in real time, not about proving the plan makes money.

assumptions: Fictional demo trade, illustrative prices, account currency USD
Plan: buy EUR/USD at 1.08500, stop 1.08300 (20 pips), 0.10 lot, pip value 1 USD
Actual fill: 1.08510 (1 pip worse, from slippage)
steps: Planned risk = 20 pips × 1 USD = 20 USD.
Actual stop distance = 1.08510 − 1.08300 = 21 pips.
Actual risk = 21 × 1 USD = 21 USD, 1 USD more than planned.
The learner records both numbers in the Journal. Small differences like this are normal in live conditions.

assumptions: Fictional learner, first week of forward testing
Plan allows 2 trades per day; 5 trading days
steps: Setups appeared on 3 of the 5 days. The learner took 5 trades in total.
On one quiet day, the learner felt bored and took a trade that was not in the plan.
The Journal flags that trade as a rule break.
Lesson learned: waiting is part of the plan. A day with no trades can be a day of perfect discipline.

lessons.explainSimpler: Replay is practising with the answers hidden. Forward testing is practising in real time, at the speed of the real market.
lessons.commonMistake: Changing the plan every few demo trades. Then no version gets enough trades to learn from.

quickCheck.prompt: What does a forward test add that a replay test does not?

options.text: Real-time waiting, changing spreads, slippage and your live reactions
options.explanation: Right: these only show up when you trade in real time.

options.text: Proof that the plan works, because it now uses real-time prices
options.explanation: No: real-time prices do not prove anything. No test can show that a plan will work in future.

quickCheck.prompt: Planned stop 30 pips. Fill 2 pips worse than planned. Pip value 1 USD. What is the actual risk?

options.text: 30 USD, the planned risk
options.explanation: No: the worse fill added 2 pips.

options.text: 32 USD
options.explanation: Right: 32 pips × 1 USD = 32 USD.

options.text: 28 USD
options.explanation: No: a worse fill increases the distance to the stop.

quickCheck.prompt: Why can demo results differ from real trading?

options.text: Demo money is pretend, so emotions differ, and fills may differ too
options.explanation: Right: demo is useful practice, not a copy of real trading.

options.text: They cannot differ, since demo accounts use live prices
options.explanation: No: prices may be similar, but fills, costs and feelings can differ.

doItNow.instructions: Run the pre-trade checklist, then place one demo trade on MetaTrader exactly as your plan says, with a stop loss and take profit. Follow the task card if you need a reminder of the steps. Take a screenshot of the chart at entry.

lessons.title: Journaling and reviewing demo trades

inOneLine.simple: Log every demo trade in your [[trading-journal]] with a screenshot, then review it. The [[process-score]] judges how you followed your plan, never the profit.
inOneLine.balanced: Add demo trades by hand with a screenshot, or import your MetaTrader statement. Each review goes: thesis → plan vs. actual → rules followed? → result (kept separate from decision quality) → one lesson → next learning goal.

explain.simple: A trade you do not write down is a trade you cannot learn from. In the Journal, add each MetaTrader demo trade: pair, direction, entry, stop, target, size, exit, and a screenshot of the chart. You can also export your demo history from MetaTrader and import it in the Journal. Then review each trade in six steps. What was my idea? Did I do what I planned? Did I follow my rules? What was the result? What is one lesson? What will I work on next? The app gives a process score. It never uses profit. A winning trade that broke your rules scores lower than a losing trade that followed them.
explain.balanced: Separating result from decision quality is the core skill here. Over a few trades, a bad decision can win and a good decision can lose. If you judge by result, you learn the wrong lessons. The process score looks at things like: was the stop set before entry, was risk within the limit, did the entry match the rules, and was the review done. Imported trades are marked "Imported from MT statement" and kept separate from replay and paper trades, so sources never mix.

assumptions: Fictional demo trade A: in plan, stop set, risk 20 USD (within limit)
Stop hit; result −20 USD
Fictional demo trade B: not in plan, stop moved further away during the trade
Price came back; result +15 USD
steps: Trade A: followed every rule. Result was a loss. Process: good.
Trade B: broke two rules. Result was a gain. Process: poor.
The process score rates A above B.
Lesson from B: moving the stop happened to work this time, but it removes the limit on the loss. The habit matters more than this one result.

assumptions: Fictional review of one demo trade, filled in by the learner
steps: Thesis: "Price broke above the session high on the 1-hour chart."
Plan vs. actual: entry planned 1.27200, filled 1.27215. Stop and size as planned.
Rules followed? Yes, all of them.
Result: −1R. Decision quality: good, the setup matched the plan.
One lesson: "I entered 2 minutes before a news release; my plan should say how long to wait."
Next learning goal: add a news timing rule as a new plan version.

lessons.explainSimpler: Judge the cook by whether they followed the recipe, not by whether one dinner guest liked it.
lessons.commonMistake: Only journaling the losing trades, or only the winners. Every trade goes in, or the review is skewed.

quickCheck.prompt: Which trade gets the better process score?

options.text: A rule-breaking trade that made money
options.explanation: No: profit is never part of the process score.

options.text: A planned trade with a stop that lost its planned amount
options.explanation: Right: following the plan is what scores, whatever the result.

quickCheck.prompt: In the review flow, why is "result" separate from decision quality?

options.text: Because good decisions can lose and bad ones can win over a few trades
options.explanation: Right: judging by result teaches the wrong lessons.

options.text: Because results do not matter, so the journal does not record them
options.explanation: No: results are recorded; they are just not the measure of a good decision.

doItNow.instructions: Export your demo account history from MetaTrader by following the task card, then import it in Journal. Open each imported trade, add a screenshot, and complete the six-step review. If your app version cannot export, add your demo trades by hand with screenshots instead.

lessons.homework: Keep going until you have 20 or more demo trades logged with screenshots and reviewed.

lessons.title: Leverage and margin

inOneLine.simple: Leverage lets a small deposit, called margin, hold a big trade. It makes losses bigger as well as gains.
inOneLine.balanced: Required [[margin]] = trade value ÷ [[leverage]], converted to your account currency. Leverage changes the deposit needed, not the profit or loss per pip.

explain.simple: With leverage, your broker lets you open a trade much bigger than the money you put down. The money set aside is called margin. At 1:30 leverage, 1 dollar of margin holds 30 dollars of trade. Your profit or loss is based on the full trade size, not on the margin. So a small move in price can make a large dent in your account. Margin is a deposit. It is not the most you can lose.
explain.balanced: Required margin = units × price (in the quote currency) ÷ leverage, then converted into the account currency. Leverage limits are set by brokers and, in many places, by regulators, and they can differ between instruments. Higher leverage means less margin per trade, which makes it easy to open trades that are too big. Risk is set by size and stop distance, not by leverage, but leverage is what lets oversized trades happen. Losses can exceed the margin, and in some cases the account balance.

assumptions: Illustrative prices and leverage, not any broker's actual terms
Account currency USD
EUR/USD price 1.1000
Size 0.10 lot = 10,000 EUR (100,000-unit contract)
Leverage 1:30
steps: Trade value in USD = 10,000 × 1.1000 = 11,000 USD.
Required margin = 11,000 ÷ 30 = 366.67 USD (rounded).
Pip value = 10,000 × 0.0001 = 1 USD per pip.
A 100-pip move against you = 100 × 1 = 100 USD lost, more than a quarter of the margin.
A 100-pip move for you = 100 USD gained. Leverage magnifies both directions.

assumptions: Illustrative prices and leverage
Account currency USD
USD/JPY price 150.00
Size 0.10 lot = 10,000 USD
Leverage 1:50
steps: The base currency is USD, so the trade value is already 10,000 USD.
Required margin = 10,000 ÷ 50 = 200 USD.
If the same trade used 1:20 leverage instead, margin = 10,000 ÷ 20 = 500 USD.
The profit or loss per pip is the same in both cases: 10,000 × 0.01 = 100 JPY, about 0.67 USD at 150.00.

lessons.explainSimpler: Leverage is like putting down a small deposit on something big. If its price falls, you lose on the whole thing, not just the deposit.
lessons.commonMistake: Thinking that margin is the most you can lose, or that high leverage is a free bonus. Margin is only the deposit. Losses come from the full trade size, and with high leverage it is easy to open a trade far too big for the account.

quickCheck.prompt: GBP/USD at 1.2500, 0.10 lot (10,000 GBP), leverage 1:50, account in USD. What margin is required?

options.text: 200 USD
options.explanation: No: that uses 10,000 without converting GBP to USD first.

options.text: 250 USD

options.explanation: No: that is the full trade value, before leverage.

quickCheck.prompt: Which statement about leverage is true?

options.text: It magnifies losses as well as gains
options.explanation: Right: profit and loss come from the full trade size, in both directions.

options.text: It limits your loss to the margin
options.explanation: No: losses can be larger than the margin.

options.text: It only magnifies gains
options.explanation: No: a move against you is magnified in exactly the same way.

doItNow.instructions: Open the margin calculator. For each trade on your list of 10, enter the pair, size, price, leverage and account currency, and write down the required margin. Do at least two by hand first.

lessons.homework: Finish your list of 10 trades with pip value and required margin for each. Include at least two pairs where the account currency is not the quote currency.

lessons.title: Lot sizes

inOneLine.simple: A lot is the unit for trade size. Bigger lots mean each pip is worth more money.
inOneLine.balanced: By common convention 1.00 [[lot]] is 100,000 units of the [[base-currency]], 0.10 is 10,000 and 0.01 is 1,000, but your broker's [[contract-size]] decides the real number.

explain.simple: You choose your trade size in lots. Usually a standard lot is 100,000 units of the first currency in the pair. A mini lot (0.10) is 10,000 units. A micro lot (0.01) is 1,000 units. MetaTrader calls the size 'volume' and shows it in lots. Brokers can use a different contract size, so check it for each symbol before you trade.
explain.balanced: Size in units = lots × [[contract-size]]. With the common 100,000-unit contract, 0.25 lots is 25,000 units of the base currency. The size you pick sets how much each [[pip]] is worth and how much [[margin]] the trade needs. The smallest size and the size steps allowed also depend on the broker.

assumptions: Contract size 100,000 units per lot (check your broker)
Trade on EUR/USD, so the units are euros
A made-up broker symbol whose contract specification says 10,000 units per lot
This is only to show why checking matters; it is not any real broker's setting
steps: The same 'lot' number gives a size ten times smaller than with a 100,000-unit contract, so pip value and margin are ten times smaller too.

lessons.explainSimpler: Lots are like box sizes. A standard box holds 100,000, a mini box 10,000, and a micro box 1,000. Check the label on your broker's boxes.
lessons.commonMistake: Thinking 1.00 lot is a small trade because the number looks small. With a 100,000-unit contract, 1.00 lot on EUR/USD moves about 10 USD per pip. Start practice with 0.01 lots and always check the contract size.

quickCheck.prompt: With a 100,000-unit contract, how many units is 0.05 lots?

options.explanation: No: that would be 0.005 lots.
No: that would be 0.50 lots.

quickCheck.prompt: Where should you check how many units one lot is for a symbol?

options.text: Your broker's contract specification for that symbol
options.explanation: Right: the broker sets the contract size, and it can differ between symbols.

options.text: Nowhere: one lot is always 100,000 units everywhere
options.explanation: No: 100,000 is a common convention, not a rule every broker follows.

doItNow.instructions: Open the pip value calculator. Enter EUR/USD with 0.01, 0.10 and 1.00 lots and a 100,000-unit contract. Write down the pip value for each and notice how it grows with size.

lessons.homework: Find your demo broker's contract specification for EUR/USD (often on its website) and write down the contract size and the smallest volume allowed.

lessons.title: Moving-average trend following

inOneLine.simple: Hold a position while price stays on the right side of a moving average that points in the same direction, and step aside when it crosses back.
inOneLine.balanced: The rule reacts only to moves that have already happened, so it is always late. It accepts many small losses in sideways markets in exchange for staying in during long trends.

explain.simple: The simplified version here uses a daily chart and a 50-period exponential [[moving-average]] (EMA 50). A long is allowed when a candle closes above the average and the average is higher than it was 10 candles ago. The position is closed when a candle closes back below. The stop sits 2 × [[atr]] from the entry, and the size risks no more than 1% of the account. This is a simplified educational version, not any trader's system.
explain.balanced: Because the average is built from past closes, the entry comes after part of the move and the exit after part of the reversal. In a range, price crosses a flat average again and again, producing a run of small losses ([[whipsaw]]). The rule set works only if occasional long trends pay for those losses and the costs. The 50-period setting is an example; testing many settings on the same data and keeping the best invites [[overfitting]].

assumptions: Illustrative EUR/USD daily chart (simulated)
50-period average: 1.0950 ten candles ago, 1.1010 now; latest close 1.1030
ATR 0.0035; account 10,000 USD (simulated); 1 pip = 1 USD per 10,000 units
steps: The close (1.1030) is above the average (1.1010), and the average has risen from 1.0950: a long is allowed.
If the order fills at 1.1030, the stop is 2 × 0.0035 = 0.0070 below, at 1.0960: 70 pips.
1% risk = 100 USD. 100 ÷ 70 ≈ 1.43 USD per pip, which is about 14,286 units. Round down to 14,000 units.
Check: 14,000 units = 1.40 USD per pip; 1.40 × 70 = 98 USD at the stop, within the 100 USD limit.

assumptions: An illustrative 60-candle stretch (simulated)
40 sideways candles, then a 20-candle trend
Spread cost 1.5 pips per trade
steps: In the sideways part the rule enters and exits 6 times, losing about 25 pips each: 6 × 25 = 150 pips lost.
The trend then gives one trade of about 300 pips.
Before costs: 300 − 150 = +150 pips. Spread: 7 trades × 1.5 = 10.5 pips. After costs: about +139.5 pips.
If the trend had not come, or had been shorter, the same rules would have ended with a loss.

lessons.explainSimpler: Follow the arrow on the average: stay in while price is above a rising line, get out when it falls back below.
lessons.commonMistake: Dropping the rules after a run of whipsaw losses. Those losses are the normal cost of the method, and skipping trades by feel means the next trend may be missed.

quickCheck.prompt: Average 1.2500 now (1.2460 ten candles ago), close 1.2530, ATR 0.0020. Where is a 2 × ATR stop for a long filled at 1.2530?

options.text: 1.2510, one ATR below
options.explanation: No: that uses 1 × ATR. The rule uses 2 × 0.0020 = 0.0040.

options.text: 1.2460, the old average
options.explanation: No: the old average is part of the trend test, not the stop.

quickCheck.prompt: Why do trend-following rules often have more losing trades than winning ones?

options.text: They are built to lose most trades
options.explanation: No: losing often is a side effect, not the aim.

options.text: Moving averages never change direction
options.explanation: No: they do change direction, but late.

options.text: Most crosses happen in sideways markets and soon reverse
options.explanation: Right: most crosses come in sideways markets and reverse soon after, so most trades are small losses; occasional long trends pay for them.

doItNow.instructions: In Chart Lab, choose Strong uptrend and turn on EMA 50. Find the first close above the rising average and the first close back below it. Then choose Range and count the false starts.

lessons.title: MACD: the gap between two averages

inOneLine.simple: MACD shows how far a fast average is from a slow one. Because it is built from averages, it lags too.
inOneLine.balanced: With the usual settings, the [[macd|MACD]] line = EMA 12 − EMA 26, the signal line = EMA 9 of the MACD line, and the histogram = MACD line − signal line.

explain.simple: Take two moving averages: a fast one (12 periods) and a slow one (26 periods). When price has been rising, the fast one sits above the slow one, and the MACD line is positive. When price has been falling, it is negative. The signal line is an average of the MACD line, and the histogram is the gap between them. A growing gap means the recent move has been speeding up. A shrinking gap means it has been slowing.
explain.balanced: MACD is in price units, so a MACD of 0.0015 on EUR/USD and 0.30 on USD/JPY cannot be compared directly. Crosses of the MACD and signal lines come after the averages turn, so they are late by design. In a range, the lines cross back and forth near zero and most crosses lead nowhere. MetaTrader's built-in MACD usually draws the MACD line as bars and the signal as a line, with no separate histogram, while Chart Lab draws the histogram as bars. Apps also differ in small details, such as which kind of average the signal line uses, so values can differ slightly between apps. Check what each part means in each app.

assumptions: Illustrative EUR/USD H4 values
steps: The MACD line is positive, so the fast average is above the slow one: price has been rising recently.
The histogram is positive, so the MACD line is above its own average. It describes the recent past, not the next candle.

assumptions: Illustrative USD/JPY H4 values; 1 pip = 0.01
steps: MACD line = 150.40 − 150.10 = 0.30, which is 30 pips.
On EUR/USD, a gap of 30 pips would show as 0.00300. The numbers look very different for the same size of gap.
So compare MACD with its own history on the same pair, not across pairs.
If the pair then moves sideways, the two EMAs drift together and the MACD line moves toward zero, with frequent crosses.

lessons.explainSimpler: MACD measures the distance between a quick average and a slow one. Wide gap: a strong recent move. Small gap: not much happening.
lessons.commonMistake: Treating each MACD and signal line cross as a buy or sell signal. The crosses come late, and in sideways markets most of them reverse.

quickCheck.prompt: EMA 12 = 1.25300 and EMA 26 = 1.25500. What is the MACD line?

options.explanation: Right: 1.25300 − 1.25500 = −0.00200, so the fast average is below the slow one.

options.text: +0.00200 (fast above slow)
options.explanation: No: the fast EMA (1.25300) is below the slow one (1.25500), so fast − slow is negative.
No: that is the midpoint, not the difference.

quickCheck.prompt: Why does MACD lag price?

options.text: It is calculated from moving averages of past prices
options.explanation: Right: averages always run behind price.

options.text: It waits for each candle to close
options.explanation: No: the lag comes from averaging past prices, not from waiting for a close.

quickCheck.prompt: Can you say a MACD of 0.30 on USD/JPY is stronger than 0.00150 on EUR/USD?

options.text: No: MACD is in each pair's own price units
options.explanation: Right: compare it only with its own history on the same pair.

options.text: Yes: 0.30 is a bigger reading, so the move behind it is stronger
options.explanation: No: yen pairs are quoted with far fewer decimal places, so the numbers are on different scales.

doItNow.instructions: In Chart Lab, show MACD below the chart. Choose the Range scenario and count the MACD and signal line crosses. Then choose the Breakout scenario and see how far price had already moved before the lines crossed.

lessons.title: Equity, free margin and margin level

inOneLine.simple: As open trades lose money, your free margin and margin level fall. Too low, and the broker can close your trades.
inOneLine.balanced: [[equity|Equity]] = [[balance]] ± open profit or loss; [[free-margin|free margin]] = equity − used margin; [[margin-level|margin level]] = equity ÷ used margin × 100%.

explain.simple: Your balance is the money in the account before open trades. Equity is the balance plus or minus what your open trades are making or losing right now. Free margin is the equity left after the margin your trades use. Margin level compares equity with used margin as a percentage. If margin level drops to a level set by your broker, you get a margin call: a warning. If it drops further, to the stop-out level, the broker closes trades for you. Each broker sets its own levels.
explain.balanced: These numbers move with every price change. A [[margin-call]] usually means you cannot open new trades and should act. A [[stop-out]] means the broker starts closing positions at market prices, often the largest loser first, without asking. The margin call and stop-out levels are broker-specific and can differ by account type, so read your broker's terms. In a fast market or a [[gap]], the closing price can be worse than the stop-out level suggests.

assumptions: Illustrative numbers only
Account currency USD
Balance 1,000 USD
One open trade using 200 USD of margin
The trade currently shows a loss of 150 USD
steps: Free margin = 850 − 200 = 650 USD.
The balance is still 1,000 USD, because the trade is not closed yet.

assumptions: Same account: balance 1,000 USD, used margin 200 USD
A made-up broker with a margin call at 100% and a stop-out at 50%; real levels differ by broker
steps: Margin call at 100% means equity = 200 × 100% = 200 USD.
That happens when the open loss reaches 1,000 − 200 = 800 USD.
Stop-out at 50% means equity = 200 × 50% = 100 USD.
That happens when the open loss reaches 1,000 − 100 = 900 USD.
At that point most of the account is already gone. A stop-out is not protection; it is the last step.

lessons.explainSimpler: Margin level is a fuel gauge. When it gets low, the broker warns you. When it gets very low, the broker switches the engine off by closing your trades.
lessons.commonMistake: Watching only the balance. The balance does not change until a trade closes, while equity and margin level can fall fast. Another mistake is waiting for a margin call to act. By then, much of the account may be lost.

quickCheck.prompt: Equity is 500 USD and used margin is 250 USD. What is the margin level?

options.explanation: No: that divides margin by equity. Margin level is equity ÷ margin.

options.text: 250 USD
options.explanation: No: 250 is the margin in dollars, not the margin level.

quickCheck.prompt: Balance 2,000 USD, open loss 300 USD, used margin 400 USD. What is the free margin?

options.explanation: No: that uses the balance, not the equity, so the open loss is missed.
No: that is the equity. Free margin also subtracts the used margin.

quickCheck.prompt: Who sets the margin call and stop-out levels?

options.text: Each broker, and they can differ
options.explanation: Right: check your own broker's terms for the exact levels.

options.text: One rule for every broker
options.explanation: No: there is no single universal level.

doItNow.instructions: On your demo account in MetaTrader, open the Trade tab. Read your balance, equity, margin, free margin and margin level. Then follow the task card to see how they change with one small demo trade.

lessons.homework: Find your demo broker's margin call and stop-out levels in its terms or account information, and write them down.

lessons.title: Market orders

inOneLine.simple: A market order opens a trade now, at the best price available. You buy at the ask and sell at the bid.
inOneLine.balanced: A [[market-order]] trades immediately: buys fill near the [[ask]], sells near the [[bid]]. Speed is certain; the exact price is not.

explain.simple: A market order says: open my trade now. A buy fills at the ask, the higher price. A sell fills at the bid, the lower price. To close, you do the opposite: a buy is closed by selling at the bid, and a sell is closed by buying at the ask. That is why a new trade shows a small loss straight away. It is the spread.
explain.balanced: Market orders favour speed over price. The fill can differ from the price on screen if the market moves while the order travels, which is called [[slippage]]. Profit or loss on a buy = (closing bid − opening ask) in pips × [[pip-value]]. On a sell = (opening bid − closing ask) in pips × pip value.

assumptions: Illustrative prices, not live data
Account currency USD
EUR/USD bid 1.10000, ask 1.10012
Buy 0.10 lot = 10,000 EUR; pip value 1 USD
No slippage in this example
steps: The buy fills at the ask: 1.10012.
To close now you would sell at the bid: 1.10000.
Open result right away = −1.2 × 1 USD = −1.20 USD. That is the spread cost.

assumptions: Illustrative prices
Account currency USD
Sell 0.10 lot GBP/USD = 10,000 GBP; pip value 1 USD
Later: bid 1.24800, ask 1.24820
steps: The sell fills at the bid: 1.25000.
To close, you buy at the ask: 1.24820.
Profit = 18 × 1 USD = 18 USD.

lessons.explainSimpler: A market order is like saying 'I'll take it at whatever the price is now.' You get in fast, but you start a little behind because of the spread.
lessons.commonMistake: Working out a sell trade's result from the bid on the chart. A sell closes at the ask, which is higher than the bid by the spread, so the real result is a bit worse than the chart line suggests.

quickCheck.prompt: You have an open buy trade. At which price will it close?

options.text: The bid
options.explanation: Right: closing a buy means selling, and sells happen at the bid.

options.text: The ask
options.explanation: No: the ask is where a buy opens, not where it closes.

options.text: The price where you opened the trade
options.explanation: No: the price has moved since then. A buy closes at the current bid.

quickCheck.prompt: Buy 0.10 lot EUR/USD (pip value 1 USD) at ask 1.10050. You close at bid 1.10350. What is the result?

options.text: +30 USD
+300 USD
options.explanation: No: 0.00300 is 30 pips, and 30 × 1 USD = 30 USD. 300 USD would need a pip value of 10 USD (1 lot).

options.text: −30 USD
options.explanation: No: you bought and the price rose, so this is a profit.

doItNow.instructions: Open the P/L calculator. Enter the GBP/USD sell from the second example and check you get the same answer. Then try a buy that loses 25 pips at 0.10 lot.

lessons.homework: On your demo account, open a 0.01 lot market buy on EUR/USD and note the price it filled at and the result shown straight away. Close it and note the closing price.

lessons.title: Market structure and ranges

inOneLine.simple: Market structure is the pattern of swings. When an uptrend makes a lower low, its structure is broken and you stop calling it an uptrend.
inOneLine.balanced: [[market-structure|Structure]] has three states: higher highs and lows, lower highs and lows, or overlapping swings in a range. A break of structure changes the description. It does not predict the next move.

explain.simple: Once you have marked the swings, you can describe the chart in one of three ways. Rising swings: an uptrend. Falling swings: a downtrend. Swings that stay between a similar top and a similar bottom: a range. When an uptrend falls below its last higher low, the up pattern is broken. That does not mean price will now fall. It means the old description no longer fits, and you wait for new swings.
explain.balanced: A range has a ceiling and a floor that price has turned from more than once. Its height is ceiling minus floor. In a range, trend tools tend to give poor readings, because price keeps reversing. A break of structure can be followed by a new trend the other way, by a range, or by the old trend resuming. On a shorter [[timeframe]] you will see many small breaks of structure inside one longer swing.

assumptions: Illustrative EUR/USD H4 chart in an uptrend
Last higher lows: 1.09850, then 1.10100. Last swing high: 1.10600
Price then falls and an H4 candle closes at 1.10000
steps: The last higher low was 1.10100. The close at 1.10000 is below it by 1.10100 − 1.10000 = 10 pips.
Price has made a lower low, so the uptrend structure is broken.
The right description now is "uptrend broken, direction unclear", not "downtrend".
A downtrend description would need a lower high as well. Wait to see where the next swing high forms compared with 1.10600.

assumptions: Illustrative GBP/USD H1 chart
steps: The highs differ by at most 1.27050 − 1.26980 = 7 pips. The lows differ by at most 1.26040 − 1.25970 = 7 pips.
Neither the highs nor the lows step clearly one way, so this is a range.
Calling this an uptrend because the second high was 5 pips higher would ignore the mixed lows.

lessons.explainSimpler: Rising steps, falling steps, or a box. When the steps stop matching, the old label stops fitting.
lessons.commonMistake: Treating a break of structure as a signal that price will reverse. Often price only moves sideways, or the old trend resumes. Another mistake is calling a tiny difference between swing highs a "higher high" when the swings really overlap.

quickCheck.prompt: In an uptrend, the last higher low is 1.08500. A candle closes at 1.08420. What has happened?

options.text: The uptrend structure is broken
options.explanation: Right: price closed 8 pips below the last higher low, which is a lower low.

options.text: A downtrend is now confirmed by the lower low
options.explanation: No: a downtrend also needs a lower high. For now the direction is unclear.

options.text: Nothing, the uptrend is intact
options.explanation: No: a lower low breaks the higher-low pattern.

quickCheck.prompt: Swing highs sit near 1.3000 and swing lows near 1.2900, again and again. How do you describe this?

options.text: A range about 100 pips high
A slow uptrend
options.explanation: No: the highs and lows are not rising; they keep returning to the same levels.

options.text: A downtrend
options.explanation: No: the highs and lows are not falling; the lows keep holding near 1.2900.

quickCheck.prompt: After a break of structure, which of these can happen next? Select all that apply.

options.text: A trend the other way
options.explanation: Right, it can, but it is only one of the possibilities.

options.text: A range
options.explanation: Right: price often moves sideways after a break.

options.text: The old trend resuming
options.explanation: Right: the break can turn out to be a pause.

options.text: None of these: a break always leads to a reversal
options.explanation: No: a break of structure guarantees nothing about what comes next.

doItNow.instructions: Start a replay on the strong uptrend scenario. Mark each new swing low as it forms. Pause when a candle closes below the last higher low, and write "structure broken" with the price. Then keep going and note what happened next: new downtrend, range, or uptrend resumed.

lessons.title: Moving averages and lag

inOneLine.simple: A moving average is the average of the last few closing prices. It smooths the chart, but it always runs behind price.
inOneLine.balanced: A [[moving-average]] is a [[lagging-indicator]]: it only moves after price has moved. The longer the period, the smoother the line and the bigger the lag.

explain.simple: An MA 20 on an H1 chart adds up the last 20 hourly closes and divides by 20. Each new candle adds one close and drops the oldest. Plotted as a line, it shows the general direction more calmly than the candles. When price is above a rising average, people often describe the trend as up. But because it is built from old prices, it turns late. In a sideways market price crosses it again and again, and each cross means very little.
explain.balanced: Simple MA (SMA): every close counts equally. Exponential MA (EMA): recent closes count more, so it reacts faster but also flips more often. Chart Lab shows MA 20 and EMA 50. Crosses of price and an average, or of two averages, are common [[indicator]] readings. Every cross is late by design, and in a range most of them reverse soon after. The period is a setting you choose. Change it and the crosses move.

assumptions: Illustrative EUR/USD H1 closes
A 5-period simple moving average, kept short so the sums are easy to check
steps: The next candle jumps and closes at 1.1100. The oldest close (1.1000) drops out.
Price is at 1.1100 but the MA is 1.1040: 60 pips behind. The average only moved 20 pips (1.1040 − 1.1020) while price moved 60 (1.1100 − 1.1040).

assumptions: Illustrative sideways GBP/USD chart between 1.2600 and 1.2700
An MA 20 that runs flat near 1.2650
steps: Price swings up to near 1.2700, down to near 1.2600, and back, crossing the flat MA each time.
Each cross above the MA looks like the start of an uptrend. Each cross below looks like a downtrend.
Over 4 full swings, that is 8 crosses, and none of them led to a lasting move.
This is where moving averages mislead most: in ranges, where they whipsaw.

lessons.explainSimpler: A moving average is like the average speed over the last few minutes of a drive. It tells you roughly how you have been going, not what the road ahead looks like.
lessons.commonMistake: Treating a moving-average cross as a signal that a trend is starting. In a range, crosses happen often and usually reverse. In a sharp turn, the cross comes late, after much of the move is over.

quickCheck.prompt: A 4-period SMA uses closes 1.2000, 1.2010, 1.2020 and 1.2050. What is it?

options.explanation: Right: the sum is 4.8080, and 4.8080 ÷ 4 = 1.2020.
No: that is the last close, not the average.
No: check the sum again. It is 4.8080, not 4.8100.

quickCheck.prompt: Where does a moving average usually give the most misleading crosses?

options.text: In a sideways range
options.explanation: Right: price keeps crossing the flat average without any lasting move.

options.text: In a steady trend
options.explanation: No: steady trends produce fewer crosses, although the average still lags.

quickCheck.prompt: Compared with an SMA of the same period, an EMA usually…

options.text: Reacts faster but flips direction more often
options.explanation: Right: it weights recent closes more, so it has less lag and more false turns.

options.text: Has no lag at all, because it only uses the latest close
options.explanation: No: an EMA still uses past closes, and every average built from past prices lags.

options.text: Predicts the next close
options.explanation: No: it only summarises past closes.

doItNow.instructions: In Chart Lab, turn on MA 20 and EMA 50. Choose the Range scenario and count how many times price crosses MA 20. Then choose the Strong uptrend scenario and note how far price had already risen before it crossed above MA 20.

lessons.title: Majors, minors, and exotics

inOneLine.simple: Pairs are grouped by how widely traded their currencies are, which affects their costs.

explain.simple: Major pairs contain the US dollar and one other widely traded currency, such as EUR/USD, USD/JPY, or GBP/USD. Minor pairs (also called crosses) pair two major currencies without the dollar, such as EUR/GBP or EUR/JPY. Exotic pairs pair a major currency with the currency of a smaller or emerging economy, such as USD/ZAR or USD/TRY. Exotics usually trade less, so their [[spread|spreads]] tend to be wider and prices can jump more.
explain.balanced: The common classification: majors are USD paired with EUR, JPY, GBP, CHF, AUD, CAD, or NZD. Crosses (minors) combine those currencies without USD. Exotics include an emerging-market or less-traded currency. Lower [[liquidity]] usually means wider spreads, larger gaps, and higher swap costs. Exact groupings vary between brokers.

assumptions: Illustrative quotes, not live prices
EUR/USD bid 1.1000, ask 1.1001 (spread 1 pip)
An exotic pair with a spread of 60 pips
steps: Opening and immediately closing EUR/USD costs about 1 pip.
Doing the same on the exotic pair costs about 60 pips.
Before a trade on the exotic even breaks even, price must move 60 times further in your favour than on EUR/USD.

assumptions: Classify each pair using the definitions above
steps: USD/CAD: major (dollar plus a major currency).
EUR/JPY: minor or cross (two majors, no dollar).
USD/ZAR: exotic (South African rand).

lessons.explainSimpler: Majors include the dollar, minors leave the dollar out, and exotics include a less-traded currency that usually costs more to trade.
lessons.commonMistake: Assuming every pair costs the same to trade. Always check the spread before you practise on a pair, especially exotics.

quickCheck.prompt: EUR/GBP is usually classed as…

options.text: A major
options.explanation: No: majors include the US dollar.

options.text: A minor (cross)
options.explanation: Right: it pairs two major currencies without the dollar.

options.text: An exotic, since neither currency is the US dollar
options.explanation: No: exotic pairs include a currency from a smaller or emerging economy. Both the euro and the pound are major currencies.

quickCheck.prompt: Why do exotic pairs usually have wider spreads?

options.text: They are usually traded less, so liquidity is lower
options.explanation: Right: fewer buyers and sellers usually means a wider gap between bid and ask.

options.text: They are newer pairs, so brokers have not settled their spreads yet
options.explanation: No: spreads reflect how much trading there is, not how new a pair is. Fewer buyers and sellers usually means a wider gap.

options.text: They are only traded at night
options.explanation: No: exotic pairs can be traded whenever the market is open. The wider spread comes from lower liquidity.

doItNow.instructions: In MetaTrader on your demo account, open the quotes list and add 5 pairs: 3 majors, 1 minor, and 1 exotic. Note each pair's spread.

lessons.homework: Check the spread on EUR/USD and on your exotic pair at two different times of day, and write both down.

lessons.title: Pending orders: limits and stops

inOneLine.simple: A pending order waits for price to reach your level. Limits buy lower or sell higher. Stops buy higher or sell lower.
inOneLine.balanced: [[pending-order|Pending orders]]: buy limit below price, sell limit above, buy stop above, sell stop below. Nothing happens unless price reaches the level.

explain.simple: You do not have to trade now. A pending order waits. A buy limit sits below the current price: you want to buy cheaper. A sell limit sits above: you want to sell higher. A buy stop sits above the current price: you want to buy only if price rises to that level. A sell stop sits below: you want to sell only if price falls to that level. If price never gets there, no trade opens.
explain.balanced: In MetaTrader, buy pending orders are triggered by the [[ask]] and sell pending orders by the [[bid]]. A [[limit-order]] aims for your price or better. A [[stop-order]] becomes a market order once triggered, so it can fill worse than its level, especially in fast markets or [[gap|gaps]]. Many brokers set a minimum distance between the current price and a pending order, and you can usually add a stop loss and take profit when you place it.

assumptions: Illustrative prices
EUR/USD bid 1.09990, ask 1.10000
steps: Buy limit at 1.09500: below the ask. Triggers if the ask falls to 1.09500.
Sell limit at 1.10500: above the bid. Triggers if the bid rises to 1.10500.
Buy stop at 1.10500: above the ask. Triggers if the ask rises to 1.10500.
Sell stop at 1.09500: below the bid. Triggers if the bid falls to 1.09500.

assumptions: Illustrative prices
A buy stop on EUR/USD at 1.10500, for a possible breakout
Size 0.10 lot; pip value 1 USD
steps: Price rises quickly and the ask jumps from 1.10490 to 1.10520.
The order triggers and becomes a market order.
It fills at 1.10520, 2 pips above the level.
That slippage costs 2 × 1 USD = 2 USD compared with the planned price.

lessons.explainSimpler: Limit: 'get me a better price than now.' Stop: 'only get me in if price moves past this point.'
lessons.commonMistake: Mixing up limit and stop orders. Putting a buy limit above the current price, or a buy stop below it, is the wrong way round. The platform will usually reject it, or you may end up placing an order you did not intend.

quickCheck.prompt: EUR/USD ask is 1.10000. You want to buy only if price drops to 1.09700. Which order?

options.text: Buy limit at 1.09700
options.explanation: Right: a buy limit sits below the current price.

options.text: Buy stop at 1.09700
options.explanation: No: a buy stop sits above the current price.

options.text: Sell limit at 1.09700
options.explanation: No: that would open a sell, and a sell limit sits above the price.

quickCheck.prompt: Where does a sell stop go?

options.text: Below the current bid
options.explanation: Right: a sell stop triggers if price falls to the level.

options.text: Above the current bid
options.explanation: No: a sell order above the price is a sell limit.

quickCheck.prompt: A pending order's price is never reached. What happens?

options.text: No trade opens
options.explanation: Right: a pending order only opens a trade if price reaches its level.

options.text: It fills at the end of the day anyway
options.explanation: No: it waits until it triggers, expires, or you delete it.

doItNow.instructions: On your demo account, place a buy limit on EUR/USD below the current price, with a stop loss and take profit. Check it in the Trade tab, then delete it. Follow the task card.

lessons.homework: For EUR/USD at today's price, write down one example level for each of the four pending order types and say why each one is on that side of the price.

lessons.title: Pip value in your account currency

inOneLine.simple: Pip value tells you how much money one pip is worth on your trade.
inOneLine.balanced: [[pip-value|Pip value]] = units × pip size, in the [[quote-currency]]. If your account uses another currency, convert it at the current rate.

explain.simple: To turn pips into money, multiply your trade size in units by the size of one pip. The answer is in the second currency of the pair. For EUR/USD that is US dollars. If your account is also in US dollars, you are done. If not, you convert the answer into your account currency.
explain.balanced: Pip value = units × pip size, measured in the [[quote-currency]]. If the account currency is the quote currency, no conversion is needed. Otherwise divide or multiply by the exchange rate between the quote currency and the account currency. Because that rate moves, pip value can change a little while a trade is open. Profit or loss = pips moved × pip value.

assumptions: Illustrative prices, not live data
Account currency USD
Contract size 100,000 units per lot
Trade 1: EUR/USD, 0.10 lot = 10,000 EUR
Trade 2: USD/JPY, 1.00 lot = 100,000 USD, price 150.00
steps: Trade 1: pip value = 10,000 × 0.0001 = 1 USD per pip. The account is in USD, so no conversion.
Trade 2: pip value = 100,000 × 0.01 = 1,000 JPY per pip.
Convert JPY to USD: 1,000 ÷ 150.00 = 6.666… USD per pip, about 6.67.
A 20-pip move on Trade 2 is 20 × 6.666… = 133.33 USD. Round at the end, not in the middle, or small errors grow.

assumptions: Illustrative prices
Account currency USD
EUR/GBP, 0.10 lot = 10,000 EUR
GBP/USD rate used for conversion = 1.2500
steps: Pip value in the quote currency = 10,000 × 0.0001 = 1 GBP per pip.
Convert GBP to USD: 1 × 1.2500 = 1.25 USD per pip.
A 40-pip move = 40 × 1.25 = 50 USD.

lessons.explainSimpler: Size times one pip gives money in the second currency. If your account uses a different currency, change it over at today's rate.
lessons.commonMistake: Assuming one pip is always worth 10 USD per lot. That is only true when USD is the quote currency and the account is in USD. For USD/JPY, EUR/GBP or a non-USD account the value is different.

quickCheck.prompt: EUR/USD, 1.00 lot (100,000 EUR), account in USD. What is one pip worth?

options.text: 1 USD
options.explanation: No: that is the pip value for 10,000 units (0.10 lot).

options.text: 10 USD
options.explanation: Right: 100,000 × 0.0001 = 10 USD, and the account is already in USD.

options.text: 100 USD
options.explanation: No: that would need 1,000,000 units.

quickCheck.prompt: USD/JPY at 125.00, 0.10 lot (10,000 USD), account in USD. What is one pip worth?

options.explanation: No: 100 is the pip value in yen. It still needs converting to dollars.

options.text: 0.80 USD
1 USD
options.explanation: No: that ignores the yen pip size and the conversion.

quickCheck.prompt: Before any conversion, pip value comes out in which currency?

options.text: The quote currency
options.explanation: Right: the price is quoted in the second currency, so pip value is too.

options.text: The base currency
options.explanation: No: the size is in the base currency, but price steps are in the quote currency.

options.text: Always the account currency
options.explanation: No: pip value comes out in the quote currency first. It only matches your account currency when the two are the same, or after converting.

doItNow.instructions: Open the pip value calculator. Work out the pip value in your account currency for EUR/USD, USD/JPY and EUR/GBP at 0.10 lot. Do one by hand first, then check it with the calculator.

lessons.homework: Start your list of 10 trades: for each, write the pair, size in lots, account currency, and pip value. You will add margin in the next lesson.

lessons.title: Pips and pipettes

inOneLine.simple: A pip is the usual small step in a currency price. A pipette is one tenth of a pip.
inOneLine.balanced: Price moves are counted in [[pip|pips]]: 0.0001 for most pairs and 0.01 for most yen pairs. The extra digit many platforms show is a [[pipette]].

explain.simple: Traders count price moves in pips. For most pairs, like EUR/USD, one pip is 0.0001, the fourth digit after the dot. For pairs with the Japanese yen, like USD/JPY, one pip is 0.01, the second digit after the dot. Many platforms show one more digit than that. That last digit is a pipette. Ten pipettes make one pip.
explain.balanced: A 5-digit quote such as 1.10253 has a pip in the fourth decimal and a [[pipette]] in the fifth. A 3-digit yen quote such as 150.253 has a pip in the second decimal and a pipette in the third. MetaTrader often calls a pipette a 'point', so a distance of 50 points on a 5-digit pair is only 5 pips. Always check whether a number is in pips or points.

assumptions: Illustrative prices, not live market data
EUR/USD quoted to 5 decimals; 1 pip = 0.0001
USD/JPY quoted to 3 decimals; 1 pip = 0.01
steps: EUR/USD moves from 1.10250 to 1.10750.
USD/JPY moves from 150.000 to 150.450.
Change = 0.450. 0.450 ÷ 0.01 = 45 pips (450 pipettes).

assumptions: Illustrative prices
GBP/USD quoted to 5 decimals; 1 pip = 0.0001
steps: GBP/USD moves from 1.25003 to 1.25010.
Change = 0.00007, which is 7 pipettes.
7 pipettes ÷ 10 = 0.7 pips.

lessons.explainSimpler: A pip is like one centimetre on a ruler for price. Most pairs use the fourth digit after the dot. Yen pairs use the second.
lessons.commonMistake: Treating the last digit on the screen as a pip. On a 5-digit quote the last digit is a pipette, so a 30-point move is only 3 pips. Yen pairs are another trap: using 0.0001 for USD/JPY makes your pip count 100 times too big.

quickCheck.prompt: EUR/USD moves from 1.2000 to 1.2025. How many pips is that?

options.text: 2.5 pips
options.explanation: No: 0.0025 is 25 steps of 0.0001, not 2.5.

options.text: 25 pips
250 pips
options.explanation: No: 250 pips would be a move of 0.0250.

quickCheck.prompt: USD/JPY moves from 148.20 to 148.50. How many pips is that?

options.text: 30 pips
options.explanation: Right: for yen pairs a pip is 0.01, and 0.30 ÷ 0.01 = 30 pips.

options.text: 3,000 pips
options.explanation: No: that uses 0.0001 as the pip, which is wrong for yen pairs.

options.text: 3 pips
options.explanation: No: 3 pips on a yen pair would be a move of 0.03.

quickCheck.prompt: On a 5-digit EUR/USD quote, how many pipettes make one pip?

options.explanation: Right: a pipette is one tenth of a pip.
No: 100 pipettes would be 10 pips.
No: a pipette is smaller than a pip, not the same size.

doItNow.instructions: Pick three pairs, including one yen pair. For each one, write down two made-up prices and work out the move in pips and in pipettes. Check the yen pair uses 0.01 per pip.

lessons.homework: In MetaTrader on your demo account, note the price of EUR/USD and USD/JPY now and again in an hour. Work out how many pips each one moved.
