lessons.title: Limits, when to stop, and the pre-trade checklist

inOneLine.simple: Your plan also says how much you can lose in a day, how many trades you take, and when you stop. A [[pre-trade-checklist]] checks each trade against it.
inOneLine.balanced: A daily loss limit and a maximum trade count cap the damage from a bad day or a bad mood. The pre-trade checklist asks five questions before every trade: in my plan? stop set? risk within limit? important news due soon? calm, and not trying to win back a loss?

explain.simple: Even good rules lose sometimes. Bad days happen. Your plan should say when to stop. A daily loss limit stops you after you lose a set amount. A maximum number of trades stops you from trading too much. Add plain stop rules too, such as "stop if I feel angry" or "stop before a big news release". Then, before each trade, the app shows a short checklist. Is this trade in my plan? Is a stop loss set? Is the risk within my limit? Is there important news due soon for this market? Am I calm, and not trying to win back a loss? If an answer raises a caution (for example no stop, risk over your limit, news due soon, not calm, or not sure), wait or skip that trade. The app lists the cautions; the decision to wait is yours.
explain.balanced: Limits work best as numbers you can check, not feelings. Write them as an amount of money or a count of trades. The pre-trade checklist sits before you go to MetaTrader or place a paper trade. It is short on purpose, so you use it every time. When you want to change a limit, do it after the session, save a new plan version, and note why. Then you can compare versions in your journal instead of drifting without noticing.

assumptions: Fictional demo account, balance 2,000 USD
Example risk per trade: 1% = 20 USD (example only)
Example daily loss limit: 3% = 60 USD
Example maximum: 4 trades per day
Losses equal the planned risk (no slippage)
steps: Trade 1: stop hit, −20 USD. Day total −20 USD.
Trade 2: target hit, +40 USD. Day total +20 USD.
Trade 3: stop hit, −20 USD. Day total 0 USD.
Trade 4: stop hit, −20 USD. Day total −20 USD. That is 4 trades, the maximum, so the learner stops for the day even though the loss limit was not reached.

assumptions: Fictional paper trade idea on GBP/USD
A major news release is due in 15 minutes
The learner's plan says: no new trades from 30 minutes before major news
steps: In my plan? Yes, the setup matches the entry rule.
Stop set? Yes.
Risk within limit? Yes.
Important news due soon? Yes, within 30 minutes. That raises a caution, and the plan says no new trades now.
One caution is enough. The learner skips the trade and writes down why.

lessons.explainSimpler: Limits are the brakes. The checklist is checking the mirrors before you pull out.
lessons.commonMistake: Raising the daily loss limit in the middle of a losing day "just this once". That turns the limit into a suggestion.

quickCheck.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the five pre-trade checklist questions?

options.text: Is a stop loss set?
options.explanation: No: this is one of the five questions.

options.text: Will this trade win?
options.explanation: Right: nobody can know that. The checklist checks your process, not the outcome.

options.text: Am I calm, and not trying to win back a loss?
options.explanation: No: this is one of the five questions.

quickCheck.prompt: The setup is in your plan, the stop is set, risk is within your limit and you are calm. A major release is due in 10 minutes, and your plan says no new trades within 30 minutes of major news. What do you do?

options.text: Take it: four out of five is good enough
options.explanation: No: the checklist is not a score. One answer that raises a caution means you wait or skip that trade.

options.text: Skip it and note why
options.explanation: Right: the news rule says no, so you wait.

quickCheck.prompt: When is the right time to change your daily loss limit?

options.text: After the session, saved as a new plan version
options.explanation: Right: calm changes, recorded, so you can compare versions.

options.text: When you hit it and want one more trade
options.explanation: No: that is exactly when the limit is meant to stop you.

doItNow.instructions: In More → Tools → Trading plan, set your risk per trade, daily loss limit, maximum trades per day, and your "when to stop" rules. Save the plan. Then open the pre-trade checklist and run it on one paper trade idea, even if you do not take the trade.

lessons.homework: Read your saved plan out loud. It should fit on one page. Anything you would not follow on a bad day, simplify.

lessons.title: Entry, exit, stop and target rules

inOneLine.simple: Good rules are clear enough that someone else could follow them and get the same trades.
inOneLine.balanced: Write each rule as "if this, then that", using things you can see on the chart at the time. Vague rules ("buy when it looks strong") cannot be tested or reviewed.

explain.simple: Your plan needs four kinds of rule. An entry rule says when to open a trade. A stop rule says where your idea is wrong, so you get out. A target rule says where you take the gain. An exit rule covers anything else, like closing before the weekend. Each rule should be something you can check on the chart. "Buy when it looks strong" is not a rule. "Buy when a 1-hour candle closes above the level I marked earlier" is a rule. You enter these in the plan builder under entry, exit, stop and target.
explain.balanced: Test each rule with one question: could another person follow it and take the same trade? If not, make it more specific. Decide the [[stop-loss]] from the chart first, then choose the position size so the money at risk fits your limit. Do not pick a stop distance to fit a size. A [[take-profit]] can be set as a multiple of the stop distance (for example 2R), or at a level on the chart. Neither choice makes a trade more likely to win; it only defines what you aim for.

assumptions: Illustrative prices, EUR/USD, account currency USD
Buy at 1.10000; the chart puts the stop at 1.09700 (30 pips below)
0.10 lot, pip value 1 USD
Plan's example risk limit per trade: 50 USD
No slippage in this example
steps: Money at risk = 30 pips × 1 USD = 30 USD.
30 USD is within the 50 USD limit, so the trade passes the risk rule.
Target at 2R = 2 × 30 pips = 60 pips above entry = 1.10600. This is a goal, not a promise.

assumptions: Fictional rule rewrite
Same learner, same pair
steps: Vague: "Sell when the trend is down and it looks weak."
Clearer: "On the 1-hour chart, if price has made a lower high and a lower low, sell when a candle closes below the most recent low."
Stop rule: "Stop goes a few pips above the most recent lower high."
Target rule: "Take profit at 2 times the stop distance, or close at the end of the session, whichever comes first."

lessons.explainSimpler: Write rules like a recipe: exact steps someone else could follow and get the same dish.
lessons.commonMistake: Choosing the lot size first, then squeezing the stop to fit it. The stop should come from where the idea is wrong, and the size should fit the stop.

quickCheck.prompt: Which of these is a rule you can test?

options.text: "Buy when the market feels bullish"
options.explanation: No: feelings cannot be checked on a chart or repeated.

options.text: "Buy when a 1-hour candle closes above the level I marked before the session"
options.explanation: Right: anyone can check it on the chart at the time.

quickCheck.prompt: Stop distance 40 pips, pip value 1 USD, plan risk limit 30 USD. What should you do?

options.text: Take the trade; 40 USD is close enough
options.explanation: No: 40 × 1 = 40 USD, which breaks the 30 USD limit.

options.text: Move the stop to 30 pips so it fits
options.explanation: No: the stop should come from the chart, not from the size.

options.text: Use a smaller size, or skip the trade
options.explanation: Right: reduce size so risk fits the limit, or pass on the trade.

doItNow.instructions: In More → Tools → Trading plan, write your entry, exit, stop and target rules. For each, ask: could someone else follow this and take the same trade? Rewrite any rule that fails that test.

lessons.title: Why write a trading plan

inOneLine.simple: A [[trading-plan]] is your rules, written down before you trade, while you are calm.
inOneLine.balanced: A plan turns many in-the-moment choices into decisions made in advance. It sets what you trade, when, how you enter and exit, and how much you risk, so each trade can be checked against it.

explain.simple: During a trade, it is hard to think clearly. Price moves, and fear or excitement push you to act. A trading plan answers the big questions before that happens. What do I trade? When? What tells me to enter? Where is my stop? How much can I lose today? If you write these down first, you only need to follow them. You build yours in More → Tools → Trading plan. Start simple. A short plan you follow is better than a long one you ignore.
explain.balanced: The plan builder covers: instruments, sessions, timeframe, entry rules, exit rules, [[stop-loss]] and [[take-profit]] rules, risk per trade, daily loss limit, maximum trades per day, and when to stop. The plan is versioned. When you change a rule, you save a new version, so later you can compare how each version was followed. A plan does not make trades win. It makes your behaviour consistent enough to learn from, because you can tell whether a result came from the rules or from breaking them.

assumptions: Fictional learner, demo account balance 10,000 USD
Example risk per trade: 1% of balance (an example, not a recommendation)
Example daily loss limit: 2% of balance
Every trade has a stop loss and the loss equals the planned risk (no slippage)
steps: Risk per trade = 1% × 10,000 USD = 100 USD.
Daily loss limit = 2% × 10,000 USD = 200 USD.
200 USD ÷ 100 USD = 2. So the plan says: stop for the day after 2 full losses.
The learner writes "Stop after 2 losses or 200 USD down, whichever comes first" in the plan.

assumptions: Fictional learner with no written plan
Paper account, illustrative trades
Each trade was chosen "by feel"
steps: Trade 1: no stop, closed by hand at −35 USD.
Trade 2: bigger size "to win it back", closed at −80 USD.
Trade 3: a winner of +60 USD, closed early from fear.
At the end, the learner cannot say which choices came from a rule and which from a feeling. There is nothing to review against. A written plan fixes that.

lessons.explainSimpler: A trading plan is a recipe. You decide the recipe before you cook, not while the pan is on fire.
lessons.commonMistake: Writing a plan, then changing it in the middle of a trade because the market "looks different". Changes belong between sessions, saved as a new version.

quickCheck.prompt: When should you write or change your trading plan?

options.text: Before or between trading sessions, while calm
options.explanation: Right: decisions made in advance are less driven by fear or excitement.

options.text: During a trade, as soon as price moves against your plan
options.explanation: No: that is when emotions are strongest and rules get broken.

options.text: Whenever you feel like it
options.explanation: No: a plan changed on a whim is not a plan. Change it calmly, before or between sessions.

quickCheck.prompt: A demo balance is 5,000 USD. Example risk per trade is 1%. What is the risk per trade in money?

options.text: 5 USD
options.explanation: No: that would be 0.1%.

options.text: 50 USD
options.explanation: Right: 1% × 5,000 USD = 50 USD.

options.text: 500 USD
options.explanation: No: that would be 10%.

quickCheck.prompt: What can a trading plan do for you?

options.text: Make most of your trades win
options.explanation: No: no plan can promise results. Following rules keeps your behaviour consistent; it does not make trades win.

options.text: Keep your behaviour consistent, so you can learn from your results
options.explanation: Right: a plan lets you separate the rules from rule-breaking when you review.

doItNow.instructions: Open More → Tools → Trading plan. Fill in the first part: which instruments you will trade, which sessions, and which timeframe. Keep it short. One or two pairs is enough to start.

lessons.homework: Write one sentence on why you want each rule. If you cannot explain a rule, leave it out for now.

lessons.title: Position sizing from your stop

inOneLine.simple: Choose the stop first. Then pick the trade size that makes hitting the stop cost only your planned amount.
inOneLine.balanced: [[position-sizing|Size]] in lots = money at risk ÷ (stop distance in pips × [[pip-value]] for 1 lot). Round down to the size step so you never risk more than planned.

explain.simple: Your stop goes where your trade idea is wrong. That comes from the chart, not from your wallet. Once the stop is set, you know how many pips you could lose. Divide the money you are willing to risk by what those pips cost on 1 lot. The answer is your size. A wide stop means a small size. A tight stop means a bigger size. The money at risk stays the same.
explain.balanced: Steps: money at risk = balance × your example percentage. Risk per lot = stop pips × pip value per lot, in the account currency. Size = money at risk ÷ risk per lot. Round down to the broker's [[lot]] step, then recheck the actual risk. If the size falls below the smallest lot, skip the trade instead of raising the risk. Costs such as the [[spread]] and possible [[slippage]] make the real loss larger, so the 'Position size with costs' calculator adds them in.

assumptions: Example account: 10,000 USD
Example rule: 1% risk per trade = 100 USD. A learning example, not a recommendation
EUR/USD, account in USD, pip value 10 USD for 1.00 lot
Stop loss 35 pips from entry
Size step 0.01 lot; costs ignored in this example
steps: Risk per lot = 35 × 10 = 350 USD.
Round down to 0.28 lot. Actual risk = 0.28 × 350 = 98 USD, inside the 100 USD limit.
Rounding up to 0.29 lot would risk 0.29 × 350 = 101.50 USD, which breaks the limit.

assumptions: Example account: 5,000 USD
Example rule: 1% risk per trade = 50 USD
USD/JPY at an illustrative 150.00, account in USD
Stop loss 30 pips; spread 2 pips counted as extra loss; size step 0.01 lot
steps: Without costs: risk per lot = 30 × 6.666… = 200 USD. Size = 50 ÷ 200 = 0.25 lot.
With the spread: the loss at the stop covers 30 + 2 = 32 pips. Risk per lot = 32 × 6.666… = 213.33 USD.
Size = 50 ÷ 213.33 = 0.234… lot. Round down to 0.23 lot.
Actual risk = 0.23 × 213.33 = 49.07 USD, inside the 50 USD limit. Slippage could still add to it.

lessons.explainSimpler: Stop first, size second. Money you will risk, divided by what your stop costs on 1 lot, gives the size. Always round down.
lessons.commonMistake: Picking the size first, for example always 0.10 lot, and then placing the stop wherever the money runs out. Another mistake is rounding the size up, or moving the stop closer just to trade bigger.

quickCheck.prompt: Example risk 200 USD. Stop 50 pips. Pip value 10 USD per 1.00 lot. What size?

options.text: 0.40 lot
options.explanation: Right: risk per lot = 50 × 10 = 500 USD, and 200 ÷ 500 = 0.40 lot.

options.text: 4.00 lots
options.explanation: No: that would risk 4 × 500 = 2,000 USD.

options.text: 0.04 lot
options.explanation: No: that would risk only 20 USD.

quickCheck.prompt: Your stop moves from 20 pips to 40 pips away, and your money at risk stays the same. What happens to the size?

options.text: It doubles
options.explanation: No: a wider stop with a bigger size would double the risk.

options.text: It halves
options.explanation: Right: twice the pips at risk means half the size for the same money.

options.text: It stays the same
options.explanation: No: then the money at risk would double.

quickCheck.prompt: The formula gives 0.137 lot and your size step is 0.01. Which size keeps you inside your limit?

options.text: 0.13 lot
options.explanation: Right: round down so the actual risk is at or below the plan.

options.text: 0.14 lot
options.explanation: No: rounding up risks a little more than your limit.

doItNow.instructions: Open Practice → Size it and size 20 trades so each one risks your example 1% as closely as possible without going over. Work the first two by hand, then check them in Learn → Calculators → Position size with costs.

lessons.homework: For 3 of your 20 sized trades, write the stop distance, the size, and the actual risk after rounding down.

lessons.title: Your Practice Progress Review

inOneLine.simple: The Practice Progress Review shows what you have studied and practised, and what to practise next. It is not a verdict on whether you are ready to trade real money.
inOneLine.balanced: Find it in More → Tools → Practice Progress Review. It shows each module's checkpoint and MetaTrader task, your calculation accuracy, how many of your paper and hand-entered demo trades broke no rule, which market conditions you have practised, and what to practise next. Profit and loss are not part of it. There is no pass or fail, and no "ready" badge.

explain.simple: Open More → Tools → Practice Progress Review. It has five parts. Learning objectives: for each module, whether the checkpoint is passed, not passed yet or not taken, your best score, and whether the module's MetaTrader task is done. Calculation accuracy: how many answers you got right, shown as "N of M correct" with a percentage, for pips, lots, pip value and margin; for risk, position size and reward to risk; and for the Size It drill. Following your rules: how many of your paper and hand-entered demo trades broke no rule, how many had a stop, and how many you reviewed in the journal. Market conditions practised: trending markets, ranges, breakouts, reversals, high and low volatility, and news, counted from finished replays and paper accounts. What to practise next: the gaps, with links to a lesson or a drill. It does not judge you by profit. It does not give a "ready" badge. It ends with a reminder: completing practice does not show that you are ready to trade real money.
explain.balanced: Profit and expectancy are left out on purpose. Your practice sample is small, and a small sample of results says little. Judging by profit would also push you to chase outcomes instead of improving your process. There is no pass or fail. Read the review as a study plan. A gap is listed when a checkpoint is not passed yet, when a calculation area is under 80% correct, when a market condition has no practice yet, or when you broke the same rule 2 or more times. Rule-following counts only paper trades and demo trades you entered by hand, because those are the trades checked against your rules. Practice results, simulated or demo, can differ from real trading, where costs, fills and emotions differ.

assumptions: Fictional review for a fictional learner, illustrative numbers
Risk, position size and reward to risk: 20 answers marked
Size It drill: 10 attempts
12 paper and hand-entered demo trades checked against the rules
steps: Risk, position size and reward to risk: 18 of 20 correct. 18 ÷ 20 = 90%. That is 80% or more, so it is not listed as a gap.
Size It drill: 7 of 10 correct. 7 ÷ 10 = 70%. That is under 80%, so it appears under "What to practise next" with a link to the drill.
Following your rules: "9 of 12 checked trades broke no rule. 11 had a stop. 8 were reviewed in the journal." The review shows these counts, not a percentage.
Market conditions: trending markets and ranges practised; news events not yet. "No practice yet in: news events" is listed as a gap.
There is no pass or fail and no "ready" badge. The gaps become the next study steps.

assumptions: Two fictional learners, illustrative numbers
Learner A: demo result +300 USD; 6 of 10 checked trades broke no rule; the same rule was broken 3 times
Learner B: demo result −80 USD; 10 of 10 checked trades broke no rule
steps: Neither review shows the profit or the loss.
Learner A sees "6 of 10 checked trades broke no rule", and a gap for a rule broken often (3 times).
Learner B sees "10 of 10 checked trades broke no rule" and no rule gap, despite the loss.
A small sample of results says little about the future. Following your rules is something you can practise and control.

lessons.explainSimpler: The review is a report card on your learning, not a permission slip.
lessons.commonMistake: Reading a good review as "I am ready for real money". The review measures learning and discipline in practice, not readiness to trade real money.

quickCheck.prompt: What does the Practice Progress Review measure?

options.text: Your simulated profit, to judge if you are ready
options.explanation: No: profit and loss are not part of it, and the review gives no readiness verdict.

options.text: What you have studied and practised, and the gaps to work on next
options.explanation: Right: it is a learning assessment: checkpoints, calculation accuracy, rule-following, market conditions practised, and what to practise next.

quickCheck.prompt: Does completing all the practice show that someone is ready to trade real money?

options.text: Yes, once no gaps are listed
options.explanation: No: the review is never a readiness verdict, even with no gaps.

options.text: No: completing practice does not show that
options.explanation: Right: the review ends with this reminder. Practice results can differ from real trading.

quickCheck.prompt: Which trades does the review check for rule-following?

options.text: Paper trades and demo trades you entered by hand
options.explanation: Right: those are the trades checked against your rules. The review counts how many broke no rule, had a stop, and were reviewed in the journal.

options.text: Every replay, paper and demo trade, shown as a percentage score
options.explanation: No: replay trades are not checked for rules, and the review shows counts, not a percentage.

options.text: Only the losing trades
options.explanation: No: every paper and hand-entered demo trade is checked, win or lose. A winning trade can still break a rule.

doItNow.instructions: Open your Practice Progress Review. Pick the two biggest gaps it lists and schedule the linked lessons or drills. Write one sentence on what you will practise next, and one sentence on what the review cannot tell you.

lessons.title: Noticing your own patterns: psychology on demo

inOneLine.simple: Your feelings change your decisions. Rate them in the Journal and practise in the Psychology Lab, so you can spot your own patterns.
inOneLine.balanced: Self-ratings of confidence, stress, patience and emotion, tracked across many trades, show when you tend to break rules. The Psychology Lab (Journal → Psychology Lab) lets you practise responses to FOMO, revenge trading, moving stops and more.

explain.simple: Even with pretend money, trading stirs feelings. After a loss, you may want to win it back. After a win, you may feel you cannot lose. When you see a big move without you, you may want to jump in late. These feelings are normal. The problem is acting on them. In the Journal, rate how you felt before and after each trade. Over 20 trades, you may see a pattern, like breaking rules after two losses in a row. Open Journal → Psychology Lab to practise what you would do in situations like these. This is a learning tool, not a mental-health assessment.
explain.balanced: Look for links between your ratings and your rule breaks. Common patterns include revenge trading after a loss, sizing up after losses, moving stops, and overtrading when bored. Your plan's "when to stop" rules and daily loss limit exist for these moments. When you hit the limit or have several losses in a row, the app may show a cool-down prompt. Treat it as part of your plan, not as a punishment. Demo trading lacks the fear of losing real money, so feelings with real money may well be stronger, not weaker.

assumptions: Fictional demo day; plan: example daily loss limit 60 USD, risk 20 USD per trade
Losses equal planned risk (no slippage)
steps: Loss 1: −20 USD. Day total −20 USD. Stress rating: 2 out of 5.
Loss 2: −20 USD. Day total −40 USD. Stress rating: 4 out of 5. The learner wants to "win it back".
The checklist asks "Am I calm?" Answer: no. The learner stops for the day at −40 USD, before reaching the limit.
Journal note: "After 2 losses my stress jumps. My plan now says to pause for 30 minutes after 2 losses."

assumptions: Fictional learner, 20 journaled demo trades
4 rule breaks in total
steps: The learner sorts the 4 rule breaks by the emotion rating before each trade.
3 of the 4 came right after a loss with a high stress rating.
1 came after 2 hours of waiting with a high boredom note.
The learner practises the revenge-trading and overtrading scenarios in the Psychology Lab, and adds a pause rule to the plan.

lessons.explainSimpler: Feelings are weather. You cannot stop them, but your plan is the umbrella.
lessons.commonMistake: Thinking "I am disciplined, emotions do not affect me" and skipping the ratings. The pattern only shows up if you record it.

quickCheck.prompt: You just had two losses and feel angry. What fits your plan best?

options.text: Double the size to win it back
options.explanation: No: sizing up after losses is a classic emotional mistake.

options.text: Pause, note the feeling in the Journal, and follow your stop rules
options.explanation: Right: pausing is part of the plan.

quickCheck.prompt: Why rate your emotions on every journaled trade?

options.text: To find patterns between feelings and rule breaks over many trades
options.explanation: Right: one trade shows little; many trades show patterns.

options.text: To get a score that tells you whether you are emotionally fit to trade at all
options.explanation: No: the ratings are for spotting patterns in your own journal. They are not a fitness test, and the Psychology Lab is not a mental-health assessment.

options.text: To decide which trades to delete
options.explanation: No: every trade stays in the journal. Ratings help you find patterns, not hide trades.

doItNow.instructions: Open Journal → Psychology Lab and work through at least two scenarios, such as revenge trading and moving stops. Then, on your next 5 demo trades, rate your emotion before and after each trade in the Journal.

lessons.homework: After 20 demo trades, list your rule breaks next to your emotion ratings. Write down one pattern you see, if any.

lessons.title: Interest rates, inflation and central banks

inOneLine.simple: A country's interest rate, and what people expect it to be next, is one of the big forces behind its currency.
inOneLine.balanced: [[central-bank|Central banks]] set the policy [[interest-rate]], mostly in response to [[inflation]]. Markets trade on expected future rates, so a change that was already expected may move a currency very little.

explain.simple: Inflation is how fast prices rise. A central bank's main job is usually to keep it steady. If prices rise too fast, it may raise interest rates. If the economy is weak, it may cut them. Higher rates can make a currency more attractive to hold, because savers earn more. But this is a tendency, not a law. Traders try to guess the next move in advance, so prices often change before the decision, not on it.
explain.balanced: A common chain of reasoning is: higher-than-expected inflation → markets expect higher rates → demand for the currency may rise. Each link can fail. Growth worries, risk mood, the other currency in the pair, or the bank's statement about the future can all matter more. The rate gap between two currencies also feeds the [[swap]] you pay or receive overnight. Treat every link as a hypothesis to test, not a sure thing. All examples here are fictional.

assumptions: Fictional country: Westmark, currency WMK
Hypothetical price index: 200.0 a year ago, 207.0 today
Hypothetical central-bank inflation target: 2%
Hypothetical policy rate today: 3.00%
steps: That is 1.5 percentage points above the 2% target.
Traders may expect the bank to raise rates, or to keep them high for longer.
If that expectation is already in the price, WMK may not rise on the inflation release. It is a scenario, not a forecast.

assumptions: Fictional Westmark central bank, policy rate 3.00%
Hypothetical market expectation before the meeting: a rise of 0.25 points to 3.25%
Two possible outcomes, both made up for practice
steps: Outcome A: the bank raises to 3.25%, as expected. The surprise is zero. WMK may barely move, or move on what the bank says about the future.
Outcome B: the bank holds at 3.00%. That is 0.25 points below the expected 3.25%.
In Outcome B, WMK may weaken because rates are lower than expected. It could also rise if the bank signals more rises later.
Same decision type, different reaction: what was expected matters as much as what happened.

lessons.explainSimpler: Prices rising fast → the central bank may raise rates → the currency may get stronger. But traders guess early, so by the time it happens, the move may already be over.
lessons.commonMistake: Thinking 'rates up means currency up' every time. The reaction depends on what was expected, what the bank says next, and what is happening to the other currency in the pair.

quickCheck.prompt: A fictional price index rises from 150 to 153 in a year. What is the inflation rate?

options.explanation: No: 3 is the change in points. Divide it by the starting level, 150.
No: that is the new level, not the change.

quickCheck.prompt: A fictional central bank raises rates by exactly as much as everyone expected. What is most accurate?

options.text: Its currency must rise sharply
options.explanation: No: an expected move may already be in the price.

options.text: The reaction may be small, or driven by what the bank says about the future
options.explanation: Right: with no surprise, guidance about later moves often matters more.

doItNow.instructions: Pick one currency pair you practise. For each of its two currencies, find the central bank's name and its stated inflation goal on the bank's own website. Write one sentence for each on what could make it raise or cut rates.

lessons.title: Risk per trade: the 1% example

inOneLine.simple: Decide before each trade how much money you can lose on it. Keep that amount small so a run of losses cannot wipe you out.
inOneLine.balanced: [[risk-per-trade|Risk per trade]] = balance × your chosen percentage. This lesson uses 1% as a learning example only. It is not a right number for everyone, and you can change it in your risk rules.

explain.simple: Every trade can lose. So before you enter, choose the most you are willing to lose if the stop loss is hit. Many learners use a small share of the account, such as 1%, as an example rule. With a 10,000 USD account, 1% is 100 USD. The point is not the exact number. The point is that one bad trade, or ten, should not end your practice. A small fixed share also shrinks your risk in money as the account falls, which slows the damage.
explain.balanced: Risk is set as a percentage of current balance, then turned into a position size from the stop distance. The percentage in this lesson is a configurable learning example, not advice. Fixed-percentage risk means each loss is a little smaller in money than the last while you are in a [[drawdown]]. The opposite habit, raising size to win back losses, makes drawdowns deeper and faster. A [[stop-loss]] can slip, so the real loss can be larger than the plan. Set your own example limits in More → Risk rules.

assumptions: Example account: 10,000 USD
Example rule: risk 1% of the current balance per trade. This is a learning example, not a recommendation
Every stop fills exactly at its level, with no slippage or costs
10 losses in a row
steps: Trade 1: risk = 10,000 × 0.01 = 100 USD. After the loss the balance is 9,900 USD.
Trade 2: risk = 9,900 × 0.01 = 99 USD. The money at risk shrinks as the balance falls.
After 10 losses: 10,000 × 0.99^10 = 9,043.82 USD. That is a fall of about 9.56%.
Same streak at an example 10% per trade: 10,000 × 0.90^10 = 3,486.78 USD. That is a fall of about 65.13%.

assumptions: Example account: 10,000 USD
Example rule: 1% of the current balance per trade
Three losses in a row, then one more loss
No slippage or costs
steps: Three losses: 100 + 99 + 98.01 = 297.01 USD. Balance = 9,702.99 USD.
Sticking to the rule, trade 4 risks 9,702.99 × 0.01 = 97.03 USD. If it loses, the balance is 9,605.96 USD, down about 3.94%.
Raising risk to 4% to 'win it back' means risking 9,702.99 × 0.04 = 388.12 USD. If it loses, the balance is 9,314.87 USD, down about 6.85%.
One extra loss at the bigger size left a total fall of about 6.85% instead of 3.94%, about 1.7 times the damage. Bigger size after losses is the wrong reaction.

lessons.explainSimpler: Pick a small slice of your account to risk on each trade. If you lose, the next slice gets a bit smaller. Never make the slice bigger to get money back.
lessons.commonMistake: Treating 1% as a rule everyone must use, or forgetting to recalculate it from the current balance. Another mistake is raising size after a loss to recover faster. That turns a normal losing run into a deep drawdown.

quickCheck.prompt: Your example rule is 1% risk per trade. Your balance is 8,000 USD. How much do you risk on the next trade?

options.text: 8 USD
options.explanation: No: that is 0.1% of 8,000.

options.text: 80 USD
100 USD
options.explanation: No: use the current balance, not the starting one.

quickCheck.prompt: You have lost 4 trades in a row. What does a sound risk plan say about the next trade's size?

options.text: Double it, since a win is more likely after a long losing run
options.explanation: No: past losses do not make a win more likely, and bigger size after losses makes the drawdown deeper and faster.

options.text: Keep the same percentage of the current balance, or lower it
options.explanation: Right: the rule stays the same. Some learners also pause and review after a set number of losses.

options.text: Remove the stop loss so the trade can come back
options.explanation: No: without a stop the possible loss has no limit.

quickCheck.prompt: Why is the 1% in this lesson called a learning example?

options.text: Because it is the one correct number for every trader, whatever the account size
options.explanation: No: no single percentage suits everyone.

options.text: It is a number to practise with, and you can change it in your risk rules
options.explanation: Right: it shows the method. The right number depends on the person and the plan.

options.text: Because the app sets it and you cannot change it
options.explanation: No: you can set your own example limits in More → Risk rules.

doItNow.instructions: Open More → Risk rules and set your own example limits: risk per trade, daily loss limit, and when to stop and review after losses. Then write one sentence on why you chose each number.

lessons.homework: Work out by hand what 5 losses in a row would do to a 10,000 USD example account at 1% and at 5% of the current balance.

lessons.title: Reward to risk, win rate and expectancy

inOneLine.simple: How often you win and how much you win compared with how much you lose must be looked at together.
inOneLine.balanced: Break-even [[win-rate]] = 1 ÷ (1 + reward to risk). [[expectancy|Expectancy]] = win rate × average win − loss rate × average loss, often measured in [[r-multiple|R]].

explain.simple: R is the amount you risk on a trade. A full stop-out loses 1R. If your target is twice as far as your stop, a win makes 2R. That is a 2:1 [[risk-reward-ratio|reward to risk]]. With 2:1 you only need to win 1 trade in 3 to break even, before costs. But a far target may be hit less often. A high win rate is not enough either: if wins are small and losses big, you can still lose money.
explain.balanced: Break-even win rate = 1 ÷ (1 + R:R), before costs. At 1:1 it is 50%. At 2:1 it is 33.3%. At 0.5:1 it is 66.7%. Expectancy in R = W × average win − (1 − W) × average loss. A positive figure means the inputs would make money on average over many trades. It is only arithmetic on your inputs. Real win rates drift, costs reduce results, and no method guarantees a positive expectancy.

assumptions: Example plan: stop 25 pips, target 50 pips
Example win rate: 40%; every loss is exactly −1R and every win exactly +2R
Example risk: 1R = 100 USD
Costs and slippage ignored
steps: Reward to risk = 50 ÷ 25 = 2, written 2:1.
Break-even win rate = 1 ÷ (1 + 2) = 33.3%.
At 100 USD per R, that is 20 USD per trade on average over many trades. Any single trade still wins 200 USD or loses 100 USD, and short runs can be far from the average.

assumptions: Example plan with a tight target: average win 0.4R, average loss 1R
Example win rate: 70%
Costs and slippage ignored
steps: Break-even win rate = 1 ÷ (1 + 0.4) = 1 ÷ 1.4 = 71.4%.
Even winning 7 trades in 10, this example loses money on average.
A high win rate on its own tells you little. Look at it next to the size of wins and losses.

lessons.explainSimpler: If you win big and lose small, you can be wrong often and still be fine. If you win small and lose big, you must be right very often. Check both numbers together.
lessons.commonMistake: Chasing a high win rate while letting losses run bigger than wins. Another mistake is treating a positive expectancy from a few trades, or from a backtest, as a guarantee for the future.

quickCheck.prompt: A plan uses 3:1 reward to risk. What win rate does it need to break even, before costs?

options.explanation: No: that is the break-even win rate for 2:1.
No: that would be the break-even win rate for a 1:3 plan, risking 3 to make 1.

quickCheck.prompt: Example inputs: win rate 50%, average win 1.5R, average loss 1R. What is the expectancy?

options.explanation: No: you must subtract the losing half, 0.50 × 1.
No: that is the average win, not the average per trade.

quickCheck.prompt: Which statement is true?

options.text: A 2:1 reward to risk makes a plan profitable over time, whatever its win rate
options.explanation: No: if you win less than a third of the time, it still loses, and costs push the bar higher.

options.text: A positive expectancy on your inputs does not promise future results
options.explanation: Right: real win rates and averages change, and costs reduce results.

options.text: Expectancy only matters for large accounts
options.explanation: No: expectancy is arithmetic per trade, in R. It does not depend on account size.

doItNow.instructions: Open Learn → Calculators. In Break-even win rate, try reward to risk of 0.5, 1, 2 and 3. Then in Expected value per trade, find a win rate where an example 1.5:1 plan has an expectancy near zero. Check one answer by hand.

lessons.title: RSI: momentum, not a reversal signal

inOneLine.simple: RSI scores recent up moves against recent down moves on a scale of 0 to 100. A high reading means price has risen a lot lately, not that it must fall.
inOneLine.balanced: [[rsi|RSI]] = 100 − 100 ÷ (1 + RS), where RS = average gain ÷ average loss over the period, often 14. Above 70 and below 30 are labelled [[overbought-oversold|overbought and oversold]], which describes the past move only.

explain.simple: RSI looks at the last 14 candles and asks: were the up moves bigger than the down moves? If up moves were much bigger, RSI is high, near 70 or above. If down moves were bigger, RSI is low, near 30 or below. Around 50 they were similar. People call above 70 "overbought" and below 30 "oversold". Those are just names. In a strong uptrend RSI can stay above 70 for a long time while price keeps rising.
explain.balanced: RSI uses smoothed averages, so the number in your app will differ a little from a quick hand calculation. Some people look for divergence: price makes a higher high while RSI makes a lower high. Divergence can last a long time while price keeps going, so it is a description, not a timing tool. Selling every time RSI crosses 70 in a strong uptrend means selling into a rising market again and again.

assumptions: Illustrative and simplified: plain averages instead of the smoothed averages real RSI uses
Over 14 EUR/USD candles: average gain 6 pips, average loss 2 pips
steps: That is above 70, so many apps would call it overbought.
It only says up moves have been about three times the size of down moves lately. Price can keep rising with RSI above 70.

assumptions: Illustrative and simplified, as before
Over 14 candles: average gain 2 pips, average loss 8 pips
steps: That is below 30, so it would be labelled oversold.
In a strong downtrend, RSI can sit near 20 for many candles while price keeps falling. Buying just because RSI is low would mean buying into that fall.

lessons.explainSimpler: RSI is a scoreboard of recent ups versus downs. A lopsided score tells you who has been winning, not who wins next.
lessons.commonMistake: Selling just because RSI is above 70, or buying because it is below 30. In strong trends, RSI often stays at those levels while price keeps going the same way.

quickCheck.prompt: Average gain 4 pips, average loss 4 pips. Using the simplified formula, what is RSI?

options.explanation: Right: RS = 1, so RSI = 100 − 100 ÷ 2 = 50.
No: RSI is 100 only when there are no losses at all.
No: RSI is 0 only when there are no gains at all.

quickCheck.prompt: In a strong uptrend, RSI 14 stays above 70 for many candles. What does that mean?

options.text: Up moves have been much bigger than down moves recently
options.explanation: Right: that is all RSI measures.

options.text: Price is overbought, so a fall is now more likely than a rise
options.explanation: No: overbought is a label, not a forecast. In a strong uptrend, price can keep rising while RSI stays high.

options.text: The indicator is broken
options.explanation: No: RSI is working as designed. It shows that up moves have been bigger than down moves.

quickCheck.prompt: When does "RSI below 30, so buy" mislead most often?

options.text: In a strong downtrend
options.explanation: Right: RSI can stay low while price keeps falling.

options.text: In a calm, sideways range
options.explanation: No: in a calm range, "buy below 30" tends to mislead less. In a strong downtrend, RSI can stay low while price keeps falling.

options.text: Never
options.explanation: No: every indicator has conditions where it misleads.

doItNow.instructions: In Chart Lab, choose the Strong uptrend scenario and show RSI 14 below the chart. Find a stretch where RSI stayed above 70 while price kept rising. Write down how many candles it lasted. Try the Crash scenario for the same thing below 30.

lessons.title: What makes a strategy rules-based

inOneLine.simple: A rules-based strategy writes down exactly when to enter, when to exit and how much to risk, so two people applying it to the same chart make the same trades.
inOneLine.balanced: Exact rules can be tested on past and simulated charts, and the results can be compared fairly. Vague rules cannot: the result depends on who applies them and in what mood.

explain.simple: "Buy when the trend looks strong" is an opinion. "Buy on a close above the highest high of the previous 20 candles" is a rule: anyone can check whether it happened. A full rule set covers the entry, the exit, the [[stop-loss]], the position size and which markets and [[timeframe|timeframes]] it applies to. This module teaches two well-known families, moving-average trend following and channel breakouts, as simplified educational versions. Named historical versions of these systems are added to TradeLab only after a person has checked them against reliable sources.
explain.balanced: Rules make testing possible, but they do not make a strategy good. A rule set needs enough trades to judge ([[sample-size]]), results measured in R so different trades compare fairly ([[r-multiple]]), and costs included. Trend and breakout rules usually lose more often than they win and rely on a few large winners, so a long [[losing-streak]] is part of their normal behaviour. Named historical versions of these systems are added to TradeLab only after a person has checked them against reliable sources.

assumptions: Illustrative EUR/USD daily candles (simulated)
Rule: enter long on a close above the highest high of the previous 20 candles
Before day 1, the highest high of the previous 20 candles is 1.1180
steps: Day 1 closes at 1.1175. That is below 1.1180, so there is no entry, even though the day's high reached 1.1190.
Day 2: the previous 20 candles now include day 1, so the level rises to 1.1190. Day 2 closes at 1.1195, above 1.1190: the rule triggers.
The order fills at day 3's open, because the signal is only known once day 2 has closed.
Anyone applying the rule to these candles reaches the same answer: that is what makes it testable.

assumptions: 30 replay trades following one rule set (illustrative practice results, not real performance)
11 winners averaging +2.1R; 19 losers of −1R each
steps: Expectancy = 4.1 ÷ 30 ≈ +0.14R per trade.
Win rate = 11 ÷ 30 ≈ 37%: most trades lost, yet the total is positive in this sample.
30 trades is a small sample. A few different results would change the conclusion, so this says little about the future.

lessons.explainSimpler: A recipe instead of a feeling: if the rule is written exactly, anyone can follow it and check it.
lessons.commonMistake: Changing the rules after every loss. Each change creates a new strategy with no test behind it, and the losing streaks that trend and breakout rules normally have are never sat through long enough to judge them.

quickCheck.prompt: Which rule is specific enough to test?

options.text: Buy on a close above the highest high of the last 20 candles
options.explanation: Right: anyone can check whether it happened, so the result does not depend on who applies it.

options.text: Buy when the trend feels strong and the news is good
options.explanation: No: "feels strong" and "good news" mean different things to different people.

options.text: Buy when momentum is building
options.explanation: No: "building" is not defined, so two people would trade it differently.

quickCheck.prompt: 30 trades: 11 winners averaging +2.1R and 19 losers of −1R. What is the expectancy per trade?

options.text: About +1.1R per trade
options.explanation: No: that is the average win minus the average loss (2.1 − 1), which ignores how often each happens.

options.text: About +0.14R
About −0.27R, since most trades lost
options.explanation: No: a low win rate can still give a positive total when winners are larger than losers.

doItNow.instructions: Open Replay with the Breakout scenario. Before you start, write your entry, exit, stop and size rules in one sentence each. Take 5 trades using only those rules, and note any moment you wanted to break them.

lessons.homework: Rewrite one vague trading idea of your own as exact rules for entry, exit, stop and size.

lessons.title: Scam red flags: guaranteed returns, "account managers" and signal groups

inOneLine.simple: Anyone who promises guaranteed returns, asks for your login, or pushes you to act fast is a red flag for an [[investment-scam]].
inOneLine.balanced: Real trading has no guaranteed returns. Scams often use promised profits, a friendly "account manager", and paid [[signal-group|signal groups]] with results you cannot check. Never share your MetaTrader login with anyone.

explain.simple: Trading scams often look friendly and professional. Watch for three warning signs. First, guaranteed or "safe" returns. No honest person can promise that trading will make money. Second, an "account manager" who contacts you, offers to trade for you, or asks for your MetaTrader login or remote access to your phone. Never share your login, not even for a demo account. Third, paid signal groups. They post screenshots of winning trades, but you cannot check them, and they ask you to pay or to sign up with a broker they choose. All the examples in this lesson are fictional.
explain.balanced: Scams play on feelings: excitement (big returns), trust (a friendly contact), urgency ("only today"), and social proof (a busy chat full of "members" saying thanks). An [[account-manager-scam]] often starts with a small deposit that seems to grow, then pressure to deposit more, then problems when you try to withdraw. A [[signal-group]] may earn from fees or referrals whatever happens to members' trades. A quick test: if you cannot check who they are on a regulator's official register, cannot verify the results, and they want money or your login, walk away.

assumptions: Fictional message from a made-up group, "Example Pip Club (fictional)"
Message: "Join for 99 USD a month. Our signals return 10% every week, guaranteed."
Arithmetic only, to show why the claim cannot be true
steps: Start with a fictional 1,000 USD.
After 52 weeks: 1,000 × 1.10^52 ≈ 142,000 USD. A promise like that, "guaranteed", is a red flag on its own.

assumptions: Fictional story; all names made up
A person calling themselves "support" (fictional) contacts a learner after they fill in an online form
steps: The caller is friendly and says they are the learner's personal account manager.
They ask for the MetaTrader login "to set up the account properly".
They then push for a bigger deposit "before the opportunity closes".
Red flags: unsolicited contact, a request for the login, and urgency. The right move is to refuse, stop contact, and check the firm on a regulator's official register.

lessons.explainSimpler: If someone promises easy money, asks for your password, or rushes you, stop. That is the scam talking.
lessons.commonMistake: Thinking "it is only a demo, so sharing my login is harmless". It builds the habit scammers rely on, and the same people may later ask for a real account.

quickCheck.prompt: A stranger offers to manage your MetaTrader account for you and asks for your login. What do you do?

options.text: Share it, since they seem professional
options.explanation: No: never share your MetaTrader login with anyone.

options.text: Refuse and stop contact
options.explanation: Right: no genuine helper needs your login.

quickCheck.prompt: A signal group promises "guaranteed 5% a week". What is the best reading?

options.text: A confident group, worth paying for
options.explanation: No: confidence is not evidence, and no one can guarantee trading returns.

options.text: A red flag: guaranteed returns are a classic sign of a scam
options.explanation: Right: real trading has no guarantees.

quickCheck.prompt: Which of these is a red flag?

options.text: Urgency: "only today", "spots are limited"
options.explanation: Right: pressure to act fast stops you from checking.

options.text: A lesson that says losses are a normal part of trading
options.explanation: No: honest material talks about losses.

options.text: A demo account with no real money
options.explanation: No: practising on a demo account is not a red flag.

doItNow.instructions: Think of any trading ad, message or group you have seen. Without naming anyone, write down which red flags it showed: guaranteed returns, requests for a login, urgency, unverifiable results, or pressure to pay. If you have never seen one, write the three questions you would ask before trusting a trading offer.

lessons.title: Crypto "forex" schemes, fake brokers, pump-and-dumps and recovery scams

inOneLine.simple: Fake brokers, crypto "forex" schemes, [[pump-and-dump|pump-and-dumps]] and [[recovery-scam|recovery scams]] all try to get your money in, then make it hard or impossible to get out.
inOneLine.balanced: Warning signs include deposits only in crypto or to personal accounts, a platform you cannot find on any regulator's official register, sudden hype about a small asset, and anyone asking for a fee to "recover" lost money. Never pay to recover money.

explain.simple: Some scams set up a fake broker. The website and app look real. Your balance seems to grow. But when you try to withdraw, there are new "fees", "taxes" or delays. Crypto "forex" schemes are similar: you deposit crypto into a platform that promises forex or "AI trading" profits, and the money is hard to trace once it is gone. In a pump-and-dump, people hype a small asset so its price jumps, then sell to the buyers they attracted, and the price can collapse. Finally, after a loss, someone may offer to "recover" your money for a fee. This is a second scam. Never pay anyone to recover money. All examples here are fictional.
explain.balanced: A fake broker may copy the look, the name or the details of a real firm, so check the exact name, website and contact details against a regulator's official register, reached on your own, not through a link they send. Hype messages often come with countdowns and screenshots. A [[recovery-scam]] may claim to be a lawyer, an investigator or an official, and may already know details of your loss, sometimes because it is run by the same people. If you have lost money to a scam, report it through official channels in your country, and do not send more money to anyone who promises to get it back.

assumptions: Fictional platform "Example Crypto Platform (fictional)", all numbers made up
Learner deposits the equivalent of 500 USD in crypto
The dashboard shows the balance at 1,200 USD after a month
steps: The learner asks to withdraw 1,200 USD.
The platform asks for a "release fee" of 15%: 15% × 1,200 = 180 USD.
After paying, a new "tax" of 10% appears: 10% × 1,200 = 120 USD.
The 1,200 USD balance was a number on a screen. The learner has now sent 500 + 180 + 120 = 800 USD and received nothing. Each new fee is a red flag.

assumptions: Fictional story; all names made up
Weeks after the loss above, a "Sample Recovery Service (fictional)" calls
steps: The caller knows the platform name and the amount lost.
They promise to get the money back for an upfront fee of 300 USD.
This is a recovery scam. Paying would add to the loss.
The right move: do not pay, stop contact, and report the original loss through official channels.

lessons.explainSimpler: If getting your money out costs more money, or getting it back costs a fee upfront, it is a scam.
lessons.commonMistake: Paying a "withdrawal fee" or "tax" to release a balance. Each payment usually leads to another request.

quickCheck.prompt: A platform says you must pay a fee before you can withdraw your profits. What is the best reading?

options.text: A normal withdrawal charge; pay it
options.explanation: No: repeated surprise fees to release money are a classic fake-broker sign.

options.text: A warning sign; stop paying and check the firm on an official register
options.explanation: Right: this is how many fake platforms keep taking money.

quickCheck.prompt: Someone offers to recover your scam losses for an upfront fee. What do you do?

options.text: Pay, if they already know the details of your case, since that shows they are real
options.explanation: No: a scammer can know the details, for example from the first scam. Never pay upfront to recover money. This is a recovery scam.

options.text: Refuse, and report the loss through official channels
options.explanation: Right: upfront recovery fees are a second scam.

quickCheck.prompt: What is a pump-and-dump?

options.text: Hyping a small asset to push its price up, then selling to those who bought the hype
options.explanation: Right: late buyers are often left with big losses.

options.text: A normal method: buying a strongly rising asset early and selling once the rise slows down
options.explanation: No: that describes ordinary trend trading. A pump-and-dump is price manipulation: hype first, then selling to late buyers.

options.text: A type of order
options.explanation: No: it is not an order type. It is price manipulation: hype first, then selling to late buyers.

doItNow.instructions: Write a short note to your future self: "If anyone asks me to pay a fee to withdraw, to recover money, or to join a hot tip, I will..." Finish the sentence with the steps you will take: stop, do not pay, check the firm yourself, report through official channels.

lessons.title: Trading sessions

inOneLine.simple: Forex trades around the clock on weekdays, but activity rises and falls as different financial centres open and close.

explain.simple: There is no single forex exchange. Banks and brokers in different cities trade during their working day, so the market runs from Monday morning in Asia to Friday evening in New York. People usually talk about the Sydney, Tokyo, London, and New York [[trading-session|sessions]]. When London and New York are both open, many pairs trade most actively, and spreads are often tighter.
explain.balanced: Session times are conventions, not official hours, and they shift with daylight saving time in each city. Activity in a pair is usually highest when its home markets are open, for example EUR and GBP pairs during London hours. Quiet periods and the weekly open can bring wider spreads and gaps.

assumptions: Approximate convention: London ≈ 08:00–17:00 London time; New York ≈ 08:00–17:00 New York time
Your time zone is West Africa Time (UTC+1, no daylight saving)
Winter: London is UTC+0 and New York is UTC−5
If you live in another time zone, convert from UTC in the same way
steps: London 08:00 (UTC+0) = 09:00 your time.
New York 08:00 (UTC−5) = 13:00 UTC = 14:00 your time.
London closes about 17:00 London time = 18:00 your time, so the overlap is roughly 14:00–18:00 your time in winter.

In summer both cities move their clocks forward one hour, so these times come one hour earlier for you. The US and UK change their clocks on different dates, so for a few weeks each spring and autumn the gap between London and New York is an hour different from usual.

assumptions: Summer: London is UTC+1 and New York is UTC−4
Your time zone stays UTC+1
steps: London 08:00 = 08:00 your time.
New York 08:00 = 12:00 UTC = 13:00 your time.
Overlap is roughly 13:00–17:00 your time.

lessons.explainSimpler: The market is open on weekdays, day and night. It is usually busiest when London and New York are both open, which is the afternoon in West Africa.
lessons.commonMistake: Thinking every hour is the same. Spreads and how much prices move can change a lot between busy and quiet hours.

quickCheck.prompt: When is EUR/USD usually most active?

options.text: When London and New York are both open
options.explanation: Right: the overlap of the two largest centres usually brings the most activity.

options.text: On Saturday
options.explanation: No: the main forex market is closed at the weekend.

options.text: During the Asian session, when Tokyo is open
options.explanation: No: EUR/USD is usually quieter then. Activity usually peaks when London and New York are both open.

quickCheck.prompt: Why do session times in your local time change during the year?

options.text: London and New York switch to daylight saving time
options.explanation: Right: their clocks move, so the times shift for you.

options.text: The market changes its official opening hours every month
options.explanation: No: sessions are conventions based on local business hours.

options.text: Your phone's clock is wrong
options.explanation: No: the shift is real. London and New York move their clocks for daylight saving, on dates that can differ from yours.

doItNow.instructions: Using today's date, work out roughly when the London–New York overlap starts and ends in your time zone. Write it down and compare it with when you are free to study.

lessons.title: Stop loss and take profit

inOneLine.simple: A stop loss closes a losing trade at a level you chose. A take profit closes a winning trade at a level you chose.
inOneLine.balanced: A buy closes at the [[bid]], so its [[stop-loss]] and [[take-profit]] trigger on the bid. A sell closes at the [[ask]], so its levels trigger on the ask.

explain.simple: Before you open a trade, decide two prices. The stop loss is where your idea is wrong, so you get out. The take profit is where you are happy to bank the gain. For a buy, the stop loss goes below your entry and the take profit above. For a sell, it is the other way round. A buy is closed by selling, at the bid. A sell is closed by buying, at the ask. So a sell's stop can trigger when the ask touches it, even if the chart's bid line has not.
explain.balanced: Risk in money = stop distance in pips × [[pip-value]]. Set the stop first from your analysis, then choose a size that keeps that risk acceptable. A stop loss becomes a market order when triggered, so the fill can be worse than the level. A take profit normally fills at its level or better. Many brokers enforce a minimum distance from the current price. You can move a stop after entry, but moving it further away to avoid a loss defeats its purpose.

assumptions: Illustrative prices
Account currency USD
Buy 0.10 lot EUR/USD at ask 1.10012; pip value 1 USD
Stop loss 1.09512 (50 pips below); take profit 1.11012 (100 pips above)
No slippage in this example
steps: The buy closes at the bid, so the stop triggers when the bid falls to 1.09512.
Planned loss = 50 × 1 USD = 50 USD.
The take profit triggers when the bid rises to 1.11012.
Planned gain = 100 × 1 USD = 100 USD. Neither result is guaranteed: price may hit either level first, or neither.

assumptions: Illustrative prices
Sell 0.10 lot GBP/USD at bid 1.25000; pip value 1 USD
Spread 2 pips
Stop loss 1.25300 (30 pips above); take profit 1.24400 (60 pips below)
steps: The sell closes at the ask, so the stop triggers when the ask rises to 1.25300.
With a 2-pip spread, that happens when the bid is about 1.25280, 2 pips below the stop on a bid chart.
Planned loss = 30 × 1 USD = 30 USD.
The take profit triggers when the ask falls to 1.24400. Planned gain = 60 × 1 USD = 60 USD.

lessons.explainSimpler: Stop loss: 'get me out if I'm wrong.' Take profit: 'get me out when I've got enough.' Buys watch the bid. Sells watch the ask.
lessons.commonMistake: Placing a sell's stop exactly at a level seen on the bid chart. Because the sell closes at the ask, the spread can trigger it early. Another mistake is moving the stop further away when price gets close.

quickCheck.prompt: You hold a sell trade. Which price triggers its stop loss?

options.text: The ask
options.explanation: Right: a sell is closed by buying, and buys happen at the ask.

options.text: The bid, the price you sold at
options.explanation: No: the bid closes buy trades, not sell trades.

quickCheck.prompt: Buy 0.10 lot EUR/USD (pip value 1 USD) with a 40-pip stop. What is the planned loss if the stop fills at its level?

options.text: 4 USD
options.explanation: No: that would be a 4-pip stop.

options.text: 40 USD
options.explanation: Right: 40 pips × 1 USD = 40 USD.

options.text: 400 USD
options.explanation: No: that would need a pip value of 10 USD, which is 1.00 lot.

quickCheck.prompt: For a buy trade, where do the stop loss and take profit go?

options.text: Stop loss below entry, take profit above
options.explanation: Right: a buy loses if price falls and gains if it rises.

options.text: Stop loss above entry, take profit below it
options.explanation: No: that is the layout for a sell trade.

options.text: Both below entry
options.explanation: No: a take profit below entry would close a buy at a loss.

doItNow.instructions: On your demo account, place a 0.01 lot market order with a stop loss and take profit, move the stop, then close the trade. Follow the task card. Repeat until you have done 5 demo trades.

lessons.homework: For each of your 5 demo trades, write down the entry, stop loss, take profit, planned loss in money, and how the trade closed.

lessons.title: Support and resistance

inOneLine.simple: Support is where falling price has turned up before. Resistance is where rising price has turned down before.
inOneLine.balanced: Mark [[support]] and [[resistance]] from earlier [[swing-low|swing lows]] and [[swing-high|swing highs]], as zones rather than single lines. They show where price reacted in the past, not where it must react next time.

explain.simple: Look back on the chart for places where price turned more than once at about the same price. Turning up from below makes a support area. Turning down from above makes a resistance area. Draw these as zones a few pips wide, because price rarely turns at exactly the same price twice. A level is a place to watch, not a wall. Price can go straight through it.
explain.balanced: Good zones come from clear swing points on your chosen [[timeframe]]. Levels from a longer timeframe usually stand out more on shorter ones. Use wicks or bodies, but be consistent. When price breaks through a zone, the old support sometimes acts as resistance later, and the other way round. Often it does not. The more you draw, the more likely price is near some line by chance, so keep only the clearest few.

assumptions: Illustrative EUR/USD H4 prices
Three earlier swing lows at 1.08020, 1.07980 and 1.08050
Current bid 1.08400
steps: The lowest low is 1.07980 and the highest is 1.08050, so the zone runs from 1.07980 to 1.08050.
Distance from the current bid to the top of the zone = 1.08400 − 1.08050 = 35 pips.
If price falls into the zone, it may turn up again, move sideways, or break through. The zone tells you where to pay attention, not what will happen.

assumptions: Illustrative GBP/USD H1 prices
Resistance zone 1.26450–1.26500 from two earlier swing highs
Price later closes at 1.26600, then falls back to 1.26480 and the next candle closes at 1.26550
steps: The close at 1.26600 is 10 pips above the top of the old resistance zone (1.26600 − 1.26500).
Price comes back into the old zone at 1.26480. This is a [[retest]].
The next close at 1.26550 is back above the zone. For now, the old resistance acted like support.
This is one outcome. On another chart, price could have closed back below 1.26450 and kept falling.

lessons.explainSimpler: Support: a floor price has bounced from before. Resistance: a ceiling price has turned from before. Floors and ceilings in markets can break.
lessons.commonMistake: Drawing a single thin line and expecting price to turn at that exact price. Another mistake is filling the chart with so many lines that price is always near one.

quickCheck.prompt: Price has turned up three times near 1.0950. What is that area called?

options.text: Support
options.explanation: Right: support is where falling price has turned up before.

options.text: Resistance
options.explanation: No: resistance is where rising price has turned down.

quickCheck.prompt: Swing highs at 1.27120, 1.27080 and 1.27150. How wide is the resistance zone they form?

options.text: 7 pips
3 pips
options.explanation: No: that is only the gap between 1.27150 and 1.27120. The zone runs from the lowest to the highest of the three.

options.text: 70 pips
options.explanation: No: 0.00070 is 7 pips.

quickCheck.prompt: Price reaches a strong support zone. What will it do?

options.text: It must bounce
options.explanation: No: support describes the past. It can break.

options.text: It can bounce, move sideways or break through
options.explanation: Right: the zone tells you where to watch, not the outcome.

doItNow.instructions: On your demo account, draw horizontal lines at two support and two resistance areas on a EUR/USD H4 chart. Follow the task card.

lessons.title: Swaps: the cost of holding overnight

inOneLine.simple: Keep a trade open overnight and you may pay, or sometimes receive, a small amount called a swap.
inOneLine.balanced: A [[swap]] is a daily financing adjustment on open leveraged positions. It differs for buys and sells, by symbol and by broker, and can be negative or positive.

explain.simple: If you hold a trade past your broker's daily cut-off time, the broker adds or takes away a small amount. This is the swap. Often it is a cost. Sometimes it is a credit. Buys and sells on the same pair usually have different swaps. Some brokers charge extra on one night of the week to cover the weekend. Which night, and how much, depends on your broker, so check its contract specification.
explain.balanced: Swaps reflect the interest rate difference between the two currencies plus the broker's own charge, so they change over time. Brokers show them in different units, such as points or money per lot. Positive swaps can turn negative when rates or broker terms change, so they are not reliable income. For trades held for days or weeks, swaps can add up and should be counted in your costs, next to the [[spread]].

assumptions: Illustrative swap, not any broker's real rate
Swap for this buy trade: −0.50 USD per night for 0.10 lot
The trade is held for 4 nights
This made-up broker charges three nights' worth on one of those nights
steps: Normal nights: 3 × 1 = 3 swap charges.
The extra night counts as 3 charges.
Total charges = 3 + 3 = 6.
Total swap = 6 × −0.50 = −3.00 USD.

assumptions: Illustrative swap: +0.20 USD per night for 0.10 lot on a sell trade
Held for 10 nights, with no extra charges in this example
The broker may change swap rates at any time
steps: Total swap = 10 × 0.20 = +2.00 USD.
If the rate changed to −0.20 USD halfway through, the total would be 5 × 0.20 + 5 × (−0.20) = 0.00 USD.

lessons.explainSimpler: Holding a trade overnight is like borrowing overnight. Usually you pay a little rent. Sometimes you get a little back.
lessons.commonMistake: Ignoring swaps on trades held for a long time, or holding a trade just to collect a positive swap. Swap rates can change, and price moves usually matter far more than the swap.

quickCheck.prompt: Which statement about swaps is true?

options.text: They can be positive or negative and differ by broker
options.explanation: Right: they depend on the pair, the direction and the broker's terms.

options.text: They are always a fixed fee the same at every broker
options.explanation: No: they vary by broker, symbol and direction, and change over time.

options.text: They apply to trades opened and closed in the same day
options.explanation: No: swaps apply when a trade is held past the broker's daily cut-off.

quickCheck.prompt: A trade's swap is −0.40 USD per night. You hold it 5 nights with no extra charges. What is the total swap?

options.explanation: No: that is only one night.
No: a negative swap is a cost, so the total is negative.

doItNow.instructions: Find your demo broker's contract specification for EUR/USD, usually on its website. Write down the buy swap, the sell swap, the units they are shown in, and which night, if any, is charged extra.

lessons.homework: Compare the buy and sell swaps on EUR/USD and on one exotic pair at your demo broker. Note which ones are costs and which are credits.

lessons.title: Timeframes

inOneLine.simple: The timeframe is how much time one candle covers. Changing it changes how the same market looks.
inOneLine.balanced: Four H1 candles combine into one H4 candle: the first open, the highest high, the lowest low and the last close. Longer [[timeframe|timeframes]] hide the moves inside each candle.

explain.simple: On an M15 chart each candle covers 15 minutes. On H1 it is one hour, on H4 four hours, and on D1 one day. A 1-hour chart and a 1-day chart of EUR/USD show the same prices, grouped differently. Shorter timeframes show more detail and more back-and-forth. Longer ones show the bigger picture. Neither is the true one. They answer different questions.
explain.balanced: To build a longer candle from shorter ones: open = the first candle's open, close = the last candle's close, high = the highest high, low = the lowest low. A [[trend]] on D1 can sit alongside a move the other way on M15, because each covers a different stretch of time. Many people choose one main timeframe for decisions and look at one longer timeframe for context. Spreads stay the same whatever chart you watch, so on short timeframes they are a bigger share of a typical candle.

assumptions: Illustrative prices for four EUR/USD H1 candles in a row
steps: H4 open = candle 1 open = 1.10000. H4 close = candle 4 close = 1.10040.
The H4 candle has a 4-pip body (1.10040 − 1.10000) and a 30-pip range (1.10200 − 1.09900).
On H4 you see one small up candle. On H1 you can see price rose about 20 pips, then fell back. The longer timeframe hides that.

assumptions: Forex trades about 24 hours a day on weekdays
Illustrative chart that shows 100 candles on screen
steps: On M15 there are 4 candles per hour, so 100 candles cover 100 ÷ 4 = 25 hours, about one day.
On H1, 100 candles cover 100 hours, a little over 4 trading days.
On D1, 100 candles cover 100 trading days, roughly 5 months.
If the D1 chart rises over those months while the last day on M15 falls, both are true. They describe different windows of time.

lessons.explainSimpler: A timeframe is like zooming a map: street view and country view show the same place at different detail.
lessons.commonMistake: Flicking between timeframes until one shows what you hoped to see. Choose your timeframe before you look, and stick to it for that analysis.

quickCheck.prompt: How many H1 candles cover the same time as one H4 candle?

options.explanation: Right: an H4 candle covers four hours.
No: one H1 candle covers only one hour.
No: 24 H1 candles cover a whole day, like one D1 candle.

quickCheck.prompt: You combine four H1 candles into one H4 candle. Which price becomes the H4 close?

options.text: The close of the last H1 candle
options.explanation: Right: the H4 period ends when the fourth hour ends.

options.text: The highest close of the four
options.explanation: No: the close is simply the last price in the period.

options.text: The average of the four closing prices
options.explanation: No: candles do not average prices.

quickCheck.prompt: The D1 chart shows an uptrend and the M15 chart shows a fall. Which is correct?

options.text: Both: they describe different stretches of time
options.explanation: Right: a short fall can happen inside a longer rise.

options.text: Only D1, because the longer timeframe is always the true trend
options.explanation: No: neither timeframe is the true one. They answer different questions.

options.text: Only M15, because it is more recent
options.explanation: No: both charts include the latest prices.

doItNow.instructions: On your demo account, open a EUR/USD chart and switch between M15, H1, H4 and D1. Follow the task card and note how the same latest price looks on each.

lessons.title: Planning around news releases

inOneLine.simple: Check the economic calendar before you trade, and decide in advance what you will do around big releases.
inOneLine.balanced: Around major releases, [[spread|spreads]] often widen, [[volatility]] jumps and stops can suffer [[slippage]]. Plan with the [[economic-calendar]]: stay out, close before, or trade smaller with a wider stop.

explain.simple: An economic calendar lists upcoming releases, their time, the forecast and the last figure. Around big ones, prices can jump in seconds. The spread, which is the gap between buy and sell prices, can get much wider. A stop loss can fill well past its level. So many learners make a simple rule: no new trades shortly before a big release for the currencies they trade. Whatever you choose, decide it before the event, not during it.
explain.balanced: Choices before a high-importance release: (1) no trade, (2) close or reduce open trades beforehand, (3) trade with a wider stop and a smaller size so the money at risk stays the same. Even option 3 does not cap the loss: a [[gap]] or fast move can fill a stop far past its level. Always check the calendar's time zone, and note that the actual figure may be revised later. These are planning habits, not ways to predict the move.

assumptions: Illustrative prices and hypothetical spreads
Buy 0.10 lot EUR/USD; pip value 1 USD
Stop loss 20 pips below entry, so the planned loss is 20 USD = 1R
Normal spread 1 pip; during a release the spread widens to 8 pips
The release makes price jump, and the stop fills 10 pips past its level
steps: Planned loss = 20 × 1 USD = 20 USD.
Actual loss = (20 + 10) × 1 USD = 30 USD. That is 1.5R, not 1R.
A new trade opened during the release would also pay the wider spread: 8 pips × 1 USD = 8 USD, instead of 1 USD.
Nothing about the trade idea changed. The timing alone made the loss bigger.

assumptions: Example risk: 50 USD per trade, a learning example
EUR/USD, pip value 10 USD for 1.00 lot
Normal stop 25 pips; the learner wants a 50-pip stop around a release
steps: Normal day: size = 50 ÷ (25 × 10) = 0.20 lot.
Around the release: size = 50 ÷ (50 × 10) = 0.10 lot.
Planned risk stays at 50 USD, with a smaller size and a wider stop.
Slippage can still make the loss bigger than 50 USD. Skipping the trade is also a valid plan.

lessons.explainSimpler: Big news can make prices jump and costs spike. Look at the calendar first. Decide before the news: sit out, close, or go smaller.
lessons.commonMistake: Trading straight into a big release without checking the calendar, then being surprised by a wide spread or a stop filled far away. Another mistake is reading the calendar in the wrong time zone.

quickCheck.prompt: Buy 0.10 lot (pip value 1 USD), stop 15 pips. A release makes the stop fill 5 pips past its level. What is the loss?

options.text: 15 USD
options.explanation: No: that is the planned loss. The fill was 5 pips worse.

options.text: 20 USD
options.explanation: Right: (15 + 5) × 1 USD = 20 USD.

options.text: 5 USD
options.explanation: No: that is only the slippage part.

quickCheck.prompt: You keep the same money at risk but double your stop distance for a news day. What should happen to the size?

options.text: Halve it
options.explanation: Right: twice the pips at risk needs half the size for the same money.

options.text: Keep it the same
options.explanation: No: that doubles the money at risk.

quickCheck.prompt: What is the main reason to check an economic calendar before a trade?

options.text: To know which way price will move
options.explanation: No: the calendar shows when events happen, not what the market will do.

options.text: To know when spreads, volatility and slippage may jump, and plan for it
options.explanation: Right: it is a timing and risk tool, not a prediction tool.

doItNow.instructions: Open any economic calendar you trust and find 3 upcoming high-importance events for the currencies you practise. For each, write: the time in your local time, the consensus and the previous figure, one way price could react to a higher number and one to a lower number, and your plan (no trade, close before, or smaller size with a wider stop). After the events, write what actually happened and how well your plan held up.

lessons.homework: After each of your 3 events, note how wide the spread got on your demo or paper account, if you were watching.

lessons.title: Trends: higher highs and lower lows

inOneLine.simple: An uptrend makes higher highs and higher lows. A downtrend makes lower highs and lower lows. Anything else is sideways or unclear.
inOneLine.balanced: Mark the [[swing-high|swing highs]] and [[swing-low|swing lows]], then compare each with the one before. The [[trend]] is a description of those swings, not a forecast.

explain.simple: Price rarely moves in a straight line. It goes up, dips, goes up again. The turning points at the top are swing highs. The turning points at the bottom are swing lows. If each high is higher than the last, and each low is higher than the last, you can call it an uptrend. If each high and low is lower, it is a downtrend. If they overlap or mix, call it sideways or unclear. "Unclear" is a valid answer.
explain.balanced: A swing point is only confirmed after the candles that come after it. One common rule: a swing high is a candle whose high is above the highs of the 2 candles on each side.
