Different rules mark different swings, so be consistent. Use the same [[timeframe]] for every swing you compare. A trend so far says nothing certain about the next candle. Trends end, and the last swings before a turn often look just like the ones before.

assumptions: Illustrative EUR/USD H4 swing points, in time order
Swing low 1.09500, swing high 1.10200, swing low 1.09850, swing high 1.10600, swing low 1.10100
steps: Highs: 1.10200, then 1.10600. The second is higher, so that is a higher high.
Lows: 1.09500, then 1.09850, then 1.10100. Each is higher, so these are higher lows.
Higher highs and higher lows: you can describe this as an uptrend so far.
If the next low falls below 1.10100, that description no longer fits.

assumptions: Illustrative USD/JPY H1 swing points, in time order
For USD/JPY, 1 pip = 0.01
Swing high 151.80, swing low 150.90, swing high 151.20, swing low 150.30, swing high 150.70
steps: Highs: 151.80, 151.20, 150.70. Each is lower: lower highs.
Lows: 150.90, then 150.30. The second is lower: a lower low.
Lower highs and lower lows: a downtrend so far.
The highs fell by 60 pips (151.80 − 151.20 = 0.60) and then 50 pips (151.20 − 150.70 = 0.50). The size of each step varies. It does not have to be regular.

lessons.explainSimpler: Up stairs: each step higher. Down stairs: each step lower. Flat or messy: no clear trend.
lessons.commonMistake: Calling a trend from one or two candles, or from the last big move. Compare swing points, not single candles. Another mistake is assuming the trend must continue.

quickCheck.prompt: Swing highs: 1.2650, 1.2700, 1.2760. Swing lows: 1.2600, 1.2640, 1.2690. What do the swings describe?

options.text: An uptrend
options.explanation: Right: both the highs and the lows are rising.

options.text: A downtrend
options.explanation: No: a downtrend needs lower highs and lower lows.

options.text: Sideways
options.explanation: No: the swings are not overlapping. Each one is higher.

quickCheck.prompt: Swing highs: 1.1050, then 1.1048. Swing lows: 1.0990, then 1.1000. What is the best description?

options.text: Sideways or unclear
options.explanation: Right: the high slipped lower while the low rose. That is a mix, not a trend.

options.text: A clear uptrend, as the lows are rising
options.explanation: No: rising lows alone are not enough. An uptrend needs higher highs too, and 1.1048 is below 1.1050.

options.text: A clear downtrend
options.explanation: No: a downtrend needs lower lows, and 1.1000 is above 1.0990.

quickCheck.prompt: A chart shows a clear uptrend. What does that tell you about the next candle?

options.text: Nothing certain: a trend describes the past
options.explanation: Right: trends can stop or turn at any time.

options.text: It will probably close higher, because the trend is up
options.explanation: No: a trend describes the past. It does not tell you what the next candle will do.

options.text: It will close lower
options.explanation: No: a trend does not tell you the next candle, either way.

doItNow.instructions: In Practice, open the Find the trend drill. For each chart, mark the last few swing highs and lows, then answer up, down or sideways. Aim for 20 charts in total over this module.

lessons.title: Beyond the labels: choosing what to study

inOneLine.simple: Labels like 'forex is always liquid' or 'stocks are safe' are wrong. Every market changes with the time, the product and the conditions, so choose what to study by what fits you.
inOneLine.balanced: [[liquidity|Liquidity]], [[spread|spreads]] and [[volatility]] change with the [[trading-session|session]], the instrument and the news. Choose a market by your schedule, your account size versus the smallest sensible position, the costs you can measure, and the data you can study.

explain.simple: You will hear one-line labels: forex is always liquid, stocks are safe, futures are only for professionals, penny stocks are a cheap way to start. Each is wrong as a rule. A major currency pair can be busy at one hour and thin at another, and around news its spread can widen a lot. An ordinary share can fall sharply. A penny stock's low price says nothing about its risk; thin trading can make it expensive to get in and out. Instead of labels, test the conditions: when you would trade, what it would cost, and how big the smallest position would be for your account.
explain.balanced: A practical way to choose: (1) When can you study and practise? Match it to the market's active hours. (2) What is the smallest position, and does a normal stop on it fit your risk per trade? (3) What are the round-trip costs, measured on a demo or in the simulator at your chosen times? (4) What data do you need, and can you get it? (5) What can make price jump, and can you live with that? Write the answers down. Choosing a market to study is not a prediction of profit in it.

assumptions: Illustrative spreads, not any broker's terms
A currency pair at a broker: spread 1.0 pip in busy hours, 4.0 pips in quiet hours
0.10 lot, so 1 pip = 1 USD
A fictional penny stock: bid 0.50 USD, ask 0.55 USD; buy 2,000 shares
steps: Forex, 10 trades in busy hours: spread cost = 10 × 1.0 × 1 USD = 10 USD.
The same 10 trades in quiet hours: 10 × 4.0 × 1 USD = 40 USD, four times as much. Same pair, different time.
Penny stock: buy at the ask, 2,000 × 0.55 = 1,100 USD. Selling straight away at the bid gives 2,000 × 0.50 = 1,000 USD.
That is a 100 USD loss before price moves at all: 100 ÷ 1,100 ≈ 9.1%. A low share price did not mean a low cost.

assumptions: Practice account 2,000 USD; risk 1% per trade = 20 USD
Example index future (fictional specs): 10 USD per point; planned stop 20 points
EUR/USD, 0.01 lot = 0.10 USD per pip, 0.10 lot = 1 USD per pip; planned stop 20 pips
Fictional share at 20.00 USD; planned stop 1.00 USD below entry
steps: Future: 1 contract × 20 points × 10 USD = 200 USD at risk, 10% of the account. The smallest position is too big for this account and this stop.
Forex: 0.10 lot × 20 pips = 20 pips × 1 USD = 20 USD, which is 1%. The size can be cut in steps of 0.01 lot.
Shares: 20 USD ÷ 1.00 USD per share = 20 shares, costing 20 × 20.00 = 400 USD, with 20 USD at risk.
So for this account, the fictional future does not fit a 1% rule, while the other two do. The answer changes with the account, the stop and the contract.

lessons.explainSimpler: Do not trust slogans about markets. Check three things for yourself: when you can trade it, what it costs then, and whether the smallest trade fits your risk.
lessons.commonMistake: Choosing a market because of a slogan, a low share price, or because it is popular online. Another mistake is studying several markets at once before you can explain the costs and risks of one.

quickCheck.prompt: Why is 'forex is always liquid' a poor rule?

options.text: Liquidity changes with the time, the pair and the news
options.explanation: Right: spreads can widen in quiet hours and around releases, even on major pairs.

options.text: Forex is never liquid at any time
options.explanation: No: that is just the opposite slogan. Liquidity varies.

options.text: Liquidity only matters in the stock market, not in forex trading
options.explanation: No: liquidity affects spreads and fills in every market.

quickCheck.prompt: Account 3,000 USD, risk 1% = 30 USD. A fictional future is worth 10 USD per point, and your stop would be 15 points. Does 1 contract fit the rule?

options.text: Yes: 15 points is a small stop
options.explanation: No: a small number of points can still be a lot of money. Convert it first.

options.text: No: 150 USD at risk, which is 5%
options.explanation: Right: 15 × 10 = 150 USD, and 150 ÷ 3,000 = 5%, well above 30 USD.

options.text: Yes, if the margin is below 3,000 USD
options.explanation: No: margin tells you whether you can open it, not whether the risk fits your rule.

doItNow.instructions: In the Fundamental Analysis Lab, open the market comparison screen and read every row, including each caveat. Pick the market you are most drawn to and write down: the hours you could study it, the smallest position, what a normal stop on that position would risk for your practice account, and one way it could cost more than you expect.

lessons.homework: Write a one-page note: which market you will study first, why, and the three things you will check about the exact product before your first practice trade.

lessons.title: How the five markets differ

inOneLine.simple: The same price move can mean very different things in different markets, because what you hold, how you pay, and how much leverage is involved all differ.
inOneLine.balanced: Buying a [[share]] with your own cash is ownership; a forex position at a broker, a [[futures-contract]] or many commodity products are contracts, often with [[leverage]] and [[margin]]. Hours, costs and margin rules depend on the exchange, the broker and the jurisdiction.

explain.simple: When you buy an ordinary share with your own money, you own a small part of a company, and the most you can lose is what you paid. Penny stocks are shares too, but often of tiny companies whose shares trade thinly. In forex at a retail broker, and in futures, you usually hold a contract rather than the thing itself, and you put down margin instead of the full value. That changes everything about risk. Commodities such as gold or oil can be traded in several ways, often through futures or broker contracts. Each market also has its own trading hours and its own costs, such as spreads, commissions, overnight charges and the cost of rolling futures.
explain.balanced: Useful questions for any market: What do I actually hold? Who is on the other side? When can I trade, and when are there gaps? What does a trade cost, in money, both ways? Is there leverage, and what happens when margin runs short? What can make the price jump? The answers differ by product as well as by market: a commodity can be reached through a [[futures-contract]], a broker's contract or a fund, each with different rules. Use the market comparison screen as a map, and check the rules of the exact product and broker before practising.

assumptions: Illustrative prices and margins, not any broker's or exchange's terms
Fictional share at 20.00 USD; buy 50 shares with your own cash
EUR/USD at 1.1000, 0.10 lot (10,000 EUR), leverage 1:30, account in USD
Example index future (fictional specs): 10 USD per point, price 4,000.00, initial margin 2,000 USD
In each case price moves 2% against you
steps: Shares: cost = 50 × 20.00 = 1,000 USD. A 2% fall loses 1,000 × 0.02 = 20 USD, which is 2% of the money you put in.
Forex: trade value = 10,000 × 1.1000 = 11,000 USD; margin = 11,000 ÷ 30 = 366.67 USD. A 2% move loses 11,000 × 0.02 = 220 USD, about 60% of the margin.
Future: notional = 4,000 × 10 = 40,000 USD. A 2% move is 80 points, so the loss is 80 × 10 = 800 USD, 40% of the 2,000 USD margin.
Same 2% move, three very different results. The difference comes from what you hold and how much leverage you use, not from the market's name.

assumptions: Illustrative holding costs, not any broker's terms
Hold each position for 20 nights
Forex: hypothetical overnight swap of −0.80 USD per night on 0.10 lot
Shares bought with your own cash; no borrowing
Example commodity future (fictional specs): 100 units; rolled once at a calendar spread of 0.70 USD per unit in contango
steps: Forex: 20 × −0.80 = −16 USD in overnight swaps.
Shares: no overnight financing charge, because nothing was borrowed. Trading costs still apply when you buy and sell.
Future: no nightly charge, but the roll buys the later month 0.70 × 100 = 70 USD per contract higher, plus fees on two trades.
Each market has a different cost of time. Ignoring it can turn a small planned edge into a loss.

lessons.explainSimpler: Owning a share is like buying a thing outright. Forex and futures are more like a deposit on a big deal. A small move against a big deal can cost a lot.
lessons.commonMistake: Comparing markets by price alone, or by what someone online says about them. Compare what you hold, the costs, the leverage and the margin rules for the exact product you would use, at your broker, in your country.

quickCheck.prompt: You buy fictional shares worth 1,000 USD with your own cash, no borrowing. Price falls 5%. What do you lose?

options.text: 5 USD
options.explanation: No: 5% of 1,000 is 50, not 5.

options.text: 500 USD
options.explanation: No: that would be a 50% fall.

options.text: 50 USD
options.explanation: Right: 1,000 × 0.05 = 50 USD. Without leverage, the loss is the same share of what you paid.

quickCheck.prompt: What is the key difference between buying a share with cash and holding a futures contract?

options.text: Futures always cost less to trade than shares
options.explanation: No: costs depend on the product and the broker. No market is always cheaper.

options.text: You own nothing; it is a contract on margin
options.explanation: Right: you put down margin on a contract, so the loss can exceed what you put down.

options.text: Shares can only rise, while futures can fall
options.explanation: No: share prices can fall too, all the way to zero.

doItNow.instructions: Open the Fundamental Analysis Lab and go to the market comparison screen. Read the rows on ownership vs contract, leverage, margin and typical costs. For each of the five markets, write one sentence on what you would actually hold and one on what could make you lose more than you planned.

lessons.title: Buying calls and puts: value at expiry, breakeven and the most you can lose

inOneLine.simple: When you buy an option, the most you can lose is the premium you paid. To make money at expiry, the price must move past the strike by more than that premium.
inOneLine.balanced: At expiry a call is worth max(price − strike, 0) per unit and a put max(strike − price, 0). Buyer P/L = (value − premium) × units per contract × contracts. [[breakeven|Breakeven]]: call = strike + premium, put = strike − premium. An [[out-of-the-money]] option expires worthless.

explain.simple: A call buyer wants the price to rise above the strike. A put buyer wants it to fall below the strike. At expiry, work out what the option is worth: for a call, the price minus the strike; for a put, the strike minus the price. If that comes out below zero, the option is worth nothing. Then take away the premium you paid. The price where you exactly get your premium back is the breakeven. Below it (for a call) or above it (for a put), you lose money even if the price moved your way. If the option is worth nothing at expiry, you lose the whole premium.
explain.balanced: A bought option has a known worst case: the premium paid, plus fees. That makes it different from a futures contract or a short sale. But a known loss is not a small risk. An option can expire worthless, and the whole premium is lost; holding many contracts means losing many premiums. A bought call's gain has no fixed ceiling, because the price can keep rising. A bought put's gain is largest if the underlying falls to zero: (strike − premium) × units. One exception to check: depending on the contract and the broker, an option that is in the money at expiry may be exercised automatically, and for a contract that settles by delivery the buyer of a call would then have to pay strike × units for the underlying. These sums are for expiry only. Before expiry the option's price also includes [[time-value]], which the next lessons cover.

assumptions: Example option (fictional specs): one contract covers 100 units
Buy 1 call, strike 50.00, premium 2.00 USD per unit
Held to expiry; fees left out
steps: Premium paid = 2.00 × 100 = 200 USD. That is the most this position can lose.
Breakeven at expiry = 50.00 + 2.00 = 52.00.
Price at expiry 56.00: value = 56.00 − 50.00 = 6.00 per unit. P/L = (6.00 − 2.00) × 100 = 400 USD gain.
Price at expiry 51.00: value = 1.00 per unit. P/L = (1.00 − 2.00) × 100 = 100 USD loss. The price rose above the strike, but not past the breakeven.
Price at expiry 48.00: value = 0. The call expires worthless. P/L = (0 − 2.00) × 100 = 200 USD loss, the whole premium.

assumptions: Same fictional contract size: 100 units per contract
Buy 2 puts, strike 40.00, premium 1.50 USD per unit
Held to expiry; fees left out
steps: Premium paid = 1.50 × 100 × 2 = 300 USD. That is the most this position can lose.
Breakeven at expiry = 40.00 − 1.50 = 38.50.
Price at expiry 35.00: value = 40.00 − 35.00 = 5.00 per unit. P/L = (5.00 − 1.50) × 100 × 2 = 700 USD gain.
Price at expiry 42.00: value = 0. Both puts expire worthless: a 300 USD loss.
Largest possible gain, only if the price fell to 0: (40.00 − 1.50) × 100 × 2 = 7,700 USD. This is a limit, not a likely outcome.

lessons.explainSimpler: Work out what the option is worth at expiry, never less than zero. Take away what you paid. If it is worth nothing, you lose everything you paid, and no more.
lessons.commonMistake: Thinking you are in profit as soon as the price passes the strike. You must also cover the premium: a call only breaks even at strike + premium. Another mistake is treating 'I can only lose the premium' as 'this is safe': the whole premium is lost often enough that each trade must be sized as if it could go to zero.

quickCheck.prompt: Fictional: you buy 1 call, strike 30.00, premium 1.20 USD per unit, 100 units per contract. At expiry the price is 33.00. What is your profit or loss?

options.text: A 300 USD gain
options.explanation: No: that is the value at expiry, 3.00 × 100. Take away the 120 USD premium.

options.text: A 180 USD gain
A 120 USD loss
options.explanation: No: that would be the result if the call expired worthless. Here it is in the money.

quickCheck.prompt: Fictional: you buy a put, strike 60.00, premium 2.50 USD per unit. What is the breakeven price at expiry?

options.explanation: No: that is the call formula, strike + premium. A put needs the price to fall.
No: at 60.00 the put is worth nothing and the whole premium is lost.
Right: put breakeven = strike − premium = 60.00 − 2.50 = 57.50.

quickCheck.prompt: You bought 1 call. What is the most you can lose if you hold it to expiry (fees aside)?

options.text: The premium you paid
options.explanation: Right: if the call expires worthless you lose the premium, and nothing more.

options.text: There is no fixed limit
options.explanation: No: that is true for a seller of an uncovered call, not for a buyer.

options.text: The strike × units
options.explanation: No: a buyer never has to use the right, so the strike is not at risk.

doItNow.instructions: Work out this lesson's call example by hand first. Then open the option-at-expiry calculator and enter Call, Buy (hold), Contracts 1, Units per contract 100, Strike price 50, Premium per unit 2. Try Price of the underlying at expiry 56, 51 and 48, and check the profit or loss shows +400.00, −100.00 and −200.00, with a breakeven of 52.00. Then switch to Put, Contracts 2, Strike price 40, Premium per unit 1.50, try 35 and 42, and check +700.00 and −300.00.

lessons.homework: Draw a simple payoff line for the fictional call in this lesson: price at expiry along the bottom from 44 to 60, profit or loss up the side. Mark the strike, the breakeven and the most you could lose.

lessons.title: What an option is: calls, puts, strike, premium and expiry

inOneLine.simple: An option gives its buyer the right, but not the duty, to buy or sell something at a set price before or on a set date. The buyer pays a price for that right.
inOneLine.balanced: A [[call-option|call]] is a right to buy and a [[put-option|put]] is a right to sell the [[underlying]] at the [[strike-price]], until or at [[expiry]]. The buyer pays the [[option-premium|premium]]; the seller, or [[option-writer|writer]], receives it and takes on the obligation.

explain.simple: An option is a contract between two sides. The buyer pays a price, called the premium, and gets a choice. With a call, the choice is to buy the underlying (the share or other thing the option is based on) at a fixed price, called the strike. With a put, the choice is to sell at the strike. The choice lasts until a set date, called expiry. The buyer never has to use it. The seller is different: the seller keeps the premium but must carry out the deal if the buyer uses the right. Using the right is called exercise. When that happens, a seller is picked to fulfil it, which is called assignment.
explain.balanced: Exchange-listed options are standardised contracts, and each one has a specification. It names the underlying, how many units one contract covers, the strikes and expiry dates on offer, the [[exercise-style]] and how the contract settles. American style can be [[exercise|exercised]] on any trading day up to expiry; European style only at expiry. Some options end with the underlying changing hands, others settle in cash. The premium is usually quoted per unit of the underlying, so the money for one contract is premium × units per contract. In this module one contract covers 100 units, but only because the examples are fictional. Never assume a contract size: check the exact contract's specification.

assumptions: Example option (fictional specs): one contract covers 100 units of a fictional share
Share price today 50.00 USD
Call option: strike 52.00, premium 1.50 USD per unit
Fees left out
steps: Premium for 1 contract = 1.50 × 100 = 150 USD. The buyer pays it; the seller receives it.
The buyer now holds the right to buy 100 units at 52.00. The seller has the duty to sell 100 units at 52.00 if assigned.
If the share is at 55.00 at expiry, the right to buy at 52.00 is worth 55.00 − 52.00 = 3.00 per unit, or 3.00 × 100 = 300 USD for the contract.
If the share is at 49.00 at expiry, nobody would pay 52.00 for something worth 49.00. The call expires worthless, and the buyer has lost the 150 USD premium.
The next lesson works out profit and loss, which also counts the premium paid.

assumptions: Same fictional contract size: 100 units per contract
Fictional share price today 40.00 USD
Put option: strike 38.00, premium 1.20 USD per unit
steps: Premium for 1 contract = 1.20 × 100 = 120 USD.
The buyer holds the right to sell 100 units at 38.00. The seller must buy them at 38.00 if assigned.
If the share is at 35.00 at expiry, the right to sell at 38.00 is worth 38.00 − 35.00 = 3.00 per unit, or 300 USD for the contract.
If the share is at 41.00 at expiry, selling at 38.00 makes no sense. The put expires worthless and the 120 USD premium is gone.

lessons.explainSimpler: A call is a paid ticket to buy at a fixed price. A put is a paid ticket to sell at a fixed price. The ticket runs out on a set date. The buyer can use it or not; the seller must go along if it is used.
lessons.commonMistake: Mixing up the two sides. The buyer has a right and a known cost; the seller has an obligation. Another mistake is forgetting the contract size: a premium of 1.50 is per unit, so one contract costs 1.50 × the units it covers, which you must read from the specification.

quickCheck.prompt: Which option gives its holder the right to sell the underlying at the strike price?

options.text: A call
options.explanation: No: a call is a right to buy at the strike.

options.text: A put
options.explanation: Right: a put is a right to sell at the strike, until or at expiry.

options.text: Any option, after expiry
options.explanation: No: after expiry the option no longer exists, so there is no right left.

quickCheck.prompt: Fictional option: premium 0.80 USD per unit, one contract covers 100 units (fictional). You buy 2 contracts. What premium do you pay?

options.text: 80 USD
options.explanation: No: that is the premium for one contract. You bought 2.

options.text: 160 USD
1.60 USD
options.explanation: No: that leaves out the 100 units each contract covers.

quickCheck.prompt: You sold (wrote) a call option. The buyer exercises it. What happens to you?

options.text: You are assigned and must sell at the strike
options.explanation: Right: the writer has the obligation, and assignment makes it due.

options.text: You can choose to refuse
options.explanation: No: only the buyer has a choice. The seller must carry out the deal.

options.text: You must buy at the strike
options.explanation: No: that is what an assigned put seller must do.

doItNow.instructions: Open the option-at-expiry calculator. Set Option type to Call, Position to Buy (hold), Contracts 1, Units per contract 100, Strike price 52, Premium per unit 1.50 and Price of the underlying at expiry 55. Check that Value per unit at expiry shows 3.00 and Premium paid shows 150.00. Change the price at expiry to 49 and see it expire worthless. Then write, one line each, the seven things you would read in a real option's specification: underlying, units per contract, call or put, strike, expiry date, exercise style and settlement.

lessons.homework: Write a one-page 'option spec card' with blank fields for underlying, call or put, units per contract, strike, expiry date, exercise style, settlement and premium per unit. Fill it in for the two fictional options in this lesson.

lessons.title: What is in a premium: intrinsic value, time value and volatility

inOneLine.simple: Before expiry, an option's price has two parts: what it would be worth right now, and extra for the time left. The extra part melts away as expiry gets closer.
inOneLine.balanced: Premium = [[intrinsic-value]] + [[time-value]]. Whether an option is [[in-the-money|in]], [[at-the-money|at]] or [[out-of-the-money|out of]] the money decides its intrinsic value. Time value shrinks as expiry nears ([[time-decay]]) and is usually higher when [[implied-volatility]] is higher.

explain.simple: Intrinsic value is what the option would be worth if it expired right now. A call with the price above the strike has some; so does a put with the price below the strike. That option is 'in the money'. An option with no intrinsic value is 'out of the money', or 'at the money' if the strike equals the price. Anything a buyer pays above intrinsic value is time value: paying for the chance that the price moves further before expiry. As expiry gets closer, there is less time for that move, so time value tends to shrink. At expiry it is zero. That is why an option can lose value even when the price moves your way, if the move is small or slow.
explain.balanced: Time value depends on time left and on how big the market expects future swings to be. Implied volatility is that expectation, worked backwards from option prices. When it is high, premiums are usually higher, because a large move looks more likely; when it falls, premiums can drop even if the underlying price does not move. Time value is usually largest for options near the money and smaller for options far in or far out of the money. Professional pricing models exist, but this module does not use them: the numbers in this lesson are made-up quotes to show the parts of a premium, and the app's calculator only works out value at expiry.

assumptions: Example options (fictional specs and fictional quotes): one contract covers 100 units
Share price 55.00 USD, some weeks before expiry
Calls quoted at: strike 50.00 for 6.50, strike 55.00 for 2.40, strike 60.00 for 0.90 USD per unit
steps: Strike 50 call is in the money. Intrinsic = 55.00 − 50.00 = 5.00. Time value = 6.50 − 5.00 = 1.50.
Strike 55 call is at the money. Intrinsic = 0. Time value = all of it, 2.40.
Strike 60 call is out of the money. Intrinsic = 0. Time value = 0.90.
If the share is still 55.00 at expiry, all time value is gone: the 50 call is worth 5.00, the 55 and 60 calls are worth 0.
So a buyer of the 50 call at 6.50 would lose (5.00 − 6.50) × 100 = 150 USD at expiry, even though the price did not move at all.

assumptions: Same fictional contract size: 100 units per contract
Buy 1 call, strike 60.00, for 0.90 USD per unit (90 USD) with the share at 55.00
Some days later the share is 57.00 and the call's fictional quote is 0.60
steps: The share moved your way, from 55.00 to 57.00.
The call is still out of the money, so it is all time value, and there is less time left.
Its value fell from 0.90 to 0.60: (0.60 − 0.90) × 100 = 30 USD down.
If the share is still 57.00 at expiry, the call is worth 0 and the whole 90 USD is lost.
If expected swings had also calmed down (lower implied volatility), the quote could have fallen further. This is a made-up case to show the mechanism, not a prediction.

lessons.explainSimpler: Premium = what it is worth now + extra for time left. The extra fades as the date gets closer and is gone at expiry. Only the 'worth now' part is left.
lessons.commonMistake: Thinking you only need to be right about direction. With a bought option you also need the move to be big enough and soon enough to beat the time value you paid. Another mistake is calling an option 'cheap' because its premium is small: an out-of-the-money option is all time value, and it can easily expire worthless.

quickCheck.prompt: Fictional: share at 47.00. A put with strike 50.00 is quoted at 4.20 USD per unit. What are its intrinsic value and time value?

options.text: Intrinsic 0, time value 4.20
options.explanation: No: that treats it like a call. A put has intrinsic value when the price is below the strike.

options.text: Intrinsic 3.00, time value 1.20
options.explanation: Right: 50.00 − 47.00 = 3.00 intrinsic, and 4.20 − 3.00 = 1.20 time value.

options.text: Intrinsic 3.00, time value 7.20
options.explanation: No: time value is premium minus intrinsic, not premium plus intrinsic.

quickCheck.prompt: Fictional: share at 80.00. Which option is out of the money?

options.text: A call with strike 75.00
options.explanation: No: the right to buy at 75.00 when the price is 80.00 is worth 5.00, so it is in the money.

options.text: A put with strike 70.00
options.explanation: Right: the right to sell at 70.00 when the price is 80.00 is worth nothing now.

options.text: A call with strike 80.00
options.explanation: No: a strike equal to the price is at the money.

quickCheck.prompt: You bought an out-of-the-money call. The share rises slowly but stays below the strike, and the call's price falls. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: Time decay: the time value is shrinking
options.explanation: Right: with less time left and no intrinsic value, the premium tends to fall.

options.text: The quote must be wrong
options.explanation: No: an option can lose value while the price moves your way, if the move is small or slow.

options.text: Calls lose value whenever the price rises
options.explanation: No: a rising price helps a call. Here time decay outweighed a small move.

doItNow.instructions: Use the option-at-expiry calculator to see that only intrinsic value is left at expiry. Enter Call, Buy (hold), Contracts 1, Units per contract 100, Strike price 50, Premium per unit 6.50 and Price of the underlying at expiry 55. Check that Value per unit at expiry is 5.00 and the profit or loss is −150.00: the 1.50 of time value paid is gone. Then enter Strike price 60, Premium per unit 0.90, price at expiry 57, and check −90.00. Remember the calculator cannot price an option before expiry.

lessons.homework: For a fictional share at 40.00, write down two calls and two puts, one in the money and one out of the money each, with made-up premiums. For each, split the premium into intrinsic value and time value.

lessons.title: Options risk: leverage, spreads, specifications and a practice plan

inOneLine.simple: A small premium controls a lot of units, so options can win or lose fast. Read the contract, watch the spread, and keep it in simulation.
inOneLine.balanced: Options carry [[leverage]]: a premium far smaller than the units' value controls them, so the whole premium can be lost on a small or slow move. Some options trade thinly, with wide [[spread|bid-ask spreads]]. Check the full specification before any study trade, and set plan rules in advance.

explain.simple: With an option, a small amount of money is tied to a much bigger amount of the underlying. If the price moves a lot your way, the gain can be large compared with what you paid. If it does not, you can lose everything you paid, quickly. That is leverage. Options can also be costly to trade. Some have few buyers and sellers, so the gap between the price to buy (ask) and the price to sell (bid) can be wide. Buying and selling straight back can lose money even if nothing moves. Before studying any option, read its specification, and keep all practice in a simulator.
explain.balanced: Leverage makes position size matter more, not less. Spending the same money on options as on the underlying is a much bigger bet. [[liquidity|Liquidity]] differs a lot between strikes and expiry dates; strikes far from the price and far-off expiries can trade rarely, and spreads can widen in fast markets. Your specification checklist: the [[underlying]], units per contract, call or put, [[strike-price]], [[expiry]] date, [[exercise-style]], and settlement (delivery or cash). Simple plan rules for study: buy only, never sell uncovered; set a fixed most-premium-at-risk per trade; write the reason, the breakeven and the exit before entering; and review each case afterwards.

assumptions: Fictional share price 50.00 USD; one option contract covers 100 units (fictional specs)
Choice A: buy 100 units of the share for 5,000 USD
Choice B: buy 1 call, strike 50.00, premium 2.00 USD per unit, for 200 USD
Held to expiry; fees left out
steps: Price at expiry 56.00: A gains 6.00 × 100 = 600 USD, which is 600 ÷ 5,000 = 12% of the money spent. B gains (6.00 − 2.00) × 100 = 400 USD, which is 400 ÷ 200 = 200% of the money spent.
Price at expiry 50.00: A gains or loses nothing. B loses the whole 200 USD, which is 100% of the money spent.
Price at expiry 48.00: A loses 2.00 × 100 = 200 USD, or 4%. B also loses 200 USD, but that is 100% of what it cost.
Spending the full 5,000 USD on calls instead buys 5,000 ÷ 200 = 25 contracts. At 50.00 or below at expiry, all 5,000 USD is lost.
The same money in options is a far bigger bet. This is a made-up case to show the mechanism.

assumptions: Fictional option quoted bid 1.80, ask 2.20 USD per unit; 100 units per contract
Fictional share quoted bid 49.99, ask 50.01
steps: Buy 1 option at the ask: 2.20 × 100 = 220 USD.
Sell it straight back at the bid: 1.80 × 100 = 180 USD.
Loss = 220 − 180 = 40 USD before the price has moved at all.
Buying and selling 100 units of the share straight back costs (50.01 − 49.99) × 100 = 2 USD.
A wide spread means the price must move further in your favour just to get back to even.

lessons.explainSimpler: A small payment controls a lot, so it can grow or vanish fast. Buying and selling can cost a lot if few people trade that option. Read the rules first and practise only in a simulator.
lessons.commonMistake: Buying many cheap options because each one costs little. Size by the total premium you could lose, assuming it all goes to zero. Another mistake is ignoring the spread and the specification: units per contract, exercise style and settlement all change what a trade means.

quickCheck.prompt: Which item belongs on your option specification checklist?

options.text: Settlement: delivery or cash
options.explanation: Right: settlement is part of the contract's specification, along with units per contract, strike, expiry and exercise style.

options.text: What a forum expects the price to do
options.explanation: No: opinions are not part of a contract's specification.

options.text: How much the option rose last week
options.explanation: No: past price moves are not part of the specification.

quickCheck.prompt: Fictional option: bid 0.90, ask 1.10 USD per unit, 100 units per contract. You buy 2 contracts and sell them straight back. What do you lose?

options.text: 20 USD
options.explanation: No: that is the spread cost for one contract. You traded 2.

options.text: 40 USD
0.20 USD
options.explanation: No: that is the spread per unit. Multiply by units and contracts.

quickCheck.prompt: Fictional: you buy 4 calls at a premium of 2.50 USD per unit, 100 units each. All four expire out of the money. What is lost?

options.text: 250 USD
options.explanation: No: that is the premium for one contract. You bought 4.

options.text: 10 USD
options.explanation: No: that leaves out the 100 units each contract covers.
Right: 2.50 × 100 × 4 = 1,000 USD, the whole premium paid.

doItNow.instructions: Write your options study rules on one page. Include: you will study options only in simulation and the calculator; the most premium you would put at risk on one fictional trade; that you will not sell uncovered options; the seven items you check in a specification; and the three things you write before any study trade (reason, breakeven, exit). Then work through 5 fictional option cases by hand and check each in the option-at-expiry calculator.

lessons.homework: Pick one fictional option from this module. Write its full specification card, its breakeven, its largest possible loss, and the spread cost of buying and selling one contract at the quotes you make up.

lessons.title: Selling (writing) options: premium, assignment and uncovered risk

inOneLine.simple: An option seller collects the premium up front, but takes on a duty. The premium is the most the seller can make, and the loss can be far bigger.
inOneLine.balanced: An [[option-writer]] receives the [[option-premium|premium]] and can be [[assignment|assigned]]. Seller P/L is the buyer's P/L with the sign flipped. An [[uncovered-option|uncovered]] sold call has no fixed limit on loss; a sold put can lose up to (strike − premium) × units if the price falls to zero.

explain.simple: Every option has a buyer and a seller. The seller, also called the writer, is paid the premium at the start. If the option expires worthless, the seller keeps it all. That is the best case, and it is also the limit: the seller can never make more than the premium. If the option ends in the money, the seller must carry out the deal. A call seller must sell at the strike, even if the price has shot up. A put seller must buy at the strike, even if the price has collapsed. The seller's loss is the buyer's gain, so it can be many times the premium received.
explain.balanced: Selling a call while owning the units it covers is a [[covered-call]]: if assigned, you deliver units you hold, so the call's loss is offset, but you give up gains above the strike and keep nearly all the risk of the units falling (the premium cushions a fall only slightly). Selling a call without owning them is [[uncovered-option|uncovered]], or naked: the price can keep rising, so there is no fixed limit on the loss. Selling a put while setting cash aside to buy at the strike is a [[cash-secured-put]]; the cash makes the purchase possible but does not shrink the loss. With American-style options, assignment can come at any time before expiry. Brokers usually require approval and [[margin]] before you can write options, and margin can be raised. In this app, selling options is something to study in the calculator, not to do.

assumptions: Example option (fictional specs): one contract covers 100 units
Sell (write) 1 call, strike 50.00, premium 2.00 USD per unit, without owning the units (uncovered)
Held to expiry; fees and margin left out
steps: Premium received = 2.00 × 100 = 200 USD. That is the most this position can make.
Price at expiry 49.00: the call expires worthless. The seller keeps the 200 USD.
Price at expiry 56.00: the call is worth 6.00 per unit. Seller P/L = −(6.00 − 2.00) × 100 = 400 USD loss.
Price at expiry 70.00: the call is worth 20.00 per unit. Seller P/L = −(20.00 − 2.00) × 100 = 1,800 USD loss, nine times the premium received.
There is no price where this stops: every 1.00 rise beyond that adds another 100 USD of loss.

Covered version: if the seller already owned 100 units bought at 50.00, at 70.00 the units gain (70.00 − 50.00) × 100 = 2,000 USD and the call loses 1,800 USD, a total of 200 USD gain. Everything above the strike was given up.

assumptions: Same fictional contract size: 100 units per contract
Sell (write) 1 put, strike 40.00, premium 1.50 USD per unit
Held to expiry; fees and margin left out
steps: Premium received = 1.50 × 100 = 150 USD.
Price at expiry 42.00: the put expires worthless. The seller keeps 150 USD.
Price at expiry 35.00: the seller is assigned and must buy 100 units at 40.00 that are worth 35.00. P/L = −(5.00 − 1.50) × 100 = 350 USD loss.
Worst case, price falls to 0: loss = (40.00 − 1.50) × 100 = 3,850 USD.
Cash-secured: setting aside 40.00 × 100 = 4,000 USD means the purchase could be paid for. It does not make the 3,850 USD worst case any smaller.

lessons.explainSimpler: The seller is paid first and hopes nothing happens. If something does happen, the seller pays the buyer's gain, and that can be far more than was collected.
lessons.commonMistake: Seeing a small premium that is usually kept and thinking it is easy money. Many small wins can be wiped out by one large loss, and with an uncovered call that loss has no ceiling. Another mistake is thinking a covered call has no risk: the units you own can still fall a long way.

quickCheck.prompt: Fictional: you sell 1 uncovered call, strike 20.00, premium 1.00 USD per unit, 100 units per contract. At expiry the price is 26.00. What is your profit or loss?

options.text: A 100 USD gain
options.explanation: No: you would keep the 100 USD only if the call expired worthless. It ended 6.00 in the money.

options.text: A 500 USD loss
options.explanation: Right: the call is worth 6.00, so −(6.00 − 1.00) × 100 = −500 USD.

options.text: A 600 USD loss
options.explanation: No: that forgets the 100 USD premium you received.

quickCheck.prompt: What is the most an option seller can make on one trade held to expiry?

options.text: There is no fixed limit
options.explanation: No: that describes the loss on an uncovered sold call, not the gain.

options.text: Strike × units per contract
options.explanation: No: the seller never receives the strike as profit.

options.text: The premium received
options.explanation: Right: the best case is the option expiring worthless and the seller keeping the premium.

quickCheck.prompt: Fictional: you sell 1 put, strike 30.00, premium 2.00 USD per unit, 100 units per contract. What is the largest possible loss at expiry?

options.text: 200 USD
options.explanation: No: that is the premium received, which is the most you can make.
Right: if the price falls to 0, the loss is (30.00 − 2.00) × 100 = 2,800 USD.
No: that forgets the 200 USD premium received.

doItNow.instructions: Open the option-at-expiry calculator and set Position to Sell (write). Enter Call, Contracts 1, Units per contract 100, Strike price 50, Premium per unit 2. Try Price of the underlying at expiry 49, 56 and 70, and check +200.00, −400.00 and −1800.00. Read the Largest possible loss line: it has no fixed limit. Then switch to Put, Strike price 40, Premium per unit 1.50, and check that the largest possible loss is 3850.00. Write one sentence on why a buyer and a seller of the same option end up with opposite results.

lessons.homework: Make a table for the fictional uncovered call in this lesson with prices at expiry of 45, 50, 52, 55, 60, 70 and 80. For each, write the seller's profit or loss. Mark where the losses pass the premium received, then pass 5 times it.

lessons.title: Low float, dilution and reverse splits

inOneLine.simple: A small [[float]] makes prices jumpy. [[dilution|Dilution]] shrinks your slice of the company. A [[reverse-split|reverse split]] changes the share count, not the business.
inOneLine.balanced: Check three things on any small share: how many shares can actually trade, how fast the share count has been growing, and whether reverse splits keep following that growth. Together they often tell you more than the price chart.

explain.simple: The float is the number of shares the public can actually trade. If insiders hold most shares, the float is small, and a modest amount of buying or selling can move the price a long way, up or down. Dilution happens when a company creates new shares, usually to raise cash. You still own the same number of shares, but they are a smaller part of a bigger pile. A reverse split swaps several old shares for one new one. The price per share goes up, but your total value does not change on the day. All companies here are fictional.
explain.balanced: Small companies that lose money often pay their bills by selling new shares again and again. Each round dilutes existing holders, and the price per share tends to drift down. When it gets very low, the company may do a reverse split to lift the price, then keep issuing. A pattern of 'dilute, reverse split, dilute again' is a strong reason to look harder. One reverse split is not proof of anything bad on its own, but repeated ones deserve questions.

assumptions: Fictional Cindervale Tech (fictional) has 20 million shares
You own 10,000 shares
The company issues 10 million new shares to raise cash
steps: Before: 10,000 ÷ 20,000,000 = 0.0005, so you own 0.05% of the company.
After: shares outstanding = 20 million + 10 million = 30 million.
Your slice fell by one third (from 1 share in every 2,000 to 1 in every 3,000), even though you did nothing.

assumptions: You own 10,000 shares of a fictional company at 0.12 USD
The company does a 1-for-10 reverse split
Separately: a fictional share with 50 million shares outstanding, 45 million held by insiders, average daily volume 100,000
steps: Before the split: 10,000 × 0.12 = 1,200 USD.
After: 10,000 ÷ 10 = 1,000 shares, at about 0.12 × 10 = 1.20 USD. Value = 1,000 × 1.20 = 1,200 USD. Nothing has changed.
If the price then drifts back to 0.60, your 1,000 shares are worth 600 USD.
The low-float share: float ≈ 50 million − 45 million = 5 million shares.
A 200,000-share buy order is 200,000 ÷ 100,000 = 2 days of normal volume, and 200,000 ÷ 5,000,000 = 4% of the float. Orders that size can move the price sharply.

lessons.explainSimpler: Dilution is the pizza being cut into more slices: you keep your slices, but each one is smaller. A reverse split is glueing slices together: fewer, bigger slices, same pizza.
lessons.commonMistake: Seeing a share 'jump' from 0.12 to 1.20 after a reverse split and thinking it went up tenfold. The share count fell by the same factor, so nothing was gained.

quickCheck.prompt: You hold 2,000 shares at 0.30 USD. The company does a 1-for-5 reverse split. What do you hold straight after?

options.text: 2,000 shares at 1.50 USD
options.explanation: No: the share count also falls. 2,000 at 1.50 would be 3,000 USD, more than you had.

options.text: 400 shares at 0.30 USD
options.explanation: No: the price rises by the same factor the share count falls.

options.text: 400 shares at about 1.50 USD
options.explanation: Right: 2,000 ÷ 5 = 400 shares; 0.30 × 5 = 1.50. Value 600 USD before and after.

quickCheck.prompt: A company goes from 100 million to 150 million shares. You own 50,000. What happened to your stake?

options.text: It shrank from 0.05% to about 0.033%
It stayed at 0.05%, as you still own 50,000
options.explanation: No: your share count is the same, but the total grew, so your percentage fell.

options.text: It fell by half, to 0.025%
options.explanation: No: 0.025% would need 200 million shares. 50,000 ÷ 150 million ≈ 0.033%.

quickCheck.prompt: Why can a low float make a share's price jumpy?

options.text: Low float means the company is losing money
options.explanation: No: float is about who holds the shares, not about profit.

options.text: Few shares can trade, so small orders move price
options.explanation: Right: with few tradable shares, modest buying or selling can shift the price a lot.

options.text: Insiders sell their shares every day
options.explanation: No: float is about tradable shares. Insiders often hold, and nothing makes them sell daily.

doItNow.instructions: Work out by hand two checks on a fictional company. 1) It goes from 40 million to 64 million shares: work out your new percentage if you own 20,000 shares. 2) It then does a 1-for-8 reverse split: work out your new share count and the new price if the old price was 0.08. Confirm your total value is the same before and after the split.

lessons.title: Gaps, halts, short-selling limits, and when to stay out

inOneLine.simple: In small shares, the hard part is often getting out. Overnight [[gap|gaps]] and [[trading-halt|trading halts]] can skip right past your stop, so sometimes the best trade is no trade.
inOneLine.balanced: A [[stop-loss]] cannot fill while trading is halted and fills at the next available price after a gap. [[short-selling|Short selling]] small shares is often impossible, costly, or open to unlimited losses. Before any trade, ask: if this goes wrong, can I get out, and at what cost?

explain.simple: News about small companies often comes out when the market is closed, such as a new share sale or a failed product. The next day, the price can open far away from where it closed. Your stop-loss then fills at that new price, not at your level. A trading halt is a pause in trading. While it lasts, you cannot sell at all. When trading restarts, the price may be much lower. Some traders try to profit from falls by short selling, but small shares can be hard or impossible to borrow, and a sudden spike can cause losses with no upper limit. All examples here are fictional.
explain.balanced: Put together, these risks mean your planned loss and your real loss can be very different. A good test before entering: 'What is the worst realistic exit?' If the answer is 'I might not be able to sell for days' or 'a gap could cost three times my planned risk', the position must be much smaller, or skipped. Staying out is a real decision with real value: no setup is worth it when you cannot get enough information, the spread eats most of the expected move, the share is being heavily promoted, or your order would be a large part of daily volume.

assumptions: Fictional share bought: 2,000 shares at 0.80 USD, stop-loss at 0.70 USD
After the close, the company announces a large new share sale
Next morning the first trade is at 0.45 USD
steps: The stop triggers at the open and fills near 0.45, the first available price.
700 ÷ 200 = 3.5. The real loss was 3.5 times the plan, and in a thin market the fill could be even lower.

assumptions: Fictional short sale: 2,000 shares sold short at 0.50 USD
A promotion pushes the price to 1.50 USD before the trader buys back
Borrowing costs left out to keep it simple
steps: Money received from the short sale: 2,000 × 0.50 = 1,000 USD.
Cost to buy back: 2,000 × 1.50 = 3,000 USD.
Loss = 3,000 − 1,000 = 2,000 USD, twice the 1,000 USD the trader took in.
A share cannot fall below zero, but it can rise without a fixed limit. That is why short losses have no fixed cap.
Many small shares cannot be borrowed at all, so a broker may simply refuse the short.

lessons.explainSimpler: Before you go in, picture the worst way out. If the door might be locked (a halt) or might open somewhere far away (a gap), stay out or go very small.
lessons.commonMistake: Believing a stop-loss sets your maximum loss. It is an order, not a guarantee. Gaps and halts can make the real loss several times the planned one.

quickCheck.prompt: Bought 1,000 shares at 1.20, stop at 1.00. The share opens at 0.60 after bad news. Roughly what is the loss?

options.text: 200 USD, as the stop limits it
options.explanation: No: 200 USD is the planned loss. A gap fills the stop at the first available price.

options.text: 1,200 USD, the whole amount
options.explanation: No: the shares still have a price of about 0.60, so not everything is lost.

options.text: About 600 USD, three times the plan
options.explanation: Right: (1.20 − 0.60) × 1,000 = 600 USD, three times the planned 200.

quickCheck.prompt: What happens to your stop-loss during a trading halt?

options.text: It cannot fill until trading starts again
options.explanation: Right: no trading means no fills. When trading restarts, the price may have moved far past your stop.

options.text: It fills at your stop during the halt
options.explanation: No: nothing trades during a halt, and there is no guarantee of your price afterwards.

options.text: It may fill at the last price before the halt
options.explanation: No: nothing trades during a halt, so nothing fills at that price. The first fill comes when trading resumes, often far away.

quickCheck.prompt: Which situation is the clearest case for staying out?

options.text: A small share with on-time reports and a 1% spread
options.explanation: No: this may still carry risk, but it is not the clearest case here.

options.text: Your order is 5% of a normal day's volume
options.explanation: No: that needs care with size and orders, but it is not the clearest case.

options.text: Heavily promoted, no recent filings, bids for few shares
options.explanation: Right: several red flags plus a hard exit. Staying out is the best decision.

doItNow.instructions: In Chart Lab, load the News shock scenario and then the Crash scenario, both with the Volume pane on. For each, mark where a stop-loss 10% below the entry would have been and where it would really have filled. Then write your personal 'stay out' list: three conditions under which you will not trade a small share at all.

lessons.title: Low volume, wide spreads and thin order books

inOneLine.simple: With few buyers and sellers, you pay a big [[spread]] to get in, and you may not be able to get out at the price you see.
inOneLine.balanced: Low daily volume, a wide spread and a thin [[order-book|order book]] mean the price shown is only good for a few shares. A larger order moves through several worse prices, so the real cost of trading can be far bigger than it looks.

explain.simple: [[volume|Volume]] is the number of shares traded in a period. Many small shares trade only a few thousand times a day. With so few traders, the gap between the price buyers will pay (bid) and the price sellers want (ask) is often wide. If you buy at the ask and sell straight away at the bid, you lose the whole spread. On a big share that might be a tiny fraction of a percent. On a penny stock it can be several percent or more. All numbers here are fictional.
explain.balanced: The order book shows how many shares are waiting at each price. In a thin book, the best bid might be for only a few thousand shares. Sell more than that with a [[market-order|market order]] and you fill at the next bid down, then the next, which is a form of [[slippage]]. A [[limit-order|limit order]] protects your price but may only fill in part, or not at all. A useful habit: compare your order size with the average daily volume. If your order is a large share of a normal day's trading, you may struggle to exit.

assumptions: Simulated practice penny stock: bid 0.40 USD, ask 0.44 USD
You buy 5,000 shares at the ask, then sell at once at the bid
No commission, to keep the arithmetic simple
steps: Spread = 0.44 − 0.40 = 0.04 USD per share.
Cost to buy: 5,000 × 0.44 = 2,200 USD.
Value if you sell at once: 5,000 × 0.40 = 2,000 USD.
Loss from the spread alone = 2,200 − 2,000 = 200 USD, about 9.1% of 2,200. The price had to rise 10% (0.40 to 0.44) just to get back to even.
Compare a simulated large share with bid 50.00 and ask 50.02: the spread is 0.02, about 0.04% of the ask.

assumptions: Simulated order book for the same share. Bids: 3,000 shares at 0.40, 2,000 at 0.38, 5,000 at 0.35
Average daily volume: 40,000 shares
You sell 10,000 shares with a market order
steps: At the 0.40 you saw on screen it would have been 4,000 USD. The thin book cost you 290 USD more.
Your order was 10,000 ÷ 40,000 = 25% of a normal day's volume. That is a warning that exiting will be hard.

lessons.explainSimpler: If hardly anyone is trading, the price on the screen is only good for a small amount. Sell more and you get worse and worse prices.
lessons.commonMistake: Looking only at the last traded price. The last trade might have been 200 shares an hour ago. What matters is the current bid, the size waiting at it, and how much trades on a normal day.

quickCheck.prompt: Simulated share: bid 0.90, ask 1.00. You buy 1,000 shares and sell at once. What do you lose to the spread?

options.text: 10 USD
options.explanation: No: the spread is 0.10 per share, and 0.10 × 1,000 is 100, not 10.

options.text: 900 USD
options.explanation: No: that is what you get back when you sell, 1,000 × 0.90.

options.text: 100 USD

quickCheck.prompt: A share trades about 20,000 shares a day. You plan to buy 15,000. What is the main concern?

options.text: Your order is most of a normal day's volume, so getting out may be slow and costly
options.explanation: Right: compared with daily volume, your order is huge, so exits can be hard.

options.text: None, as long as you use a market order so that the whole order fills straight away
options.explanation: No: a market order fills, but in a thin book it can fill at much worse prices.

options.text: Only the spread, since 15,000 shares is a normal order size
options.explanation: No: whether an order is normal depends on daily volume. 15,000 is three quarters of a day's trading.

quickCheck.prompt: What does a limit order do in a thin market?

options.text: It guarantees the whole order fills at your price
options.explanation: No: it protects the price, but it may fill only in part or not at all.

options.text: Caps your price, but may fill only in part
options.explanation: Right: you choose price protection and accept the risk of not filling.

options.text: It makes the spread narrower for everyone
options.explanation: No: one order may add a little depth, but it does not fix a thin market.

doItNow.instructions: In Paper trading, open the Practice penny stock (prices are simulated). Write down the bid, the ask and the maximum order size. Work out the spread as a percentage of the ask. Then place a small practice buy with a limit order, and note how far the price must rise before you would break even after the spread.

lessons.title: Promotions and pump-and-dump schemes

inOneLine.simple: When a tiny share is being hyped hard, ask who is selling to you. In a [[pump-and-dump]], the people doing the hyping sell to the buyers they attract.
inOneLine.balanced: A [[stock-promotion|promotion]] of a thinly traded share can push the price up for a while. When the promoters stop buying and start selling, the price can collapse, and late buyers may find almost no one to sell to. Learning to spot this is about protecting yourself, never about joining in.

explain.simple: A pump and dump has a pattern. First, someone buys a lot of a cheap, thinly traded share. Next comes the 'pump': excited emails, posts, newsletters or chat messages promising huge gains, often with a deadline like 'before Friday'. New buyers push the price up. Then the 'dump': the early holders sell into that buying. When the buying stops, the price can fall very fast. Late buyers are left holding shares that few people want. Taking part in this kind of scheme is market manipulation and is illegal in many places. This lesson teaches you to recognise it and stay away. All examples are fictional.
explain.balanced: Warning signs often come together: a sudden jump in price and volume with no real company news; big claims about a new product, a 'major deal' or a hot sector, with no revenue to back them; paid-promotion disclosures in small print; insiders or large holders selling while the stock is being promoted; and late, thin or missing company reports. No single sign proves a scheme, but several together are a strong reason to stay out. Many market regulators publish investor alerts about promotions; checking those, and the company's official filings, is part of doing your own homework.

assumptions: Fictional story about Glimmerpeak Lithium Dreams (fictional)
A late buyer buys 4,000 shares at 1.10 USD near the top of a promotion
After the promotion ends, the bid falls to 0.25 USD
steps: Value at the new bid: 4,000 × 0.25 = 1,000 USD.
Loss = 4,400 − 1,000 = 3,400 USD, which is 3,400 ÷ 4,400 ≈ 77% of the money put in.
To get back to 1.10 from 0.25, the price would need to rise 1.10 ÷ 0.25 = 4.4 times, a gain of +340%.
And the bid at 0.25 may be for only a few hundred shares, so even selling at 0.25 may not be possible.

assumptions: A fictional message received by a learner, from an unknown sender
"Tiny lithium explorer about to sign a MAJOR deal. Our target: 10x by Friday. Buy before the news!"
Small print at the bottom: 'The writer has been paid 50,000 USD by a shareholder to distribute this message.'
steps: Red flag 1: a huge price target with a short deadline (urgency).
Red flag 2: 'about to sign' a deal with no named partner and no official filing.
Red flag 3: the writer was paid by a shareholder, who may want to sell into your buying.
Red flag 4: it came unasked, from someone you cannot identify.
Sensible action: do not buy, do not forward it, check the company's official filings and your regulator's investor alerts.

lessons.explainSimpler: If strangers are working very hard to get you to buy a tiny share quickly, they probably want to sell it to you. Walk away.
lessons.commonMistake: Thinking you can buy early in a pump and sell before the dump. You do not know where you are in the scheme, the price can fall faster than you can sell, and a thin market may not let you out at all.

quickCheck.prompt: A newsletter's small print says the writer was paid by a shareholder. Why does that matter?

options.text: It shows the company is well funded and stable
options.explanation: No: a shareholder paying for promotion says nothing good about the company's finances.

options.text: The person paying may want to sell as you buy
options.explanation: Right: the person paying may profit from selling while you buy.

options.text: Paid newsletters are checked by regulators
options.explanation: No: do not assume anyone has checked the claims for you.

quickCheck.prompt: You bought a promoted share at 0.80. It now bids 0.20. How much must it rise to get back to 0.80?

options.explanation: Right: 0.80 ÷ 0.20 = 4 times, which is a gain of +300%.
No: 75% is the size of the fall. Getting back needs a much bigger percentage rise.
No: 0.60 is the price gap, not the percentage needed.

quickCheck.prompt: A tiny share jumps 300% in two days on huge volume, with no company news. What is the best first step?

options.text: Buy a small amount quickly so that you do not miss out
options.explanation: No: chasing an unexplained spike is how late buyers get caught in a dump.

options.text: Stay out and check filings, news and regulator alerts
options.explanation: Right: an unexplained spike is a reason to investigate, not to buy.

options.text: Wait a day, then buy if the price is still rising
options.explanation: No: a rise that lasts another day is still unexplained. Check filings, news and regulator alerts first.

doItNow.instructions: Open the Fundamental Analysis Lab and work through the Penny Stock Red Flag Detector case on the heavily promoted company. Tick every sign you think is a warning, then read the explanations. Write down the two signs you missed, if any, and what you would check next.

lessons.title: What penny stocks and microcaps are

inOneLine.simple: A [[penny-stock]] is a low-priced share in a very small company. A low price does not mean cheap, and small companies carry extra risks.
inOneLine.balanced: There is no single worldwide definition. Markets, regulators and brokers draw the line differently, by share price, by company size, or both. Company size means market value, and a [[microcap]] is a company with a very small one.

explain.simple: People use the words 'penny stock' in different ways. In some places it means a share with a low price. In others it means a share in a tiny company. The rules and the exact limits depend on the country and on who is using the word, so check the meaning where you are. The more useful number is the company's total value, called market value: share price × number of shares. A share priced at 0.10 can belong to a bigger company than a share priced at 40. Many very small companies trade on an [[otc-market|over-the-counter (OTC) market]] rather than a main exchange, where reporting rules are often lighter. All examples in this lesson are fictional.
explain.balanced: What penny stocks and microcaps tend to share is not the price but the conditions: low [[liquidity]], wide [[spread|spreads]], little independent research, and sometimes thin or late company reports. Those conditions make them easier to push around with [[stock-promotion|promotions]]. Trading OTC is not wrong in itself, and some small companies are real, honest businesses. But less information means you must check more for yourself, and sometimes the honest answer is that you cannot check enough.

assumptions: Fictional Company A (fictional): share price 0.10 USD, 2,000 million shares
Fictional Company B (fictional): share price 40.00 USD, 1 million shares
Market value = share price × shares outstanding
steps: Company B: 40.00 × 1,000,000 = 40,000,000 USD, so 40 million USD.
Company A has the lower share price but is 5 times bigger by market value (200 ÷ 40 = 5).
The share price alone tells you almost nothing about the size of a company.

assumptions: Fictional Pebblebrook Minerals (fictional): share price 0.25 USD, 40 million shares
It trades over the counter and publishes short, irregular reports
steps: Market value = 0.25 × 40,000,000 = 10,000,000 USD, so 10 million USD. That is a microcap by most people's use of the word.
'Only 0.25 a share' sounds cheap, but cheap compared with what? You would need revenue, cash and debt to judge value.
The irregular reports mean you may not be able to find those figures.
First question for any small share: can I find enough reliable information to judge it at all?

lessons.explainSimpler: Penny stocks are shares in tiny companies. A small price per share is not a bargain. The real questions are how big the company is, how much you can find out about it, and how easy it is to sell.
lessons.commonMistake: Thinking a share at 0.05 can 'easily' go to 1.00 because the number is small. A rise from 0.05 to 1.00 is a 20-fold increase in the whole company's value, whatever the price per share looks like.

quickCheck.prompt: Fictional share: price 0.50 USD, 30 million shares outstanding. What is the market value?

options.text: 60 million USD
options.explanation: No: that is 30 million ÷ 0.50. Market value multiplies the two.

options.text: 15 million USD
0.50 USD
options.explanation: No: that is the price of one share, not the value of the company.

quickCheck.prompt: Which statement about the meaning of 'penny stock' is most accurate?

options.text: It means any share priced below one unit of currency, in every country
options.explanation: No: there is no single worldwide rule. Different markets and regulators draw the line differently.

options.text: It only means shares that trade on over-the-counter markets
options.explanation: No: trading venue is part of the picture in some uses, but it is not the whole definition anywhere you can assume.

options.text: It varies by market, often based on low price or small company size
options.explanation: Right: check how the term is used where you are.

quickCheck.prompt: A share trades over the counter. What does that tell you?

options.text: Reporting rules are often lighter, so check more yourself
options.explanation: Right: OTC trading is not a scam in itself, but information can be thinner.

options.text: It must be a scam and should be reported to a regulator
options.explanation: No: many OTC shares are not scams. The venue alone does not prove fraud.

options.text: It can mean the company is big enough to skip an exchange
options.explanation: No: OTC trading says nothing good about size. Many OTC shares are small, and information can be thinner.

doItNow.instructions: Make up two fictional companies with different share prices and share counts, so that the one with the lower share price is the bigger company. Work out both market values. Then write one sentence on why a low share price is not the same as a cheap company.

lessons.title: The balance sheet: cash, debt and return on capital

inOneLine.simple: The balance sheet shows what a company has and what it owes on one day. Debt minus cash is net debt, and profit compared with all the money tied up shows how well that money is used.
inOneLine.balanced: [[balance-sheet|Balance sheet]]: cash, debt and equity. [[net-debt|Net debt]] = debt − cash. [[return-on-capital|Return on capital]] = operating profit ÷ (debt + equity). [[return-on-equity|ROE]] = net income ÷ equity.

explain.simple: The income statement covers a whole year. The balance sheet is a snapshot of one day. Start with three lines. Cash is money in the bank. Debt is money borrowed that must be repaid with interest. Equity is roughly what would be left for shareholders if the company sold everything at its book value and paid all its debts. Debt minus cash is net debt: what the company would still owe if it used all its cash to repay lenders.
explain.balanced: Debt is not bad in itself, but it adds a fixed cost, interest, that must be paid in good years and bad. Compare debt with operating profit: if operating profit covers interest many times over, a dip is easier to survive. Return on capital compares operating profit with all the money lenders and owners have put in, so it shows how productively that money is used. Return on equity can look high just because a company borrowed a lot, so read it with debt. This app uses operating profit ÷ (debt + equity); other sources may define return on capital differently.

assumptions: Example Quickling Apps Co (fictional), Year 3, millions of USD
Cash 71; debt 160; equity 183; operating profit 40; interest 16; net income 18
steps: Return on capital = 40 ÷ (160 + 183) = 40 ÷ 343 = about 11.7%.
Return on equity = 18 ÷ 183 = about 9.8%.
Operating profit covers interest 40 ÷ 16 = 2.5 times. A fall in operating profit of more than 60% would leave too little to cover the interest.

assumptions: Example Faxworth Office Machines (fictional), millions of USD
Debt 150 in every year; interest 12 every year
Operating profit: Year 1 80, Year 3 40; cash in Year 3 71
steps: Net debt in Year 3 = 150 − 71 = 79.
Interest as a share of operating profit: Year 1 = 12 ÷ 80 = 15%; Year 3 = 12 ÷ 40 = 30%.
The debt did not grow, but the profit that pays for it halved.
The same debt is riskier for a company whose profit is shrinking.

lessons.explainSimpler: Cash minus debt shows the cushion. Profit compared with all the money tied up shows how hard that money works.
lessons.commonMistake: Judging debt by its size alone. 150 million of debt can be easy for one company and dangerous for another; compare it with profit and cash flow.

quickCheck.prompt: Debt 90, cash 120 (fictional, millions USD). What is net debt?

options.text: −30: the company has net cash
options.explanation: Right: 90 − 120 = −30, so cash is larger than debt.

options.text: 30: the company owes more than it holds
options.explanation: No: cash is larger than debt here.

options.text: 210: debt and cash added together
options.explanation: No: net debt subtracts cash from debt.

quickCheck.prompt: Operating profit 60, debt 100, equity 200 (fictional). What is return on capital, as this app defines it?

options.explanation: No: that uses equity only.
No: that uses debt only.

quickCheck.prompt: Company A and Company B each owe 200. A's operating profit is 100; B's is 20. Which is true?

options.text: Both carry the same debt risk
options.explanation: No: the same debt weighs far more on the smaller profit.

options.text: B's debt is far riskier than A's
options.explanation: Right: B has much less profit to pay interest and repay debt.

options.text: A's debt is riskier, as A earns more
options.explanation: No: more profit makes the same debt easier to carry.

doItNow.instructions: Open the Fundamental Analysis Lab → Company analysis. For each fictional company, write down Year 3 net debt and return on capital. Which company has net cash? Which has the lowest return on capital, and is its debt growing or shrinking compared with its profit?

lessons.title: Business quality, competition and risks

inOneLine.simple: Numbers show what happened. To judge what might happen next, ask how the company makes money, what protects it from rivals, and what could go wrong.
inOneLine.balanced: Understand the [[business-model]], look for a possible [[competitive-advantage]] (steady margins and [[return-on-capital]] are one clue, not proof), and list the risks: competition, debt, management decisions, and customers or products that could fade.

explain.simple: Start with the business model: what does the company sell, who pays, and what does it cost to serve them? Then ask what stops a rival from taking those customers. A trusted brand, lower costs, or customers who find it hard to switch can all help. Finally list what could go wrong: new competitors, a product going out of fashion, too much debt, or managers making poor choices with the company's money.
explain.balanced: Figures give clues. Margins that hold steady for years, and a return on capital that stays high, suggest something protects the business, but advantages can fade and the past does not promise the future. Thin margins combined with debt make a business fragile: a small price cut can wipe out profit. Management risks include spending on deals that do not pay off, raising debt to fund dividends, or explanations for weak cash flow that keep changing. These are judgements, so write down your reasoning and what would change your mind.

assumptions: Fictional companies from the Fundamental Analysis Lab, millions of USD
Operating margin, Years 1 to 3: Example Steadybrook Pantry Foods (fictional) 14.8%, 14.9%, 15.0%; Example Faxworth Office Machines (fictional) 16.0%, 14.0%, 10.8%
Return on capital in Year 3: Steadybrook 156 ÷ (100 + 654); Faxworth 40 ÷ (150 + 422)
steps: Steadybrook return on capital = 156 ÷ 754 = about 20.7%. Its margin barely moved.
Faxworth return on capital = 40 ÷ 572 = about 7.0%. Its margin fell every year.
Steady margins and high returns are a clue that something protects Steadybrook, for now.
Faxworth's falling margin fits a product losing customers. Neither clue is proof; both need a reason you can explain.

assumptions: Illustrative scenario: a rival forces each company to cut prices by 5%
Year 3 costs and interest stay the same; tax ignored for simplicity
Quickling: revenue 450, cost of sales 270, operating expenses 140, interest 16. Steadybrook: revenue 1,040, cost of sales 624, operating expenses 260, interest 4
steps: Quickling revenue = 450 × 0.95 = 427.5. Profit before tax = 427.5 − 270 − 140 − 16 = 1.5. Before the cut it was 24.
Steadybrook revenue = 1,040 × 0.95 = 988. Profit before tax = 988 − 624 − 260 − 4 = 100. Before the cut it was 152.
Quickling's profit almost disappears; Steadybrook's falls by about a third.
Thin margins plus interest make a business fragile when competition bites.

lessons.explainSimpler: How does it make money, who could take that away, and what could go wrong? The numbers are clues to those answers, not the answers.
lessons.commonMistake: Treating a strong business as safe from change, or treating a strong business as a reason to buy at any price. Advantages can fade, and price still matters.

quickCheck.prompt: A company's operating margin has held near 20% for many years while rivals tried to compete. What is the fairest reading?

options.text: It has a permanent advantage over rivals
options.explanation: No: advantages can fade; past margins do not promise future ones.

options.text: A clue that something protects it
options.explanation: Right: steady high margins are a clue worth explaining, not proof.

options.text: Its shares are a good investment now
options.explanation: No: business quality and the price paid are separate questions.

quickCheck.prompt: Revenue 100, all costs 92, interest 6 (fictional). A rival forces a 5% price cut; costs stay the same. What is profit before tax now?

options.explanation: Right: 95 − 92 − 6 = −3. Thin margins plus interest turn a small cut into a loss.
No: that is the profit before the price cut.
No: that only counts the price cut.

quickCheck.prompt: Which is a management risk worth noting?

options.text: The company has changed its ticker code
options.explanation: No: a ticker change says little about how the company is run.

options.text: The share price fell sharply last week
options.explanation: No: a price move is not a management decision.

options.text: Borrowing to keep paying a dividend
options.explanation: Right: paying dividends with debt rather than cash can weaken the company.

doItNow.instructions: Open the Fundamental Analysis Lab → Company analysis and pick one fictional company. Write: its business model in one sentence, one possible competitive advantage, three risks, and one figure you would watch to see whether your view is wrong. Read its notes on the screen to compare.

lessons.homework: Do the same short write-up for a second fictional company and compare the two.

lessons.title: Cash flow: does profit turn into cash?

inOneLine.simple: Profit is an accounting figure; cash flow is money actually received. When profit keeps rising but cash does not, find out why.
inOneLine.balanced: Operating [[cash-flow]] from the [[cash-flow-statement]] shows cash the business really collected. [[free-cash-flow|Free cash flow]] = operating cash flow − capital expenditure. Profit that does not become cash over time is a warning sign worth investigating.

explain.simple: A company records a sale as revenue when it makes the sale, even if the customer will pay months later. So profit can rise while the bank account does not. The cash flow statement shows the money actually coming in and going out. Operating cash flow is the cash from day-to-day business. Free cash flow is what is left after the company spends on equipment, buildings and software (capital expenditure). That is the cash it can use to repay debt, pay dividends or save.
explain.balanced: For most steady businesses, operating cash flow is close to or above net income over several years. When it falls far below, ask why. Possible reasons include customers paying more slowly, unsold stock building up, or accounting choices that record profit early. These are hypotheses: the figures alone do not tell you which. Negative free cash flow is not always bad; a growing company may be investing heavily. The question is how it is paying for it, and for how long.

assumptions: Example Gadgetmoor Wholesale Co (fictional), millions of USD
Net income: Year 1 39, Year 2 45, Year 3 52.5
Operating cash flow: 38, 18, 2. Capital expenditure: 10, 12, 15
steps: Cash compared with profit: Year 1 = 38 ÷ 39 = about 0.97; Year 2 = 18 ÷ 45 = 0.40; Year 3 = 2 ÷ 52.5 = about 0.04.
Free cash flow: Year 1 = 38 − 10 = 28; Year 2 = 18 − 12 = 6; Year 3 = 2 − 15 = −13.
Profit rose every year, but by Year 3 almost none of it arrived as cash.
Debt rose from 60 to 75 in Year 3 to cover the gap. This needs investigating before trusting the profit figure.

assumptions: Example Quickling Apps Co (fictional), Year 3, millions of USD
Net income 18; operating cash flow 20; capital expenditure 45
Debt: Year 2 110, Year 3 160
steps: Operating cash flow is a little above net income: 20 ÷ 18 = about 1.11. Profit is turning into cash.
Free cash flow = 20 − 45 = −25. The company spends more than it brings in.
