Debt rose by 160 − 110 = 50 to pay for the spending.
Different problem from Gadgetmoor: here cash follows profit, but the investment is funded by borrowing. Ask whether that spending is likely to pay off before the debt becomes a burden.

lessons.explainSimpler: Profit is what the accounts say you earned. Cash is what actually arrived. Over time, the two should roughly match.
lessons.commonMistake: Trusting rising profit without checking operating cash flow. Profit that never turns into cash can be a sign of trouble the income statement does not show.

quickCheck.prompt: Operating cash flow 90, capital expenditure 35 (fictional, millions USD). What is free cash flow?

options.explanation: No: capital expenditure is subtracted, not added.
No: that is the capital expenditure itself.

quickCheck.prompt: Net income rises three years in a row while operating cash flow falls each year. What is a sensible next step?

options.text: Find out why cash is lagging
options.explanation: Right: profit that does not become cash is a warning sign to investigate.

options.text: Ignore it, since profit is rising
options.explanation: No: profit is an accounting figure; cash shows what was collected.

options.text: Treat it as proof of fraud
options.explanation: No: there are several possible reasons; the figures alone do not prove any one.

quickCheck.prompt: A growing company has negative free cash flow because it spends heavily on new equipment. Which question matters most?

options.text: Is its ticker short and easy to remember?
options.explanation: No: that has nothing to do with cash.

options.text: Is the dividend yield high?
options.explanation: No: a firm with negative free cash flow often pays no dividend.

options.text: How is it paying, and for how long?
options.explanation: Right: spending funded by rising debt or new shares cannot go on for ever.

doItNow.instructions: Open the Fundamental Analysis Lab → Company analysis. For each fictional company, compare Year 3 net income with operating cash flow, and work out free cash flow. Which company's profit is least backed by cash? Write two questions you would want its managers to answer.

lessons.title: Dividends and earnings reports

inOneLine.simple: A dividend is cash a company pays its shareholders from profit. An earnings report is the company's regular update on its revenue and profit.
inOneLine.balanced: A [[dividend]] is paid at the company's choice and can be cut. [[dividend-yield|Dividend yield]] = dividend per share ÷ price; [[payout-ratio]] = dividends ÷ net income. An [[earnings-report]] can move the price sharply, mostly because of the gap between the results and what was expected.

explain.simple: Some companies share part of their profit with shareholders as cash: a dividend. The company's board decides whether to pay one and how much. It can raise it, cut it or stop it. Listed companies also publish an earnings report on a regular schedule, showing how much they sold and how much profit they made. Share prices often move a lot around these reports.
explain.balanced: Two ratios help you read a dividend. Dividend yield compares the yearly dividend per share with the price. Payout ratio compares the dividends with the profit. A very high yield often appears after the price has fallen, sometimes because buyers expect a cut. A payout ratio near or above 100% leaves little room for a bad year. Around earnings reports, prices react to results compared with expectations (see [[surprise]]), so a company can report higher profit and still see its price fall. Prices can also [[gap]] from one session to the next around a report.

assumptions: Example Steadybrook Pantry Foods (fictional), Year 3, millions of USD
Dividends paid 87; net income 114; 200 million shares; price 6.80 USD
You own 1,000 shares; tax on dividends ignored
steps: Dividend per share = 87 ÷ 200 = 0.435 USD.
Your dividend = 1,000 × 0.435 = 435 USD for the year.
Dividend yield = 0.435 ÷ 6.80 = about 6.4%.
Payout ratio = 87 ÷ 114 = about 76%. About three quarters of the profit was paid out.

assumptions: Example Steadybrook Pantry Foods (fictional); illustrative expectations, not a forecast
Last year's EPS 0.555 USD; this year's reported EPS 0.57 USD
Before the report, buyers on average expected EPS of 0.60 USD
steps: Change from last year = 0.57 ÷ 0.555 − 1 = about +2.7%. Profit grew.
Compared with expectations: 0.57 − 0.60 = −0.03 USD, below what was expected.
One possible reaction is a falling price, because buyers had priced in 0.60.
Another is little change, if buyers had already lowered their hopes. The same number can cause different reactions.

lessons.explainSimpler: Dividends are a share of profit paid in cash, by choice, not by promise. Earnings reports are the scorecard, judged against what people expected.
lessons.commonMistake: Picking a share only for its high dividend yield. The yield is based on past payments, and a very high one can be a sign the market expects the dividend to be cut.

quickCheck.prompt: Dividend 0.30 USD per share; price 10.00 USD. What is the dividend yield?

options.explanation: No: that is ten times too small.

quickCheck.prompt: Net income 50; dividends paid 55 (fictional, millions USD). What is the payout ratio, and what does it suggest?

options.text: 110%: more is paid out than earned
options.explanation: Right: 55 ÷ 50 = 1.10. That cannot continue for ever without cash or borrowing.

options.text: 91%: the dividend looks fully covered
options.explanation: No: that divides 50 by 55, the wrong way round.

options.text: 5%: almost all profit is kept
options.explanation: No: that is the difference, 55 − 50, not a ratio.

quickCheck.prompt: A company reports profit up 10%, but below what buyers expected. What could happen to the price?

options.text: It must rise, since profit grew
options.explanation: No: prices react to results compared with expectations.

options.text: A miss like this often pushes the price down
options.explanation: Right: a miss against expectations can push the price down even when profit grew.

options.text: It may only react once the next report is out
options.explanation: No: prices can move at any time, often sharply around a report.

doItNow.instructions: In the Fundamental Analysis Lab, open Example Steadybrook Pantry Foods (fictional) and check its dividend per share, dividend yield and payout ratio. Then open Example Faxworth Office Machines (fictional) and write down how its dividends paid changed from Year 1 to Year 3.

lessons.title: The income statement: from revenue to EPS

inOneLine.simple: The income statement starts with everything a company sold and subtracts costs step by step until only the owners' profit is left.
inOneLine.balanced: [[income-statement|Income statement]]: [[revenue]] − cost of sales = gross profit; − operating expenses = operating profit; − interest − tax = net income ([[earnings]]); ÷ shares = [[eps]]. Each profit ÷ revenue gives a [[profit-margin]].

explain.simple: Read the income statement from top to bottom. Revenue is all the money from sales. Take away the cost of making what was sold (cost of sales) and you get gross profit. Take away the costs of running the company, such as wages, rent and marketing (operating expenses), and you get operating profit: what the business itself earned. Take away interest on debt and tax and you reach net income, the profit that belongs to the owners. Divide that by the number of shares and you get earnings per share, or EPS.
explain.balanced: Margins turn each profit line into a percentage of revenue, which makes companies of different sizes comparable. Gross margin shows pricing power and production cost; operating margin shows how efficiently the whole business runs; net margin shows what is left after lenders and tax. Watch the trend: revenue growing faster than profit means costs are growing faster too. Net income is an accounting figure, so the next step is to check it against cash flow.

assumptions: Example Steadybrook Pantry Foods (fictional), Year 3, millions of USD
Revenue 1,040; cost of sales 624; operating expenses 260; interest 4; tax 38; 200 million shares
steps: Gross profit = 1,040 − 624 = 416. Gross margin = 416 ÷ 1,040 = 40%.
Operating profit = 416 − 260 = 156. Operating margin = 156 ÷ 1,040 = 15%.
Net income = 156 − 4 − 38 = 114. Net margin = 114 ÷ 1,040 = about 11%.
EPS = 114 million ÷ 200 million shares = 0.57 USD.

assumptions: Example Quickling Apps Co (fictional), millions of USD
Year 3: revenue 450; cost of sales 270; operating expenses 140; interest 16; tax 6; 100 million shares
Year 2: revenue 300; net income 15
steps: Gross profit = 450 − 270 = 180. Gross margin = 40%, the same as Steadybrook.
Operating profit = 180 − 140 = 40. Operating margin = 40 ÷ 450 = about 8.9%.
Net income = 40 − 16 − 6 = 18. Net margin = 18 ÷ 450 = 4%. EPS = 18 ÷ 100 = 0.18 USD.
Revenue grew 450 ÷ 300 − 1 = 50%, but net income grew only 18 ÷ 15 − 1 = 20%. Costs and interest are eating most of the growth.

lessons.explainSimpler: Sales, minus costs, minus interest and tax, equals the owners' profit. Divide by shares for EPS.
lessons.commonMistake: Looking only at revenue growth. A company can grow sales fast while its margins shrink, so profit grows slowly or not at all.

quickCheck.prompt: Revenue 200, cost of sales 120, operating expenses 50 (fictional, millions USD). What is the operating profit?

options.explanation: No: that is gross profit; operating expenses still need to come off.
No: that subtracts only the operating expenses.

quickCheck.prompt: Net income 30 million USD and 60 million shares. What is EPS?

options.text: 0.50 USD
options.explanation: Right: 30 ÷ 60 = 0.50 USD per share.

options.text: 2.00 USD
options.explanation: No: that divides the shares by the profit.

options.text: 30 USD
options.explanation: No: that ignores the number of shares.

quickCheck.prompt: Revenue rose 40% but net income rose only 5%. What does that most likely mean?

options.text: The company is shrinking overall
options.explanation: No: revenue grew a lot.

options.text: Margins got wider
options.explanation: No: wider margins would make profit grow faster than revenue.

options.text: Costs grew faster than sales
options.explanation: Right: margins shrank, so profit lagged revenue.

doItNow.instructions: Open the Fundamental Analysis Lab → Company analysis and choose Example Quickling Apps Co (fictional). Work out gross, operating and net profit for Year 3 by hand, then check them against the screen. Do the same for Example Steadybrook Pantry Foods (fictional) and compare the margins.

lessons.homework: For each of the four fictional companies, write down the Year 1 and Year 3 operating margin and say whether it rose or fell.

lessons.title: Market capitalisation: size, not quality

inOneLine.simple: Market cap is share price × number of shares. It tells you how big the market thinks a company is, not how good it is.
inOneLine.balanced: [[market-capitalisation|Market cap]] = share price × shares outstanding. Two companies with the same market cap can have very different [[earnings]], so compare size with profit before drawing conclusions.

explain.simple: You cannot compare two companies by their share prices alone, because one may have far more shares than the other. Multiply the price by the number of shares and you get the market capitalisation, or market cap: what it would cost, at today's price, to own every share. It moves whenever the share price moves. Market cap measures size in the market's eyes. It does not tell you whether the business is profitable, growing, or worth that price.
explain.balanced: Market cap reflects what buyers expect the company to earn in future, as well as what it earns now. A company with a large market cap and small profits is priced for growth; if that growth does not arrive, the price can fall a long way. Market cap also ignores debt: two companies with the same market cap can owe very different amounts. Compare it with profit using [[pe-ratio|P/E]], which you will meet in the company-analysis module.

assumptions: Fictional companies from the Fundamental Analysis Lab, Year 3 figures, millions of USD
Example Quickling Apps Co (fictional): price 14.40 USD, 100 million shares, net income 18
Example Steadybrook Pantry Foods (fictional): price 6.80 USD, 200 million shares, net income 114
steps: Quickling market cap = 14.40 × 100 million = 1,440 million USD.
Steadybrook market cap = 6.80 × 200 million = 1,360 million USD.
They are almost the same size by market cap.
But Steadybrook's net income is 114 ÷ 18 = about 6.3 times Quickling's. The market is paying for Quickling's expected growth, not its current profit.

assumptions: Example Quickling Apps Co (fictional), 100 million shares
Illustrative: the share price falls from 14.40 USD to 10.80 USD in one day; nothing in the business changes that day
steps: New market cap = 10.80 × 100 million = 1,080 million USD.
The market cap fell by 360 million USD, exactly 25%.
The company's revenue, profit and debt were the same at the end of the day. Only the market's price changed.

lessons.explainSimpler: Price × shares = market cap. It is the price tag for the whole company, not a quality score.
lessons.commonMistake: Calling a company "bigger" or "better" because its share price is higher. A 100 USD share can belong to a smaller company than a 5 USD share if it has far fewer shares.

quickCheck.prompt: Price 4.00 USD, 300 million shares. What is the market cap?

options.text: 75 million USD
options.explanation: No: that divides the shares by the price.

options.text: 304 million USD
options.explanation: No: the price and shares are multiplied, not added.

options.text: 1,200 million USD
options.explanation: Right: 4.00 × 300 million = 1,200 million USD.

quickCheck.prompt: Company X shares cost 100 USD and Company Y shares cost 5 USD. What can you say about their size?

options.text: Nothing yet; you need the share counts
options.explanation: Right: size is price × shares, so the price alone tells you nothing.

options.text: X is bigger, since its price is higher
options.explanation: No: X might have far fewer shares than Y.

options.text: Y is cheaper, so better value
options.explanation: No: a low price per share is not the same as good value.

doItNow.instructions: Open the Fundamental Analysis Lab → Company analysis. For each of the four fictional companies, write down the market cap and the Year 3 net income. Which company has the largest market cap compared with its profit?

lessons.title: Shares, exchanges and tickers

inOneLine.simple: A share is a small piece of ownership in a company. Shares are bought and sold on an exchange, under a short code called a ticker.
inOneLine.balanced: A [[share]] is a fractional claim on a company's profits and assets. Your stake = your shares ÷ shares outstanding. Shares trade on a [[stock-exchange]] under a [[ticker]], and the price is set by buyers and sellers, not by the company.

explain.simple: Imagine a company split into 50 million equal pieces. Each piece is one share. If you own some of those pieces, you own a small part of the business. Shares are traded on a stock exchange, a market with rules about who can list and how orders are matched. Each company has a short code of letters, its ticker, so it fits on a quote screen. The price you see is simply the last price a buyer and a seller agreed on.
explain.balanced: Owning shares gives you a share of future profits if the company pays them out as [[dividend|dividends]], and usually a vote. It does not give you a fixed return: the price can fall as well as rise, and the company owes shareholders nothing back. If the company issues new shares, each existing share becomes a smaller slice. Tickers can look alike, so always check the full company name before you place even a simulated order.

assumptions: Fictional company with 50 million shares outstanding
You buy 500 shares at 8.00 USD each; costs ignored
Illustrative dividend of 0.20 USD per share; a learning example, not a forecast
steps: Your stake = 500 ÷ 50,000,000 = 0.00001, which is 0.001% of the company.
A dividend of 0.20 USD per share pays you 500 × 0.20 = 100 USD.
If the price falls to 6.00 USD, your shares are worth 500 × 6.00 = 3,000 USD: 1,000 USD less than you paid, a 25% fall.

assumptions: Same fictional company and your same 500 shares
The company issues 10 million new shares, so there are now 60 million
steps: You own the same number of shares, but a smaller slice of the company.
Each share now has a claim on a smaller part of the profit, unless the new money helps profit grow enough to make up for it.

lessons.explainSimpler: A share is a slice of a company. The exchange is where slices are swapped. The ticker is the slice's name tag.
lessons.commonMistake: Thinking that a share price of 1 USD is "cheap" and 100 USD is "expensive". The price of one share means little without knowing how many shares there are and how much the company earns.

quickCheck.prompt: A fictional company has 20 million shares. You own 2,000. What fraction of the company do you own?

options.explanation: No: that would need 20,000 shares.
No: that would need 200,000 shares.

quickCheck.prompt: Who sets the price of a share on an exchange?

options.text: The company, at its yearly meeting
options.explanation: No: the company does not set its trading price.

options.text: The exchange, using a fixed formula
options.explanation: No: the exchange matches orders, it does not choose the price.

options.text: Buyers and sellers trading
options.explanation: Right: the price is where buyers and sellers last agreed.

quickCheck.prompt: Two companies have tickers that differ by one letter. What should you do before a simulated order?

options.text: Check the full company name
options.explanation: Right: similar tickers can belong to very different companies.

options.text: Pick the one with the lower price
options.explanation: No: a lower price per share says nothing about value.

options.text: Assume they are the same firm
options.explanation: No: similar codes can be unrelated companies.

doItNow.instructions: Open Practice → Paper trading and choose the "Practice ordinary share" instrument. Note the simulated bid and ask. Place a simulated buy of 10 shares and write down what it cost, then what you would get if you sold straight away at the bid.

lessons.homework: In one sentence each, explain to a friend what a share, an exchange and a ticker are.

lessons.title: Growth vs value, swing trading vs investing

inOneLine.simple: Growth investors pay up for companies they hope will grow fast; value investors look for low prices compared with profit. Swing traders hold for days or weeks; long-term investors hold for years.
inOneLine.balanced: [[growth-investing|Growth]] and [[value-investing|value]] are about what you pay for, and swing trading and long-term investing are about how long you hold. Each has its own risks: growth can disappoint, cheap can be cheap for a reason, swings need a [[stop-loss]], and long holds need the ability to sit through large falls.

explain.simple: A growth approach looks for companies whose revenue and profit may rise quickly, and often accepts a high price compared with today's profit. A value approach looks for companies whose price seems low compared with what they earn. Neither is "right": both can lose money. Separately, you need to decide how long you plan to hold. A swing trader aims to catch a price move over days or weeks, using the chart, a stop and a target. A long-term investor holds for years and focuses on the business itself.
explain.balanced: The style decides which questions matter. A growth buyer must ask what happens if growth slows, because a high [[pe-ratio|P/E]] can fall a long way. A value buyer must ask why the price is low: some businesses are shrinking. A swing trader needs a [[trading-plan]], position sizing and a stop, and pays the [[spread]] more often. A long-term investor still needs a plan: what would prove the idea wrong, and can they afford to hold through a big fall? Mixing the two, for example turning a failed swing trade into a "long-term investment" to avoid taking the loss, is a common trap.

assumptions: Fictional companies from the Fundamental Analysis Lab, Year 3
Example Quickling Apps Co (fictional): price 14.40 USD, EPS 0.18 USD
Illustrative scenarios only, not forecasts
steps: If EPS grows 50% a year for two years: 0.18 × 1.5 × 1.5 = 0.405 USD. P/E at the same price = 14.40 ÷ 0.405 = about 35.6. Still high.
If growth stops instead and buyers will only pay a P/E of 20: price = 20 × 0.18 = 3.60 USD.
That is (14.40 − 3.60) ÷ 14.40 = 75% below today's price, with the same profit as today.

assumptions: A fictional share at 20.00 USD; 200 shares; costs ignored
Swing trader: stop at 19.00 USD, target 22.00 USD, plans to hold days to weeks
Long-term investor: no tight stop, plans to hold years
steps: Swing trader's risk = (20.00 − 19.00) × 200 = 200 USD. Reward at target = (22.00 − 20.00) × 200 = 400 USD. That is 2:1.
Long-term investor: if the price falls 30% to 14.00 USD, the paper loss is (20.00 − 14.00) × 200 = 1,200 USD.
The investor must be able to sit through that without being forced to sell, and must know what business change would make them sell.
Same share, same price, very different risks and plans.

lessons.explainSimpler: Growth: paying up for hoped-for growth. Value: looking for a low price, and asking why it is low. Swing: days to weeks with a stop. Long-term: years, judged on the business.
lessons.commonMistake: Turning a losing swing trade into a long-term investment so you do not have to take the loss. The original plan had a stop for a reason.

quickCheck.prompt: A share's P/E is 60 because buyers expect fast growth. What is the main risk?

options.text: Growth slows and the P/E falls
options.explanation: Right: if growth disappoints, the price can drop sharply even if profit holds.

options.text: Dividend is too high
options.explanation: No: high-P/E growth firms often pay little or no dividend.

options.text: There is no risk if the firm is good
options.explanation: No: a good business at a very high price can still be a poor investment.

quickCheck.prompt: Your swing trade hits its stop. What fits the plan?

options.text: Hold it as a long-term investment instead
options.explanation: No: that changes the plan to avoid taking the planned loss.

options.text: Buy more to lower your average price
options.explanation: No: that adds risk to an idea the stop said was wrong.

options.text: Exit as planned and review the trade
options.explanation: Right: the stop marks where the idea was wrong.

quickCheck.prompt: A share has a P/E of 4. What should a value-minded learner ask first?

options.text: Why is the price this low?
options.explanation: Right: some companies are cheap because their business is shrinking.

options.text: How quickly can I buy some shares?
options.explanation: No: a low P/E alone is not a reason to act.

options.text: Is the ticker short?
options.explanation: No: the ticker says nothing about value.

doItNow.instructions: Before your next simulated trade on the "Practice ordinary share", write three lines: your style (swing or long-term), how long you plan to hold, and exactly what would make you exit. Then place the simulated trade and keep the note in your journal.

lessons.homework: After the simulated trade closes, write whether you followed the exit you planned.

lessons.title: Valuation: a good company at a high price

inOneLine.simple: Valuation compares the price with what you get for it. A great business can be a poor investment if you pay too much.
inOneLine.balanced: [[pe-ratio|P/E]] = price ÷ [[eps]]. Earnings yield = EPS ÷ price. [[dividend-yield|Dividend yield]] = dividend per share ÷ price. [[payout-ratio|Payout ratio]] = dividends ÷ net income. [[valuation|Valuation]] tools compare price with profit; they never say what the price will do next.

explain.simple: Knowing a company is good is only half the question. The other half is the price. The P/E ratio tells you how many years of today's profit you are paying for. A P/E of 12 means you pay 12 times one year's profit per share. Turn it upside down and you get the earnings yield: profit as a percentage of the price. The dividend yield and the payout ratio show how much of that profit comes back to you as cash.
explain.balanced: A high P/E means the price already assumes strong future growth. If the business does well but less well than assumed, the price can still fall. A low P/E means low expectations, which can be justified if profits are shrinking. P/E is meaningless when earnings are zero or negative, and it uses one year's profit, which may be unusual. These ratios are tools for asking questions, not signals to buy or sell.

assumptions: Example Steadybrook Pantry Foods (fictional), Year 3
Price 6.80 USD; EPS 0.57 USD; dividends 87 and net income 114, millions of USD; 200 million shares
steps: Earnings yield = 0.57 ÷ 6.80 = about 8.4%.
Dividend per share = 87 ÷ 200 = 0.435 USD. Dividend yield = 0.435 ÷ 6.80 = about 6.4%.
Payout ratio = 87 ÷ 114 = about 76%.

assumptions: Same fictional company and the same business; illustrative scenario, not a forecast
Imagine the price rises to 22.80 USD with no change in the business
Profit then grows 2% a year for 5 years, and buyers later pay a P/E of 12 again
steps: EPS after 5 years = 0.57 × 1.02⁵ = about 0.629 USD.
Price at a P/E of 12 = 12 × 0.629 = about 7.55 USD.
That is about 67% below 22.80 USD. The business did fine; the price paid was the problem.

lessons.explainSimpler: Good company and good price are two separate questions. P/E tells you how much you are paying for each dollar of today's profit.
lessons.commonMistake: Assuming a great company is a great investment at any price. If the price already assumes more than the business later delivers, the investment can lose money while the company does well.

quickCheck.prompt: Price 15.00 USD, EPS 0.60 USD. What are the P/E and the earnings yield?

options.text: P/E 9, earnings yield 11%
P/E 25, earnings yield 4%
P/E 4, earnings yield 25%
options.explanation: No: these are swapped.

quickCheck.prompt: Two fictional firms are equally good businesses. One has a P/E of 10, the other a P/E of 50. What follows?

options.text: The P/E 50 firm is the better business
options.explanation: No: a high P/E reflects expectations, not proven quality.

options.text: Both are equally good investments right now
options.explanation: No: paying five times more for the same profit changes the outcome.

options.text: The P/E 50 price assumes much more growth
options.explanation: Right: if that growth does not arrive, the price has further to fall.

quickCheck.prompt: A company made a loss this year. What is its P/E?

options.text: Not meaningful, as earnings are negative
options.explanation: Right: P/E needs positive earnings; with a loss, it tells you nothing.

options.text: Zero, so very cheap
options.explanation: No: a P/E is not zero when there is a loss.

options.text: Very high, so expensive
options.explanation: No: there is no meaningful P/E without positive earnings.

doItNow.instructions: Open the Fundamental Analysis Lab → Company analysis. List the four fictional companies from lowest to highest P/E. Next to each, write one reason the market might be paying that price and one thing that would make that price look too high.

lessons.title: Volume and liquidity in shares

inOneLine.simple: Volume is how many shares changed hands. When volume is low, getting in and out at a fair price is harder.
inOneLine.balanced: [[volume|Volume]] counts shares traded in a period. Low volume usually comes with low [[liquidity]] and a wider [[spread]], so an order can move the price against you. Compare your order size with typical daily volume.

explain.simple: Every time a buyer and a seller agree, the shares traded are added to the volume for that period. A share that trades millions of times a day is easy to buy or sell in small amounts without moving the price much. A share that trades a few thousand times a day is different: there may be no buyer at the price you want, so you either wait or accept a worse price. That ease of trading is called liquidity.
explain.balanced: Liquidity shows up in two places. First, the [[spread]] between [[bid]] and [[ask]]: thin markets usually have wider spreads, which you pay every time you trade. Second, the size of your order compared with daily volume: a big order in a thin share can push the price as it fills. Volume also changes over time, often rising around news and earnings reports. A volume spike shows that more shares traded; on its own it does not say which way price will go next.

assumptions: Two fictional shares, both priced around 10 USD
Share A trades about 2,000,000 shares a day; Share B about 20,000
You want to sell 5,000 shares of either
steps: In Share A, 5,000 ÷ 2,000,000 = 0.25% of a typical day's volume. Small.
In Share B, 5,000 ÷ 20,000 = 25% of a typical day's volume. Large.
In Share B there may not be enough buyers near the current price, so you might need to accept lower prices or sell over several days.
The same order is easy in one share and hard in the other.

assumptions: Illustrative quotes for two fictional shares; costs other than the spread ignored
Share A: bid 10.00 USD, ask 10.02 USD
Share B: bid 0.50 USD, ask 0.55 USD
You buy 1,000 shares at the ask and sell them straight back at the bid
steps: Share A: buy for 1,000 × 10.02 = 10,020 USD; sell for 1,000 × 10.00 = 10,000 USD. Lost 20 USD, about 0.2% of 10,020.
Share B: buy for 1,000 × 0.55 = 550 USD; sell for 1,000 × 0.50 = 500 USD. Lost 50 USD, about 9.1% of 550.
In Share B, price has to rise about 10% (from 0.50 to 0.55) just for the bid to reach what you paid.

lessons.explainSimpler: Lots of trading means easy in, easy out. Little trading means you may get stuck or pay up.
lessons.commonMistake: Looking only at the price chart and ignoring volume and the spread. A trade that looks fine on the chart can lose money at entry in a thin share, and may be hard to exit.

quickCheck.prompt: A share trades about 40,000 shares a day. Your simulated order is 10,000 shares. What share of daily volume is that?

options.explanation: No: 10,000 ÷ 40,000 is a quarter, not 4%.
Right: 10,000 ÷ 40,000 = 0.25, a large part of a day's trading.
No: that would be 16,000 shares.

quickCheck.prompt: Bid 2.00 USD, ask 2.10 USD. You buy 100 shares and sell them back at once. What does the spread cost?

options.text: 10 USD
options.explanation: Right: you pay 210 USD and get back 200 USD.

options.text: 1 USD
options.explanation: No: the gap is 0.10 USD on each of 100 shares.

options.text: 0.10 USD
options.explanation: No: that is the gap for one share only.

quickCheck.prompt: Volume jumps to five times its usual level. What does that tell you on its own?

options.text: Price is likely to rise next
options.explanation: No: high volume says many shares traded, not which way price goes next.

options.text: The company has good news
options.explanation: No: the reason is unknown from volume alone.

options.text: More shares changed hands
options.explanation: Right: that is all volume measures. The reason and direction need more work.

doItNow.instructions: In Chart Lab, open the Breakout scenario and show the Volume pane. Note the volume on the breakout candle compared with the ten candles before it. Repeat with the False breakout scenario. Write down whether volume alone would have told you in advance which breakout would hold.

lessons.title: Consolidation and channels

inOneLine.simple: Consolidation is price going sideways in a box. A channel is price swinging between two sloping, roughly parallel lines.
inOneLine.balanced: A [[consolidation]] is a pause where price stays inside a flat range. A [[channel]] is a [[trend]] whose swings stay between two parallel lines. Both are drawn by you, after the fact, so write down which swing points you used.

explain.simple: After a move, price often goes sideways for a while. Highs stop rising and lows stop falling. That pause is called consolidation. You can draw a box around it: the top at the recent highs, the bottom at the recent lows. A channel is different. Price is still trending, but its swings stay between two lines with the same slope. In a rising channel, you draw one line under the higher lows and a parallel line over the higher highs.
explain.balanced: Both shapes depend on the points you choose. Pick different swing lows and the line moves. So write a rule, for example "the lower line joins the last two swing lows; the upper line is parallel through the highest high between them". Compare a box's height with [[atr|ATR]]: a box only about 2 ATR tall is narrow compared with recent movement. A consolidation can end with a [[breakout]] either way, or go on for a long time. A channel line is not a wall. Price can overshoot it, stop short of it, or the slope can change.

assumptions: Illustrative commodity prices, in USD
For 30 candles, highs stayed between 82.20 and 82.40 and lows between 80.10 and 80.30
ATR 14 is 1.10
steps: Box top = 82.40, box bottom = 80.10.
In ATR terms: 2.30 ÷ 1.10 ≈ 2.1 ATR.
So the box is narrow compared with the usual candle-to-candle movement. That describes the pause. It does not say which way price leaves it, or when.

assumptions: Illustrative stock prices
Lower line joins swing lows at 100.0 (candle 10) and 104.0 (candle 30)
Upper line is parallel and passes through a swing high of 106.0 at candle 20
Your rule: the channel is broken by a close at least 0.5 beyond a line
steps: At candle 40, the lower line = 100.0 + 0.2 × (40 − 10) = 106.0.
The upper line = 106.0 + 0.2 × (40 − 20) = 110.0, so the channel is 4.0 wide.
Candle 40 closes at 105.2: that is 106.0 − 105.2 = 0.8 below the lower line, more than 0.5. Under your rule, the channel is broken. It says the old pattern stopped, not what comes next.

lessons.explainSimpler: A box is a pause. A channel is a slope with two rails. You draw both, so draw them the same way every time.
lessons.commonMistake: Moving your lines after each new candle so price always "respects" them. A line you keep redrawing is not telling you anything.

quickCheck.prompt: A box runs from 45.20 to 46.70. ATR 14 is 0.50. How tall is the box in ATR?

options.text: 1.5 ATR
options.explanation: No: 1.50 is the height in price. Divide by ATR: 1.50 ÷ 0.50 = 3.

options.text: 0.33 ATR
options.explanation: No: that is ATR ÷ height. Height ÷ ATR = 3.

options.text: 3 ATR

quickCheck.prompt: What is the main difference between a consolidation and a channel?

options.text: A channel slopes; a consolidation goes sideways
options.explanation: Right: a channel is a trend with parallel rails, a consolidation is a flat pause.

options.text: A channel is reliable; a consolidation is not
options.explanation: No: both are shapes you draw. Neither is reliable on its own.

options.text: A consolidation always ends with a breakout up
options.explanation: No: it can break either way, or keep going sideways.

quickCheck.prompt: Price closes 0.3 below your lower channel line. Your rule says a break needs 0.5. What do you do?

options.text: Call it broken, since price is below the line
options.explanation: No: your written rule needs 0.5. Changing it after the fact is fitting the chart to your view.

options.text: Redraw the line lower so price is back inside
options.explanation: No: moving lines to fit each candle makes the channel meaningless.

options.text: Not broken under your rule; keep watching
options.explanation: Right: apply the rule you wrote, the same way each time.

doItNow.instructions: In Chart Lab, open the Range scenario. Use the Zone tool to draw a box around the sideways stretch, then measure its height against ATR 14 in the lower pane. Next open Downtrend. Use the Trend line tool to join two swing highs, then draw a parallel line through the lowest low between them. Count how many times price closed outside your lines.

lessons.title: Fibonacci retracements: a convention, not a forecast

inOneLine.simple: Fibonacci retracements are lines at set percentages of a move. Some traders watch them. They do not predict where a pullback stops.
inOneLine.balanced: A [[fibonacci-retracement]] tool draws levels at 23.6%, 38.2%, 50%, 61.8% and 78.6% of a chosen swing. They are a convention for describing how deep a [[pullback]] went. With five levels close together, price will usually be near one of them.

explain.simple: Pick a swing, say from a low to a high. The tool draws lines at fixed shares of that move, counted back from the high: 23.6%, 38.2%, 50%, 61.8% and 78.6%. The 50% line is not a Fibonacci ratio, but most tools include it. Some traders watch these lines, and some place orders near them. If the lines matter at all, it is because people watch them, not because of anything special in the numbers. Think of them as a shared way of labelling depth, like saying "about halfway back".
explain.balanced: The levels depend on which swing you pick, and different people pick different swings. Five levels inside one move leave little space between them, so almost any pullback ends "near a level" if you allow some tolerance. That makes them look accurate after the fact. Treat them as a ruler, not a signal. If you use them, write the anchor rule (which swing low and high) and the tolerance before you look, and judge them like any other rule, on a test you set up in advance.

assumptions: Illustrative stock prices
Swing low 40.00, swing high 50.00, so the move is 10.00
Levels are counted back down from the high
steps: If you anchor on an earlier low of 38.00 instead, the move is 12.00 and the 61.8% level is 50.00 − 7.416 ≈ 42.58. Same chart, different lines.

assumptions: Same 40.00 to 50.00 swing
The five levels are 47.64, 46.18, 45.00, 43.82 and 42.14
You count "near a level" as within 0.60 either side
steps: Each level covers a band 1.20 wide, for example 46.18 ± 0.60 = 45.58 to 46.78.
The bands run from 41.54 to 48.24, a span of 6.70.
Allowing for small overlaps, the five bands cover about 5.96 of that span.
5.96 ÷ 6.70 ≈ 89%. So most pullbacks in that zone would end "near a Fibonacci level" by chance alone.

lessons.explainSimpler: Fibonacci lines are tick marks on a ruler. They help you describe how far price came back. They do not tell price where to stop.
lessons.commonMistake: Drawing the tool on several swings until one level lines up with a turn, then calling it proof. Or treating a level as a reason to enter without a stop.

quickCheck.prompt: Swing low 1.1000, swing high 1.1200. Where is the 50% retracement?

options.explanation: No: that is 25% of the move above the low. The move is 200 pips; halfway is 1.1100.
No: that is only 50 pips back from the high, which is 25%.

quickCheck.prompt: Price turns exactly at the 61.8% line. What does that show?

options.text: The level caused price to turn there
options.explanation: No: with five levels close together, some turns land on a level by chance.

options.text: The 61.8% level works for this market
options.explanation: No: one turn is one example. It says nothing about how often that happens.

options.text: Only where this pullback ended
options.explanation: Right: it describes the depth. It does not show the line has predictive power.

quickCheck.prompt: Two learners draw Fibonacci levels on the same chart and get different lines. Why?

options.text: They picked different swing points
options.explanation: Right: the levels depend entirely on the chosen start and end of the move.

options.text: One of them used the wrong ratios
options.explanation: No: the tool uses the same ratios for everyone. The anchors differ.

options.text: Fibonacci levels may shift as new candles form
options.explanation: No: once the two anchors are chosen, the levels stay put. New candles do not move them.

doItNow.instructions: In Chart Lab, open the Pullback scenario. Write your anchor rule first, for example "the lowest low and highest high of the last swing up". Use the Fibonacci tool from that low to that high. Note which level the pullback ended nearest, then redraw from a different low and see how the lines move.

lessons.title: Market regimes: why a method behaves differently

inOneLine.simple: A market regime is the kind of market you are in: trending or ranging, and calm or jumpy. The same rules behave very differently in each.
inOneLine.balanced: Classify each period with a written rule on two questions: is it trending or ranging, and is [[volatility]] high or low compared with its own past? A [[market-regime]] label lags, and regimes change without warning.

explain.simple: Ask two questions about a chart. First: has price gone somewhere, or gone back and forth? That is trend or range. Second: are candles bigger or smaller than usual for this market? That is high or low volatility. Together they give four boxes, such as "trending and calm" or "ranging and jumpy". A rule built for one box can do badly in another. A moving-average cross follows a trend, but in a range it flips back and forth, and each flip is a small loss plus costs. A "buy near the bottom of the range" rule does the opposite: it suits a range and keeps buying into a falling trend.
explain.balanced: Turn the questions into numbers so you classify the same way each time. One simple version: trending if the net move over the last 20 candles is at least 3 × [[atr|ATR]] 14; high volatility if ATR 14 is at least 1.5 × its own 100-candle average, low if it is 0.75 × or less. The thresholds are your choice, and changing them moves periods between boxes. That is why you test how sensitive your results are to them. The label always describes the recent past: by the time 20 candles show a trend, part of it is over. When reviewing a [[backtest]], split results by regime. A method that only made money in one box depends on that box coming back.

assumptions: Illustrative EUR/USD prices
Rule: trending if |close now − close 20 candles ago| ≥ 3 × ATR 14
High volatility if ATR 14 ≥ 1.5 × its 100-candle average; low if ≤ 0.75 ×
Close now 1.0950; close 20 candles ago 1.0800; ATR 14 = 40 pips; its 100-candle average = 30 pips
steps: In ATR: 150 ÷ 40 = 3.75, which is at least 3. Trending.
Volatility: 40 ÷ 30 ≈ 1.33. That is below 1.5 and above 0.75, so normal.
Label: trending, normal volatility. It describes the last 20 candles only.

assumptions: Illustrative commodity prices, in USD
Same rule
Close now 74.20; close 20 candles ago 73.60; ATR 14 = 0.90; its 100-candle average = 0.50
steps: In ATR: 0.60 ÷ 0.90 ≈ 0.67, well below 3. Ranging.
Volatility: 0.90 ÷ 0.50 = 1.8, at least 1.5. High volatility.
Label: ranging, high volatility: big candles going nowhere. Trend-following rules tend to flip back and forth here, paying costs each time.

lessons.explainSimpler: A regime is the weather. A good umbrella rule is useless on a sunny day. Check the weather label, but remember it is yesterday's weather.
lessons.commonMistake: Judging a method on one kind of market and assuming the result carries over. Or redefining the regime after the fact so the losing periods "do not count".

quickCheck.prompt: Net move over 20 candles: 2.40. ATR 14: 1.20. Its 100-candle average: 0.80. Using this lesson's rule, what is the label?

options.text: Trending, high volatility
options.explanation: No: 2.40 ÷ 1.20 = 2 ATR, below the 3 ATR needed for a trend.

options.text: Ranging, high volatility
options.explanation: Right: 2 ATR is below 3, so ranging; 1.20 ÷ 0.80 = 1.5, so high volatility.

options.text: Ranging, normal volatility
options.explanation: No: 1.20 ÷ 0.80 = 1.5, which meets the high-volatility threshold.

quickCheck.prompt: A moving-average cross rule loses many small trades in a row. The market has been ranging. What is a fair reading?

options.text: The rule is broken and should be dropped at once
options.explanation: No: a few losses in one regime are what this rule does by design in a range.

options.text: The rule flips back and forth in ranges, as built
options.explanation: Right: in a range, price keeps crossing a flat average. Split results by regime before judging.

options.text: The range will now turn into a trend
options.explanation: No: nothing here says when the regime changes.

quickCheck.prompt: Why does a regime label always lag?

options.text: It is measured on closed, past candles
options.explanation: Right: by the time the window shows a trend, part of it is over.

options.text: The broker delays the indicator data
options.explanation: No: the delay comes from using past candles, not from the broker.

options.text: It does not lag if you use ATR instead
options.explanation: No: ATR also averages past candles.

doItNow.instructions: In Chart Lab, open four scenarios in turn: Strong uptrend, Range, High volatility and Low volatility. Show ATR 14 below the chart and SMA 20 on it. For each, write the label your rule gives on the last 20 candles. Then open Sideways and count how many times price crossed the SMA 20.

lessons.title: Multi-timeframe analysis

inOneLine.simple: Look at a higher timeframe for the bigger picture and a lower one for detail. They often disagree, and that is normal.
inOneLine.balanced: [[multi-timeframe-analysis|Multi-timeframe analysis]] means choosing two or three [[timeframe|timeframes]] in advance: one for context, one for entries. The higher one may show an uptrend while the lower one shows a [[pullback]]. Agreement between them is not a forecast.

explain.simple: Each timeframe shows the same price history in different-sized candles. A daily chart might show a clear uptrend. The 1-hour chart of the same days might show price falling for the last 20 hours. Both are true at once: the fall is a pullback inside the bigger uptrend. One approach is to use a higher timeframe to decide which direction you are interested in, and a lower one to plan the entry and [[stop-loss]].
explain.balanced: Pick your timeframes before you look, and keep them. Switching until one chart agrees with your idea is a form of cherry-picking. The timeframe you use for the stop decides its distance, and the distance decides the size: a stop under a daily swing low is usually far wider than one under an hourly low, so the [[position-sizing|position size]] must be smaller for the same money at risk. Indicators change meaning too: a 20-period average on a daily chart covers about four weeks of trading; on a 1-hour chart it covers less than a day. Higher and lower timeframes agreeing means two views of the same prices agree, not that the move will continue.

assumptions: Illustrative EUR/USD prices; account in USD
Example risk limit: 50 USD per trade. A learning example, not a recommendation
Pip value 10 USD for 1.00 lot; size step 0.01 lot
Stop under the last 1-hour swing low: 20 pips away. Stop under the last daily swing low: 90 pips away
steps: 1-hour stop: size = 50 ÷ (20 × 10) = 0.25 lot. Risk = 0.25 × 200 = 50 USD.
Daily stop: size = 50 ÷ (90 × 10) = 0.0555… lot, rounded down to 0.05 lot.
Actual risk at 0.05 lot = 0.05 × 900 = 45 USD.
Same idea, same money at risk, but the size differs by five times. The timeframe you base the stop on matters.

assumptions: A market that trades 24 hours a day, 5 days a week
You compare a daily (D1) chart with a 4-hour (H4) and a 1-hour (H1) chart
steps: One D1 candle = 24 ÷ 4 = 6 H4 candles = 24 H1 candles.
20 D1 candles = 20 × 6 = 120 H4 candles = 20 × 24 = 480 H1 candles.
So a 20-period moving average on H1 covers 20 hours, under one day of trading.
A "trend" on H1 can be a single wiggle on D1. Say which timeframe you mean whenever you name a trend.

lessons.explainSimpler: Zoomed out, you see the road. Zoomed in, you see the bumps. Pick both zoom levels before you look.
lessons.commonMistake: Flicking through timeframes until one agrees with what you wanted to do, or calling a 1-hour dip a "trend change" without checking the daily chart.

quickCheck.prompt: The daily chart shows an uptrend. The 1-hour chart has fallen for 15 hours. What is the plainest description?

options.text: The daily trend has now reversed downward
options.explanation: No: 15 hours is a small part of a daily chart. The daily structure may be intact.

options.text: The 1-hour chart is giving a false reading
options.explanation: No: both charts show the same prices, just in different candle sizes.

options.text: A pullback in a daily uptrend, so far
options.explanation: Right: both views can be true at once.

quickCheck.prompt: Same 50 USD risk, pip value 10 USD per lot. Stop A is 25 pips, stop B is 100 pips. What sizes?

options.text: A 0.20 lot, B 0.05 lot
A 0.05 lot, B 0.20 lot
options.explanation: No: the wider stop needs the smaller size.

options.text: Both 0.20 lot
options.explanation: No: at 100 pips, 0.20 lot would risk 200 USD.

quickCheck.prompt: You switch from H1 to M15 to H4 until one chart agrees with your trade idea. What is the problem?

options.text: You pick the view that fits your idea
options.explanation: Right: decide your timeframes first, then read them as they are.

options.text: M15 charts are too short to show any trend
options.explanation: No: any timeframe can show a trend on its own scale.

options.text: M15 is more current than H4
options.explanation: No: every timeframe shows the same latest price. The problem is choosing the one that agrees with you.

doItNow.instructions: Write down two timeframes before you start, for example 1d for context and 1h for detail. In Chart Lab, open the Pullback scenario. Zoom out to see the whole chart and name the trend. Then zoom in on the last 20 candles and name what they show. Write one sentence that is true of both views. Then do the "Find the trend" drill in Practice and say which scale you judged each chart on.

lessons.title: Pullbacks or reversals?

inOneLine.simple: A pullback is a move against the trend that leaves its structure intact. A reversal breaks the structure and starts a new one. At the time, they look the same.
inOneLine.balanced: In an uptrend, a [[pullback]] falls but stays above the last higher low. A [[reversal]] breaks that low and then builds lower highs and lower lows. You only know which one it was after more candles.

explain.simple: Trends do not move in straight lines. In an uptrend, price rises, dips, then rises again. The dip is a pullback, as long as it stays above the last swing low. If price falls below that swing low, the uptrend's structure is broken. If it then makes a lower high and a lower low, it has the shape of a downtrend. That is a reversal. The hard part: every reversal starts out looking like a pullback.
explain.balanced: Use [[market-structure]] to tell them apart, with a written rule, such as "a close below the last higher low breaks the uptrend". Measure how deep a pullback went as a share of the last swing up. A deep pullback is not automatically a reversal, and a shallow one can still turn into one. A broken structure can also repair itself: price closes below the low, then climbs back and makes a new high. On a higher [[timeframe]], a reversal on your chart may be just a pullback. None of these labels predicts the next move.

assumptions: Illustrative index futures prices, in points
Uptrend: swing lows at 4,500 and 4,580, latest swing high at 4,700
Rule: a close below the last higher low (4,580) breaks the uptrend
steps: Price falls to 4,620. Depth = 4,700 − 4,620 = 80 points.
Last swing up = 4,700 − 4,580 = 120 points. Share given back = 80 ÷ 120 ≈ 67%.
4,620 is still above 4,580, so under the rule it is a pullback. The structure is intact.
Two thirds is a deep pullback. Depth alone does not make it a reversal, and staying above the low does not mean the trend resumes.

assumptions: Same chart, a different path
Price closes at 4,560, then rallies to 4,650, then closes at 4,540
steps: Close at 4,560 is below 4,580: the uptrend structure is broken.
The rally stops at 4,650, below the 4,700 high: a lower high.
The close at 4,540 is below 4,560: a lower low.
Now it has the shape of a downtrend, so you would call it a reversal. Even so, it can turn again.

lessons.explainSimpler: A pullback is a step back on the same path. A reversal is a turn onto a new path. From the first step, you cannot tell which.
lessons.commonMistake: Calling every pullback "the reversal" and trading against the trend, or calling a broken structure "just a pullback" because you are holding a trade.

quickCheck.prompt: Swing low 1.2580, swing high 1.2700. Price drops to 1.2640. What share of the swing has it given back?

options.explanation: No: 60 is the pips given back. The swing is 120 pips, so 60 ÷ 120 = 50%.

quickCheck.prompt: In an uptrend, price closes below the last higher low. What has happened?

options.text: A reversal is now certain
options.explanation: No: the structure is broken, but price can still recover and make a new high.

options.text: The uptrend structure is broken
options.explanation: Right: it no longer fits the uptrend definition. What comes next is unknown.

options.text: Nothing; it is just a deep pullback
options.explanation: No: a pullback stays above the last higher low.

quickCheck.prompt: Why is it hard to tell a pullback from a reversal while it is happening?

options.text: Because pullbacks run deeper than reversals
options.explanation: No: depth does not decide it. A shallow fall can become a reversal.

options.text: Because indicators hide the difference
options.explanation: No: the problem is that the future candles are not visible yet.

options.text: Every reversal starts as a move against the trend
options.explanation: Right: the first candles look the same. Only later structure shows which it was.

doItNow.instructions: Start a replay on the Pullback scenario. Mark each swing low as it forms. When price falls, write "pullback" or "reversal" before revealing the next candle, with your reason. Then do the same on the Reversal scenario. Compare how often your first call was right.

lessons.title: Relative strength: comparing two markets

inOneLine.simple: Relative strength compares one market with another, or with an index. It shows which did better over a window, not which will do better next.
inOneLine.balanced: [[relative-strength|Relative strength]] is a ratio: price of A ÷ price of B. A rising ratio means A outperformed B over that window, even if both fell. It is not the same as [[rsi|RSI]], which looks at one market on its own.

explain.simple: Divide one price by another, every candle, and plot the result as a line. If the line rises, the first market did better than the second. If it falls, it did worse. Traders use it to compare a stock with its index, one commodity with another, or two related markets. It answers "which was stronger?", not "is it going up?". Both markets can fall while the ratio rises, because the first one fell less.
explain.balanced: The answer depends on the window you choose. Start the comparison a month earlier and the leader may change. Markets with different [[volatility]] are hard to compare: a jumpy market can lead in one window and lag badly in the next. In forex, the ratio of two pairs that share a currency is itself a third pair: EUR/USD ÷ GBP/USD = EUR/GBP. So you are really reading the cross rate, not the strength of either pair. Leadership can change at any time, so a strong ratio describes the past. And [[correlation|correlated]] markets often move together, so a small ratio change may be noise.

assumptions: Fictional stock A and a fictional index, illustrative prices
Start: A = 50, index = 4,000
End of the window: A = 55, index = 4,200
steps: A outperformed the index over this window. That is a description of these dates only.

assumptions: Same start: A = 50, index = 4,000
End of a different window: A = 47, index = 3,600
steps: Ratio change ≈ +4.4%, so A shows relative strength.
Yet someone holding A still lost 6%. Relative strength is not the same as going up.

lessons.explainSimpler: Relative strength is a race between two runners. It tells you who is ahead, not whether either is running uphill.
lessons.commonMistake: Confusing relative strength with RSI, or thinking a rising ratio means the market itself is rising.

quickCheck.prompt: Commodity X goes from 20 to 22. Commodity Y goes from 40 to 42. Which outperformed?

options.text: Y, because it rose 2 like X but from a higher price
options.explanation: No: compare percentages. X rose 10%, Y rose 5%.

options.text: X, because it rose 10% against Y's 5%
Neither: both rose by 2
options.explanation: No: the same move in price is a different move in percent.

quickCheck.prompt: The ratio of stock A to its index rises while both fall. What does that mean?

options.text: A fell less than the index
options.explanation: Right: the ratio rises when A does better, including by falling less.

options.text: A is rising
options.explanation: No: A can fall while its ratio to the index rises.

options.text: The ratio is miscalculated
options.explanation: No: this happens whenever A falls less than the index.

quickCheck.prompt: How is relative strength different from RSI?

options.text: Two names for the same indicator
options.explanation: No: RSI scores one market's ups against its own downs. Relative strength compares two markets.

options.text: RS compares two markets; RSI measures one market's moves
options.explanation: Right: RSI is about a single market's recent moves.

options.text: RS is RSI set to a longer period
options.explanation: No: changing RSI's period still scores one market against itself. Relative strength needs a second market.

doItNow.instructions: Pick two markets you could compare, for example a stock and its index, or two commodities. Using the closing prices shown in your demo platform, write down both prices today and in 5 trading days. Work out each percentage change and the change in the ratio. Then write one sentence on what the ratio does and does not tell you.

lessons.title: Return statistics, indicator correlation and parameter sensitivity

inOneLine.simple: Look at the whole spread of results, not just the average. Two indicators built from the same prices are not two confirmations. A result that vanishes when you nudge a setting is fragile.
inOneLine.balanced: Describe a test by its [[return-distribution]]: average, median, spread and worst run. Check [[indicator-correlation]]: RSI and MACD both come from recent closes, so they often agree. Check [[parameter-sensitivity]]: neighbouring settings should give similar results.

explain.simple: An average can hide a lot. Ten trades can average a small gain while most of them lose, if one or two big winners pull the average up. So also look at the median (the middle trade), the worst losing run and what happens if you remove the best trade. Next, indicators. RSI, MACD and moving averages are all calculated from recent closing prices. When they agree, that is partly because they are measuring the same thing. Counting them as separate votes overstates your evidence. Finally, settings. If a 20-candle average gives a great result but 18 and 22 give losses, the 20 result is probably luck.
explain.balanced: Good questions for any test: How many trades? What is the average in R ([[r-multiple|R-multiples]]), and the median? What share of the total came from the best one or two trades? What was the longest losing run and the deepest [[drawdown]]? For indicators: if two of them tend to turn on the same candles, treat them as one input; a second input should use different information, such as structure or volume. For settings: test a small grid of neighbours. A broad plateau of similar results is more believable than a single sharp peak, which is a sign of [[overfitting]]. None of this proves a method has an edge; it only tells you how fragile the result is.

assumptions: Fictional 10 replay trades, results in R
steps: Win rate = 3 ÷ 10 = 30%.
Sorted, the middle trades are both −1R, so the median is −1R. The typical trade lost.
Remove the single +4R trade: total = 2 − 4 = −2R. One trade decided the sign. With 10 trades, this says very little.

assumptions: Fictional backtests of a moving-average rule over the same data, net results in R
Plan B, same lengths: +3, +4, +5, +4, +2
steps: Plan A at length 20 looks best of all: +12R.
But its neighbours lose. Average across the five settings = (−4 − 1 + 12 − 2 − 5) ÷ 5 = 0R.
Plan B never reaches +12R, but every setting is positive. Average = (3 + 4 + 5 + 4 + 2) ÷ 5 = 3.6R.
Plan A's peak is fragile: a small change wipes it out. Plan B is less sensitive. Neither result proves anything about the future.

lessons.explainSimpler: An average is one number for a whole crowd. Two thermometers in the same room are not two weather reports. A recipe that only works at exactly 180 degrees is fussy.
lessons.commonMistake: Reporting only the average, counting RSI and MACD agreeing as "double confirmation", or publishing the one setting that worked best.

quickCheck.prompt: Results in R: +5, −1, −1, −1, −1. What are the average and the median?

options.text: Average +0.2R, median −1R
options.explanation: Right: total = 5 − 4 = +1R, ÷ 5 = +0.2R; the middle value sorted is −1R.

options.text: Average +1R, median −1R
options.explanation: No: +1R is the total. Divide by 5 trades.

options.text: Average +0.2R, median +0.2R
options.explanation: No: the median is the middle trade once sorted: −1R.

quickCheck.prompt: RSI 14 and MACD both turn up on the same candle. How much evidence is that?

options.text: Two independent confirmations
options.explanation: No: both are built from recent closes, so they often turn together.

options.text: More like one reading of the same price moves
options.explanation: Right: correlated indicators largely repeat each other.

options.text: None at all, because indicators are useless
options.explanation: No: they describe recent price behaviour. They just do not add up as separate votes.

quickCheck.prompt: Length 30 gives +15R; lengths 28 and 32 give −3R and −4R. What does that suggest?

options.text: Length 30 is the right setting to use
options.explanation: No: a lone peak with losing neighbours is likely luck in this sample.

options.text: The test needs a longer average
options.explanation: No: the issue is how sensitive the result is, not the length itself.

options.text: The +15R is fragile and may be luck
options.explanation: Right: high parameter sensitivity is a sign of overfitting.

doItNow.instructions: Take your last 20 or more replay trades from the Journal. Write down the total, average and median in R, the win rate, the longest losing run, and the total without your single best trade. Then list the indicators in your plan and mark any two that are built from the same closing prices.

lessons.title: Volatility-adjusted position sizing

inOneLine.simple: When a market moves more, your stop needs more room, so your size must be smaller. Then a loss at the stop costs the same money in calm and jumpy markets.
inOneLine.balanced: [[volatility-adjusted-sizing|Volatility-adjusted sizing]]: set the stop from the market's movement, for example 2 × [[atr|ATR]], then size = money at risk ÷ (stop distance × value per unit of price). The money at risk stays fixed.

explain.simple: In the position sizing lesson, the stop came first and the size followed. Here the stop distance comes from how much the market has been moving. One way is to use a multiple of ATR, such as 1.5 or 2 × ATR, so a calm market gets a tight stop and a jumpy market a wide one. Then you divide your money at risk by what that stop distance costs per share, per contract or per lot. A jumpy market ends up with a smaller position. The money lost at the stop is about the same.
explain.balanced: Check the ATR stop against the chart too: if it lands in the middle of a [[support]] zone, move it to where the idea is wrong and recompute the size. Round down to the size step. Some markets cannot be sized finely: one futures contract may already be more risk than your limit, and then the answer is to skip. ATR describes the past, so it can be low just before a jump. A [[gap]] or [[slippage]] can still push the loss past the stop. Costs add to the loss; the "Position size with costs" calculator includes them.

assumptions: Fictional account: 20,000 USD. Example risk: 0.5% = 100 USD. A learning example, not a recommendation
Two fictional stocks, both priced at 40.00
Stock A: ATR 14 = 0.80. Stock B: ATR 14 = 2.00
Stop = 2 × ATR. Whole shares only; costs ignored
steps: A: stop distance = 2 × 0.80 = 1.60. Shares = 100 ÷ 1.60 = 62.5, round down to 62. Risk = 62 × 1.60 = 99.20 USD.
Position value: A = 62 × 40 = 2,480 USD; B = 25 × 40 = 1,000 USD.
Same money at risk, very different position sizes. The jumpy stock gets the smaller position.

assumptions: Fictional futures contract: 1 point = 50 USD per contract. Fictional specification
Example risk limit: 1,000 USD. Stop = 1.5 × ATR
Week 1: ATR 14 = 12 points. Week 2: ATR 14 = 30 points
steps: Week 1: stop = 1.5 × 12 = 18 points. Risk per contract = 18 × 50 = 900 USD.
Contracts = 1,000 ÷ 900 ≈ 1.11, round down to 1. Actual risk = 900 USD.
Week 2: stop = 1.5 × 30 = 45 points. Risk per contract = 45 × 50 = 2,250 USD.
1,000 ÷ 2,250 ≈ 0.44, which rounds down to 0 contracts. You cannot trade less than one, so the plan says skip.

lessons.explainSimpler: Big waves need a longer rope, and a longer rope means a smaller boat. The rope always costs the same.
lessons.commonMistake: Keeping the same size when the stop gets wider, so the loss at the stop doubles. Or rounding up to "make the trade possible".

quickCheck.prompt: EUR/USD ATR 14 = 15 pips. Stop = 2 × ATR. Risk 60 USD; pip value 10 USD per lot. What size?

options.text: 0.40 lot
options.explanation: No: that uses a 15-pip stop. The stop is 2 × 15 = 30 pips.

options.text: 0.20 lot
options.explanation: Right: 30 pips × 10 USD = 300 USD per lot, and 60 ÷ 300 = 0.20.

options.text: 2.00 lots
options.explanation: No: check the units. 60 ÷ 300 = 0.20 lot.

quickCheck.prompt: ATR doubles and you keep the same 2 × ATR stop. To keep the same money at risk, what happens to size?

options.text: Size roughly halves
options.explanation: Right: the stop doubles, so the size halves for the same money at risk.

options.text: Size doubles too
options.explanation: No: that would risk four times as much.

options.text: Size stays the same
options.explanation: No: the same size with twice the stop doubles the loss at the stop.

quickCheck.prompt: One futures contract would risk 1,800 USD at your stop. Your limit is 1,000 USD. What does the plan say?

options.text: Trade one contract anyway; it is the minimum
options.explanation: No: that breaks the risk limit by 800 USD.

options.text: Tighten the stop until one fits
options.explanation: No: the stop belongs where the idea is wrong, not where the size fits.

options.text: Skip it: even one contract breaks the limit
options.explanation: Right: if the smallest size breaks the limit, the answer is no trade.

doItNow.instructions: In Chart Lab, open High volatility with ATR 14 below the chart. Read the last ATR value and turn it into pips (0.00100 = 10 pips), set a stop at 2 × ATR, and work out the size by hand for an example 10,000 USD account risking 1%. Check it in Learn → Calculators → Position size. Repeat on Low volatility and compare the two sizes. Then do 10 charts of the Size it drill in Practice.

lessons.title: Volume and gaps: what they can and cannot confirm

inOneLine.simple: Volume shows how much traded during a candle. A gap is a jump between one candle and the next. Both describe what happened, not what happens next.
inOneLine.balanced: [[volume|Volume]] measures participation, and a [[gap]] measures a jump in price. A move on heavy volume had more trading behind it than usual. That does not make it more likely to continue, and a gap does not have to "fill".

explain.simple: Volume is the amount traded in each candle: shares for a stock, contracts for a futures market. It usually shows as bars under the chart. Compare a bar with the recent average, not with zero. Forex has no single exchange, so a forex platform shows tick volume instead: how many times your broker's price changed. That is a rough stand-in, not the whole market. A gap is a jump in price with no trading in between. Stocks and futures can gap between one session's close and the next open. Forex mostly gaps when the market reopens after the weekend.
explain.balanced: Volume can tell you that a move happened with more or less trading than usual. It cannot tell you who was buying or selling, or whether the move will last. A [[breakout]] on heavy volume can still fail, and a quiet move can keep going. Volume also rises at the open, the close and around news, so compare with the same time of day where you can. A gap means orders resting inside it, including a [[stop-loss]], fill at the first price after the jump. People say gaps "fill", meaning price returns to the old close. Some do, some do not, and there is no rule that says when.

assumptions: Fictional stock, illustrative numbers
20-day average volume: 400,000 shares
Today price closes above a resistance zone on 1,000,000 shares
steps: Relative volume = today ÷ average = 1,000,000 ÷ 400,000 = 2.5.
So about 2.5 times the usual amount traded today.
That says many more shares changed hands during the breakout than on a typical day.
It does not say the breakout will hold. Every share bought was also sold by someone.

assumptions: Fictional stock, illustrative prices
You sold short 200 shares at 52.00 with a stop at 53.00
It closes at 52.40, then opens the next morning at 54.10
steps: The open is already above the stop, so the stop fills near 54.10.
Actual loss ≈ (54.10 − 52.00) × 200 = 420 USD, more than twice the plan.

lessons.explainSimpler: Volume is how loud the crowd was. A gap is a jump in the film. Neither tells you the ending.
lessons.commonMistake: Treating a high-volume breakout as "confirmed", or expecting every gap to fill. On forex, reading tick volume as if it were the whole market's trading.

quickCheck.prompt: Average volume is 250,000 shares. Today 750,000 shares trade. What is the relative volume?

options.text: One third of the average
options.explanation: No: that is average ÷ today. Divide today by the average.

options.text: 3 times the average
500,000, so 2 times

quickCheck.prompt: A breakout happens on 3 times the usual volume. What can you say?

options.text: It is confirmed and should keep going
options.explanation: No: heavy volume describes the past move. Breakouts on heavy volume can still fail.

options.text: Volume tells you nothing at all here
options.explanation: No: it tells you trading was heavier than usual during the move.

options.text: Heavy trading, but it may still fail
options.explanation: Right: volume describes participation, not what happens next.

quickCheck.prompt: On a forex platform, what does the volume pane usually show?

options.text: Tick volume: how often the broker's price changed
options.explanation: Right: forex has no single exchange, so platforms count price changes at their own feed.

options.text: Every trade in that pair, across all banks and brokers
options.explanation: No: no single platform sees all forex trading.

options.text: Volume from the broker's own clients only
options.explanation: No: it counts price changes in the broker's feed, not the shares or lots its clients traded.

doItNow.instructions: In Chart Lab, choose the Breakout scenario and show Volume below the chart. Find the breakout candle and compare its volume bar with the 10 bars before it. Then open the False breakout scenario and check: did the failed move also have a tall volume bar? Finally, open News shock and look for a jump between one candle's close and the next open.

lessons.title: Out-of-sample and walk-forward testing

inOneLine.simple: Choose your rules on one stretch of data, then test them unchanged on data you did not use. Walk-forward testing repeats this step by step through time.
inOneLine.balanced: Tune on [[in-sample]] data, then judge on [[out-of-sample]] data you kept aside. [[walk-forward-testing|Walk-forward testing]] rolls the window: tune on one block, test on the next, move on, and judge only the joined test blocks.

explain.simple: The earlier backtest lessons showed how a test can fool you: small samples, bias and overfitting. Here is a way to keep part of the data honest. Split your history in two. Use the first part to build and tune the rules. Then run the finished rules, without any change, on the second part. That second part is out-of-sample. If the results fall apart there, the tuning probably fitted noise. Walk-forward testing does this many times: tune on a block, test on the next block, slide forward, repeat.
explain.balanced: Decide the split before you look. Once you have seen the out-of-sample results and changed a rule because of them, that data has become in-sample; you need fresh data to test again. Expect out-of-sample results to be weaker than in-sample, because tuning always picks up some noise. Joined walk-forward test blocks give a fairer picture than one lucky split, and show how the rules cope as [[market-regime|regimes]] change. But the test blocks are still the past, still a limited [[sample-size|sample]], and still open to [[look-ahead-bias]] if anything from the future leaks in. A [[forward-test]] on a demo account is the next step after this, not a replacement.

assumptions: Fictional history of 600 candles
Walk-forward set-up: tune on 200 candles, test on the next 100, then slide forward by 100
steps: Round 1: tune on candles 1–200, test on 201–300.
Round 2: tune on 101–300, test on 301–400. Round 3: tune on 201–400, test on 401–500.
Round 4: tune on 301–500, test on 501–600.
Joined test blocks: 4 × 100 = 400 candles, each tested with rules tuned only on earlier candles. Compare with a single split: tune on 1–400, test once on 401–600, only 200 test candles.

assumptions: Fictional results, in R
In-sample: +18R over 60 trades
Out-of-sample, rules unchanged: +2R over 25 trades
steps: In-sample average = 18 ÷ 60 = +0.3R per trade.
Out-of-sample average = 2 ÷ 25 = +0.08R per trade.
The average fell by more than two thirds. Some of the in-sample result was probably tuning to noise.
25 trades is a small sample, so even +0.08R is very uncertain. The honest reading: no strong evidence either way yet.

lessons.explainSimpler: In-sample is the practice exam you studied from. Out-of-sample is a paper you have never seen. Walk-forward is sitting a new paper each term.
lessons.commonMistake: Peeking at the out-of-sample results, tweaking the rules, and testing again on the same data. After the first look, it is no longer out-of-sample.

quickCheck.prompt: Tune on 300 candles, test on the next 100, slide by 100. With 700 candles, how many test rounds?

options.explanation: No: the first 300 candles are only used for tuning.

quickCheck.prompt: Out-of-sample results are poor. You change one rule and test again on the same data. What is that data now?

options.text: Still out-of-sample, as before
options.explanation: No: the change was made after seeing it, so it has shaped the rules.

options.text: In-sample; get fresh data
options.explanation: Right: once results guide a change, that data is used up for testing.

options.text: Part of a walk-forward test
options.explanation: No: walk-forward tests each block once with rules tuned on earlier data.

quickCheck.prompt: In-sample: +0.4R per trade. Out-of-sample: +0.1R per trade. What is the most reasonable reading?

options.text: Some of the in-sample result was likely fitted to noise
options.explanation: Right: a drop is expected after tuning. The test shows how much.

options.text: The out-of-sample period was unlucky; trust in-sample
options.explanation: No: in-sample was used to choose the rules, so it flatters them.

options.text: The rules may need retuning on the out-of-sample data
options.explanation: No: tuning on the test data uses it up. You would then need fresh data to test again.

doItNow.instructions: Before opening Replay, write down 6 periods across different regimes and number them. Take 5 replay trades on each of periods 1–3 and adjust at most one rule. Save that plan version. Then take 5 trades on each of periods 4–6 with no changes at all. Compare the average R of the two halves in the Journal.

lessons.homework: Write three sentences: what changed between your in-sample and out-of-sample halves, what might explain it, and why 15 trades per half still cannot settle the question.

mtTasks.title: Add and remove indicators
mtTasks.summary: Add a [[moving-average]], Bollinger Bands, RSI, MACD and ATR to a demo chart, check their settings, then remove them.

steps.text: Check you are on your demo account before you start.
Open a EUR/USD candlestick chart on H1.
Open the indicators menu. It is often shown as an "f" icon at the top of the chart. It depends on your app version.
Choose to add an indicator to the main window, then pick Moving Average. Indicators are often grouped, for example under Trend. Set the period to 20 and the method to Simple, then add it.
Add Bollinger Bands to the main chart. Check the period is 20 and the deviation is 2.
Add RSI in a separate window below the chart. Check the period is 14. The app may let you show the 30 and 70 levels.
Add MACD in a separate window. Check the settings are 12, 26 and 9. Note how this app draws it: often the MACD line as bars and the signal as a line.
Add ATR in a separate window and check the period is 14. Read its value and convert it to pips: on EUR/USD, divide by 0.0001.
Scroll back through the chart. Find one place where the MA or MACD crossed late, after price had already moved a lot.
Remove each indicator. Open the indicators list, then tap or press and hold an indicator and choose delete (it depends on your app version).

afterQuestions.prompt: ATR 14 on your EUR/USD H1 chart shows 0.00110. What does that mean?

options.text: Price has moved about 11 pips per candle recently, in either direction
options.explanation: Right: ATR measures the size of moves, not their direction.

options.text: Price will rise 11 pips next hour
options.explanation: No: ATR has no direction and does not forecast.

afterQuestions.prompt: Why did the moving average cross come after price had already moved?

options.text: It is built from past closes, so it lags
options.explanation: Right: every average runs behind price.

options.text: Your app was slow to update
options.explanation: No: the lag comes from the maths, not the app.

mtTasks.title: Add 5 pairs to your quotes list
mtTasks.summary: Use the Quotes tab to add 3 majors, 1 minor and 1 exotic [[currency-pair]], and note each one's [[spread]].

steps.text: Open MetaTrader and go to the Quotes tab.
Tap the button to add a symbol, usually shown as a plus sign at the top of the Quotes tab.
Search for or browse to a major pair such as EUR/USD, then tap it to add it. Some brokers add extra letters to symbol names, for example a suffix after EURUSD.
Add two more majors, such as USD/JPY and GBP/USD.
Add one minor (cross) pair, such as EUR/GBP.
Add one exotic pair, such as USD/ZAR, if your broker offers it.
Go back to the Quotes tab and check all 5 pairs are listed.
For each pair, write down the bid and ask and work out the spread in pips.

afterQuestions.prompt: Of the pairs you added, which type usually shows the widest spread?

options.text: The exotic pair
options.explanation: Right: exotics usually trade less, so their spreads tend to be wider.

options.text: EUR/USD
