options.explanation: No: EUR/USD is among the most traded pairs and usually has one of the tightest spreads.

afterQuestions.prompt: You search for EURUSD and see a name like EURUSD with extra letters on the end. What does that most likely mean?

options.text: It is a different currency pair
options.explanation: No: it is still euro against US dollar. Check the symbol's details if unsure.

options.text: Your broker names its symbols with a suffix
options.explanation: Right: brokers can add letters to symbol names, often for different account types.

mtTasks.title: Open a chart and change its timeframe
mtTasks.summary: Open a EUR/USD [[candlestick]] chart and switch between M15, H1, H4 and D1 to see how the same prices look on each [[timeframe]].

steps.text: Check you are on your demo account before you start.
In the Quotes tab, tap EUR/USD and choose the option to open its chart. You can also open the Chart tab and pick the symbol there.
If the chart shows bars or a line, switch it to candlesticks. The chart type is usually in the chart settings or in a menu at the top of the chart. It depends on your app version.
Find the timeframe control. It is usually a label such as H1 at the top of the chart, or a round menu that appears when you tap the chart. It depends on your app version.
steps.mt4: In MT4, tapping the chart often shows a round menu with the timeframes around it.
steps.mt5: In MT5, the timeframe is often shown as a label or button at the top of the chart.

steps.text: Choose M15. Note roughly how many hours of price the screen shows.
Switch to H1, then H4, then D1. Each time, note whether the last part of the chart looks like it is rising, falling or moving sideways.
Pinch to zoom out on D1 to see more candles, then switch back to H1.
Write down one sentence for each timeframe describing what you saw.

afterQuestions.prompt: The last price was the same on every timeframe. Why did the charts look different?

options.text: Each candle covers a different length of time
options.explanation: Right: the same prices are grouped into bigger or smaller candles.

options.text: Each timeframe uses different prices
options.explanation: No: it is the same market, grouped differently.

afterQuestions.prompt: H4 looked like it was rising and M15 looked like it was falling. Which is right?

options.text: Both: they cover different windows of time
options.explanation: Right: a short fall can sit inside a longer rise.

options.text: H4, because it is longer
options.explanation: No: neither timeframe is the true one.

mtTasks.title: Read balance, equity and margin
mtTasks.summary: Find your [[balance]], [[equity]], [[margin]], [[free-margin|free margin]] and [[margin-level|margin level]] in the Trade tab, and watch them change with one small demo trade.

steps.text: Check you are on your demo account before you start.
Open the Trade tab. With no trades open, write down the balance, equity, margin and free margin. Margin level may be blank when nothing is open.
Go to the Quotes tab, tap EUR/USD and choose the option to trade.

On the order screen, set the volume to 0.01 and place a market buy. Leaving stop loss and take profit empty is for this short check only: you will close the trade a moment later. In your own practice, always set a stop loss.
Go back to the Trade tab. Write down the balance, equity, margin, free margin and margin level again.
Check: equity minus margin should equal free margin, and equity ÷ margin × 100 should match the margin level, allowing for prices moving while you read.
Tap or press and hold the open position (it depends on your app version), then choose the option to close it.
Read the balance once more. It now includes the result of the closed trade.

afterQuestions.prompt: While the trade was open, which number changed with every price tick?

options.text: Equity
options.explanation: Right: equity includes the open profit or loss, so it moves with price.

options.text: Balance
options.explanation: No: the balance only changes when a trade is closed or a charge is applied.

afterQuestions.prompt: What happened to free margin when you opened the trade?

options.text: It went up
options.explanation: No: opening a trade ties up margin, so less is free.

options.text: It went down by about the margin the trade used
options.explanation: Right: free margin = equity − used margin, so opening a trade reduces it.

mtTasks.title: Place, edit and close a demo trade with SL and TP
mtTasks.summary: Open a demo [[market-order]] with a [[stop-loss]] and [[take-profit]], move the stop, then close the trade and find it in your history.

steps.text: Check you are on your demo account before you start.
Before opening the app's order screen, decide on paper: buy or sell, the stop loss price, and the take profit price.
Go to the Quotes tab, tap EUR/USD and choose the option to trade.
Make sure the order type is a market order, not a pending order.
Set the volume to 0.01.
Enter your stop loss and take profit prices. For a buy, the stop goes below the price and the target above. For a sell, the other way round.
Tap buy or sell to place the order.
Open the Trade tab. Check the position shows your stop loss and take profit.
Tap or press and hold the position (it depends on your app version), then choose the option to modify it. Move the stop loss closer to the entry price and save.
Check the Trade tab shows the new stop loss.
Tap or press and hold the position (it depends on your app version), then choose the option to close it.
Open the History tab and find the closed trade. Note the open price, close price and result.

afterQuestions.prompt: If you placed a buy, which price on the Quotes tab would trigger your stop loss?

options.text: The bid
options.explanation: Right: a buy is closed by selling at the bid, so the bid triggers its stop and target.

options.text: The ask
options.explanation: No: the ask triggers the stop on a sell trade.

afterQuestions.prompt: Right after the order filled, the trade showed a small loss. Why?

options.text: The stop loss was hit
options.explanation: No: if the stop had been hit, the trade would have closed and moved to history.

options.text: The spread
options.explanation: Right: you opened at one side of the quote and would close at the other, so you start behind by the spread.

mtTasks.title: Save your demo account history as a statement
mtTasks.summary: Save your [[demo-account]] trade history from MetaTrader as an HTML report, then import it in the Journal. The export option and its name depend on your app version and platform.

steps.text: Check you are logged in to your demo account, not a real one. Only import demo statements.

On your phone, open the History tab and set the period so it covers your demo trades. Look for an option to save, share or export a report. It depends on your app version: many phone versions do not have one.
If your phone app cannot export the history, log in to the same demo account in the desktop MetaTrader terminal on a computer.
In the desktop terminal, open the history list in the bottom panel.
steps.mt4: Open the Terminal window and choose the Account History tab.
steps.mt5: Open the Toolbox window and choose the History tab.

steps.text: Right-click inside the history list and choose a period that covers all your demo trades.
Right-click again and look for the report option. The exact name depends on your version.
steps.mt4: It is usually called "Save as Report" or "Save as Detailed Report".
steps.mt5: It is usually called "Report", with a choice of formats.

steps.text: Choose HTML if you are offered a format. The Journal import reads HTML statements.
Save the file, then move it to your phone, for example by sending it to yourself. Keep it private: it shows your account number and history.
In TradeLab, open the Journal and choose the option to import an MT statement. Pick the file.
Check the preview: the number of closed trades and their prices should match your MetaTrader history. Trades already imported are skipped.
Confirm the import. Then open each imported trade, add a chart screenshot, and complete the review.

afterQuestions.prompt: Someone in a chat offers to export your statement for you if you send your MetaTrader login. What do you do?

options.text: Send it; it is only a demo account
options.explanation: No: never share MetaTrader logins. It builds a habit scammers rely on.

options.text: Refuse and export it yourself
options.explanation: Right: never share your login, demo or real.

afterQuestions.prompt: Your phone app has no option to save a report. What can you do?

options.text: Export it from the desktop terminal, or add your trades by hand with screenshots
options.explanation: Right: on some app versions the desktop terminal is the way to export.

options.text: Give up on journaling these trades
options.explanation: No: you can still log them by hand in the Journal.

mtTasks.title: Mark support and resistance with horizontal lines
mtTasks.summary: On a EUR/USD H4 chart, draw horizontal lines at two [[support]] and two [[resistance]] areas, then check how price reacts later.

steps.text: Check you are on your demo account before you start.
Open a EUR/USD candlestick chart and set the timeframe to H4.
Zoom out until you can see at least 100 candles. Look for places where price turned up more than once at about the same price (support) and turned down more than once (resistance).
Open the drawing tools. They are usually called objects, often shown as a shapes icon at the top of the chart. It depends on your app version.
steps.mt4: In MT4, look for an objects or shapes icon on the chart toolbar, then the option to add an object.
steps.mt5: In MT5, look for an objects or shapes icon on the chart toolbar, then choose from the list of objects.

steps.text: Choose the horizontal line. Place it at your first support area, then drag it to adjust. If the app places it in the middle of the screen, drag it into place.
Add a second support line and two resistance lines the same way. Four lines in total is enough.
For each line, write down its price and the dates of the turns it is based on.
Come back after a few days. For each line, note whether price reached it, and if so whether it turned, went sideways, or broke through.
To remove a line, tap or press and hold it (it depends on your app version), then choose delete. You can also delete objects from the objects list.

afterQuestions.prompt: Price reached one of your support lines and went straight through. What does that show?

options.text: Levels describe the past and can break
options.explanation: Right: support is a place to watch, not a wall.

options.text: The line was drawn wrong, so it would have held otherwise
options.explanation: No: even well-drawn levels break often.

afterQuestions.prompt: Why is a zone often better than one exact line?

options.text: Price rarely turns at exactly the same price twice
options.explanation: Right: wicks and the spread blur the edges, so a few pips of width is more honest.

options.text: Zones always hold, lines do not
options.explanation: No: zones can break too.

mtTasks.title: Open a demo account
mtTasks.summary: Install MetaTrader, open a [[demo-account]], and learn to tell a demo account from a real one before you practise.

steps.text: Install the MetaTrader app from the Play Store. Use whichever version your chosen broker supports.
steps.mt4: Search the Play Store for MetaTrader 4.
steps.mt5: Search the Play Store for MetaTrader 5.

steps.text: Open the app and go to its accounts screen. Choose the option to open a new demo account.
Pick a broker's demo server. If you are not sure which one, choose a broker you have checked is regulated where you live.
Fill in the demo form. A demo account never needs a deposit or card details. If you are asked for payment, stop: you are not opening a demo.
Write down the login number and password the app shows, and keep them private.
On the accounts screen, look for a label or server name that says the account is a demo. If you cannot tell, do not place any trades until you are sure.
Open the Quotes tab and check that prices are showing. Your demo account is ready.

afterQuestions.prompt: How much money did you need to deposit to open the demo account?

options.text: None
options.explanation: Right: a demo account uses pretend money, so no deposit is ever needed.

options.text: A small deposit to activate it
options.explanation: No: if a demo asks for a deposit, it is not a demo. Stop and check what you are signing up for.

afterQuestions.prompt: You open MetaTrader and are not sure whether the account is demo or real. What should you do?

options.text: Place a small trade and see what happens
options.explanation: No: on a real account even a small trade risks real money.

options.text: Check the accounts screen for the demo label before trading
options.explanation: Right: always confirm you are on demo before any practice trade.

mtTasks.title: Place and delete a pending order
mtTasks.summary: Place a buy [[limit-order|limit]] below the current price with a stop loss and take profit, find it in the Trade tab, then delete it.

steps.text: Check you are on your demo account before you start.
In the Quotes tab, note the current ask for EUR/USD.
Tap EUR/USD and choose the option to trade.
Change the order type from market to buy limit.
Set the volume to 0.01.
Enter a price about 50 pips below the current ask. If the app rejects it, check that the price is below the ask and not too close to it.
Enter a stop loss below your limit price and a take profit above it.
Place the order. Open the Trade tab and find it in the list of pending orders, separate from open positions.
Tap or press and hold the pending order (it depends on your app version), then choose the option to delete or cancel it.
Check the order has gone from the Trade tab.

afterQuestions.prompt: Why did your buy limit need a price below the current ask?

options.text: A buy limit aims to buy cheaper than now
options.explanation: Right: buy limits sit below the price; buy stops sit above it.

options.text: All pending orders must be below the price
options.explanation: No: sell limits and buy stops sit above the current price.

afterQuestions.prompt: While your pending order waited, did it show a profit or loss as an open trade?

options.text: Yes, it counted as an open trade
options.explanation: No: until it triggers there is no position, so there is no profit or loss yet.

options.text: No, nothing is open until it triggers
options.explanation: Right: a pending order only becomes a position if price reaches its level, so it has no profit or loss until then. Margin for pending orders is usually zero, but some brokers reserve some; check your broker's contract specification.

mtTasks.title: Read the bid, ask and spread
mtTasks.summary: Find the [[bid]] and [[ask]] for EUR/USD in the Quotes tab and work out the [[spread]] in [[pip|pips]].

steps.text: Open MetaTrader and go to the Quotes tab.
Find EUR/USD in the list. Each symbol shows two prices.
The lower price is the bid: where you can sell. The higher price is the ask: where you can buy.
Write both prices down at the same moment.
Subtract the bid from the ask. Divide by 0.0001 to get the spread in pips.
Do the same for USD/JPY, but divide by 0.01, because yen pairs use a different pip size.

afterQuestions.prompt: You see EUR/USD at 1.08452 and 1.08467. What is the spread?

options.text: 1.5 pips
15 pips
options.explanation: No: 0.00015 is 15 pipettes, which is 1.5 pips.

afterQuestions.prompt: Which of the two prices you saw would you get if you bought at market?

options.text: The lower one, the bid
options.explanation: No: the bid is where you sell.

options.text: The higher one, the ask
options.explanation: Right: buys fill at the ask.

psychScenarios.title: Only hearing one side
psychScenarios.situation: You have decided EUR/USD should rise and you are planning a demo buy. You read three posts that agree with you and skip one that argues the opposite. On the chart, price has just closed below the level your plan says would cancel the idea.
psychScenarios.question: What do you do next?

responses.text: Treat the idea as cancelled, as your plan says. Write down what would make you look at it again.
responses.explanation: You set this level in advance so you would not have to argue with yourself now. Acting on it keeps the plan honest.

responses.text: Ignore the break. The posts agree with you.
responses.explanation: Looking only for views that match yours is called confirmation bias. Here it is overriding the rule you set to protect you.

responses.text: Read the opposing post too, then decide.
responses.explanation: Hearing both sides is a good habit. But your plan already gave the answer, and opinions should not override it.

psychScenarios.takeaway: Decide in advance what would prove your idea wrong, and act on it when you see it.

psychScenarios.title: The trade you will not take
psychScenarios.situation: After two losing demo trades this week, you see a setup that meets every rule in your plan. Your [[stop-loss|stop loss]] and size are already worked out, and the risk is within your own limit. But your finger hovers over the button and you do not take it.
psychScenarios.question: What do you do?

responses.text: Skip it. It feels safer not to trade until you feel confident again.
responses.explanation: Skipping avoids a possible loss, but your results stop reflecting your plan. You also learn nothing about whether the plan works.

responses.text: Take it, but with a stop so tight that price can barely move.
responses.explanation: A stop placed out of fear, not where the setup needs it, is likely to be hit by normal price movement.

responses.text: Wait for extra confirmation beyond your rules, then enter late.
responses.explanation: Waiting longer changes your entry and your reward compared with your risk. You are no longer trading the plan you tested.

responses.text: Take the trade as planned. The risk is set, and a loss here is a cost you accepted in advance.
responses.explanation: Your plan already decided how much you can lose. Following it is how you find out whether the plan works.

psychScenarios.takeaway: When the risk is set in advance, following the plan matters more than how the trade feels.

psychScenarios.title: The move that left without you
psychScenarios.situation: You are practising on a [[demo-account|demo account]]. EUR/USD has risen 60 pips in the last hour without you. Your plan says to buy only on a pullback to a level you marked this morning, and price is nowhere near it. You feel you are missing out.
psychScenarios.question: What do you do next?

responses.text: Buy now at market before it goes any higher.
responses.explanation: This trade comes from the feeling, not from your plan. Chasing a move often means a worse entry and no clear place for your stop.

responses.text: Stay out, write the move in your journal, and keep waiting for your planned level.
responses.explanation: Your plan did its job: it kept you out of a trade it did not cover. Noting the move lets you review it calmly later.

responses.text: Buy a small size now, just to be in the trade.
responses.explanation: Smaller size limits the damage, but it is still a trade outside your plan. It also trains the habit of acting on the urge.

responses.text: Place a [[pending-order|pending order]] at the level your plan marked, with your usual [[stop-loss|stop loss]].
responses.explanation: This turns the plan into an order. If price comes back, you are in on your terms. If not, you missed nothing your plan wanted.

psychScenarios.takeaway: A move you missed is not a loss. The next trade only counts if it fits your plan.

psychScenarios.title: Just a little more
psychScenarios.situation: Your demo trade on USD/JPY is 45 pips in profit and close to your [[take-profit|take profit]] at 50 pips. It looks strong. You start imagining it running 150 pips and want to remove the target.
psychScenarios.question: What do you do next?

responses.text: Remove the take profit and the [[stop-loss|stop loss]] so nothing gets in the way.
responses.explanation: With no stop, nothing limits how much of the gain, or more, you can give back.

responses.text: Leave the target where your plan put it. If you want to test a different exit, write it down and try it on future trades.
responses.explanation: Exits chosen before the trade are part of what you are testing. A new idea can be tested properly, not on a feeling mid-trade.

responses.text: Close half at your target and let the rest run with the stop moved to your entry price.
responses.explanation: A plan can include this kind of exit on purpose. Decided mid-trade on a feeling, though, it is not your plan, and you cannot tell if it helps.

psychScenarios.takeaway: Exits are decided before the trade, when you are calm. Change them in review, not in the moment.

psychScenarios.title: The big green candle
psychScenarios.situation: You are scrolling through charts in the simulator when a big green candle appears on gold. Without checking your plan, you open the order ticket. You have not set a [[stop-loss|stop loss]] or worked out your size.
psychScenarios.question: What do you do next?

responses.text: Cancel the ticket and run your pre-trade checklist. If the setup passes, enter with a stop and a size you worked out.
responses.explanation: A short pause turns a sudden urge into a decision you can explain and review later.

responses.text: Enter now and add the stop later, once you see where price goes.
responses.explanation: Without a stop, the trade has no planned limit. "Later" often comes after price has already moved against you.

responses.text: Enter with your smallest [[lot]] size so it does not matter.
responses.explanation: Small size limits the damage, but it still rewards the habit of entering without a plan.

psychScenarios.takeaway: A short pause and a checklist turn a sudden urge into a decision you can review.

psychScenarios.title: Lock in the win, hope on the loss
psychScenarios.situation: You have two demo trades open. One is 30 pips in profit. The other is 35 pips down and close to its [[stop-loss|stop loss]]. You want to close the winner now to lock something in, and remove the stop on the loser so it has time to come back.
psychScenarios.question: What do you do?

responses.text: Close the winner and remove the stop on the loser.
responses.explanation: This is the pattern that leads to small wins and large losses. Without a stop, the losing trade has no limit.

responses.text: Close both trades now to end the discomfort.
responses.explanation: This does stop the risk. But it is a decision made to escape a feeling, not one from your plan, so it tells you little about the plan.

responses.text: Leave the winner, but move the stop on the loser a bit further away.
responses.explanation: Moving a stop further away makes the loss you agreed to bigger.

responses.text: Leave both trades with the stops and [[take-profit|targets]] you planned.
responses.explanation: Loss aversion means losses feel bigger than gains of the same size. Your planned levels were set before that feeling kicked in.

psychScenarios.takeaway: Losses feel bigger than equal gains. Planned stops and targets stop you acting on that feeling.

psychScenarios.title: Just give it more room
psychScenarios.situation: Your demo trade on EUR/GBP is 3 pips from your [[stop-loss|stop loss]], which you placed using the rule in your plan. You want to move the stop 20 pips further away "to give it room."
psychScenarios.question: What do you do?

responses.text: Move the stop further away. It will probably turn around.
responses.explanation: Moving the stop away makes the loss bigger than the one you planned. "Probably" is a hope, not a rule.

responses.text: Close the trade now, before the stop is hit.
responses.explanation: This keeps the loss within your plan. But it is still a decision made on a feeling, and it blurs what your stop rule would have done.

responses.text: Remove the stop and watch the trade closely instead.
responses.explanation: Watching is not a limit. If price moves fast, there is nothing to stop the loss growing.

responses.text: Leave the stop where it is. If it is hit, review later whether your stop rule needs work.
responses.explanation: The stop was set when you were calm. If the rule needs changing, a review is the place to do it.

psychScenarios.takeaway: A stop is a decision made when you were calm. Moving it further away means that if price gets there, you lose more than you planned.

psychScenarios.title: Six wins in a row
psychScenarios.situation: You have won 6 [[demo-account|demo]] trades in a row. You feel you have figured the market out. You are thinking of skipping your pre-trade checklist and risking three times your usual amount on the next trade.
psychScenarios.question: What do you do next?

responses.text: Go ahead. Six wins show the method works.
responses.explanation: Six trades is a very small sample, and a run of wins can happen by chance. Tripling risk makes the next loss three times as big.

responses.text: Use the bigger size, but still do the checklist.
responses.explanation: Keeping the checklist is good. Changing size because of a streak, rather than a planned rule, is still a reaction.

responses.text: Keep your usual size and checklist, and review the 6 trades to see whether each one followed your rules.
responses.explanation: This checks whether the wins came from your process or from luck. Your risk stays where you set it when calm.

psychScenarios.takeaway: A winning streak is a reason to check your process, not to loosen it.

psychScenarios.title: Five trades by lunchtime
psychScenarios.situation: Your trading plan allows up to 3 [[demo-account|demo]] trades a day. It is midday and you have already taken 5. The last three did not meet all your entry rules. You took them because the market was moving and you felt you should be doing something.
psychScenarios.question: What do you do next?

responses.text: Stop trading for the day and check all 5 trades against your rules in your journal.
responses.explanation: You have reached your own daily limit. Reviewing now shows which trades fit your plan and which came from restlessness.

responses.text: Keep going. More trades mean more chances to win.
responses.explanation: Every trade has costs, like the [[spread]]. Trades that do not meet your rules add risk and cost, not chances.

responses.text: Keep trading, but only take setups that meet every rule.
responses.explanation: Better than before, but you are already over your limit. The limit exists for days exactly like this one.

responses.text: Raise your daily limit to 8 so you are no longer breaking the rule.
responses.explanation: Changing a rule mid-session to fit what you already did removes its purpose. Rule changes belong in a calm review.

psychScenarios.takeaway: Trade count is not progress. A few trades that follow your rules beat many that do not.

psychScenarios.title: Five losses in a row
psychScenarios.situation: You have followed a written plan on your [[demo-account|demo account]] for six weeks. You followed your rules on every trade, but the last five were losses. When you backtested the plan earlier, it also had losing runs of five or more. You feel like quitting the plan.
psychScenarios.question: What do you do?

responses.text: Quit the plan and look for a new one.
responses.explanation: Any method has losing runs. Switching every time one happens means you never find out whether a plan works.

responses.text: Change several rules at once to stop the losses.
responses.explanation: With several changes at once, you cannot tell which one helped or hurt. Your earlier testing no longer applies.

responses.text: Compare this run with the losing runs in your backtest and journal. If it is within what you saw before and you followed your rules, carry on.
responses.explanation: This judges the plan on evidence, not on how the last five trades felt. You already saw runs like this when you tested it.

responses.text: Carry on, but cut your size in half for a while.
responses.explanation: Lowering risk is not dangerous, and a plan can include it on purpose. If yours does not, write it down as a rule first so it is not just a reaction.

psychScenarios.takeaway: A losing run your plan has shown before is normal. Judge the plan on many trades and on how well you followed it.

psychScenarios.title: Breakouts do not work anymore
psychScenarios.situation: Your last three breakout trades in the simulator all failed. Today a breakout setup appears that meets every rule in your plan. You think, "Breakouts do not work anymore," and want to drop the strategy.
psychScenarios.question: What do you do?

responses.text: Drop breakouts for good. The last three trades proved it.
responses.explanation: Three trades is far too few to judge a method. Recent results feel more important than they are.

responses.text: Take the trade as planned, then look at a bigger record, such as your journal or a backtest over many trades, before judging the strategy.
responses.explanation: A strategy is judged on many trades. A bigger record shows whether three losses in a row is unusual for it or normal.

responses.text: Trade the opposite way, expecting the breakout to fail.
responses.explanation: This is the same mistake turned around: a new idea built on just three trades, with no plan or testing behind it.

responses.text: Skip just this one and keep watching.
responses.explanation: It avoids a hasty change, but skipping valid setups makes your record less useful for judging the strategy.

psychScenarios.takeaway: The last few results feel like the whole story. Judge a method on many trades, not the latest ones.

psychScenarios.title: Winning it back
psychScenarios.situation: On your paper account, a GBP/USD trade just hit your [[stop-loss|stop loss]] for a loss of 40 USD. It was a planned trade with a planned stop. You feel angry and want to win the money back before the session ends.
psychScenarios.question: What do you do next?

responses.text: Open a new trade straight away in the opposite direction.
responses.explanation: This trade is driven by wanting to undo the loss, not by a setup in your plan.

responses.text: Take the next trade at double the size, so one win covers the loss.
responses.explanation: Raising size to recover a loss adds risk at the moment your judgement is under the most pressure. A second loss would be twice as big.

responses.text: Step away for a set time, then log the trade and check whether you followed your plan.
responses.explanation: A pause breaks the link between the loss and the next decision. If you followed your plan, the loss was a cost you already accepted.

responses.text: Stay at the screen and watch closely for the next setup.
responses.explanation: Watching is not trading, but staying glued to the chart while upset makes a rushed entry more likely.

psychScenarios.takeaway: A planned loss is part of trading. The next trade should come from your plan, not from wanting to get even.

psychScenarios.title: One big trade to get even
psychScenarios.situation: Your paper account started at 10,000 USD and is down 300 USD after four losses this week. Your own limit is to risk 50 USD per trade. You are tempted to risk 300 USD on the next trade to get back to even in one go.
psychScenarios.question: What do you do next?

responses.text: Risk 300 USD. One win and you are back to even.
responses.explanation: One loss at this size would double your drawdown. Raising size to recover losses risks the most when you are under the most pressure.

responses.text: Keep to your 50 USD limit, or less, and check whether the four losses followed your rules.
responses.explanation: Your limit was set when you were calm. Checking the losses tells you whether this is a process problem or a normal run of losses.

responses.text: Risk 100 USD as a middle ground.
responses.explanation: It is still raising size to win back losses, just more slowly. The limit you set does not change because of recent results.

responses.text: Stop trading for the rest of the week and review your journal.
responses.explanation: Pausing to review is a sound process step. Coming back with a clear head makes rule-following easier.

psychScenarios.takeaway: Raising size to win back losses makes the next loss bigger. Keep risk to the limit you set when calm.

psychScenarios.title: Too much work to stop now
psychScenarios.situation: You spent two weekends building a strategy and testing it on simulated practice charts. Over 100 simulated trades it lost money after costs like the [[spread]], and you cannot find a rule that clearly fixes it. You do not want to give up because of all the time you put in.
psychScenarios.question: What do you do next?

responses.text: Start trading it on your demo account anyway. You have invested too much to stop.
responses.explanation: The time you spent is gone whichever way you choose. Continuing because of it is called the sunk cost trap.

responses.text: Keep changing rules until the backtest shows a profit.
responses.explanation: Changing rules until past results look good can produce a strategy that only fits that one set of data.

responses.text: Write down what you learned from the test, set the strategy aside, and start from a fresh idea.
responses.explanation: The test gave you a clear answer, which is useful. Your notes keep the lessons even though the strategy did not work.

responses.text: Leave it for a month and look at it again then.
responses.explanation: Some distance can help you think clearly, but it does not change what the test showed.

psychScenarios.takeaway: Time already spent is gone either way. Decide based on what the evidence shows now.

companies.name: Example Faxworth Office Machines (fictional)
companies.summary: A fictional maker of an old type of office machine. Revenue falls every year, profit is shrinking faster, and the dividend was cut. It looks cheap on P/E, and may be cheap for a reason.
companies.assumptions: All figures are fictional and in millions of USD, except the share price. The same tax rate (25% of pre-tax profit), tax rules and accounting apply to every company. No one-off items, share issues or buybacks. Ratios use Year 3 and the current share price. Simulated for learning; not a real firm.
notes: Revenue fell from 500 to 370 million in two years as customers move to newer products. Net income fell by more than half.
The P/E of 5 uses Year 3 earnings. If earnings keep falling, next year's P/E at the same price would be higher, so the low number may not stay low.
The dividend was cut from 30 to 10 million. A high dividend yield based on past payments can disappear.
Debt of 150 million stays the same while profit shrinks, so the interest bill takes a bigger share of operating profit each year.

companies.name: Example Gadgetmoor Wholesale Co (fictional)
companies.summary: A fictional wholesaler whose reported profit rises every year, while the cash coming in from operations shrinks almost to zero. Profit and cash are telling different stories.
companies.assumptions: All figures are fictional and in millions of USD, except the share price. The same tax rate (25% of pre-tax profit), tax rules and accounting apply to every company. No one-off items, share issues or buybacks. Ratios use Year 3 and the current share price. Simulated for learning; not a real firm.
notes: Net income grew from 39 to 52.5 million, but operating cash flow fell from 38 to 2 million. Profit that does not turn into cash is a warning sign worth investigating.
Possible reasons, as hypotheses only: customers taking longer to pay, unsold stock piling up, or generous accounting choices. The figures alone do not say which.
Free cash flow turned negative in Year 3 and debt rose to cover the gap.
Questions for management: why is cash lagging profit, and when do they expect it to catch up?

companies.name: Example Quickling Apps Co (fictional)
companies.summary: A fictional app maker growing revenue about 50% a year. Margins are thin, free cash flow is negative, and growth is partly paid for with new debt. The share price is high compared with its earnings.
companies.assumptions: All figures are fictional and in millions of USD, except the share price. The same tax rate (25% of pre-tax profit), tax rules and accounting apply to every company. No one-off items, share issues or buybacks. Ratios use Year 3 and the current share price. Simulated for learning; not a real firm.
notes: Fast revenue growth, but operating expenses grew even faster in Year 3 (+56% vs +50%), so the operating margin slipped from 10% to under 9%.
Spending on equipment and software (capital expenditure) is bigger than the cash the business brings in, so free cash flow is negative and debt has doubled in two years.
The high P/E means buyers are paying today for profits the company has not made yet. If growth slows, the price has a long way to fall even if the business is fine.
Competitive position unclear: other fictional app makers could copy its product, and customers may switch easily.

companies.name: Example Steadybrook Pantry Foods (fictional)
companies.summary: A fictional food maker with slow, steady growth of about 2% a year. It turns most of its profit into cash, pays out roughly three quarters of its profit as dividends, and trades on a low P/E.
companies.assumptions: All figures are fictional and in millions of USD, except the share price. The same tax rate (25% of pre-tax profit), tax rules and accounting apply to every company. No one-off items, share issues or buybacks. Ratios use Year 3 and the current share price. Simulated for learning; not a real firm.
notes: Operating cash flow is higher than net income every year, and free cash flow comfortably covers the dividend.
Return on capital of about 21% suggests the business earns well on the money tied up in it, under these fictional figures.
Slow growth: the low P/E may reflect that buyers expect little growth. A high payout leaves less to reinvest.
Risk to watch: a cheaper rival or a change in what shoppers want could squeeze the steady margin.

redFlagCases.title: Shrinking slices: dilution on repeat

facts.label: Price
facts.value: 0.09 USD (simulated), after a 1-for-15 reverse split last quarter

facts.label: Shares outstanding
facts.value: Adjusted for the 1-for-20 split: 50 million three years ago → 180 million → 600 million before the latest 1-for-15 split (40 million after it)

facts.label: Recent reverse splits
facts.value: 1-for-20 two years ago; 1-for-15 last quarter

facts.label: Revenue trend
facts.value: Small and flat: about 0.4 million USD a year for three years

facts.label: Cash
facts.value: Enough for about 4 months at the current rate of spending, according to its latest report

facts.label: Financing
facts.value: Loans that convert into new shares at a discount to the market price

facts.label: Average daily volume
facts.value: About 300,000 shares

facts.label: Filings and disclosures
facts.value: Filed on time; reports describe one product in early testing

facts.label: Promotion activity
facts.value: None found

redFlagCases.question: Which of these are warning signs?

signs.text: The split-adjusted share count went from 50 million to 600 million in three years.
signs.explanation: That is 12 times as many shares. Someone who owned 1% of the split-adjusted shares (500,000) at the start would own about 0.083% before the latest split, unless they kept buying.

signs.text: Two reverse splits in two years.
signs.explanation: One reverse split proves little. Repeated ones, each after heavy dilution, suggest a cycle of issuing shares, the price sinking, and the split resetting it.

signs.text: Cash covers only about 4 months of spending.
signs.explanation: With little revenue, the company will likely need to raise more money soon, and recent history suggests that means more new shares.

signs.text: Loans convert into shares at a discount to the market price.
signs.explanation: Lenders can receive shares cheaply and sell them, which can push the price down and add more dilution. Worth reading the terms closely.

signs.text: Reports are filed on time.
signs.explanation: A good sign for transparency. The problem here is not hidden information but what the information shows.

signs.text: There is no sign of paid promotion.
signs.explanation: Also a good sign. Not every struggling small company is a pump and dump; some are real businesses running out of money.

signs.text: The company is working on a product in early testing.
signs.explanation: Not a warning sign. Many small companies are early-stage. But an early product does not pay today's bills.

investigate: Read the terms of the convertible loans: the discount, any limits, and how many shares could be created.
Check how many new shares the company is allowed to issue without asking shareholders.
Work out the cash runway yourself from the latest report: cash divided by monthly spending.
List every share issue and reverse split over the last few years, with dates.
Ask what has to go right for existing shareholders to benefit, given the likely future dilution.
redFlagCases.verdict: This company looks open about its situation, with no promotion and on-time filings, but the situation itself is the risk: repeated dilution, repeated reverse splits, a short cash runway and discounted convertible loans. Even if the product succeeds, existing holders may own a much smaller slice by then. For a learner, staying out is the sensible decision until the financing problem is clearly solved.

redFlagCases.title: The hot tip with no business behind it

facts.label: Price
facts.value: 0.62 USD, up from 0.08 USD three weeks ago (simulated)

facts.label: Average daily volume
facts.value: About 9 million shares in the last two weeks, up from about 50,000 before

facts.label: Spread
facts.value: Bid 0.58 / ask 0.62

facts.label: Revenue trend
facts.value: No revenue in any of the last three reported years

facts.label: Shares outstanding
facts.value: 300 million → 420 million over the last year

facts.label: Where it trades
facts.value: Over the counter

facts.label: Filings and disclosures
facts.value: Latest annual report is two months late; no official filing about any new deal

facts.label: Promotion activity
facts.value: Newsletters and social posts calling it 'the next big lithium play' with a 10x target. Small print: writers were paid by a shareholder

facts.label: Insider selling
facts.value: A director has filed to sell 15 million shares during the last two weeks

redFlagCases.question: Which of these are warning signs?

signs.text: The price rose about 675% in three weeks with no official company news.
signs.explanation: (0.62 − 0.08) ÷ 0.08 = 6.75, so +675%. A move that size with no filing to explain it often means buying is being driven by hype, not by the business.

signs.text: The promotion was paid for by a shareholder.
signs.explanation: Someone who owns shares and pays for hype may want to sell into the buying it creates. That is the classic pump-and-dump setup.

signs.text: The company has no revenue but is promoted as 'the next big' play.
signs.explanation: Big claims with no business results behind them are a warning sign. Promises are not revenue.

signs.text: A director is selling a large block during the promotion.
signs.explanation: Insiders selling while outsiders are being urged to buy is one of the strongest warning signs.

signs.text: The annual report is late and there is no filing about the 'deal'.
signs.explanation: Missing or late official information means the claims cannot be checked, and the excitement rests on rumours.

signs.text: The share trades over the counter.
signs.explanation: Not a red flag on its own: many OTC shares are not scams. It does mean reporting may be lighter, so you have to check more for yourself.

signs.text: The company has a professional website and a CEO interview video.
signs.explanation: Not a warning sign, but not evidence of anything good either. A polished website costs little and proves nothing about the business.

signs.text: The spread is about 6% of the ask (0.04 ÷ 0.62).
signs.explanation: Wide, and a real cost, but not unusual for a small share and not a sign of fraud. It matters more for whether you could trade at a sensible cost.

investigate: Read the company's official filings: is there any record of the deal, any revenue, and how much cash is left?
Check your regulator's investor alerts and any trading suspensions for this company.
Find out who paid for the promotion and how much, from the disclosure in the small print.
Look at insider and large-holder filings: who has been selling, and when?
Compare the share count over time: 300 million to 420 million is a 40% increase in one year.
redFlagCases.verdict: Several strong red flags together: an unexplained spike, paid promotion, no revenue, insider selling during the hype, and late filings. This is the pattern of a possible pump and dump. Staying out is the best decision here. There is nothing to analyse that could justify the price, and late buyers in this pattern often find the bid disappears when the promotion stops.

redFlagCases.question: You are thinking of buying 20,000 shares. Which of these are warning signs?

signs.text: Revenue has grown slowly and the company makes a small profit.
signs.explanation: A steady, profitable business is not a warning sign. 8.0 to 8.6 is +7.5%, and 8.6 to 9.1 is about +5.8%.

signs.text: The share count has not changed in three years.
signs.explanation: No dilution: a good sign. Your slice of the company is not being shrunk.

signs.text: Audited reports are filed on time and there is no promotion.
signs.explanation: Good signs of an honest business. Not every small share is a scam.

signs.text: Your 20,000-share order is more than 3 days of normal volume.
signs.explanation: 20,000 ÷ 6,000 ≈ 3.3 days. Buying and later selling that much could move the price against you and take days. This is a liquidity warning, not a fraud warning.

signs.text: The spread is about 10.5% of the ask (0.20 ÷ 1.90).
signs.explanation: You start roughly 10% behind. The share must rise from 1.70 to 1.90 bid just to break even on a round trip.

signs.text: Insiders hold about 60%, so the float is only about 4.8 million shares.
signs.explanation: 12 million × 40% = 4.8 million tradable shares. A small float can make the price jumpy. It is a risk to manage, not evidence of wrongdoing.

investigate: Look at the order book: how many shares are bid near the price, not just the best price?
Work out a size you could sell within a day or two at normal volume.
Read the audited reports: cash, debt and whether profits turn into cash.
Check whether the family's holding is locked up or could come to market, and how that might affect the price.
redFlagCases.verdict: Not every small stock is a scam, and nothing here suggests fraud. The real risk is liquidity: a wide spread, low daily volume and a small float. The question is not 'is this honest?' but 'can I get out?'. A 20,000-share position is too big for this market. Staying out is sensible if you cannot accept a slow, costly exit. If you still want exposure, go much smaller, use limit orders, and plan your exit before you enter.

marketScenarios.title: A bigger crude draw than expected (fictional)
marketScenarios.setup: Fictional Northland publishes a weekly report on crude oil held in storage. This week forecasters expected a small draw. The report shows a much bigger draw. In the same report, stocks of refined fuel rose more than expected. All countries, reports and figures are fictional.
marketScenarios.pricedIn: Over the three days before the report, the simulated crude price had already risen, as several private estimates pointed to a large draw. Many traders were already positioned for a tight number.
marketScenarios.question: Surprise = −4.2 − (−1.5) = −2.7 million barrels, a much bigger draw than expected. Which reactions are plausible?

reactions.text: Price rises and holds for the rest of the day.
reactions.explanation: A big draw hints at tighter supply. If traders weigh that most, the rise can hold.

reactions.text: Price jumps, then gives back the move within the hour.
reactions.explanation: Much of the draw was expected by private estimates and priced in. Traders who bought early may sell into the jump, and the rise in fuel stocks points the other way.

reactions.text: Price barely moves because the fuel build offsets the crude draw.
reactions.explanation: Reports have several parts. If traders focus on the fuel build as a sign of weaker fuel demand, the two can cancel out.

reactions.text: Price must rise all week, because a bigger draw always means higher prices.
reactions.explanation: No reaction is certain. A draw is a tendency towards higher prices, not a rule, and later news can take over.

reactions.text: Price falls because a draw shows nobody wants oil.
reactions.explanation: This reasoning is wrong: a draw means more was used than added. Price could still fall, but for other reasons, such as it being priced in, not because of this one.

marketScenarios.takeaway: The same big draw can lead to a lasting rise, a quick reversal or almost nothing, depending on what was priced in and on the other parts of the report. Work out the surprise, then list the scenarios. Never treat one as certain.

marketScenarios.title: An outage at a gas field in winter (fictional)
marketScenarios.setup: Fernmoor Energy (fictional) runs the Kestrel Basin gas field (fictional), which supplies about 8% of a fictional region's natural gas. On a cold winter morning it announces an unplanned shutdown after equipment damage. Its first statement says repairs should take 'around two weeks'. All firms, places and figures are fictional.
marketScenarios.pricedIn: Gas in storage in the region is above its usual level for this time of year, after a mild autumn. Weather forecasts call for a normal winter, not an unusually cold one. The market was calm before the news.
marketScenarios.question: How might the simulated regional gas price react?

reactions.text: A sharp jump on the news, then a partial fall back as storage is seen to cover the gap.
reactions.explanation: Sudden supply losses often bring a first jump. Full storage and a short expected outage can cool it once traders do the sums.

reactions.text: A steady rise over several days as the repair is delayed and a cold spell arrives.
reactions.explanation: If the outage lasts longer than first said and demand rises, the cushion shrinks. The size and length of a disruption matter as much as the headline.

reactions.text: Only a small move, because ample storage and normal weather make 8% manageable.
reactions.explanation: With high stored stock, losing 8% of supply for two weeks may not change the picture much.

reactions.text: The price doubles and stays there until spring.
reactions.explanation: Nothing in the setup supports a certain, extreme, lasting move. Storage is high and the outage is expected to be short. Treat certain-sounding calls with suspicion.

marketScenarios.takeaway: A supply shock's effect depends on how big it is, how long it lasts, how much is in storage and what the weather does. The first jump is a reaction to uncertainty; what follows depends on new information. Think in scenarios, not certainties.

marketScenarios.title: A bigger harvest estimate than expected (fictional)
marketScenarios.setup: A fictional agriculture office in fictional Westmark publishes its harvest estimate for a grain. The estimate comes in above what forecasters expected and above last year. At the same time, a fictional neighbouring region is in a dry spell, and its crop is still in the fields. All places, offices and figures are fictional.
marketScenarios.pricedIn: Good weather all summer had led many traders to expect a large crop, and the simulated grain price had drifted lower for weeks. Some private estimates were even higher than the official consensus.
marketScenarios.question: Surprise = 126.0 − 120.0 = +6.0 million tonnes, a bigger crop than expected. Which reactions are plausible?

reactions.text: Price falls, as more supply is coming than expected.
reactions.explanation: A bigger crop is more supply. That tends to weigh on price, as a tendency only.

reactions.text: Price hardly moves, or even rises, because the big crop was already priced in.
reactions.explanation: The price had already fallen for weeks and some estimates were higher still. Traders who sold early may buy back after the report.

reactions.text: Price rises because the dry spell next door takes over the story.
reactions.explanation: Supply is about the whole market. Worry about the neighbouring crop could outweigh good news at home.

reactions.text: Price must fall exactly 5%, since the crop is 5% above the consensus.
reactions.explanation: 6.0 ÷ 120.0 = 5%, but price does not move one-for-one with a surprise. There is no fixed formula for the reaction.

marketScenarios.takeaway: A bigger-than-expected harvest points to more supply, but what was priced in and what is happening elsewhere can lead to very different reactions. Seasonal reports are scenarios, not forecasts.

marketScenarios.title: Westmark's budget (fictional): a bigger deficit than expected
marketScenarios.setup: The fictional Westmark government announces next year's budget, with higher spending and tax cuts. Its planned deficit is larger than forecasters expected. At the same time, the central bank is trying to bring 3.4% inflation back to its 2% target. All figures are made up; this is a practice scenario, not a forecast.
marketScenarios.pricedIn: Partly. Some extra spending had been widely expected, so a deficit close to last year's was in prices. The size of the tax cuts was not expected.
marketScenarios.question: The planned deficit is 4.5% of GDP against a 3.0% consensus, a +1.5-point surprise. Which reactions are plausible?

reactions.text: WMK rises, as traders expect the central bank to keep rates higher for longer to offset the extra spending.
reactions.explanation: Plausible: [[fiscal-policy]] that adds to demand can push [[monetary-policy]] to stay tighter.

reactions.text: WMK falls, as lenders worry about faster-rising debt and ask for more interest.
reactions.explanation: Plausible: a sharp rise in [[government-debt]] can worry lenders and investors in the currency.

reactions.text: WMK swings both ways during the day as traders weigh the two stories.
reactions.explanation: Plausible: when two forces clash, the price can move back and forth before settling.

reactions.text: Westmark shares and index futures rise on hopes that tax cuts boost growth.
reactions.explanation: Plausible: tax cuts can lift growth hopes, though higher rates could weigh on them later.

reactions.text: Nothing moves, because a budget only matters once the money is spent.
reactions.explanation: Not plausible: markets react to plans and expectations, not only to money already spent.

marketScenarios.takeaway: Fiscal news can pull a currency two ways at once: through what the central bank may do, and through worries about debt. List both chains before deciding which you think matters more, and expect to be wrong sometimes.

marketScenarios.title: Westmark growth (fictional) misses, but last quarter is revised up
marketScenarios.setup: Fictional Westmark publishes its quarterly [[gdp|GDP]] estimate. The headline growth figure is below the consensus, but the same report revises the previous quarter up from 0.6% to 0.9%. Inflation is above the central bank's target. All figures are made up; this is a practice scenario, not a forecast.
marketScenarios.pricedIn: Moderate. Recent jobs data had been strong and traders expected solid growth. Their bets implied rates staying high for some time. Over the two quarters together, growth of 0.9% then 0.2% is about the same as the 0.6% then 0.5% expected before the revision.
marketScenarios.question: Growth comes in at 0.2% against a 0.5% consensus, a −0.3-point surprise, while the previous quarter is revised up by 0.3 points. Which reactions are plausible?

reactions.text: WMK dips on the headline miss, then recovers as traders notice the revision.
reactions.explanation: Plausible: fast reactions often follow the headline; slower ones take in the whole report.

reactions.text: WMK falls and stays lower as traders expect rates to be cut sooner.
reactions.explanation: Plausible: if traders focus on the latest quarter's slowdown, rate expectations can shift down.

reactions.text: Little net change, since growth over two quarters is about as expected.
reactions.explanation: Plausible: the miss and the revision roughly cancel out over the two quarters.

reactions.text: WMK must fall sharply, because revisions never matter to markets.
reactions.explanation: Not plausible: revisions change the picture of the economy and can matter a lot.

marketScenarios.takeaway: A headline miss is not the whole story. Read revisions and the full report, and remember that growth is read alongside jobs and inflation.

marketScenarios.title: Westmark inflation (fictional) beats forecasts: a calm market
marketScenarios.setup: Fictional Westmark publishes its monthly [[inflation]] figure. The [[central-bank]] targets 2%. Over the past month WMK has moved sideways, and the economic calendar showed no other big release that day. All figures are made up; this is a practice scenario, not a forecast.
marketScenarios.pricedIn: Little. Most traders expected the central bank to hold its [[interest-rate]] at the next meeting, and few had bet on a high inflation number. WMK had been flat going into the release.
marketScenarios.question: Inflation comes in at 3.4% against a 3.0% consensus, a +0.4-point surprise. Which reactions are plausible?

reactions.text: WMK rises and holds as traders start to expect a rate rise.
reactions.explanation: Plausible: little was priced in, so a higher-than-expected number can shift rate expectations and the currency with them.

reactions.text: WMK rises at first, then gives some back as traders read the rest of the report.
reactions.explanation: Plausible: other parts of a report, such as which prices drove the rise, can soften the first reaction.

reactions.text: WMK hardly moves because a bigger story elsewhere dominates the day.
reactions.explanation: Plausible: a release can be outweighed by other news or by the general mood in markets.

reactions.text: WMK is certain to rise by a fixed amount for every 0.1 points of surprise.
reactions.explanation: Not plausible: there is no fixed exchange rate between surprise and price. Reactions vary from day to day.

reactions.text: WMK cannot move until the central bank actually meets.
reactions.explanation: Not plausible: prices move on what traders expect the bank to do, long before it meets.

marketScenarios.takeaway: With little priced in, a surprise has more room to move the price. But even then, several reactions are plausible. Compare this with the crowded version of the same release.

marketScenarios.title: Westmark inflation (fictional) beats forecasts: a crowded market
marketScenarios.setup: The same fictional Westmark [[inflation]] release, with exactly the same numbers as the calm scenario. The difference is the run-up: WMK has risen steadily for three weeks while commentary focused on a high inflation number. All figures are made up; this is a practice scenario, not a forecast.
marketScenarios.pricedIn: A lot. Many traders had already bought WMK in the hope of a high number, and their bets already implied a good chance of a rate rise at the next meeting. Some expected an even higher figure than the 3.0% consensus.
marketScenarios.question: Inflation comes in at 3.4% against a 3.0% consensus, the same +0.4-point surprise. Which reactions are plausible?

reactions.text: WMK spikes, then falls back as early buyers take profit.
reactions.explanation: Plausible: when a move is crowded, good news can be the moment people who bought early choose to sell.

reactions.text: WMK rises further, because 3.4% was above even what most buyers had hoped for.
reactions.explanation: Plausible: if positioning was for a smaller beat, the number can still add to the move.

reactions.text: WMK falls straight away, because some traders had bet on an even higher figure.
reactions.explanation: Plausible: against what some traders expected, 3.4% may feel like a disappointment.

reactions.text: WMK must rise and hold, because that is one plausible outcome in the calm scenario.
reactions.explanation: Not plausible as a rule: the number is the same, but what was priced in is not, so the reaction can differ.

reactions.text: Nobody will sell WMK today, because the number beat the consensus.
reactions.explanation: Not plausible: there are always sellers, and profit-taking after a crowded run-up is common.

marketScenarios.takeaway: Same release, same surprise, different setup. When much is priced in, the reaction can be small, short-lived, or even the 'wrong' way. Always ask what the market was set up for, not only what the number was.

cells.forex: Needs a broker; leverage limits and product rules differ by country, and some brokers are unregulated.
cells.stocks: Needs a broker with access to the exchange; account minimums and fees vary.
cells.penny_stocks: Some brokers limit or block trading in them; some venues have extra rules and warnings.
cells.commodities: Product choice depends on the broker and country; some routes need larger accounts.
cells.futures: Often needs an approved account; one contract can be large compared with a small account.

marketComparison.caveat: Access depends on your country, the regulator, the broker and the account type. Check that any broker is properly regulated where you live before opening an account.

cells.forex: Studied approaches include trend following, range trading and trading around news, each with its own risks.
cells.stocks: Long-term investing, swing trading and value or growth approaches are widely studied.
cells.penny_stocks: Often the best-tested decision is to stay out; strategies here face high costs and manipulation risk.
cells.commodities: Trend following, spread trading and supply-and-demand analysis are commonly studied.
cells.futures: Trend following, spread trading such as [[calendar-spread|calendar spreads]], and hedging are commonly studied.

marketComparison.caveat: These are approaches people study, not recommendations. No strategy works in every market or period; test any idea on simulated or historical data first.

cells.forex: Prices, an [[economic-calendar]], interest-rate and inflation news for both currencies, and your broker's spreads and swaps.
cells.stocks: Prices and volume, company reports and filings, and the market's general mood.
cells.penny_stocks: Filings, share count changes, trading volume and any promotion activity, and whether information is reliable at all.
cells.commodities: Supply and demand news, inventories, the futures curve, and the currency it is priced in.
cells.futures: The contract specification, margin levels, the futures curve and the underlying market's own data.

marketComparison.caveat: What is available, how reliable it is and whether it costs money depends on the market, the venue and the provider. Check the source of any data you use.

cells.forex: Commonly offered through margin; maximum [[leverage]] is set by the broker and often capped by the regulator.
cells.stocks: Not needed when you pay in full; some accounts allow borrowing, which adds leverage and risk.
cells.penny_stocks: Borrowing to buy is often restricted or unavailable; even without it, price swings can be large.
cells.commodities: Often leveraged through futures or broker contracts; funds may have little or none.
cells.futures: Built in: the margin is a small part of the [[notional-value]], so leverage is usually high.

marketComparison.caveat: Limits depend on the jurisdiction, the regulator, the broker, the account type and the product, and can change. Higher allowed leverage is not a reason to use it.

cells.forex: Major pairs are often heavily traded, but [[liquidity]] can thin out in quiet hours, on holidays and around big news.
cells.stocks: Large, well-known companies are often heavily traded; smaller ones can be thin.
cells.penny_stocks: Often thin: little trading one day, a sudden rush the next, and it can be hard to sell.
cells.commodities: Varies widely between commodities, products and times of day.
cells.futures: Often concentrated in one or two contract months; far-dated months can be thin.

marketComparison.caveat: No market is always liquid. Liquidity depends on the instrument, the time, the venue and current conditions, and it can vanish in a fast market.

cells.forex: Leverage, gaps around news and weekends, widening spreads, and broker-related risks.
cells.stocks: Company-specific falls, gaps on news, and the share losing most of its value.
cells.penny_stocks: Thin trading, wide spreads, dilution, promotions and manipulation, halts, and being unable to sell.
cells.commodities: Leverage, supply shocks, roll costs and sudden gaps.
cells.futures: Leverage, [[gap|gaps]], margin calls and forced liquidation; losses can exceed the margin.

marketComparison.caveat: Risks differ by product, broker and jurisdiction as well as by market. Every market can lose money, and past calm is not a guarantee.

cells.forex: A deposit per trade set by the broker; falling too low can bring a [[margin-call]] and a [[stop-out]].
cells.stocks: None if you pay in full; a borrowing account has margin rules of its own.
cells.penny_stocks: Usually paid in full; many brokers restrict borrowing against these shares.
cells.commodities: Depends on the route: futures margin, broker contract margin, or full payment for a fund.
cells.futures: [[initial-margin|Initial]] and [[maintenance-margin|maintenance]] margin per contract, with daily [[mark-to-market]] settlement.

marketComparison.caveat: Margin rules are set by exchanges, brokers and regulators and can be raised at short notice. In every market, required margin is a deposit, not the most you can lose.

cells.forex: Buy or sell a pair in [[lot|lots]]; profit or loss is counted in [[pip|pips]] times [[pip-value]].
cells.stocks: Buy shares and later sell them; short selling, where allowed, has its own rules and costs.
cells.penny_stocks: Like shares, but orders can fill slowly or only in part, and the price you see may not be available in size.
cells.commodities: Usually through a futures contract or broker contract, with that product's own sizing and rules.
cells.futures: Buy or sell whole contracts; profit or loss is ticks moved × [[tick-value]] × contracts, settled daily.

marketComparison.caveat: Order types, sizes, fills and settlement depend on the venue and broker. Learn the exact product's rules before practising.

cells.forex: At a retail broker you usually hold a contract on the rate, not the currencies themselves.
cells.stocks: Bought with your own cash, a share is part-ownership of the company; borrowing to buy changes the risk.
cells.penny_stocks: Also part-ownership, but small companies can issue many new shares, shrinking each holder's slice.
cells.commodities: Most practice-level routes are contracts or funds; owning the physical goods is a different business with storage costs.
cells.futures: A contract to buy or sell later, held on [[margin]]; nothing is owned until settlement, if ever.

marketComparison.caveat: Product type decides this, not the market name. A broker's contract on a share is not the same as owning the share, so read what the product actually is.

cells.forex: Many brokers offer near round-the-clock trading on weekdays, but activity rises and falls with each [[trading-session]].
cells.stocks: Set by each exchange, often a fixed day session; some offer limited trading before and after it.
cells.penny_stocks: Follow the venue they trade on; trading in an individual stock can also be halted.
cells.commodities: Depends on the product; futures hours are set by the exchange, broker contracts by the broker.
cells.futures: Set by the exchange for each contract, often with daily breaks; activity often shifts to the next month near expiry.

marketComparison.caveat: Hours differ by exchange, broker, product and time zone, and change around holidays. Check the exact schedule; a market can be open yet thin.

cells.forex: Mainly the [[spread]], sometimes a commission, plus [[swap|overnight swaps]] on positions held past the daily cut-off.
cells.stocks: Spread and commission, which vary by broker; holding with your own cash has no financing charge.
cells.penny_stocks: Spreads can be a large share of the price, so getting in and out can cost a lot before price moves.
cells.commodities: Spread and commission, plus storage-related costs built into the product, such as roll costs in futures.
cells.futures: Commission and exchange fees per contract, the spread, and the cost of rolling to a later month.

marketComparison.caveat: Costs depend on the broker, account type, product, size, time of day and conditions. Measure them on a demo or in the simulator at the times you would trade.

cells.forex: Often modest day to day for major pairs, but releases and policy surprises can bring sharp moves.
cells.stocks: Varies by company and sector; company news such as earnings can move a share a lot in one day.
cells.penny_stocks: Can be extreme: large daily swings, sudden spikes and falls, and gaps.
cells.commodities: Can be high; supply news, inventories and weather-type events can move prices quickly.
cells.futures: Follows the underlying, but leverage makes each move large compared with the margin.

marketComparison.caveat: [[volatility|Volatility]] changes over time and with conditions. A calm period says little about the next one, and leverage turns a small move into a big result.

cells.forex: Exchange rates between two currencies, quoted as a [[currency-pair]].
cells.stocks: [[share|Shares]] in companies, usually listed on a stock exchange.
cells.penny_stocks: Shares in very small companies with a low price per share, often thinly traded, sometimes outside the main exchanges.
cells.commodities: Raw materials such as metals, energy and farm goods, reached through futures, broker contracts or funds.
cells.futures: Standardised contracts on an underlying such as an index, a currency, a rate or a [[commodity]], each with its own specification.

marketComparison.caveat: What exactly you can trade depends on the broker, the exchange and where you live. The same market name can cover very different products.

labConcepts.title: Balance sheet, debt and net debt
labConcepts.summary: The balance sheet is a one-day snapshot of cash, debt and equity. Net debt = debt − cash. Compare debt with operating profit to see how heavy it is.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: When a single day's cash is unusually high or low, when debt is due soon but the balance sheet does not show when, or when you judge debt by its size without comparing it with profit.
labConcepts.goodExample: A fictional food maker holds more cash than debt, so it has net cash and its operating profit covers interest many times.
labConcepts.badExample: A fictional office-machine maker keeps the same debt while its operating profit halves, so interest takes twice the share of profit.

labConcepts.title: Business quality and competitive position
labConcepts.summary: How the company makes money, what protects it from rivals, and what could go wrong, including how managers use the company's money. Figures are clues; the reasons need explaining.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: When past margins are treated as a promise, when a strong brand or product is assumed to last for ever, or when a good business is treated as a reason to pay any price.
labConcepts.goodExample: A fictional food maker's margins hold steady while it pays dividends from free cash flow, a clue that something protects the business for now.
labConcepts.badExample: A fictional app maker with thin margins and rising debt: a 5% price cut forced by a rival would wipe out almost all its profit before tax.

labConcepts.title: Cash flow vs profit
labConcepts.summary: Operating cash flow is the cash the business actually collected. Free cash flow = operating cash flow − capital expenditure. Over time, cash should roughly follow profit.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: In a single year, when a big order or a delayed payment shifts cash between years, or for a young company investing heavily on purpose.
labConcepts.goodExample: A fictional food maker's operating cash flow is above its net income every year, and free cash flow covers its dividend.
labConcepts.badExample: A fictional wholesaler reports rising profit while its operating cash flow falls almost to zero and it borrows to fill the gap.

labConcepts.title: Commodity supply and demand scenarios
labConcepts.summary: Work through fictional inventory reports, supply disruptions and harvest estimates. Compare the actual with the expected, note what was already priced in, and list several plausible reactions instead of one prediction.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: Supply and demand explain tendencies, not exact moves. Reactions can be swamped by other news, by positioning, by currency and rate moves, or by details in the same report. A report may also be revised later.
labConcepts.goodExample: Working out that a draw was 2.7 million barrels bigger than expected, then noting that private estimates had already priced much of it in, and writing three possible reactions with a reason for each.
labConcepts.badExample: Seeing 'big draw' in a headline and assuming the price must rise all week, without checking the consensus, the rest of the report, or what the market had already expected.

labConcepts.title: Income statement: from revenue to EPS
labConcepts.summary: Revenue minus cost of sales gives gross profit; minus operating expenses gives operating profit; minus interest and tax gives net income. Divide by the number of shares for EPS.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: When one-off gains or costs distort a single year, when accounting choices record sales before cash is collected, or when you read one year without the trend.
labConcepts.goodExample: A fictional food maker grows revenue 2% a year and net income grows at about the same pace, so its margins hold steady.
labConcepts.badExample: A fictional app maker grows revenue 50% in a year, but net income grows only 20% because costs and interest grow almost as fast.

labConcepts.title: Employment and growth
labConcepts.summary: [[gdp|GDP]] growth and the [[employment-report]] show how strongly an economy is running. Read together with [[inflation]], they shape what traders expect a central bank to do next.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: When early figures are later revised, when parts of a report disagree (for example jobs added vs. the unemployment rate), or when one noisy month is read as a trend.
labConcepts.goodExample: A learner reads fictional Westmark's GDP, jobs and inflation together, notes that all three point the same way, and writes two plausible reactions with a reason for each.
labConcepts.badExample: A learner reacts to a single weak GDP headline without noticing that the previous quarter was revised up, so growth over two quarters was about as expected.

labConcepts.title: Policy and government debt
labConcepts.summary: [[monetary-policy|Monetary policy]] (the central bank's rates) and [[fiscal-policy|fiscal policy]] (the government's spending and taxes) both affect growth and inflation. Deficits add to [[government-debt]], and higher rates make that debt more costly.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: When the two policies pull in opposite directions, when the reaction depends on how lenders feel about the debt that day, or when one debt figure is treated as a fixed danger line. There is no single level at which debt becomes a problem.
labConcepts.goodExample: A learner reads fictional Westmark's bigger-than-expected deficit and lists two chains: the central bank keeping rates high (WMK up) and debt worries (WMK down). They plan for either.
labConcepts.badExample: A learner assumes a bigger deficit must sink the currency, ignoring that the central bank may respond with higher rates.

labConcepts.title: Rates and inflation
labConcepts.summary: A [[central-bank]] usually raises its [[interest-rate]] when [[inflation]] runs above its target and cuts when the economy is weak. Markets trade on the expected path of rates, so currencies and other markets often move before the decision, not on it.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: When the rate change was fully expected, when the bank's guidance about future moves says something different from the decision, or when other news such as risk mood or the other currency in a pair dominates.
labConcepts.goodExample: Fictional Westmark inflation comes in well above target and few traders expected it. Traders raise their rate expectations, and WMK rises and holds. The chain held this time, but it was a tendency, not a guarantee.
labConcepts.badExample: A learner sees inflation above consensus and buys WMK expecting a sure rise, but traders had already bought heavily before the release. WMK spikes, then falls back below where it started.

labConcepts.title: Surprises vs. expectations
labConcepts.summary: The [[surprise]] is actual minus [[consensus-forecast]], but the reaction also depends on what was already [[priced-in|priced in]] and how traders were positioned. The same number can bring different reactions on different days.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: When positioning is unclear, when the consensus is not what traders really expected, when other parts of a report matter more than the headline, or when a bigger story dominates.
labConcepts.goodExample: A learner compares the calm and crowded fictional Westmark inflation scenarios: same +0.4 surprise, different run-ups. They write a different most-plausible reaction for each and one outcome that would prove them wrong.
labConcepts.badExample: A learner decides 'better than expected means up' and ignores a three-week run-up in which many traders had already bought. The price falls on the news.

labConcepts.title: Margins and return on capital
labConcepts.summary: Margins show how much of each dollar of revenue becomes profit. Return on capital = operating profit ÷ (debt + equity) shows how well all the money tied up in the business is used.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: When margins are compared across very different industries, when one unusual year flatters the figures, or when return on equity looks high only because of heavy borrowing.
labConcepts.goodExample: A fictional food maker keeps its operating margin near 15% and its return on capital near 21% for three years.
labConcepts.badExample: A fictional office-machine maker's operating margin falls from 16% to under 11% and its return on capital drops to about 7%.

labConcepts.title: Penny stock red flags
labConcepts.summary: Read a fictional small-company profile (price, volume, spread, revenue, share count, filings, promotion, insider selling) and sort the warning signs from the signs that are not. Then decide what to investigate, and whether staying out is the best decision.
