labConcepts.unreliableWhen: A checklist cannot prove fraud or prove honesty. Information on small companies can be thin, late or wrong, and a share with few red flags can still be very hard to sell. When you cannot get enough reliable information to check, treat that itself as a reason to stay out.
labConcepts.goodExample: Noticing that a share up 675% in three weeks has no revenue, a paid promotion and a director selling during the hype, and deciding to stay out and check the official filings and regulator alerts first.
labConcepts.badExample: Deciding a share is safe because it has a professional website and an exciting story, without checking revenue, share count, filings or who is paying for the promotion.

labConcepts.title: Valuation and P/E
labConcepts.summary: P/E = price ÷ EPS. Earnings yield = EPS ÷ price. Dividend yield and payout ratio show how much profit comes back as cash. A good business can be a poor investment at a high price.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: When earnings are zero or negative, when one year's profit is unusual, or when a low P/E reflects a business that is shrinking.
labConcepts.goodExample: A fictional food maker on a P/E near 12 with steady profit: the price assumes little growth, so modest results do not need to surprise anyone.
labConcepts.badExample: A fictional app maker on a P/E of 80: even fast growth may leave the price looking high, and if growth slows the price has a long way to fall.

labConcepts.title: Volatility: ATR and Bollinger Bands
labConcepts.summary: ATR shows how far price has typically moved per candle. Bollinger Bands widen when price has been jumpy and squeeze when it has been calm. Neither shows direction.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: Both describe the past, so they can be low just before a sudden news move. A band touch is not "too high", since price can ride a band in a trend. A squeeze can break either way, or not at all.
labConcepts.goodExample: Seeing ATR 14 at 12 pips and widening a 5-pip stop, then reducing the size to keep the same money at risk.
labConcepts.badExample: Selling every touch of the upper band in a strong uptrend.

chart.lookFor: Compare ATR 14 and the band width at the start and end of the chart. Then open Low volatility and look for a squeeze.

labConcepts.title: Breakouts
labConcepts.summary: A breakout is price moving out through a support or resistance zone. Decide in advance what counts, for example a close a set distance beyond the zone.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: Many breakouts fail and come back inside. Around news, fills can be worse than planned. Without a written rule, any wick looks like a breakout afterwards.
labConcepts.goodExample: Rule: a close at least 5 pips above the zone. A candle closes 8 pips above, so it counts. You still place a stop.
labConcepts.badExample: Calling a wick through the line a breakout, then changing the rule so the chart fits.

chart.lookFor: Mark the range with the Zone tool. Find the first candle that closed beyond it by your written distance. Note how far price went before its first pullback.

labConcepts.title: Candlesticks, OHLC and timeframes
labConcepts.summary: Each candle shows the open, high, low and close of one period. The timeframe sets how long that period is, from minutes to a day.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: A single candle's shape says little on its own. Very short timeframes are full of noise, and a candle that has not closed yet can still change completely.
labConcepts.goodExample: Reading a candle as "opened at 1.1000, dipped to 1.0980, closed near its high at 1.1030" and saying which timeframe it is on.
labConcepts.badExample: Calling one long green candle a buy signal, or judging a candle before it has closed.

chart.lookFor: Long-press a few candles to read their open, high, low and close. Find one with a long lower wick and say what happened inside that period. Then switch timeframe and notice that each candle now covers a different length of time.

labConcepts.title: Channels
labConcepts.summary: A channel is a trend whose swings have stayed between two roughly parallel sloping lines.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: The lines depend on which swing points you pick, and are easy to redraw to fit. Price can overshoot or fall short of a line, and the slope can change.
labConcepts.goodExample: Joining two swing highs in a downtrend, drawing a parallel line through the low between them, and writing a rule for what counts as a break.
labConcepts.badExample: Redrawing the channel after every candle so price always "respects" it.

chart.lookFor: Use the Trend line tool to join two swing highs, then draw a parallel line through the lowest low between them. Count the closes outside your lines.

labConcepts.title: Failed breakouts
labConcepts.summary: A failed breakout moves through a level, then comes back inside. You only know it failed afterwards.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: Waiting for more confirmation avoids some failures but enters later, at a worse price, and still gets caught by some. Judging after the fact makes failures look obvious.
labConcepts.goodExample: Committing to "real", "fake" or "wait" before seeing more candles, then recording how each call turned out.
labConcepts.badExample: Deciding a breakout was "obviously fake" only after seeing what happened next.

chart.lookFor: Mark the range, find the candle that closed outside it, and note how many candles passed before price was back inside.

labConcepts.title: Fibonacci retracements
labConcepts.summary: Lines at 23.6%, 38.2%, 50%, 61.8% and 78.6% of a chosen swing. A convention some traders watch for describing how deep a pullback went.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: Always as a forecast: the levels depend on the anchor points chosen, and with five levels close together, many pullbacks end near one by chance. They show no predictive power on their own.
labConcepts.goodExample: Writing the anchor rule first, drawing from the swing low to the swing high, and noting "the pullback ended near the 50% line" as a description.
labConcepts.badExample: Redrawing on different swings until a level matches a turn, then calling it proof.

chart.lookFor: Use the Fibonacci tool from the low to the high of the last swing up. Note which level the pullback ended nearest, then redraw from a different low and see the lines move.

labConcepts.title: Gaps
labConcepts.summary: A gap is a jump in price with no trading in between, such as from one session's close to the next open, or after sudden news.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: Gaps do not have to "fill", and there is no rule for when. A stop inside a gap fills at the first available price, which can be far worse than planned.
labConcepts.goodExample: Planning size so that a gap through the stop would still be survivable.
labConcepts.badExample: Holding a trade into a weekend expecting the stop to cap the loss exactly.

chart.lookFor: Find the candle where price jumped. Compare its range with ATR 14 before the jump, and see how long ATR took to catch up.

labConcepts.title: Support, resistance and consolidation
labConcepts.summary: Support and resistance are zones where price has turned before. A consolidation is a sideways box between them, often after a bigger move.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: Levels are zones, not exact lines, and every chart shows some level if you look hard enough. A box drawn after the fact always looks neat. Price can leave a consolidation either way.
labConcepts.goodExample: Drawing a zone through three earlier turns at 1.0848–1.0855 and noting the box is about 2 ATR tall.
labConcepts.badExample: Drawing a new line at every wick until the chart is full of lines, or expecting a level to hold because it held before.

chart.lookFor: Use the Zone tool to mark the top and bottom of the range where price turned at least twice. Compare the box height with ATR 14 in the lower pane.

labConcepts.title: Look-ahead and survivorship bias
labConcepts.summary: Look-ahead bias uses information that was not available at the time. Survivorship bias studies only what survived, such as methods you heard worked.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: Both make a test look better than real trading could be, and both are easy to miss on a finished chart.
labConcepts.goodExample: Deciding only on closed bars in Replay, and treating a method you heard about as an idea to test, not as proof.
labConcepts.badExample: Drawing support with a low that formed after your planned entry, then counting the trade as a win.

labConcepts.title: MACD
labConcepts.summary: MACD is the gap between a fast and a slow moving average of price, with a signal line and a histogram. It describes momentum, and it lags.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: In sideways markets, the lines cross back and forth. After a sudden move, MACD reacts late because it is built from averages.
labConcepts.goodExample: Reading a rising histogram as "the fast average is pulling away from the slow one".
labConcepts.badExample: Taking every signal-line cross as an entry in a choppy market.

chart.lookFor: Count how many times the MACD line crosses its signal line. Then open Strong uptrend and compare.

labConcepts.title: Market regime classification
labConcepts.summary: Label each period trending or ranging, and high or low volatility, with a written rule. The same method behaves differently in each regime.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: The label uses past candles, so it lags, and regimes change without warning. The thresholds are your choice; changing them moves periods between labels.
labConcepts.goodExample: Splitting backtest results by regime and finding a crossover rule did well only in trends and lost small amounts in ranges.
labConcepts.badExample: Leaving the losing ranging periods out of a test because "the rule is not meant for those".

chart.lookFor: Measure the net move over the last 20 candles in ATR terms and give the chart a label. Count how often price crossed the SMA 20. Then compare with Strong uptrend and High volatility.

labConcepts.title: Moving averages
labConcepts.summary: A moving average smooths recent closes into one line. Its slope summarises direction, and it always lags price.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: In sideways markets, price crosses a flat average again and again, so crossover rules flip back and forth. After sharp turns, the average reacts late.
labConcepts.goodExample: Price stays above a rising EMA 50 through a trend, with the SMA 20 above it.
labConcepts.badExample: Buying every time price crosses above the SMA 20 in a sideways market, and paying costs on each flip.

chart.lookFor: Watch the slope of both averages and how far behind price they turn. Then open Sideways and count how often price crosses the SMA 20.

labConcepts.title: Multi-timeframe analysis
labConcepts.summary: Use a higher timeframe for the bigger picture and a lower one for detail. Choose them before you look.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: Timeframes often disagree, and flicking between them until one agrees is cherry-picking. Two timeframes agreeing are two views of the same prices, not two confirmations.
labConcepts.goodExample: Daily uptrend, 1-hour dip: "a pullback inside the daily uptrend so far", with the stop distance taken from the timeframe written in the plan.
labConcepts.badExample: Switching from 1h to 15m to 4h until a chart matches the trade you already wanted.

chart.lookFor: Zoom out to name the trend of the whole chart, then zoom in on the last 20 candles and name what they show. Write one sentence true of both.

labConcepts.title: Pullbacks and reversals
labConcepts.summary: A pullback moves against the trend but keeps its structure. A reversal breaks the structure and builds a new one in the opposite direction.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: At the time, the two look the same. A broken structure can repair itself. On a higher timeframe, a reversal may be just a pullback.
labConcepts.goodExample: Uptrend with a last higher low at 4,580. Price dips to 4,620 and stays above it: "pullback so far".
labConcepts.badExample: Calling every dip "the top", or calling a clear break below the last higher low "just a pullback" because you hold a trade.

chart.lookFor: Mark the last higher low before the dip. Watch whether the dip stays above it. Then open the Reversal scenario and find the candle that broke the structure.

labConcepts.title: Relative strength
labConcepts.summary: Relative strength compares one market with another, or with an index, as a ratio of prices. A rising ratio means the first did better over that window.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: Results depend on the start date chosen, leadership changes without warning, and markets with very different volatility are hard to compare. The first market can fall while showing relative strength.
labConcepts.goodExample: Stock A up 10% while its index is up 5%: the ratio rose about 4.8% over that window.
labConcepts.badExample: Reading a rising ratio as "A is going up", or confusing relative strength with RSI.

labConcepts.title: Risk-to-reward planning
labConcepts.summary: Before entering, set the stop where the idea is wrong and a target, then compare the distances. A 2:1 plan risks 1 to aim for 2.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: A planned ratio says nothing about how often the target is reached. Targets placed far beyond any recent move, or stops squeezed to make the ratio look good, distort the plan.
labConcepts.goodExample: Stop below the swing low 30 pips away, target at the next resistance 60 pips away: 2:1, decided before entry.
labConcepts.badExample: Moving the stop closer to make a 3:1 ratio, inside normal candle movement.

chart.lookFor: Mark an entry after the pullback, a stop below the swing low and a target at the earlier high. Measure both distances and compare the stop with ATR 14.

labConcepts.title: RSI
labConcepts.summary: RSI scores recent up moves against recent down moves on a 0 to 100 scale. High readings mean recent up moves were bigger, not that a fall is due.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: In strong trends, RSI can stay above 70 or below 30 for many candles while price keeps going. Divergence can last a long time.
labConcepts.goodExample: Reading RSI 75 as "up moves have been about three times the down moves lately".
labConcepts.badExample: Selling because RSI is above 70 during a strong uptrend.

chart.lookFor: Find a stretch where RSI 14 stays above 70 while price keeps rising, and count the candles. Then try Crash for the same below 30.

labConcepts.title: Return statistics, indicator correlation and parameter sensitivity
labConcepts.summary: Describe a test by its whole spread of results, treat indicators built from the same prices as one input, and check that nearby settings give similar results.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: With few trades, every statistic is very uncertain. Low parameter sensitivity does not prove an edge; it only shows the result does not hinge on one number.
labConcepts.goodExample: Reporting average +0.2R alongside a median of −1R, and noting that removing the best trade turns the total negative.
labConcepts.badExample: Counting RSI and MACD agreeing as two confirmations, or publishing the one average length that worked best.

chart.lookFor: Note the candles where RSI 14 turns. Switch the lower pane to MACD and check whether it turns at about the same places.

labConcepts.title: Trends: higher highs and higher lows
labConcepts.summary: An uptrend makes higher swing highs and higher swing lows; a downtrend makes lower highs and lower lows. Anything else is sideways or unclear.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: In choppy, sideways markets, the swings overlap and the label flips back and forth. A trend describes the past and can stop at any time.
labConcepts.goodExample: Marking swing lows at 1.0950, 1.0985 and 1.1010 with rising highs between them, and calling it an uptrend so far.
labConcepts.badExample: Calling a trend from two candles, or from one big move without any swings to compare.

chart.lookFor: Mark the last four swing lows and swing highs. Check that each is higher than the one before, and that the SMA 20 slopes up. Then try the Downtrend scenario.

labConcepts.title: Volatility-adjusted position sizing
labConcepts.summary: Set the stop from the market's movement, such as 2 × ATR, then size = money at risk ÷ (stop distance × value per unit). The loss at the stop stays the same.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: ATR describes the past and can be low just before a jump. Gaps and slippage can push a loss past the stop. Some markets cannot be sized small enough, so the answer is to skip.
labConcepts.goodExample: Two stocks at 40.00: ATR 0.80 gives 62 shares and ATR 2.00 gives 25 shares, both risking about 100 USD.
labConcepts.badExample: Keeping the same size when ATR doubles, so the loss at the stop doubles too.

chart.lookFor: Read ATR 14 at the start and end of the chart. Work out a 2 × ATR stop and the size for the same money at risk at each point.

labConcepts.title: Volume
labConcepts.summary: Volume shows how much traded in each candle. Compare each bar with its recent average to see whether a move had more or less participation than usual.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: Heavy volume does not show direction or what happens next. Volume jumps at opens, closes and news. On forex, platforms show tick volume from one broker, not the whole market.
labConcepts.goodExample: Noting that a breakout candle traded about 2.5 times the 20-candle average, and still treating the breakout as unproven.
labConcepts.badExample: Calling a breakout "confirmed" because volume was high, or reading forex tick volume as total market trading.

chart.lookFor: Find the breakout candle and compare its volume bar with the 10 bars before it. Then open False breakout: did the failed move also have a tall bar?

labConcepts.title: Walk-forward and out-of-sample testing
labConcepts.summary: Tune rules on one block of data, then test them unchanged on data they have not seen. Walk-forward testing repeats this step by step through time.
labConcepts.unreliableWhen: Once a rule is changed because of out-of-sample results, that data is in-sample. The test blocks are still the past and still a small sample.
labConcepts.goodExample: Tuning on periods 1–3, saving the plan version, and testing it unchanged on periods 4–6.
labConcepts.badExample: Looking at the out-of-sample results, tweaking the rules, and testing again on the same data.

strategies.title: Breakout with volume confirmation

overview.objective: Join a breakout only when unusually heavy trading comes with it.
overview.context: Daily charts of liquid shares, where volume is reported centrally. Not suited to thinly traded penny stocks.

simple.simple: A close above recent highs counts only if [[volume]] that day is well above normal. If price closes back below the breakout level soon after, get out.
simple.balanced: Heavy volume shows that more shares changed hands, not who bought or why. It filters out some quiet breaks, but [[false-breakout|false breakouts]] still happen on high volume, and the filter also skips some breaks that would have worked. Volume in forex is broker-specific, so this version is for shares.

strategies.reasoning: If a break above resistance attracts much more trading than usual, more participants may have changed their view at that price, which could make the move more likely to hold than a quiet break. That is the reasoning; it is not evidence, and the effect, if any, varies by market and period.

rules.label: A simplified educational version, not any trader's system
rules: Use a daily chart. The breakout level is the highest high of the previous 20 days.
Enter on a close above that level, but only if that day's volume is at least 1.5 × the 20-day average volume.
Place the stop 1 × ATR below the breakout level.
If price closes back below the breakout level within 3 days, exit.
Size the position so the loss at the stop is no more than 1% of the account.

demo.lookFor: Compare volume on the breakout candle with the candles before it. Then open the False breakout scenario and check whether the failed break also had high volume.

replay.instructions: Replay the Breakout scenario with the volume pane on. Before each entry, write down the 20-day average volume and the breakout day's volume, and skip any break below 1.5 ×.

exercise.prompt: Which statements are true under the simplified rules? Pick all that apply.
exercise.situation: A fictional share, daily chart (simulated). The previous 20 days' high is 48.20 and the 20-day average volume is 300,000 shares. Today closes at 48.90 on volume of 510,000 shares. ATR is 1.10.

options.text: The volume filter passes
The close is above the breakout level
options.explanation: Right: 48.90 is above 48.20.

options.text: The stop goes at 47.10
The breakout would also pass the filter on 420,000 shares
options.explanation: No: the filter needs at least 1.5 × 300,000 = 450,000 shares.

options.text: The stop goes at 48.20, the breakout level
options.explanation: No: the rules put the stop one ATR below the breakout level.

failureAnalysis: Breakouts on heavy volume still fail, sometimes sharply.
Volume often jumps on news days, when gaps make fills worse than the chart level.
The filter skips some quiet breaks that turn into long moves.
Exiting on a close back below the level means many quick small losses.
limitations: The 1.5 × and 3-day settings are examples for learning, not tested values.
Volume shows how much traded, not who traded or why.
No claim is made that adding a volume filter improves results.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: The 20-day average volume is 400,000 shares. The breakout day trades 520,000. Does it pass the 1.5 × filter?

options.text: Yes, it is higher
options.explanation: No: higher than average is not enough; it needs 1.5 times the average.

options.text: No: it needs 1.5 × 400,000 = 600,000, and 520,000 is below that
options.explanation: Right: 520,000 is below 600,000.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: What does heavy volume on a breakout day show?

options.text: More shares traded
options.explanation: Right: that is all it measures.

options.text: That large buyers are in and the move will continue
options.explanation: No: volume does not show who traded or what comes next.

options.text: That the break is confirmed, so a false breakout is no longer possible
options.explanation: No: false breakouts happen on heavy volume too.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Two days after entry, price closes back below the breakout level. What do the rules say?

options.text: Hold on
options.explanation: No: the rules exit on a close back below the level within 3 days.

options.text: Exit: the break has failed
options.explanation: Right: a close back below the level within 3 days is the exit.

options.text: Buy more, because the price is now lower than where you entered
options.explanation: No: adding to a failed break increases the loss the rules are designed to cut.

strategies.title: Carry (concept)

overview.objective: Earn the interest-rate difference between two currencies by holding the higher-rate one.
overview.holdingPeriod: Months, because the interest builds up night by night.
overview.context: A concept page. Carry depends on central-bank rates and broker swap terms, which change.

simple.simple: Hold a currency that pays a higher interest rate against one that pays less. Each night you hold it, your broker pays or charges a [[swap]]. That is the [[carry-trade|carry]].
simple.balanced: The interest is small and arrives slowly; price moves are large and arrive quickly. If the higher-yielding currency falls, months of swaps can be lost in days. Swaps include the broker's markup and can turn negative when [[interest-rate|rates]] change.

strategies.reasoning: If the higher-yielding currency does not fall by more than the interest gained, holding it earns the difference. That is the reasoning. Nothing guarantees the currency holds its value, and the swap you actually receive is set by your broker.

exercise.prompt: Which statements are true for this fictional position? Pick all that apply.
exercise.situation: A fictional pair (simulated). You are long 20,000 units of a higher-rate currency. The swap is +1.10 USD per night after the broker's markup. You hold for 60 nights, and price falls 45 pips. At this size, 1 pip is worth 2 USD.

options.text: The interest earned is 66 USD
options.explanation: Right: 60 × 1.10 = 66 USD.

options.text: The price loss is 90 USD
options.explanation: Right: 45 pips × 2 USD = 90 USD.

options.text: The net result is −24 USD
options.explanation: Right: 66 − 90 = −24 USD.

options.text: Holding 20 more nights at the same price would turn the result positive
options.explanation: No: 80 × 1.10 = 88 USD, still below the 90 USD price loss, so the result would be −2 USD.

options.text: Swaps are the same at every broker
options.explanation: No: each broker sets its own swap, including its markup.

failureAnalysis: The higher-yielding currency falls by more than the interest earned.
Central banks change rates, and the swap shrinks or turns negative.
Many holders may sell at once when markets are stressed, giving sharp losses.
Leverage turns a small price fall into a large loss of the account.
limitations: This page explains the idea; it gives no rules to trade it.
Swap rates in examples are invented. Real ones change and differ by broker.
No claim is made that carry has made or will make money.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Long 10,000 units with a swap of +0.80 USD per night. After 30 nights, price has fallen 60 pips, with 1 pip worth 1 USD. What is the net result?

options.text: −36 USD
options.explanation: Right: swaps 30 × 0.80 = 24 USD; price −60 USD; 24 − 60 = −36 USD.

options.text: +24 USD, the swaps earned
options.explanation: No: that ignores the price loss.

options.text: −60 USD, since swaps are not paid while the position is losing
options.explanation: No: swaps are paid regardless of the price move.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: What mainly sets the swap you receive?

options.text: The chart pattern
options.explanation: No: chart patterns do not set swaps.

options.text: The two interest rates and the broker's markup
options.explanation: Right: the rate difference, less what the broker keeps.

options.text: The direction the price has trended over the past month of trading
options.explanation: No: the swap does not depend on recent price direction.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Why do carry positions tend to suffer when markets are stressed?

options.text: Brokers stop paying swaps until markets calm
options.explanation: No: swaps carry on being paid or charged during stress.

options.text: Central banks freeze rates during the stress
options.explanation: No: central banks can change rates in a crisis, but a freeze is not why carry suffers.

options.text: Many holders sell the higher-yielding currency at once
options.explanation: Right: when many sell together, price losses can outweigh months of interest in days.

strategies.title: Channel breakout

overview.objective: Enter when price closes beyond its recent range, and ride the move if it becomes a trend.
overview.holdingPeriod: Weeks to months for winners; failed breaks are usually closed within days.
overview.context: Daily charts of liquid markets. Needs room for many small losses, because most breaks fall back.

simple.simple: Mark the highest high and lowest low of the last 20 candles. A close above the top is a long signal; a close below a shorter 15-candle channel is the exit.
simple.balanced: Most [[breakout|breakouts]] fail and fall back inside the [[channel]], so the rule relies on the occasional break that becomes a long move. A shorter lookback gives more, earlier signals and more [[false-breakout|false breakouts]]. The exit channel always gives back part of a gain before it triggers.

strategies.reasoning: When price escapes a range it has held for weeks, something may have changed in supply and demand. A rule that joins every such escape, and leaves quickly when it fails, could catch the few that run far. This is the reasoning, not evidence; results depend on the market, the lookback and costs.

rules.label: A simplified educational version; not presented as any trader's documented rules
rules: Use a daily chart. The entry channel is the highest high and lowest low of the previous 20 candles, not counting the current one.
Go long on a close above the 20-candle high; go short on a close below the 20-candle low.
Exit a long on a close below the previous 15-candle low (a short on a close above the 15-candle high). That level is also the initial stop.
The order fills at the next candle's open, because the signal is only known once the candle has closed.
Size the position so the loss at the stop is no more than 1% of the account.

demo.lookFor: Turn on Channel 20 and mark each close beyond the channel. Then switch to the False breakout scenario and count how many breaks fell back inside within 5 candles.

replay.instructions: Replay the False breakout scenario with Channel 20 on. Enter only on closes beyond the channel and exit on the 15-candle channel. Record each trade in R, including the ones that fail quickly.

exercise.prompt: Which statements are true under the simplified rules? Pick all that apply.
exercise.situation: A fictional commodity priced in USD, daily chart (simulated). The previous 20 candles have a high of 152.40 and a low of 148.10. The previous 15 candles' low is 150.20. Today closes at 152.65, and tomorrow opens at 152.70.

options.text: Today's close is a long signal
options.explanation: Right: 152.65 is a close above the 20-candle high of 152.40.

options.text: From a fill at 152.70, the stop at the 15-candle low is 2.50 away
A candle that reached 152.50 but closed at 152.30 would also have been a signal
options.explanation: No: the rules use closes. A close at 152.30 is inside the channel.

options.text: If tomorrow opened at 152.90 instead, the stop would still be 2.50 away
options.explanation: No: the stop stays at 150.20, so from a fill at 152.90 it is 2.70 away.

failureAnalysis: Most breaks fall back inside the channel, giving a run of small losses.
Gaps through the channel or the exit level give worse fills than the line suggests.
The exit channel gives back part of every winning move before it triggers.
Choosing the lookback that did best on past data usually flatters the result.
limitations: The 20 and 15 candle settings are examples for learning, not tested values.
No claim is made that these rules make money; that depends on the market, period and costs.
Simulated charts in TradeLab show behaviour, not the history of any real market.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: The previous 20 candles' high is 1.0950. A candle reaches 1.0965 but closes at 1.0948. What do the rules say?

options.text: Long: the high broke out
options.explanation: No: the rules use closes, not highs.

options.text: No signal: the close is inside the channel
options.explanation: Right: 1.0948 is below 1.0950.

options.text: Long, because any trade above the channel high counts as a breakout signal
options.explanation: No: only a close above the channel high counts.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Why does the exit use a shorter channel than the entry?

options.text: To win more often
options.explanation: No: the aim is a faster exit, not a higher win rate.

options.text: Shorter channels never give false signals
options.explanation: No: shorter channels give more false signals, not fewer.

options.text: It gets out sooner when a move turns, at the cost of being shaken out of some trends by ordinary dips
options.explanation: Right: a shorter-lookback low sits closer to price, so the exit gives back less, but normal pullbacks reach it more often.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Compared with a long lookback, a short lookback usually gives…

options.text: More signals and more false breaks
options.explanation: Right: a narrower channel is broken more often, and more of those breaks fail.

options.text: Fewer signals, all of them later and more reliable
options.explanation: No: that describes a longer lookback, and later does not mean more reliable.

options.text: The same trades, only shown on a lower timeframe with smaller stops
options.explanation: No: the trades change completely with the lookback.

strategies.title: Diversification and position sizing

overview.objective: Keep any single trade, or any group of linked trades, from doing serious damage.
overview.holdingPeriod: Applies to every trade, whatever its length.
overview.context: A risk principle for all markets and strategies. It does not make any strategy profitable; it limits damage.

simple.simple: Decide how much you can lose on one trade before you enter, and size the trade from your [[stop-loss]] so you cannot lose more. Treat trades that depend on the same thing as one bigger bet.
simple.balanced: [[position-sizing|Position sizing]] turns a fixed [[risk-per-trade]] into a trade size: risk in money ÷ (stop distance × value per point). [[diversification|Diversification]] only helps when positions do not move together, and [[correlation|correlations]] tend to rise in stressed markets. Gaps can still push a loss past the stop.

strategies.reasoning: Every strategy has losing streaks. Keeping each loss small, and not stacking linked losses, could keep an account usable through a streak long enough to see whether the strategy works. That is the reasoning; it limits damage but cannot turn losing rules into winning ones.

rules.label: A simplified educational version, not anyone's documented method
rules: Risk no more than 1% of the account on any single trade.
Size each trade from the stop: risk in money ÷ stop distance = value per pip or point.
Keep total open risk at no more than 5% of the account.
Treat trades that depend on the same currency, sector or commodity as one position, and keep their combined risk at no more than 2%.
Set the size before entering, and never widen a stop to keep a losing trade open.

exercise.prompt: Which statements are true under these rules? Pick all that apply.
exercise.situation: A simulated 10,000 USD account with four open trades, each risking 1%: long EUR/USD, long GBP/USD, short USD/CHF and short USD/JPY.

options.text: Total open risk is 4%
options.explanation: Right: 4 × 1% = 4%. That is within the 5% total, but as one dollar bet it breaks the 2% limit for linked trades.

options.text: Each of the four tends to gain if the US dollar weakens broadly
options.explanation: Right: each trade is a bet against the dollar, so they are closely linked.

options.text: A fifth 1% trade, short USD/CAD, would spread the risk
options.explanation: No: it is another bet against the dollar, adding to the same exposure.

options.text: A 1% trade must not lose more than 100 USD at the stop
options.explanation: Right: 1% of 10,000 USD = 100 USD, so the size is set from the stop to keep the loss within that.

options.text: A sharp dollar rally would hit only the EUR/USD and GBP/USD trades
options.explanation: No: all four lose when the dollar rises, about 4% together, and more if prices gap past the stops.

failureAnalysis: Linked positions all lose together and the total loss is several times the per-trade limit.
Gaps jump past stops, so losses exceed the plan.
Moving stops further away to avoid a loss breaks the sizing.
Raising risk after a few wins makes the next streak more damaging.
limitations: The 1%, 2% and 5% figures are examples for learning, not recommendations for your situation.
Sizing limits losses; it does not make a strategy profitable.
Correlations change, and in stressed markets they often rise.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Account 8,000 USD, 1% risk, stop 40 pips. 1 pip is worth 1 USD per 10,000 units. What size?

options.text: 8,000 units
options.explanation: No: that is the account size, not the trade size.

options.text: 40,000 units
options.explanation: No: at 4 USD per pip, a 40-pip stop risks 160 USD, which is 2%.

options.text: 20,000 units: 80 USD ÷ 40 pips = 2 USD per pip
options.explanation: Right: 2 USD per pip is 20,000 units.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Three open trades are all long other currencies against the US dollar, at 1% risk each. What is the combined exposure most like?

options.text: One bet of about 3%
options.explanation: Right: they all depend on the dollar falling.

options.text: Three separate 1% risks that cancel each other out
options.explanation: No: they move together; they do not cancel.

options.text: Less than 1% in total, because the currencies are spread across different regions
options.explanation: No: they share the same dollar exposure.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Why risk a small fixed share of the account on each trade?

options.text: To win more often
options.explanation: No: size does not change how often a trade wins.

options.text: A losing streak then leaves the account usable
options.explanation: Right: ten 1% losses leave about 90% of the account.

options.text: Because brokers require each trade to stay below a set share of the account
options.explanation: No: brokers set margin rules, but that is not why you size small.

strategies.title: Dividend and index investing

overview.objective: Own a broad slice of the market for years, with low costs and reinvested dividends.
overview.context: Long-term saving in shares through low-cost funds. Not a short-term trading method.

simple.simple: Instead of picking shares, buy an [[index-fund]] that holds many companies. Add a fixed amount on a schedule, reinvest the [[dividend|dividends]], keep fees low and hold for years.
simple.balanced: [[diversification|Diversification]] across many companies reduces the damage any one can do, but the fund still falls when the whole market falls, sometimes by a lot and for years. Fees are taken every year whatever the result, so small differences compound. [[dividend-yield|Dividend yield]] is income, not a forecast of price.

strategies.reasoning: Over long periods, the combined profits of many companies may grow, and owning a share of all of them avoids having to pick winners. That is the reasoning, not a promise; markets can fall and stay down for many years.

rules.label: A simplified educational version, not anyone's documented method
rules: Invest a fixed amount on a fixed schedule into a broad, low-cost index fund.
Reinvest dividends.
Compare yearly fees before buying, and prefer the lower fee for the same index.
Rebalance once a year if you hold more than one fund.
Use only money you will not need for many years.

exercise.prompt: Which statements are true for this fictional plan? Pick all that apply.
exercise.situation: A fictional fund. You invest 200 a month for 3 months, at prices of 50, 40 and 50 per unit. Ignore fees.

options.text: You hold 13 units
Your average cost is about 46.15, below the simple average price of 46.67
options.explanation: Right: 600 ÷ 13 ≈ 46.15, and (50 + 40 + 50) ÷ 3 ≈ 46.67. A fixed amount buys more units when the price is low.

options.text: Investing all 600 at the first price of 50 would have bought more units
options.explanation: No: 600 ÷ 50 = 12 units, one fewer than the 13 bought month by month.

options.text: At a price of 50, the holding is worth 650
The dividend yield tells you the price will rise
options.explanation: No: yield is income relative to price, not a forecast.

failureAnalysis: A broad market fall takes the whole fund down, sometimes for years.
Needing the money during a fall forces selling at a loss.
High fees quietly reduce results every year.
Dividends can be cut.
limitations: Taxes and fees vary and are not included in the examples.
No claim is made about future market returns.
This page describes a principle, not advice for your situation.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: A share costs 40 and pays a yearly dividend of 1.60. What is the dividend yield?

options.explanation: Right: 1.60 ÷ 40 = 0.04, which is 4%.

options.text: 25%, price divided by dividend
options.explanation: No: that is 40 ÷ 1.60. Yield is the dividend divided by the price.

options.text: 1.6%, since the yield is just the dividend amount written as a percent
options.explanation: No: the dividend has to be divided by the price.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: What does a broad index fund not protect you from?

options.text: One company failing
options.explanation: No: one company is a small part of a broad fund.

options.text: A fall in the whole market
options.explanation: Right: if the market falls, the fund falls with it.

options.text: One sector falling while the rest of the market rises
options.explanation: No: a broad fund holds many sectors, so one sector falling does limited damage.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Two funds track the same index. One charges 1.0% a year, the other 0.2%. Over many years…

options.text: They end level, because they hold the same shares
options.explanation: No: the fee gap is taken every year.

options.text: The 1% fund ends ahead, because a higher fee buys better tracking
options.explanation: No: a higher fee is not a sign of better results for the same index.

options.text: The 0.8 point gap is lost each year and compounds, so the cheaper fund is likely to end ahead
options.explanation: Right: same index, so the fee difference is most of the gap.

strategies.title: Growth investing (concept)

overview.objective: Own companies whose sales and earnings are growing much faster than average.
overview.context: A concept page. High expected growth is usually already in the price.

simple.simple: [[growth-investing|Growth investing]] means buying companies whose [[revenue]] and [[earnings]] are growing fast, even if the share price looks expensive today.
simple.balanced: A high [[pe-ratio]] means the price already assumes strong growth. If growth merely slows, the share can fall sharply even while the business keeps growing. The [[peg-ratio]] compares price with growth, but only as well as the growth forecast. Issuing new shares ([[dilution]]) spreads earnings more thinly.

strategies.reasoning: If a company keeps growing its earnings faster than the market expects, its value could rise more than the high price implies. That is the reasoning; the hard part is that expectations are already high.

exercise.prompt: Which statements are true for this fictional company? Pick all that apply.
exercise.situation: A fictional company. Revenue grew from 100 million to 130 million last year. The P/E is 60, and analysts expect earnings to grow 30% a year. It is losing cash and issues about 10% more shares each year.

options.text: The PEG ratio is 2.0
Issuing 10% more shares a year dilutes each share's claim on earnings
options.explanation: Right: the same earnings are spread over more shares.

options.text: 30% growth will continue because it did last year
options.explanation: No: past growth is not a promise of future growth.

options.text: A high P/E means the price already assumes strong growth
options.explanation: Right: buyers are paying for growth they expect.

options.text: A P/E of 60 means the price is 60 times revenue per share
options.explanation: No: P/E compares the price with earnings per share, not revenue.

failureAnalysis: Growth slows, and the share falls even though the business still grows.
Forecasts of growth turn out too high.
Cash losses force the company to issue shares, diluting holders.
Rising interest rates can hit highly valued shares hardest.
limitations: This page explains the idea; it gives no rules to pick shares.
Growth forecasts are uncertain, and PEG inherits that uncertainty.
No claim is made that growth investing beats other approaches.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: A share has a P/E of 40 and expected earnings growth of 20% a year. What is its PEG ratio?

options.explanation: No: that is 20 ÷ 40, the wrong way round.
Right: P/E divided by the growth rate.

options.text: 800, from multiplying the P/E by the growth rate
options.explanation: No: PEG divides P/E by growth.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: What tends to hurt a highly valued growth share most?

options.text: Growth slowing
options.explanation: Right: the price assumed fast growth.

options.text: A small dividend paid each year
options.explanation: No: a small dividend is common and not a main risk.

options.text: Its number of shares staying exactly the same from one year to the next
options.explanation: No: a steady share count avoids dilution.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Earnings per share are 2.00 and grow 25% a year. What are they after 2 years?

options.explanation: No: that adds 0.50 twice. Growth compounds on the new, larger figure.
No: that is after one year.

strategies.title: Mean reversion with RSI and bands

overview.objective: Buy a stretched move back towards the average in a sideways market.
overview.context: Quiet, sideways markets only. In a trend the same signals keep appearing while price keeps going.

simple.simple: When price closes below the lower [[bollinger-bands|Bollinger band]] and [[rsi]] is low, in a market that has been going sideways, buy and aim for the middle band.
simple.balanced: [[mean-reversion|Mean reversion]] describes quiet ranges better than trends. A filter for the [[market-regime]] is the core of the rules: without it, buying every low reading in a falling market produces repeated losses. Win rates can look high while a few large losses decide the result.

strategies.reasoning: In a sideways market, sharp moves away from the average may be overreactions that fade. A rule that buys the stretch and takes profit at the average could then win more often than it loses. That is the reasoning only, and it breaks down when the market starts to trend.

rules.label: A simplified educational version, not any trader's system
rules: Regime filter: price has crossed the MA 20 at least 4 times in the last 40 candles.
Go long when a candle closes below the lower Bollinger band and RSI is below 30.
Place the stop 1 × ATR below the entry.
Take profit at the middle band (the MA 20).
No trade if the regime filter fails. Size for no more than 1% risk.

demo.lookFor: Find closes below the lower band with RSI under 30, and see how often price returned to the middle band. Then try Downtrend and count the same signals.

replay.instructions: Replay the Range scenario with Bollinger bands, MA 20 and RSI on. Check the regime filter before each trade. Then replay a Downtrend with the same rules and see how the filter changes things.

exercise.prompt: Which statements are true under the simplified rules? Pick all that apply.
exercise.situation: A fictional EUR/GBP chart (simulated), sideways between 0.8500 and 0.8600. The MA 20 is flat at 0.8550 and price crossed it 6 times in the last 40 candles. The latest close is 0.8495, the lower band is 0.8502, RSI is 27 and ATR is 0.0030.

options.text: The regime filter passes
options.explanation: Right: 6 crosses in 40 candles is at least 4.

options.text: The entry conditions are met
options.explanation: Right: the close is below the lower band and RSI is under 30.

options.text: The stop goes at 0.8465
The target is 0.8600, the top of the range
options.explanation: No: the target is the middle band, 0.8550.

options.text: An RSI of 27 means price has to bounce
options.explanation: No: RSI can stay low while price keeps falling.

failureAnalysis: When a range turns into a trend, the signals keep appearing and each one loses.
Small, frequent wins can be wiped out by one large loss.
Gaps on news can skip the stop.
The regime filter only looks backwards and changes late.
limitations: The band, RSI and filter settings are examples for learning, not tested values.
A high win rate here says little about the total result.
No claim is made that these rules make money.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: RSI is 25 and price closes below the lower band, in a strong downtrend that has not crossed the MA 20 for weeks. What do the rules say?

options.text: Buy
options.explanation: No: the regime filter fails.

options.text: No trade: the regime filter fails
options.explanation: Right: the rules need at least 4 crosses of the MA 20 in 40 candles.

options.text: Buy double the normal size, as the market is extremely oversold
options.explanation: No: the rules forbid the trade, and size never depends on how stretched price looks.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Why is the target the middle band rather than the upper band?

options.text: A bigger target would win more on each trade
options.explanation: No: a farther target is reached less often, and the idea is only a return to the mean.

options.text: The upper band moves too fast to use as a target
options.explanation: No: the bands move with price, but that is not why the target is the middle.

options.text: The idea is a return towards the average, not a swing to the other extreme
options.explanation: Right: the rules aim only for the move back to the mean.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Using the simplified formula, average gain is 2 pips and average loss is 8 pips. What is RSI?

options.text: 25, the ratio of gain to loss
options.explanation: No: 0.25 is the ratio; it still has to go into the formula.

options.text: 80, since losses are four times the size of gains
options.explanation: No: 80 is the 100 ÷ (1 + RS) part. RSI is 100 − 80.

strategies.title: Pullback in a trend

overview.objective: Join an existing trend after a pause, instead of chasing it.
overview.context: Markets already in a clear trend on the daily or 4-hour chart.

simple.simple: In an uptrend, wait for price to dip without breaking the last higher low. Buy when it starts rising again, with a stop under the dip.
simple.balanced: At the time, a [[pullback]] and the start of a [[reversal]] look the same; only later candles show which it was. Waiting for a close above the prior candle's high gives some sign the dip has paused, at the cost of a worse price. The stop under the pullback low defines the risk, and [[market-structure]] tells you when the trend idea is wrong.

strategies.reasoning: In a trend, dips may attract buyers who missed the earlier move, so entering after a dip gives a nearer stop than entering at the high. That is the reasoning only. It assumes the trend continues, which it often does not.

rules.label: A simplified educational version, not any trader's system
rules: Trend filter: the close is above a rising EMA 50, and the last swing low is higher than the one before.
Wait for a pullback that stays above the last higher low.
Enter on a close above the high of the previous candle after the pullback.
Place the stop just below the pullback low.
Exit at 2R, or on a close below the EMA 50, whichever comes first. Size for no more than 1% risk.

demo.lookFor: Mark the last higher low, the pullback low and the first close above the prior candle's high. Then switch to Reversal and see how the same set-up looks when the trend ends.

replay.instructions: Replay the Pullback scenario with EMA 50 on. Mark the last higher low before you trade, enter only on the trigger close, and put the stop under the pullback low.

exercise.prompt: Which statements are true under the simplified rules? Pick all that apply.
exercise.situation: A fictional daily chart (simulated). The EMA 50 is rising. The last higher low is 1.0820. Price pulls back to 1.0850. The pullback candle's low is 1.0850 and its high is 1.0885. The next candle has a high of 1.0880 and closes at 1.0875. The candle after that closes at 1.0890.

options.text: The pullback held above the last higher low
options.explanation: Right: 1.0850 stayed above 1.0820.

options.text: The entry trigger is the close at 1.0890
options.explanation: Right: it is the first close above the previous candle's high of 1.0880.

options.text: The trend will continue because the low held
options.explanation: No: a held low is a condition for the set-up, not a forecast.

options.text: A stop at 1.0845 risks 45 pips from an entry at 1.0890
The entry was the dip to 1.0850
options.explanation: No: the rules wait for a close above the previous candle's high, not the low.

failureAnalysis: A pullback that keeps falling becomes a reversal, and the stop is hit.
Waiting for the trigger means entering higher than the low, so some winners are smaller.
In choppy trends, swing lows are unclear and the rules are hard to apply.
Sharp news moves can skip the stop.
limitations: The EMA 50, the trigger and the 2R target are examples for learning, not tested values.
What counts as a swing low involves judgement unless it is defined exactly.
No claim is made that buying pullbacks makes money.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: The pullback low is 1.3420 and the last higher low 1.3380. Entry is 1.3470 with a stop at 1.3415. What is the risk?

options.text: 55 pips
90 pips, to the higher low
options.explanation: No: the stop is under the pullback low, not the higher low.

options.text: 50 pips, from the pullback low up to the entry price
options.explanation: No: the stop is 5 pips below the pullback low, at 1.3415.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: At the moment it happens, how can you tell a pullback from the start of a reversal?

options.text: By its size
options.explanation: No: pullbacks and reversals both come in all sizes.

options.text: You cannot tell for sure; later candles show it
options.explanation: Right: they look the same at the time.

options.text: A pullback always stops at a 50% retracement, a reversal goes further
options.explanation: No: there is no fixed level where pullbacks stop.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Why wait for a close above the prior candle's high instead of buying while price is still falling?

options.text: It gets a lower price than buying during the dip
options.explanation: No: it means buying at a higher price than the dip.

options.text: It is a way to catch the exact low of the pullback
options.explanation: No: it deliberately gives up the low.

options.text: It wants a sign the dip has paused, and accepts a worse price in exchange
options.explanation: Right: the trigger trades price for some evidence the pullback has stopped.

strategies.title: Range trading

overview.objective: Buy near the bottom of a sideways range and sell near the top.
overview.context: Markets that have tested the same support and resistance several times.

simple.simple: Find a market bouncing between a floor ([[support]]) and a ceiling ([[resistance]]). Buy after price bounces off the floor, aim just below the ceiling, and stop trading the range once price closes outside it.
simple.balanced: Ranges end with a breakout, often after some false ones. Waiting for a close back above support, instead of buying as price falls, avoids some breaks at a worse price. The [[risk-reward-ratio]] is limited by the height of the range.

strategies.reasoning: If many traders watch the same levels, price may keep turning near them until something changes. Trading inside those levels with a nearby stop could then have small, defined risk. That is the reasoning, not evidence; ranges end without warning.

rules.label: A simplified educational version, not any trader's system
rules: A range needs at least two touches of support and two of resistance.
Buy only after a candle closes back above support (dips below that close back inside are allowed).
Place the stop 0.5 × ATR below support.
Take profit just below resistance.
Once a candle closes outside the range, stop trading it until a new range forms. Size for no more than 1% risk.

demo.lookFor: Mark support and resistance where price turned at least twice. Note how close each turn came to the line, and what happened when price finally closed outside.

replay.instructions: Replay the Sideways scenario. Draw the range only after two touches of each side, trade only bounces that close back inside, and stop when a candle closes outside.

exercise.prompt: Which statements are true under the simplified rules? Pick all that apply.
exercise.situation: A fictional commodity in USD (simulated). Support at 85.00 was touched 3 times, resistance at 89.00 twice. The latest candle dipped to 84.80 and closed at 85.30. ATR is 1.20.

options.text: The range has enough touches for the rules
options.explanation: Right: at least two on each side.

options.text: The close back above support is an entry trigger
options.explanation: Right: the candle closed at 85.30, above 85.00.

options.text: A stop 0.5 × ATR below support is at 84.40
The target should be above 89.00, in case it breaks out
options.explanation: No: the target is just below resistance.

options.text: The dip to 84.80 ended the range
options.explanation: No: the rules end the range on a close outside it, and this candle closed inside.

failureAnalysis: A breakout through support hits the stop, sometimes with a gap.
Many touches can mean the level is weakening, not strengthening.
Targets are limited by the range height, so costs take a larger share.
Deciding where the range is involves judgement.
limitations: Touch counts and the 0.5 × ATR stop are examples for learning, not tested values.
No claim is made that ranges hold or that these rules make money.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Support is 1.2600 and resistance 1.2700. A candle closes at 1.2580. What do the rules say?

options.text: Buy, it is cheap
options.explanation: No: price is outside the range.

options.text: Wait for RSI to fall further
options.explanation: No: RSI is not part of these rules.

options.text: Do not buy: a close outside the range ends it until a new range forms
options.explanation: Right: the rules stop trading the range after a close outside it.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Entry 1.2615, stop 1.2585, target 1.2690. What is the reward-to-risk ratio?

options.explanation: Right: reward 75 pips, risk 30 pips, and 75 ÷ 30 = 2.5.

options.text: 3.3, using the full 100-pip range
options.explanation: No: use the distance from entry to target, not the range height.

options.text: 0.4, dividing the risk by the reward instead of the other way round
options.explanation: No: reward-to-risk is reward ÷ risk.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: What usually ends a range?

options.text: Time alone
options.explanation: No: ranges do not end on a schedule.

options.text: A breakout, often after false ones
options.explanation: Right: eventually price leaves the range.

options.text: Nothing: once it is established, a range keeps going until people stop trading it
options.explanation: No: ranges do end, often without warning.

strategies.title: Seasonality (read the caveats)

overview.objective: Look for price patterns that repeat at the same time of year.
overview.context: A concept page with strong warnings. Seasonal patterns are easy to find by chance and hard to confirm.

simple.simple: [[seasonality|Seasonality]] means a price tends to do something at the same time each year. A few patterns have a physical cause, like harvests or heating demand. Most patterns found by searching old charts are coincidence.
simple.balanced: With only one data point per year, even decades give a small [[sample-size]]. Searching many calendar windows and keeping the best guarantees some will look strong by chance. A known cause, a test on years not used to find the pattern ([[out-of-sample]]) and humility about the result are the minimum.

strategies.reasoning: Where a physical cycle, such as a harvest or a heating season, changes supply or demand at the same time each year, prices could show a pattern. That is the reasoning; if the cause is known, others may already have priced it in.

exercise.prompt: Which statements are true for this fictional table? Pick all that apply.
exercise.situation: A fictional commodity. A table says it rose in a given month in 8 of the last 10 years. The 8 rising years averaged +3%. The 2 falling years were −9% and −7%.

options.text: The average over all 10 years is +0.8%
Ten years are too few to rely on
options.explanation: Right: ten data points say little.

options.text: With 8 of 10 up, the chance next year is 80%
options.explanation: No: past frequency in a small sample is not a probability for next year.

options.text: The losing years were bigger than the typical rising year
options.explanation: Right: −9% and −7% against an average rise of +3%.

options.text: Seasonal patterns stay the same once found
options.explanation: No: patterns change, especially once many people trade them.

failureAnalysis: The pattern was found by chance and does not repeat.
A cause that was real gets priced in once many people know it.
One bad year can outweigh several good ones.
Supply shocks and news override the calendar.
limitations: This page gives no trading rules.
Tables of seasonal win rates are usually based on very few years.
No claim is made that any seasonal pattern exists or works.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: A pattern held in 9 of the last 12 years. What is the main problem?

options.text: It is too recent
options.explanation: No: recency is not the main issue.

options.text: Twelve years is a very small sample
options.explanation: Right: twelve data points cannot separate a pattern from chance.

options.text: Nothing: 9 of 12 is 75%, so it will come true three years in four
options.explanation: No: a frequency in a small sample is not a reliable probability.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: You searched 50 calendar windows and kept the best one. Why distrust it?

options.text: Calendar windows only work on very old data
options.explanation: No: the age of the data is not the issue; the search is.

options.text: The seasons themselves shift from year to year
options.explanation: No: the calendar is fixed; the problem is how many windows were tried.

options.text: Testing many windows makes some look good by chance, so the best one is likely flattered
options.explanation: Right: the more you search, the more you find by luck.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Which makes a seasonal pattern more believable?

options.text: A known physical cause
options.explanation: Right: a cause like a harvest gives a reason, though it may be priced in.

options.text: A higher win rate over the last few years
options.explanation: No: a few more years of wins is still a small sample.

options.text: That it appears in a chart shared widely online by many traders
options.explanation: No: popularity is not evidence, and a well-known pattern may be priced in.

strategies.title: Trend following with moving averages

overview.objective: Stay in a market while it trends, and step aside when it stops.
overview.holdingPeriod: Weeks to months; trades in sideways markets are often closed within days.
overview.context: Daily charts of liquid markets. Works on the idea of long moves, so it needs patience through many small losses.

simple.simple: Hold a position while price stays on the right side of a [[moving-average]] that points the same way. Get out when price closes back across it.
simple.balanced: The rule only reacts to moves that have already happened, so it enters late and exits late. In ranges it is whipsawed into many small losses ([[whipsaw]]); it relies on occasional long [[trend|trends]] to pay for them. The period is a setting, not a discovery: testing many periods on the same data and keeping the best invites [[overfitting]].

strategies.reasoning: If markets sometimes move in one direction for a long time, a rule that stays aboard those moves and cuts the rest early could, on balance, come out ahead. That is the reasoning only; whether it holds in a given market, period and cost level has to be tested, and it can fail for long stretches.

rules.label: A simplified educational version, not any trader's system
rules: Use a daily chart and a 50-period exponential moving average (EMA 50).
Long only when a candle closes above the average and the average is higher than it was 10 candles ago. Short is the mirror image.
Place the stop 2 × ATR from the entry price.
Size the position so the loss at the stop is no more than 1% of the account.
Exit when a candle closes back across the average, or at the stop, whichever comes first.

demo.lookFor: Find the first close above the rising EMA 50 and the first close back below it. Note how much of the move came before the entry and how much was given back before the exit.

replay.instructions: Replay a Strong uptrend with EMA 50 on. Apply the rules exactly: enter only on a close above a rising average, set a 2 × ATR stop, and exit on a close back below. Then try the Range scenario with the same rules and compare.

exercise.prompt: Which statements are true under the simplified rules? Pick all that apply.
exercise.situation: A fictional daily chart (simulated). The 50-period average rose from 1.2200 to 1.2260 over the last 10 candles. The latest close is 1.2290 and ATR is 0.0040. The simulated account is 5,000 USD, and 1 pip is worth 1 USD per 10,000 units.

options.text: A long is allowed now
options.explanation: Right: the close (1.2290) is above the average (1.2260), and the average is higher than 10 candles ago.

options.text: The stop for a long filled at 1.2290 is 1.2210
The most the trade may lose at the stop is 100 USD
options.explanation: No: 1% of 5,000 USD is 50 USD.

options.text: A size of 6,000 units keeps the loss at the stop within the limit
options.explanation: Right: 50 USD ÷ 80 pips = 0.625 USD per pip, or 6,250 units. Rounding down to 6,000 units risks 0.60 × 80 = 48 USD.

options.text: A size of 7,000 units also keeps the loss at the stop within the limit
options.explanation: No: 7,000 units is 0.70 USD per pip, and 0.70 × 80 = 56 USD, above the 50 USD limit.

failureAnalysis: In sideways markets price crosses the average again and again, and each cross is a small loss.
Sharp reversals hit before the average turns, so a large part of a gain can be given back before the exit.
Gaps can jump past the stop, so a loss can be bigger than planned.
Long losing streaks are normal. People often abandon the rules just before the next trend.
limitations: The settings (50 periods, 2 × ATR, 10 candles) are examples for learning, not tested values.
No performance claim is made here: whether the rules made or lost money depends on the market, period and costs.
Costs such as spread, swaps and slippage reduce results, and they matter more when there are many trades.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: The average is 1.1500 now and was 1.1440 ten candles ago. The latest close is 1.1530. What do the rules allow?

options.text: A long: close above a rising average
options.explanation: Right: 1.1530 is above 1.1500, and the average rose from 1.1440.

options.text: Nothing, because the average must be falling before any trade is allowed
options.explanation: No: a rising average is what allows a long.

options.text: Nothing yet: the close has to be a full ATR above the average first
options.explanation: No: the rules have no such distance condition.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Which market condition gives this rule the most losing trades?

options.text: A long steady trend
options.explanation: No: steady trends give few crosses.

options.text: A sideways range with a flat average
options.explanation: Right: price crosses a flat average often, and most crosses reverse.

options.text: A trend with small pullbacks that stay above the average
options.explanation: No: if pullbacks stay above the average, the rule stays in.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: In a simulated test, the rules lost 6 trades in a row. What is the most reasonable reading?

options.text: Stop using the rules
options.explanation: No: 6 trades are far too few to judge.

options.text: Shorten the average to 5 so it reacts faster
options.explanation: No: changing the settings after a few losses is curve fitting, and a shorter average whipsaws more.

options.text: Streaks like this are normal for trend rules; judge them on many more trades
options.explanation: Right: trend rules usually lose often and depend on a few large winners, so short streaks say little.

strategies.title: Value investing (concept)

overview.objective: Buy shares for less than a careful estimate of what the business is worth.
overview.context: A concept page. Value investing rests on estimates of a business's worth, and those estimates can be wrong.

simple.simple: [[value-investing|Value investing]] means estimating what a company is worth, then buying only when the price is well below that estimate. The gap is the [[margin-of-safety]].
simple.balanced: The estimate depends on assumptions about future cash flows, so two careful people can disagree widely. A share can look cheap because the business is shrinking: a [[value-trap]]. Cheap shares can stay cheap for years, and checking [[free-cash-flow]] and debt is part of the work, not optional.

strategies.reasoning: If the market sometimes prices a business below what its future cash flows are worth, buying at a discount could leave room for error and for the price to recover. That is the reasoning; markets may have good reasons for the low price.

exercise.prompt: Which statements are true for this fictional company? Pick all that apply.
exercise.situation: A fictional company. The share price is 30 and earnings per share are 3. Free cash flow has been negative for 3 years and debt is rising. Your estimate of its worth is 45.

options.text: The P/E ratio is 10
The margin of safety on your estimate is about 33%
Negative free cash flow and rising debt are warning signs of a possible value trap
options.explanation: Right: profits that do not turn into cash deserve a closer look.

options.text: The P/E of 10 is below the estimate's implied P/E of 12
options.explanation: No: the estimate implies 45 ÷ 3 = 15, not 12.

options.text: The estimate of 45 is a fact
options.explanation: No: it is an estimate built on assumptions.

failureAnalysis: The business keeps shrinking, so the cheap price was justified.
The estimate of worth was too optimistic.
The price stays low for years, tying up money.
Debt problems wipe out shareholders before any recovery.
limitations: This page explains the idea; it gives no rules to pick shares.
Valuation needs assumptions, and small changes to them move the estimate a lot.
No claim is made that value investing beats other approaches.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: You estimate a business is worth 80 per share. It trades at 60. What is the margin of safety?

options.text: 33%, measured on the price
options.explanation: No: the margin is measured against the estimated value, not the price.
No: 20 is the gap in money; the margin is usually given as a share of the estimate.
Right: the gap divided by the estimated value.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: A share has a P/E of 5 while similar companies trade at 15. What should you check first?

options.text: Why it is cheap
options.explanation: Right: a low P/E can mean earnings are about to fall.

options.text: Whether the price rose this week
options.explanation: No: last week's price says little about value.

options.text: Nothing more, since a low P/E alone is enough to show it is good value
options.explanation: No: that is how value traps catch people.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: What does an estimate of a business's worth rely on?

options.text: The chart
options.explanation: No: value estimates come from the business, not the chart.

options.text: Assumptions about future cash flows
options.explanation: Right: and different assumptions give different values.

options.text: A fixed formula that gives the same answer whoever uses it and whatever they assume
options.explanation: No: estimates change with the assumptions.
