calendarEvents.title: Central bank meetings and statements
calendarEvents.measures: Nothing is measured. A central bank's policy committee meets, discusses the economy and publishes a statement, and often holds a press conference or later releases the minutes of the discussion.
calendarEvents.whyItMatters: The wording of a statement can change what traders expect about future interest rates, even when rates themselves are left alone. Expectations about rates feed into currencies, bond yields, stock valuations and the cost of holding commodities.
calendarEvents.expectations: Before a meeting, analysts and traders form a view of what the bank will say, based on recent data and earlier speeches. Much of that view is already in prices before the meeting starts.
calendarEvents.surprises: A surprise here is usually about tone: a statement that sounds more worried about inflation, or more worried about growth, than expected. Traders may reprice future rate paths, but they can also disagree about what the words mean, so the first move is often reversed or extended as the press conference goes on.
calendarEvents.limits: A meeting does not tell you which way any price will go. The same statement can be read in different ways, and other news can matter more on the day. Spreads can widen and prices can jump around the release time.

samples.title: Bank of Westmark policy statement (fictional)
samples.details: The fictional Bank of Westmark publishes its statement after a two-day meeting, followed by a press conference half an hour later.

samples.title: Bank of Westmark meeting minutes (fictional)
samples.details: Minutes of an earlier fictional meeting, showing how the committee members' views differed.

calendarEvents.title: Company earnings reports
calendarEvents.measures: A listed company's results for the last quarter or year: revenue, profit, earnings per share, cash flow, and often what management expects next (guidance).
calendarEvents.whyItMatters: Earnings show how a business is actually doing. A report can change what investors are willing to pay for the shares, and a large company's results can affect its sector or a whole index.
calendarEvents.expectations: Analysts publish estimates for revenue and earnings per share. Investors also form views on guidance and on details such as margins, which are harder to summarise in one number.
calendarEvents.surprises: Beating or missing the estimates is only part of it. Weak guidance can outweigh a strong quarter, and a small miss can be ignored if the outlook improves. Shares can gap at the next open because reports often come out when the main market is closed.
calendarEvents.limits: Good results do not guarantee a rising share price, and poor results do not guarantee a fall. Small companies often have few or no analyst estimates and thin trading, so their moves can be large and unpredictable.

samples.title: Example Quickling Apps quarterly results (fictional)
samples.details: A sample after-hours earnings release with revenue, earnings per share and next-quarter guidance for a fictional company.

samples.title: Example Steadybrook Pantry Foods annual results (fictional)
samples.details: A sample before-the-open annual report, including the dividend the fictional company proposes.

calendarEvents.title: Futures expiries and rollovers
calendarEvents.measures: Nothing is measured. It is the date a futures contract month stops trading, with related dates such as the last trading day and, for physically settled contracts, the first notice day.
calendarEvents.whyItMatters: Positions in an expiring contract must be closed or rolled to a later month. Trading activity moves from one contract month to the next, and prices of the two months can differ. Holding a physically settled contract too long can mean taking or making delivery.
calendarEvents.expectations: Expiry dates are set by each exchange's contract rules and are known in advance. Check them in the exchange's own contract specification, not from memory.
calendarEvents.surprises: There is no forecast to beat, but trading near expiry can be thin in the old month, spreads can widen, and the gap between months can look like a price jump on a continuous chart that joins the contracts together.
calendarEvents.limits: An expiry does not tell you where prices are going. Charts that join contract months need to say how they were joined, or they can show jumps that never happened in any one contract.

samples.title: IDX practice future: last trading day (fictional)
samples.details: A sample last trading day for the app's fictional index future. Positions would need to be closed or rolled to the next fictional contract month before it.

calendarEvents.title: Market holidays and short sessions
calendarEvents.measures: Nothing is measured. An exchange or a country's banks close, or trade for shorter hours.
calendarEvents.whyItMatters: With fewer traders active, liquidity can be thin, spreads can widen and prices can move further on small orders. Some markets stay open while related ones close, and the next session can open with a gap.
calendarEvents.expectations: Holiday calendars are published by exchanges in advance. Check the exchange's own calendar for the market you are studying.
calendarEvents.surprises: There is no figure to beat. The risk is being caught by thin trading or a gap at the reopening, especially with positions held through the closure.
calendarEvents.limits: A holiday does not point prices in any direction. It changes how easily and cheaply you can trade, not where the market is going.

samples.title: Westmark national holiday: exchange closed (fictional)
samples.details: A sample full-day closure of the fictional Westmark exchange and banks. Other markets trade with fewer participants.

calendarEvents.title: Inflation reports
calendarEvents.measures: How fast prices of a basket of goods and services are rising, usually compared with a month earlier and a year earlier. Many reports also show a 'core' figure that leaves out the most changeable items, such as food and energy.
calendarEvents.whyItMatters: Central banks try to keep inflation near a target, so inflation figures shape expectations about interest rates. Those expectations feed into currencies, bond yields, stock valuations and commodities.
calendarEvents.expectations: Forecasters publish a consensus figure before the release. Traders compare the actual number with that consensus, and with the previous figure, which is sometimes revised.
calendarEvents.surprises: A figure above or below the consensus may change what traders expect the central bank to do. The headline and core figures can point different ways, and a revision to last month can matter as much as the new number. The first move can fade if the surprise was small or already expected by many traders.
calendarEvents.limits: An inflation surprise does not set a price direction. A higher figure can strengthen a currency in one situation and weaken it in another, depending on what was priced in and how the central bank is expected to respond.

samples.title: Westmark consumer price index (fictional)
samples.details: The fictional Westmark statistics office publishes the monthly consumer price figures, with headline and core measures.

calendarEvents.title: Inventory reports
calendarEvents.measures: How much of a commodity is held in storage, such as crude oil, fuels, natural gas or grain, and how much that changed since the last report.
calendarEvents.whyItMatters: Stocks in storage show the balance between supply and demand. A larger-than-expected fall can point to tighter supply, and a larger-than-expected rise to weaker demand or more supply.
calendarEvents.expectations: Forecasters estimate the change before the release, and private estimates may circulate earlier. Traders compare the official figure with those numbers.
calendarEvents.surprises: Reports have several parts, such as crude and refined fuels, and they can point different ways. A surprise that was already hinted at by private estimates may be priced in, and the reaction can fade within minutes.
calendarEvents.limits: A draw does not guarantee a rise, and a build does not guarantee a fall. Seasons, weather, the futures curve and wider news all matter, and futures can move sharply around the release.

samples.title: Northland weekly crude inventories (fictional)
samples.details: A sample weekly report on crude oil and refined fuels held in storage in the fictional country of Northland.

calendarEvents.title: Jobs reports
calendarEvents.measures: How many jobs were added or lost, the share of people looking for work who cannot find it (the unemployment rate), and often how fast wages are growing.
calendarEvents.whyItMatters: Jobs and wages show how strong an economy is and whether wage growth may push inflation up. Both shape expectations about interest rates, and through them currencies, stocks and commodities.
calendarEvents.expectations: A consensus forecast is published for the main figures. Earlier months are often revised, so traders look at the new figure, the revisions and the parts of the report together.
calendarEvents.surprises: A report can surprise on one figure and not another: many new jobs with slower wage growth, for example. Traders may react to the part they think the central bank will care about most, and the first move can reverse once the whole report has been read.
calendarEvents.limits: A strong jobs report is not automatically good or bad for any market. Its effect depends on expectations, on the other figures in the report and on everything else happening that day. Spreads can widen and prices can jump at the release.

samples.title: Westmark employment report (fictional)
samples.details: The fictional monthly report with jobs added, the unemployment rate and average wage growth, plus revisions to the two previous months.

calendarEvents.title: Interest rate decisions
calendarEvents.measures: The central bank's main policy interest rate: whether it is raised, cut or left where it is, and by how much.
calendarEvents.whyItMatters: The policy rate sets the base cost of borrowing and the return on holding a currency. A change, or a change in the expected path of rates, can move currencies, bond yields, stock valuations and the cost of carrying futures positions.
calendarEvents.expectations: Most decisions are widely expected. Forecasters publish a consensus, and futures and other markets show what traders think is likely. A decision that matches expectations may barely move prices because it was already priced in.
calendarEvents.surprises: A surprise is a decision that differs from what was priced in, or an expected decision that comes with an unexpected hint about the next ones. The hint often matters more than the decision. Traders may also wait for the press conference before deciding what the surprise means.
calendarEvents.limits: Higher rates do not always mean a stronger currency, and lower rates do not always mean higher stocks. What matters is the change compared with expectations, and other forces can outweigh it. Prices can gap and spreads can widen at the release.

samples.title: Bank of Westmark rate decision (fictional)
samples.details: A sample decision on the fictional Westmark policy rate. Forecasters expect no change; the statement and press conference follow.

modules.title: Commodities: supply, demand and scenarios

modules.title: Macro analysis: growth, policy, debt and expectations

modules.practicalResult: Work through all four Westmark macro scenarios in the Fundamental Analysis Lab, and for each write the surprise, what was priced in, and at least two plausible reactions with a reason for each.

modules.title: Charts, trends and structure

modules.title: Stocks: analysing a company

modules.title: Regimes, sizing and honest testing
modules.summary: Market regimes, volatility-adjusted position sizing, return statistics, indicator correlation, parameter sensitivity, and out-of-sample and walk-forward testing.
modules.practicalResult: Size 10 trades from ATR-based stops, label each replay period by regime, and run a two-part replay test: tune on the first half, then test unchanged on the second.
